News.title: Mum, 36, tragically drowned in bath at home after ‘sponge blocked plughole’
News.content:
TRAGIC DEATH Mum, 36, tragically drowned in bath at home after ‘sponge blocked plughole’







Next

A MUM tragically drowned in the bath after a sponge blocked the plughole, an inquest heard.

Cops tragically found Natasha Keryk at her home after her family became concerned they couldn’t contact her.

An inquest into the mum-of-two’s death heard that she was found in the bath with a sponge covering the plughole on October 7, 2024.

The 36-year-old’s cause of death was concluded as drowning, contributed to by acute alcohol intoxication.





Coroner Emma Mather said: “Natasha was found submerged in the bath where a sponge was covering the plug and she died from drowning.

“At the time of her death she was acutely intoxicated. Natasha was experiencing significant challenging personal issues at the time of her death and was being supported by professionals.

“Her intentions cannot be determined.”

The secretary had been rebuilding her life after the end of a long-term relationship was trying to overcome struggles with alcohol, the inquest heard.

How to get help EVERY 90 minutes in the UK a life is lost to suicide

It doesn’t discriminate, touching the lives of people in every corner of society – from the homeless and unemployed to builders and doctors, reality stars and footballers.

It’s the biggest killer of people under the age of 35, more deadly than cancer and car crashes.

And men are three times more likely to take their own life than women.

Yet it’s rarely spoken of, a taboo that threatens to continue its deadly rampage unless we all stop and take notice, now.

If you, or anyone you know, needs help dealing with mental health problems, the following organisations provide support:

CALM, www.thecalmzone.net, 0800 585 858

Heads Together,www.headstogether.org.uk

HUMEN www.wearehumen.org

Mind, www.mind.org.uk, 0300 123 3393

Papyrus, www.papyrus-uk.org, 0800 068 41 41 Samaritans,www.samaritans.org, 116 123

A post-mortem concluded she died from drowning, contributed to by acute alcohol intoxication at her home in Blackburn, Lancashire.

The coroner at Blackburn Town Hall rejected conclusions of both accidental death and of Natasha taking her own life.

Coroner Mather said she was unable to determine Natasha’s intentions before her death, and recorded a narrative conclusion.

The hearing was told the mum had been sober for several weeks before relapsing shortly before her death.



Her family said she was making progress and had been discussing future plans, “to make sure she was a good parent”.

Emma Spencer, deputy service manager at Spark – an alcohol recovery service – said she self-referred in August 2024 after difficulties in her personal life.

She said Natasha wanted to stop drinking and added: “She was really doing her best to engage and make changes to her life.”

The inquest heard she disclosed suicidal thoughts to a GP and a social worker in 2024.

A review carried out after Natasha died found that some information hadn’t been shared between agencies.



The coroner also criticised children’s services after Natasha spoke about suicidal feelings to a social worker.

A Blackburn with Darwen Council spokesperson said: “Evidence given at the inquest set out that Children’s Services remained actively involved with Natasha between July 29 and October 7, 2024.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The chronology records 24 contacts or interactions during that period, including home and unannounced visits, telephone calls, text messages, multi-agency meetings and contact through partner agencies involving the social worker.”

If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this article, please call the Samaritans for free on 116123.

News.title: Heartbreak as UK Christmas market is AXED after more than a decade in ‘incredibly difficult decision’
News.content:
Next

A BELOVED UK Christmas market has been axed after more than a decade in an “incredibly difficult decision”.

The popular event will not return this year in a move locals have called a “great shame”.



The Christmas market in Kimberley, Nottingham has been cancelled this year after the council said rising costs and a lack of volunteers made the event no longer financially viable.

In a post on Facebook, Kimberley Town Council announced that they had taken the “difficult decision” to cancel the event for a number of reasons.



The council stated that they had “no viable indoor venue option” to host the markets, “without presenting a financially unviable event”.

They also cited “rising costs” of both traffic management and security for the event which had been imposed “as a direct result of Event Management requirements set forth by higher authorities than Kimberley Town Council”.



The market had also reportedly seen a dwindling number of vendors and stall holders that presented enough variety across their stalls, which the council remarked was not appealing to either traders or visitors.

The council also stated that they had seen “a decreasing number of volunteers and decreasing availability of the volunteers remaining”.

It continued: “Our team work incredibly hard throughout the year on all the events that occur in the town for no ZERO financial gain or pay.

“Sadly as the average age of these volunteers rises and with no “fresh” legs joining the team organising and manning these events puts a huge strain on our team.”



This claim seemed to cause a slight disruption in the comments, with several people writing that they had not been contacted to volunteer at the event by the council when it took over running the markets, despite having volunteered in the past.

Another claimed they had not seen the council advertise for volunteers in the lead up to the cancellation.

The council has instead said they will be focusing their efforts on the Christmas Lights Switch On, set to take place on November 27 and are “already working on ways” to ensure the Christmas Market event goes ahead next year.

However, the council revealed they are planning to bring the market back next year, saying that it isn’t a “farewell for good”, but rather a “sad “we’ll see you next year””.

They thanked community members for understanding “the rationale behind the decision”.



Locals shared their sadness surrounding the news in the comments below.

“It’s a great shame that this event has been cancelled,” shared one.

“Disappointed to read this,” said another.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Kimberley Christmas Market previously took place in the lead up to Christmas, with a host of stalls, hot and cold foods, games and live music.

The beloved event was previously run by a local couple, who passed the reins over to the council in 2024.

News.title: What time is Andy Burnham’s speech today? When to watch his Labour conference announcement live and what to expect
News.content:
Next

PRIME MINISTER Andy Burnham is set to take to the stage for his first Labour Party conference leader’s speech.

The PM is expected to once again promise to end “politics-as-usual” and tackle issues past leaders have dodged for decades.



Here is everything you need to know about what time he speaks, how to watch live, and the major policy bombshells heading your way.

What time is Andy Burnham’s speech today?

Burnham is scheduled to deliver his keynote address today, Tuesday, September 29, 2pm.



He will speak live from the main arena at the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool.

How can I watch the Labour speech live?

You can tune in live on TV and online from 2pm across all major channels and platforms, including here with The Sun.



Watch the live stream directly on The Sun’s official YouTube channel.

What will Andy Burnham announce?

Echoing the conference slogan of “Hope again”, Burnham is expected to promise a break from the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”.

Rather than the usual Westminster spin, the PM says he will deliver an “honest conversation” with the British public on tough choices.

Social care is set to be the centrepiece of the PM’s speech.



Burnham will set out plans for a new universal care service in England, making care free at the point of use to help vulnerable pensioners and families being squeezed by rising costs.

Ministers have refused to rule out scrapping the pensions triple lock in Labour’s next manifesto in order to fund the plans, sparking debate over how to spread the costs.

Burnham will tell members that fixing social care is his personal crusade to rebuild broken public services.

He has previously said he intends to spend what “political capital” he has on social care reforms, an issue he tried to address as health secretary under Gordon Brown.

What is ‘Great British Grid’?

In a shift away from privatised power companies, the PM is also expected to announce a new publicly owned body; Great British Grid.



Operating under the Great British Energy umbrella, it marks the first public ownership in electricity networks since privatisation under Margaret Thatcher.

By taking back public control, the government aims to speed up grid connections and bring British household energy bills down in line with European nations within a decade.

Burnham will also lay out measures to tackle youth unemployment and bring vital utilities back under public control so essential services put working people first.

What else will the Prime Minister say?

Extracts from his address seen ahead of time suggest Burnham remains ready to take on the political status quo.

Burnham will say: “We can’t carry on as we are. Politics-as-usual has taken Britain backwards.



“More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.”

He will admit that while he initially wanted to give a “tub-thumping conference speech,” the “patriot in me tells me something very different is needed”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Burnham will add: “Hope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.

“I accept people will not agree with every part of it, but I believe it can turn Britain around.”

News.title: Horror moment teen girl, 14, is hit by car live on air while journalist reports on ANOTHER crash before driver flees
News.content:
Next

THIS is the horrifying moment a teenage girl is hit by a car live on air while a journalist reports on another crash.

Shocking footage showed the victim, 14, riding her e-scooter on a road in Kościerzyna, Poland before a motorist ploughs into her.



After smashing into the windscreen, the girl is sent flying before the cameraman captures the assailant fleeing down a side street.

TVP journalist Miłosz Sieliwończyk had been at the scene reporting on a young boy being fatally crushed by a car.



He said: “At one point, I heard a bang behind me and the operator’s shout: ‘Oh Jesus!’

“When I turned around, I saw a car driving away with a shattered windshield and a child lying there.”



Miłosz told the cameraman to keep filming and zoom in on the licence plate so that they could report the incident to police.

He said: “We approached the girl. She was unable to stand. I saw blood stains on the scooter.”

They quickly called the emergency services, who arrived at the scene within three minutes.

The injured teen asked to call her mum, who arrived on a bicycle a few minutes later.



Paramedics decided to take the teen to hospital for a check-up, although her injuries are not thought to be serious.

According to Miłosz, the person responsible for the accident returned to the scene a few minutes later.

He said: “He must have been in shock too, because he got out of the car and asked if something had happened.”



Police are investigating the cause of the collision.

Miłosz had been reporting live from the scene where a three-year-old boy was crushed by a car.

The child was pulled from under the vehicle by his parents and underwent extensive resuscitation attempts by firefighters and then paramedics.

However, the boy sadly succumbed to his injuries.

It comes days after a Polish footballer died after his car struck a deer.



Oskar Kordus, 20, was hit in the face when a roe deer was struck by an oncoming Volkswagen car driven by a 52-year-old and flew onto the opposite carriageway and into his path while driving.

The animal smashed through his BMW‘s front windscreen while he was driving on the DW434 section between Krajewice and Grabonóg at 6am on Monday morning.

His car then left the road and rolled into a ditch by the side of the road. The driver of the Volkswagen was unhurt.

Despite the best efforts of medical professionals, Kordus was later pronounced dead.

His club, Kania Gostyn – who play in Poland‘s fourth tier, bid the defender a heartbreaking farewell on social media.



A post said: “It is with great sadness and disbelief that we received the news of the death of our player, Oskar Kordus.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“On behalf of the entire Kani Gostyn community, we extend our deepest condolences to Oskar’s family, loved ones, and all friends.

“In these extremely difficult times, we share your grief and are with you in our thoughts and hearts. Rest in peace, Oskar.”

News.title: Two dead as boat with 60 on board capsizes after ‘machete fight’ with survivors left in water for 12 hours
News.content:
Next

TWO people have died as a packed boat capsized after a machete-wielding fiend allegedly forced people to jump into the sea.

The brutal fight erupted aboard a “makeshift vessel” carrying around 60 people trying to land off the coast of Puerto Rico.



Survivors allege that a fight broke out and that several people were severely injured after being slashed by a machete.

Terrified passengers leapt into the sea as the boat flipped over amid the turmoil.



The dramatic mid-sea horror unfolded at around 11pm on Sunday.

None of the people on board had been wearing life jackets.



They spent more than 12 hours in the water before a passing boat spotted them at around midday on Monday and alerted authorities.

US Coast Guard officers pulled at least 40 people from the water approximately 10 miles off Mona Island.

Two were found dead and several are still missing.

The search for survivors remains ongoing.



Aerial footage released by the US Coast Guard shows the overcrowded boat bobbing in wide open seas as an emergency helicopter flies towards the vessel.

It is unclear from where the boat had been travelling.

In previous years, overloaded boats of Haitians have tried to navigate the treacherous waters surrounding Mona Island.

In June 2022, 11 Haitian girls and women were killed after the migrant vessel they had been travelling on capsized in open waters.

It follows reports of two women and a child being crushed to death after a UK-bound dinghy capsized in the English Channel.



The women and ten-year-old boy who died were “likely crushed” in a stampede to get to a rescue boat, French authorities said.

The child was Eritrean and suffocated in the disaster, officials said.

Dozens more were injured when the boat carrying around 105 people went down off the coast of Wissant, near Calais.

In another harrowing incident, a toddler was allegedly thrown off a migrant boat to his death because human traffickers were annoyed with his crying.

The two-year-old boy was on the boat alongside his mum travelling across the Atlantic to Lanzarote when the tragedy took place, according to officials.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The horror follows reports of three men being arrested under allegations of gang-raping a woman on the same migrant boat back on September 16.

Enrique Espinosa, the chief of Lanzarote’s Emergency Services Consortium, claimed the alleged sexual abuse was just one of many crimes reported on board.

News.title: Man arrested over death of Brit pensioner, 85, found dead in garden of house in French village after ‘violent killing’
News.content:
VILLAGE ‘MURDER’ Man arrested over death of Brit pensioner, 85, found dead in garden of house in French village after ‘violent killing’







Next

A SUSPECT has been arrested over the alleged murder of a British pensioner who was brutally beaten to death at his isolated French home.

John Agner, 85, suffered “very violent blows” to the face in the savage attack – with cops cuffing a 60-year-old man in connection with the assault.



The horror unfolded in the tiny village of Verlus, west of Toulouse, on Friday night.

Investigators said the victim had been persistently beaten around the head, suffering “very violent facial injuries”.



A murder probe has been launched and police now say one man has been arrested.

He is thought to be part of a gang of four suspects who escaped John’s home using his stolen car.



Cops spotted John’s Kia being driven erratically in the early hours of Saturday.

Officers attempted to stop the vehicle before two men abandoned it and bolted on foot.

One man was caught and arrested shortly after.

Police traced the stolen motor back to John’s secluded home, where his body was discovered.



French reports said the pensioner was found outside the property, while its door had been left open and signs of a struggle were discovered inside.

An investigating source said John had “clearly suffered a very violent beating”, with the worst injuries around his head.

The source added: “Work is underway to find the other three men who escaped from the car.”

Jean Menvielle, the mayor of Verlus, said John was “living alone while his wife was in hospital”.

He added: “His death could have gone unnoticed for a very long time if the car hadn’t been stopped.



Menvielle said police had found no signs of a struggle inside the house, where the front door was left open.

He said: “Everything was in order, everything was still there, nothing’s was stolen – his papers, his wallet, his musical instruments.”

John had worked as a specialist wood carver in Southampton before retiring to France with his wife.

In 2003, he was commissioned to produce decorative carvings for the £5million conversion of Doxford Hall in Northumberland into a luxury hotel.

The deeply religious Brit was also a member of the Confraternity of St James, a UK-based pilgrims’ organisation.



A neighbour remembered the pensioner riding his bike and attending several village fêtes.

His wife is suffering from impaired cognition, and is due to return home from hospital in the coming days.

Menvielle described the Brit as extremely discreet and said the couple largely kept themselves to themselves.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “Everybody in the village is extremely shocked by what has happened.”

He added: “None of us understand why such a popular, friendly man was attacked. This attack makes no sense at all.”

News.title: Brit mum, 31, facing jail in Cambodia after being caught ‘trying to smuggle drugs to UK’ as she insists she was ‘set up’
News.content:
DRUG 'MULE' Brit mum, 31, facing jail in Cambodia after being caught ‘trying to smuggle drugs to UK’ as she insists she was ‘set up’







Next

A BRITISH mother is facing up to 20 years in a “hellhole” jail in Cambodia after claiming that she was unknowingly recruited as a drug mule.

Tamara Martins, from Croydon, was arrested after allegedly attempting to leave the country with 71 packages of marijuana – amounting to 34.5kg – stuffed in her luggage.



The 31-year-old claims she was the victim of a “set up” – and that she only found out about the cannabis when staff at Techo Airport asked to check her bags.

Her version of events is that she was approached by a man in a bar who asked her to transport a suitcase full of electronics back to the UK for a fee.



Tamara’s younger brother Trey is now looking after his 10-year-old niece, who does not know that her mum is in jail and may not be home for years.

Trey himself was not aware that his sister was in Cambodia until she called him sobbing.



“All I heard was her crying. She said, ‘I’ve been arrested. I’ve been arrested,” he told the Daily Mail, adding that Tamara had never had run-ins with the law in the past.

“She was extremely erratic. She was upset, asking if I could do anything to help, and saying how sorry she was.”

The siblings were able to stay in contact for the first few days while at the tourist detention centre.

Her phone was later confiscated when she was moved to a CC2 women’s prison.



Tamara is reportedly being held in a cell with over 66 people, many forced to sleep on a hard floor.

In a letter written to Trey, Tamara described the conditions in the prison as “hell,” adding that she has not been able to sleep or eat.

“I have to try and not think so much about life at home otherwise I’ll die from a broken heart… It’s really difficult and hard to see the light at the end of the tunnel,” she wrote to him.



Her brother revealed that the hardest part for his sister is being away from her daughter.

Trey has since launched a GoFundMe to raise £20,000 to secure legal representation for Tamara.

He wrote: “I never imagined I would have to write something like this about my sister.

“My sister Tamara is currently detained in Cambodia, thousands of miles away from her family and, most importantly, her young daughter here in the UK.

“Everything has happened incredibly quickly.



“We are doing everything we possibly can from here, contacting the British authorities, trying to arrange welfare support and desperately trying to secure proper legal representation for her in Cambodia.”

Trey added: “Tamara is not just somebody whose name is attached to a legal case. She is my sister. She is a daughter. And she is a mum with a little girl waiting for her.”

So far, only £825 has been raised in the last two weeks.

Tamara is now one of the 355 Brits detained in Southeast Asia after being accused of being recruited as drug mules.

Drug smuggling arrests involving Brits abroad have more than quadrupled between 2023 and 2025, according to the UK Foreign Office.



Recruits are often told luggage destined for the UK contains clothes, gold or cash – with suitcases actually containing up to 71kg of cannabis.

One British national, currently detained on cannabis offences, said about the tactic: “At the end of the day, it’s your freedom you’re risking, and once it’s gone, it’s not easy to get back.”

Another described feeling “a sense of mourning for the life I had.”

Penalties range from lengthy prison sentences to life behind bars, as well as whipping and, in some countries, the death penalty.

Minister for Consular and Crisis, Stephen Doughty, said earlier this month: “Far too many British nationals are being lured into drug smuggling schemes by criminal gangs that promise free travel or a quick way to make cash.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The reality is very different, and detainees are warning about the dire living conditions they now face decades in prison or, in some countries, the possibility of the death penalty.”

An FCDO spokesperson told The Sun: “We are supporting a British National detained in Cambodia and are in contact with the local authorities.”

News.title: Brit tourist, 26, killed in hit-and-run on holiday in Florida as heartbroken mum pays tribute to ‘wonderful soul’
News.content:
‘DEEPLY LOVED’ Brit tourist, 26, killed in hit-and-run on holiday in Florida as heartbroken mum pays tribute to ‘wonderful soul’







Next

A BRITISH tourist has died after being struck in a suspected hit-and-run while on holiday as his heartbroken family are left “shattered” with grief.

Brandon Grimes, 26, was hit at around 3am while crossing Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway in Florida, officials said.



Brandon, from Durham, was struck by the right-hand side of the car on Friday before the driver allegedly fled the scene on .

Cops recovered pieces of the smashed vehicle from the road and launched an urgent appeal for the motorist.



Police were looking for a silver 2007 to 2010 Ford Edge with a black roof and damage to its bonnet and front-right headlight.

Witnesses later spotted a car matching this description – triggering police to seize the vehicle for investigation.

No arrests have been made yet.

Brandon’s heartbroken mum Claire said her family had been “shattered” by his death.

She said: “Brandon is deeply loved by us all and will be missed beyond words. Our lives will never be the same without him.

“Brandon was a gentle, bright, funny and wonderful soul who brought so much light, love and joy to everyone who knew him.



“He was the life and soul of the party. Our family is completely devastated, and the pain of losing him this way is something no family should ever have to bear.

“Our lives have been shattered. We are completely lost without him.”

Brandon worked as a football referee and was a keen runner.



In 2024 he completed the Edinburgh marathon to raise money for a rehabilitation charity which had helped his older brother following a serious military accident.

His devastated family are working to bring the Brit home while the Florida Highway Patrol continues its investigations.

The Brit’s partner, David Jackson, 41, told Chronicle Live that loved ones were still trying to piece together what happened.

David said: “We have a lot more questions than we do answers at the moment, we don’t fully know what happened, or why, it just doesn’t make any sense.

“We are trying to get all of the information and get justice for him, while his entire family are grieving at the same time.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Looking back, it was clear that something wasn’t right, he was trying to ring me and his friend Tom who he was there with, and I got back just 15 minutes later, but I have since found out that he was already gone by then.

“We are all absolutely devastated, and the most frustrating part is that we don’t know the whole story.”

News.title: Brit, 85, 'violently murdered' in French village is named as major update issued
News.content:
Brit, 85, 'violently murdered' in French village is named as major update issued

A 60-year-old man has been arrested in connection with the murder of retired British wood carver John Agner, 85, in rural France

View 2 Images John Agner lived on the outskirts of the picturesque village of Verlus, near Toulouse (Image: Google Maps)

A British pensioner found dead in rural France with "very violent facial injuries" has been named.

‌



John Agner, 85, was found on Friday night in the garden of his isolated house on the outskirts of the village of Verlus, west of Toulouse. A 60-year-old suspect, who has not been named, has been arrested in connection with the killing.

‌



Mr Agner had been repeatedly beaten around the head, suffering "very violent facial injuries", according to one investigator.

‌



Prosecutors have opened a murder investigation and on Tuesday confirmed that "one man is in custody".

View 2 Images A murder investigation has been launched (Image: Getty Images)

He is thought to have been part of a gang of four who fled Mr Agner's house in his stolen car.

‌



The Ford Ka was involved in a 20-minute police chase, during which it failed to stop while travelling at 120kmph (74mph) in a 50kmph zone at around 2.30am on Saturday in nearby Mont-de-Marsan.

When the vehicle turned down a dead end, four men got out and fled on foot, according to a police source.

The source added: "The car’s owner was traced, and when police arrived at the scene, the deceased’s body was found."

‌



The suspect was caught nearby and transferred to the city of Agen, where prosecutors are leading the investigation.

The source said: "Work is underway to find the other three men who escaped from the car."

Jean Menvielle, the mayor of Verlus, said Mr Agner was "living alone while his wife was in hospital".

‌



He added: "His death could have gone unnoticed for a very long time if the car hadn’t been stopped."

Mr Menvielle said police had found no signs of a struggle inside the house, where the front door was left open.

He said: "Everything was in order, everything was still there, nothing was stolen - his papers, his wallet, his musical instruments."

‌



Mr Agner had worked as a specialist wood carver in Southampton before retiring to France with his wife.

In 2003, he was commissioned to produce decorative carvings for the £5m conversion of Doxford Hall in Northumberland into a luxury hotel.

Mr Agner, who was deeply religious, was a member of the Confraternity of St James, a British pilgrims' organisation.

‌



He listed his interests as walking historical pilgrimage routes across Europe, particularly in France and Spain.

His wife was suffering from impaired cognition and was due to return home from hospital in the coming days.

The murder inquiry is being supported by officers from the investigations unit of the Toulouse gendarmerie.

The investigation continues.

News.title: Britain’s rental hotspots revealed and they’re not all where you might expect
News.content:
Britain’s rental hotspots revealed and they’re not all where you might expect

Moving home is always stressful, but Gumtree have come up with one way to help as their survey reveals demand for rented properties has gathered pace across the UK

View 3 Images There are some surprises in the latest list of where we want to rent our homes

From Glasgow in the north to Plymouth in the south, Britain’s rental hotspots for 2026 have been revealed.

‌



London unsurprisingly tops the list of popular cities, but Edinburgh and Glasgow have leapfrogged Manchester, taking third and fourth place respectively.

‌



Bradford and Plymouth also make the top ten, according to Gumtree figures based on more than 2.2 million rental searches made between January and July 2026.

‌



View 3 Images There are some new names among the ever-popular destinations

Moment daredevil Prince Harry honours promise made to 102-year-old Second World War veteran READ MORE :

Demand has also gathered pace over the summer, with more than 310,000 searches made on Gumtree in July alone, up 7% on June.

The rankings suggest interest stretches beyond Britain’s biggest cities, with Bradford and Plymouth joining established rental hubs including Manchester, Leeds and Bristol.

‌



Nav Dhillon, CEO at Gumtree, said: “Britain’s renters are clearly casting the net wider, and our top ten rental hotspots show how demand is stretching across the country.

“Finding the right property is only part of the challenge. Deposits, removals and furnishing a home can quickly add to the cost, so being able to compare options and make use of second-hand can help make moving more manageable.”

Gumtree has launched a new moving feature with AnyVan, which the companies say could cut moving costs by up to 40%. There are potentially greater savings for people who pack their belongings themselves.

‌



The service provides movers with an instant estimated quote, allowing them to factor transport costs into their plans earlier.

View 3 Images Gumtree's new service helps movers work out the cost of transporting their goods

For renters looking to keep costs down, Gumtree also offers listings for second-hand furniture, appliances and homeware, alongside local services such as removals and furniture assembly.

‌



Landlords and property professionals can also use the platform to find local tradespeople and services to help manage and maintain rental properties.

Marc Clifton, CEO at AnyVan, added: “The cost of moving home often gets overlooked when budgeting for a new property, but moving everything in a three-bed home costs upwards of £500 on average, or £1,000 if you need help with the packing.

“For renters moving between furnished properties, the good news is that costs will usually be lower, as there’s less to transport.

News.title: Latest Covid and flu symptoms as cases rise
News.content:
Latest Covid and flu symptoms as cases rise

Flu and Covid cases are on the rise this autumn, though are at expected levels for the time of year

View Image Bugs tend to circulate more as the seasons change (Image: Creative Images Lab via Getty Images)

Many of us are falling ill with unpleasant bugs, as is typical at this time of year.

‌



Pupils returning to school and people spending increased time indoors create ideal conditions for colds, flu and Covid to circulate. And if you do unfortunately fall ill, it can be tricky to determine what you're suffering from. Many symptoms of Covid, flu and the common cold are similar, although there are a few distinctions that may help identify which virus you have come down with.

‌



For example, typical Covid symptoms include a high temperature, a persistent new cough, and a loss or change to your sense of taste or smell. Those with Covid may also suffer from fatigue, breathlessness, a sore throat, a runny nose, vomiting, nausea, diarrhoea, headaches, body aches, and a loss of appetite.

‌



Most people recover within a few weeks, although for some it may take significantly longer. For certain individuals, however, the illness can prove more serious, with symptoms continuing for an extended period.

According to the latest data, in the week to September 24, hospital admissions with Covid increased from 0.81 per 100,000 people to 1.2 per 100,000 people. While this represents an almost 50% rise, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) says this is an expected level for this time of year.

Separately, the UKHSA reports that influenza (flu) cases have risen slightly, though these remain at a "baseline" level for the time of year also. Of those tested via a GP swab, 10.7% tested positive for flu, up from 8.3% the previous week.

‌



The majority of people who catch flu will recover within a few days to less than two weeks, although some may go on to develop complications such as pneumonia, which can in certain cases prove fatal. The flu jab provides protection against the virus and is offered on the NHS every autumn and winter to those most at risk of serious illness.

Most eligible people can get the flu vaccine from October 1, 2026. Some people, including anyone who is pregnant, can get vaccinated from September 1, 2026.

Flu symptoms tend to appear very suddenly and can include a sudden high temperature, a dry cough, headaches, body aches, a sore throat, fatigue, difficulty sleeping, and loss of appetite. Symptoms are largely similar in children, though they may also suffer from earache, sore eyes, swollen glands and low energy levels.

‌



You can get the free NHS flu vaccine if you:

- are pregnant

- are aged 65 or over (including those who will be 65 by March 31, 2027)

‌



- are aged 18 to 64 and have certain long-term health conditions

- are the main carer for an older or disabled person, or receive a carer's allowance

- are experiencing homelessness or staying in a homeless hostel or night shelter

‌



- live in a care home

- live with someone who has a weakened immune system

Children aged two to three years, school-aged children (Reception to Year 11) and children with certain long-term health conditions are also eligible for the flu vaccine.

Article continues below

Common cold

Colds typically clear up on their own within one to two weeks. Symptoms develop gradually over two to three days, with the most common being a runny nose, sore throat, cough, sneezing, and general fatigue and tiredness.

News.title: New vape rules start on Thursday with £2.20 per 10ml tax added to cost
News.content:
New vape rules start on Thursday with £2.20 per 10ml tax added to cost

Major changes begin this week

View 3 Images It's a big change and users will notice a price hike (Image: supersizer via Getty Images)

A significant shift in vaping regulations takes effect on Thursday, October 1, including a new tax.

‌



Revealed in the 2024 Budget, the changes will introduce a £2.20 charge per 10ml imposed by HMRC on vaping products, irrespective of nicotine content. The new regulations come into effect alongside tobacco duty rises. The Government said that, combined, the measures form part of its broader strategy to create a "smoke-free generation, tackle youth vaping and help adult smokers to give up tobacco".

‌



Rachel Nixon, HMRC's director of indirect tax, said earlier this month: "With one month to go until Vaping Products Duty comes into force, manufacturers, importers and warehousekeepers should have applied to HMRC for approval and be preparing to pay any of the new excise duty due, to comply with the new requirements from October 1, 2026. Businesses that do not have approval by that date cannot produce vaping products in the UK and may be unable to trade. They could also face operational delays and may be subject to civil or criminal sanctions."

‌



View 3 Images Vaping has become popular with young people (Image: Alamy/PA)

Companies that produce vaping products, serve as UK representatives for foreign manufacturers, or warehouse duty-suspended vaping products should have secured the necessary HMRC approvals to operate from October 1, 2026, the tax authority confirmed. Firms liable for Vaping Products Duty will need to account for and settle the duty when the 'duty point' is activated, it noted.

Retailers face new regulations on vapes

HMRC also confirmed that duty-liable products released for sale in the UK would require a valid vaping duty stamp. Where products enter a duty suspension arrangement, payment of the duty is deferred until they leave duty suspension. Whether the duty is passed on to others within the supply chain remains a commercial decision, it added.

‌



HMRC also said: "Following industry feedback, approved manufacturers, UK representatives and warehousekeepers can buy transitional duty stamps until November 30, 2026, and affix them until December 31, 2026. Digital stamps are available from September 1, 2026, and can also be applied immediately to products by those approved under the Vaping Duty Stamps Scheme. Stamped vaping products, transitional or digital, cannot be released onto the market until October 1, 2026. From January 1, 2027, only digital duty stamps can be affixed to vaping products."

Digital stamps will facilitate authentication and traceability throughout the supply chain via a straightforward scanning app provided by the duty stamp supplier, HMRC confirmed. Importers will be required to pay Vaping Products Duty upon the arrival of vaping products in the UK, unless the goods enter duty suspense, such as in an approved customs warehouse.

What retailers need to do

HMRC has urged retailers and wholesalers to work alongside their suppliers to guarantee that the vaping products they stock meet the new regulations. Those that solely sell or distribute duty-paid vaping products wholesale or retail are not required to apply for Vaping Products Duty or Vaping Duty Stamps Scheme approval.

‌



They may continue to purchase and sell existing eligible unstamped stock throughout a six-month transition period running from October 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027. However, vaping products manufactured in, or imported into, the UK on or after October 1, 2026, must carry a duty stamp.

From April 1, 2027, the retail packaging of all vaping products sold or supplied in the UK must display a valid vaping duty stamp. Businesses failing to adhere to the new regulations could face civil or criminal sanctions, HMRC warned.

View 3 Images Vapes will be taxed from Thursday (Image: PA)

Article continues below

Changes consumers will see

HMRC explained: "Consumers in the UK will begin to see changes to vaping products and packaging from October 1, 2026, as Vaping Products Duty and the Vaping Duty Stamps Scheme come into effect. HMRC will provide further information to help them understand the changes.

"New rules for travellers bringing vaping products into the UK for personal use will apply from October 1, 2026. Information about the new personal allowance rules for travellers will be available on GOV.UK from October 1, 2026 and is being communicated in advance of the changes. There are different rules for travellers entering Great Britain and Northern Ireland."

News.title: Russia directly threatens nuclear strike on UK and NATO in response to Sky TV show
News.content:
Russia directly threatens nuclear strike on UK and NATO in response to Sky TV show

Russia has directly threatened to unleash nuclear weapons on Britain in a statement from its UK embassy referencing a new Sky TV show The Wargame

View 3 Images Russia issued a nuclear threat to the UK today (stock) (Image: Russian MOD / SWNS)

Russia has threatened to unleash “nuclear weapons” against Britain in a menacing statement from the country’s UK embassy.

‌



The statement referenced an article discussing a potential NATO blockade of or action against Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave on the Baltic sea. It also said the "prospect of a hypothetical strike" was explored in new Sky TV show The Wargame.

‌



“Those advocating plans to blockade or strike Kaliningrad should have no illusions about the consequences,” it said. “Any British or NATO military action against Russian territory would be met with a response using all means at Russia’s disposal, including nuclear weapons.”

‌



The statement started with the bizarre reference to the recent mini-series on Sky, which features real political figures taking part in a simulated scenario responding to a Russian attack on UK soil.

Spanish fighter jets scrambled with Romania 'alert' as Putin launches huge attack READ MORE :

The statement said: "We have noted an article in The i Paper on Kaliningrad, which suggests, among other things, that NATO could blockade the region or 'de-recognise Russian sovereignty'. The prospect of a hypothetical strike is also explored in Sky News’ recent mini-series The Wargame."

‌



Sky called the show "a provocative stress test on our leaders, our institutions and the country itself," and it appears that the Kremlin has also found it provocative.

The article in the i Paper referenced by the statement, which ran on Saturday, was headlined 'Russia’s tiny outpost in Europe could be Putin’s greatest weakness'.

View 3 Images Kaliningrad is of major strategic importance to Putin (Image: Google Maps)

‌



It discussed how Kaliningrad, and the area of NATO territory that separated the exclave from the main Russian territory, was often called “the most likely place for World War III to break out”.

The article cites former NATO officials and security analysts describing the exclave as "a vulnerability" and Russia’s "Achilles Heel".

The territory, taken from Germany by Russia after the Second World War, is of vital strategic importance to the Kremlin, allowing the Russian navy access to the Atlantic ocean. Kaliningrad is the home of Russia’s Baltic Sea fleet and 12,000 soldiers of its 11th Army Corps.

‌



View 3 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin (file) (Image: Getty)

The news comes after Lithuania and Poland have been making plans for a Russian invasion of the region.

The plans focus around an area called the Suwałki Gap which connects Kaliningrad with the Russian-allied state of Belarus via a 60-mile stretch of the Polish and Lithuanian border.

Article continues below

Lithuania and Poland are currently working together on a framework for plans in case Putin were to move his forces from Belarus across the gap to Kaliningrad, leaving Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania cut off from the rest of Europe.

View 2 Images Police launched dawn raids this morning, arresting 17 people (stock) (Image: Getty)

Major dawn raids were launched across the UK this morning as police arrested 17 people as part of probe into a suspected organised crime group.

More than 800 officers from the Met Police launched raids at 24 properties across five counties - London, Essex, Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Suffolk.

An officer taking part in the operation was stabbed in the leg while carrying out a warrant at an address in Cockfosters, Barnet, the Met said. He was treated at the scene before being taken to hospital, where his injuries were assessed as non-life changing.

News.title: What is the triple lock pension? Everything to know as Andy Burnham hints at social care reform
News.content:
What is the triple lock pension? Everything to know as Andy Burnham hints at social care reform

The state pension triple lock has become a political albatross in the years since it was introduced due to its cost and perceived unfairness, with parties having been unwilling to touch the issue

View 4 Images The triple lock was designed to protect pensioners, but it has become a controversial policy (Image: Getty Images)

The future of the state pension triple lock is unclear after Andy Burnham signalled he would be willing to pursue tough decisions to fund adult social care - but what is the controversial policy?

‌



Burnham's new social care plan sparked speculation the triple lock could come to an end after 16 years. Former Conservative Chancellor George Osborne was announced in May 2010 and came into effect in the 2011/12 financial year.

‌



Currently, the state pension is worth about £241.30 that is typically paid every four weeks. In order to qualify for the pension people need at least 10 years of National Insurance contributions to get anything and 35 years for the full amount.

‌



View 4 Images Andy Burnham is considering different ways to fund adult social care changes in England (Image: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Chancellor John Healey unveils £100m fighting fund to get young people into work READ MORE :

HMRC is issuing refunds to millions of state pensioners after tax error READ MORE :

What is the triple lock pension?

The triple lock affects anyone who receives the state pension, including those who used the older system before April 2016. Each April, the increase is automatically calculated based on inflation, a minimum safety net set at 2.5 per cent and average wage growth.

Those in favour of the triple lock argue it protects pensioners from poverty and it has been praised for lifting worse off retirees out of relative poverty. They also argue the UK's state pension is lower that other European countries and that the triple lock brings it up to the continent's overall standard.

‌



But it has proved to be controversial, despite being introduced to protect pensioners from poverty. Critics have argued since 2011/12 it has become unsustainable and is unfair on younger taxpayers.

Due to how it is measured, the pension typically grows faster than the overall UK economy. The Office for Budget Responsibility has previously warned that as the population ages, it eats into a larger cut of tax revenue, meaning there is less money to spend on other sectors such as education and defence.

View 4 Images George Osborne introduced the pension triple lock (Image: Surrey Advertiser)

‌



Pensioners are also be protected from rough economic circumstances, even as working-age taxpayers see their wages freeze or fall due to inflation. Critics have also argued the triple lock is also not effectively targeting who can benefit most with the lock applying to all eligible pensioners - including ones with considerable wealth.

Should the triple lock be scrapped, it could mean pensioners lose out on several hundred to even over one thousand pounds each year in the next few years. Returning to an earnings link to pensions could save billions of pounds over several years. But scrapping, or even tinkering with, the triple lock could lead to massive electoral consequences.

While some politicians have privately voiced concerns about retaining the triple lock in its current form, many across the political spectrum have hesitated to change it. Older voters typically turn out more than younger voters, risking a major election blowback should any party propose to scrap it.

‌



View 4 Images The triple lock has been credited with dramatically cutting the numbers of pensioners in poverty (Image: Getty Images)

When asked about the triple lock, Education Secretary Lucy Powell said solving the adult social care crisis would not happen without "big conversations" about spending. She told Sky News that she did not know what Burnham will mention in his speech, but that there could be references to the triple lock.

"We are committed to the triple lock, it's in our manifesto," she said. "The triple lock has really delivered for pensioners in this country. Over the course of this parliament, I think we're going to see state pension rising by about £2,000 a year, significantly.

Article continues below

"And that's really important so pensioners can know, pensioners watching your show today can know, that their income is secure and will continue to rise over the course of this parliament.

"I don't know what Andy's going to say about that today, but I know that what he's talking about is this big conversation about solving these big problems, but being really honest with people that they come at a cost. They do come at a cost. You can't just solve the social care crisis without having the big conversations about how you're going to do that."

News.title: Sainsbury's issues urgent 'stop using' caution over 'serious chemical risk'
News.content:
Sainsbury's issues urgent 'stop using' caution over 'serious chemical risk'

The supermarket has issued an urgent recall notice

View 2 Images Sainsbury's has issued a recall notice. (Image: Peter Dazeley/Getty Images))

Sainsbury's has urged its customers to stop using three of its products after a serious chemical risk was found. The supermarket has issued a recall notice warning shoppers of the danger.

‌



It has recalled three styles of TU Tote Shopper Bags because they contain excessive concentrations of phthalates. The Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) explained: "The products present a serious chemical risk because they contain excessive concentrations of phthalates.

‌



"Phthalates may harm the health of children, potentially causing damage to the reproductive system. The products do not meet the requirements of the REACH Enforcement Regulations 2008."

‌



As a result, Sainsbury's and Argos have recalled the products. The OPSS added: "We recommend that you stop using the products immediately and return them to your nearest Sainsbury’s or Argos store for a full refund."

View 2 Images Sainsbury's has recalled a selection of bags. (Image: OPSS)

Recalled products

Tu Pu Tan Curved Top Shopper

‌



SKU: 147160009 Item number: 147160412

Tu Black Croc Winged Tote Bag

SKU: 147165985 Item number: 147166081

‌



Tu Brown Belt Handled Core Shopper

SKU: 147789683 Item number: 147789704

Sainsbury's said: "Sainsbury’s are recalling the above products due to excessive concentrations of phthalates, which pose a chemical safety risk. Prolonged exposure to phthalates may be harmful to human health.

‌



"As a result, the products do not meet Sainsbury’s safety requirements. The products were sold through selected Sainsbury's stores, the Tu website and the Argos website.

"We are asking customers who have purchased any of these items to stop using them and return them to their local Sainsbury’s store for a full refund. For further details or if you have any questions, please visit our website Sainsburys.co.uk/help or contact our careline on 0800 028 8303."

It added: "Please share this recall notice with anyone who may have purchased, received or used one of these products. No other products have been affected by this issue. Sainsbury’s would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused."

‌



If you purchased the bags from Argos, you can visit the website Argos.co.uk or call 0800 011 3462 for the next steps.

What are phthalates?

According to Breast Cancer UK, phthalates are Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals (EDCs) that interfere with male and female sex hormones.

They are found in PVC, which is used to make plastic stronger and more flexible, or in PET, which is sometimes found in single-use bottles.

‌



It added: "Products listing "fragrance," "parfum," or "perfume" may contain these chemicals. They are used in cosmetics, toiletries, and cleaning products to make fragrances/perfumes last longer. Phthalates have been detected in the human body in blood, urine, breast milk, and breast tissue."

Phthalates may interfere with the hormone system by changing the levels of sex hormones such as testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone. They can also lower the activity of testosterone, copy the action of oestrogen or decrease the activity of oestrogen.

Breast Cancer UK added: "Some phthalates are recognised to be harmful chemicals due to their toxic effects on reproduction and/or endocrine disrupting properties.

Article continues below

"These phthalates have been restricted or banned from toys, cosmetics, beauty products and materials that come into contact with food or are used in baby products. However, manufacturers can simply swap these phthalates with unregulated ones for which the effects on our health are unknown."

News.title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes' relatives say it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
News.content:
Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.

It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.

Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.

Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.

They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns".

Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease.

He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by The Guinness Book of Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".

Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.

Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind".

"He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said.

Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts.

News.title: Temperatures to hit 26C in burst of late September warmth
News.content:
The boost in temperatures will come as a strong southerly airflow develops into Tuesday.

With unusually hot air across France and Spain - where temperatures have widely been in excess of 30C - the southerly wind will bring some of this warmth to the UK.

Temperatures across England will exceed 20C widely with the highest temperatures in south-east England where it will get into the mid-20s Celsius.

Average temperatures across England in late September are around 16 to 19C.

While there could be a lot of cloud with a few showers on Tuesday morning, sunny spells will develop over England and Wales.

It will also be warmer than average across Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland with maximum temperatures on Tuesday of 17 to 22C.

However, after starting sunny here, cloud will increase during the day.

The southerly winds will strengthen with gusts up to 50mph expected in Northern Ireland and western Scotland.

This is linked to a large and deep area of low pressure moving north in the eastern Atlantic toward Iceland.

News.title: Police arrest 17 in dawn raids on suspected organised crime group
News.content:
Police investigating a suspected organised crime group have arrested 17 people in dawn raids at 24 properties in London, Essex, Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Suffolk.

More than 800 officers took part in the arrest operations in the early hours of Tuesday.

Searches are ongoing at a number of the properties and there is expected to be a police presence for some days, the Metropolitan Police said.

An officer taking part in the operation in Cockfosters, Barnet, was stabbed in the leg while carrying out a warrant - his injuries are non-life changing.

The arrests were part of an investigation by the Met along with His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

The Met said the FCA has "disrupted" seven businesses and is "actively pursuing" another 30.

A spokesperson said: "These arrests mark a significant point in this investigation.

"Those arrested are suspected of leading or being involved at a senior level in serious and organised crime and related financial offending."

In total, 15 men aged between 26 and 65 were arrested, and two women aged 31 and 41.

They are being held on suspicion of participating in the activities of an organised crime group, money laundering, cheating the public revenue, false accounting, and conspiracy to commit GBH.

A 56-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of GBH over the stabbing.

News.title: Lives 'will be lost' unless UK does more to combat wildfires, committee chairwoman says
News.content:
Lives "will be lost" unless more is done to combat the increasing risk of wildfires, the chairwoman of the UK's Climate Change Committee (CCC) has said after a record number of blazes this summer.

Baroness Brown told BBC File on 4 Investigates "not enough action" had been taken in light of predictions the UK is facing longer, drier summers because of global warming.

Earlier this year, one man died in a wildfire in Gloucestershire, while 19 homes were destroyed in Stourbridge, near Birmingham, and villagers were evacuated in the Cairngorms.

The government said it was investing nearly Â£100m to improve national resilience capabilities, which includes piloting specially trained firefighting teams.

News.title: Migrants using longer, more dangerous routes across Channel
News.content:
A growing number of migrants are trying to cross the Channel on small boats using longer routes from beaches further south and west of Calais and Dunkirk, French authorities say.

Last week one boat set off from Normandy and spent more than 30 hours at sea, before being intercepted and taken to Dover by Border Force.

Although attempts from Normandy have been rare, authorities in neighbouring Seine-Maritime say there have already been 58 attempts this year, up from 30 last year.

The government says it is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings, with figures showing a sharp drop in arrivals this year.

Despite overall crossings dropping, the stretch of coastline used for smuggling appears to be widening.

Earlier this month another migrant boat was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight having set off from the Cherbourg area.

These locations are nearly 80 miles (128 km) from the beaches where many of the small boats have crossed in recent years, with those on board spending longer at sea.

News.title: I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree. Here's why
News.content:
As university courses go it may raise a few eyebrows, but Destiny McGowan has no doubt that hers was very useful.

In July the 21-year-old graduated from Nottingham Trent University with a degree in content creation.

As well as teaching how to best make videos and posts for Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, the course also focused on how to build audiences, engage with brands and monetise your content.

"I always wanted to be an entrepreneur, so for me the course was about the transferable skills that I believed I would gain," says Destiny, pointing to both the social media and business aspects she was taught.

It's early on in her career, and Destiny won't disclose precisely what she is earning, but says she's already making money.

In addition to posting about fashion on her own accounts, she makes videos for others, and has also been hired as a TikTok live selling host, presenting products for sale on camera.

She says the course gave her access to equipment, technology and industry contacts.

"The incredible people I've met through panels that the university hosted would take someone five to 10 years to get to that place," she explains.

Nottingham Trent says its content creation degree, which it launched in 2022, provides "hands-on experience".

Several universities in the UK now offer such courses. The University of Brighton says it teaches students how to create "content that cuts through the noise".

Meanwhile in the US, Arizona State University say its similar qualification allows students to "turn your creativity into content that connects with audiences".

Yet you'd be paying a lot of money for this. The three-year degrees at Nottingham Trent and Brighton both currently cost Â£9,790 per year for UK students, while the standard annual fee at Arizona State is $14,724 (Â£11,000) for a resident of that state.

News.title: Are Trump's US government funded ads illegal?
News.content:
President Trump has faced criticism after fronting television ads paid for by the US government.

There are laws against federal funds being used in the US for political advertising.

The White House has said they are public service announcements, rather than publicity or propaganda.

BBC Verify's Jake Horton examined the ads and spoke to legal experts about their legality.

Produced by Krystal Campos. Graphics by Sally Nicholls.

News.title: Warning more homes will be uninsurable due to flood risk
News.content:
Homes are being built today that could become uninsurable in the future due to the risk of flooding, the boss of insurance giant Aviva has said.

Amanda Blanc said the risk of flooding is "absolutely increasing", but based on current building patterns 115,000 new homes will be built in flood zones in the next decade.

"That doesn't seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built," she told the BBC.

About 6.3 million homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency, and Aviva research found one in nine homes built between 2022 and 2024 are at medium to high risk of flooding.

Blanc told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that England was "for sure" building homes that might be uninsurable at some point in the future.

"It's very well known where these flooding areas are. Let's think very carefully about homes that are being built."

Blanc said construction that borders those flood zones also needs a different approach.

"You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood," she said.

According to Aviva's research, nearly a third of new homes built in 2024 will be at risk of some flooding by 2050, and one in seven would be at medium to high risk of flooding as extreme weather becomes more acute.

Earlier this year the Met Office estimated that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters like the one experienced in the UK in 2023-2024 have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: Delays in fitting electronic tags putting victims at risk, report finds
News.content:
Almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements are not fitted on time, with significant delays putting victims in England and Wales at risk, a report has found.

The report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) says some criminals are waiting up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.

Only 55% of GPS and radio frequency tags were fitted on time, while 60% of alcohol monitoring tags were fitted promptly, according to the report's findings.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said the government was delivering the "biggest expansion of tagging in British history" with Â£100 million in funding.

Plans to significantly expand electronic monitoring were announced earlier this year as part of the Sentencing Act 2026, which aims to ease prison pressures by managing more offenders in the community.

Thousands more prisoners will be released early from October as part of the new law. Most will require tagging.

Electronic monitoring is used by the Probation Service to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order.

A total of 27,847 people were given tagging orders with equipment in England and Wales as of June 2026.

"There is a real danger that electronic monitoring creates a false sense of assurance if the technology is not matched by effective professional practice," said Martin Jones CBE, HM Chief Inspector of Probation.

"Expanding tagging programmes without addressing their weaknesses risks overpromising and underdelivering on public protection," he added.

In some cases, there were waits of more than two weeks for the equipment while one in 10 people waited five months to be tagged after the required time.

Some of the reasons for tags not being fitted on time included individuals not making themselves available.

Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman OBE said victims needed to "know immediately" if tagging was delayed because this could give a "false sense of security".

She said a "robust response" was required in the event of breaches but there were "real concerns" over how "overstretched" probation services would be able to handle this.

Data from the tags was often found to be underused with major violations raised and explored in just 46% of relevant cases, the report also found.

Inspectors discovered little evidence that electronic monitoring was being used consistently to promote behaviour change.

The three types of tags are: curfew tags; location tags; and alcohol tags. They include strict controls of an offender's punishment to manage risk, safeguarding and the protection of victims.

Those who breach their orders either immediately return to prison, are given a court order or a formal warning.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "public protection" was the government's priority.

They said: "That's why we are delivering the biggest expansion of tagging in British history, backed by Â£100 million in funding, with tag install rates up by nearly 50% since 2024.

"This is part of our record Â£700 million investment in probation and community services, recruiting 2,300 trainee officers over the last two years and a further 1,300 this year â ensuring dangerous offenders are kept under closer surveillance than ever before."

News.title: Egyptian officials convicted of kidnapping Cambridge student found dead in 2016
News.content:
Three Egyptian security officials have been convicted by a Rome court over the kidnapping of an Italian student whose tortured body was found in Cairo a decade ago.

The men, who were tried in absentia, denied the charges. On Monday they were sentenced to 10 years in prison on charges of aggravated kidnapping. A fourth Egyptian defendant was acquitted.

Giulio Regeni, 28, was studying for a doctorate at Cambridge University when he went missing while on a research trip in Egypt in 2016.

Days later, his mutilated body was found in a ditch near Cairo. An autopsy later revealed he had been tortured.

Italian and Egyptian prosecutors originally investigated the case together, but reached opposing conclusions.

Egyptian authorities argued criminal gangsters were to blame for Regeni's murder and suggested various other explanations for his death, including a car accident, failed drug deal, or botched robbery.

They also denied any state involvement in Regeni's disappearance or death.

But prosecutors in Rome concluded that the Egyptian national security agency was involved in the crime.

The four defendants were Gen Tariq Sabir, Col Usham Helmi, Col Athar Kamel Mohamed Ibrahim and Maj Magdi Ibrahim Abdelal Sharif. Sabir was acquitted.

Rome's chief prosecutor and a lawyer for Regeni's family welcomed the verdict.

"From today, people around the world can feel safer," Alessandra Ballerini, the family's lawyer, said. "Impunity can be defeated and democracies can place limits on arbitrary power."

Regeni's family have campaigned throughout the decade for justice. As the verdict was read out, there was silence from family members and supporters in court who wore yellow t-shirts and badges, the colour of their campaign, AFP reported.

News.title: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
News.content:
The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News.

Diesel prices in the UK reached a new high on Monday due to supply pressures springing from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Fuel prices are rising globally and US President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports, stating at the weekend: "We're thinking about it very seriously."

Healey, who admitted that UK diesel prices are "extreme", said the government was in discussions with the US, adding: "We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK."

Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Healey said: "We work very closely with the Americans.

"In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran."

The UK depends on the US for around a third of its diesel imports and a ban would send prices even higher.

US sources suggest that Trump is considering a ban to attempt to bring down prices for domestic consumers ahead of the critical midterm elections.

The White House said no official policy announcements have been made, adding that Trump wants to see prices at the pump fall and "is evaluating all the options on the table".

In the UK, the average price for a litre of diesel reached 199.33p on Monday, according to the RAC motoring organisation, surpassing a previous high of 199.09p in June 2022 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.23p.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

Healey said he was "very aware" of these cost of living pressures as he prepared what he called a "breathing space" Budget on 28 October.

A freeze on fuel duty, first implemented by the Conservative government in 2022, is due to expire at the end of the year. Duty is scheduled to increase by 3p in January and a further 2p in March.

Healey said: "Fundamentally, what we need is a settlement in the Middle East. We need an easing of the pressure of costs on business, the costs on households and on ordinary families that we see at the pumps in the most extreme level today for diesel."

News.title: Slipknot fans hit back after Marilyn Manson announced as support act for UK show
News.content:
Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.

The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.

Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.

Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.

Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.

While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".

Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.

One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."

Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.

However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".

News.title: Russian foreign minister questions 'what will become of UK' and future of 'the Celts'
News.content:
Russia's foreign minister has questioned the future of the UK, suggesting it looks uncertain with "the Celts" looking to hold independence referendums.

Sergei Lavrov made the comments at a youth conference where he said he did "not know what will become of the country called Great Britain", according to The Times, external.

The comments come weeks after the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland declared "Westminster's time is coming to an end" and signed an agreement to say it had no right to "block democracy".

In response to Lavrov's comments, Plaid Cymru said Wales' constitutional future was "a matter for the people of Wales", and "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit".

In the conference, Lavrov also suggested the west had too much influence in the UN Security Council, external - the five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK and the US.

According to The Times, he said: "The Celts - Wales, Ireland, Scotland - are now seeking to hold referenda.

"We do not advocate the expulsion of any of the permanent members of the security council. Although, of course, the scale of the British Empire, when it first took its seat in the UN security council at the organisation's founding, has, naturally, diminished to the utmost degree."

News.title: Mahmood signals rethink on migrants' right to remain
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is willing to rethink plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK.

The home secretary has been under pressure to water down the proposals from a significant number of Labour MPs, including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, and trade unions.

In a speech to Labour's annual conference, Mahmood acknowledged "some have said elements of these reforms are not fair".

And she said the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

Mahmood suggested doubling the time it takes for most migrants to qualify for the right from five to 10 years. Some of those who came to the UK on health and social care visas could wait up to 15 years, under the proposals.

Earlier this year, when Rayner was a backbench MP, she accused the government of "moving the goalposts", branding Mahmood's plans "un-British" - and then stuck with her criticisms when she re-joined the cabinet.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of Unison, said the proposed changes would unfairly penalise overseas care workers.

Home Office sources insist no final decision on changes to the immigration rules have been taken, and Mahmood was setting out the principles that would guide her in her conference speech.

The home secretary told delegates: "As we restore control and fairness to our asylum system, we must do the same for legal migration too.

"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did, and fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young.

"That same principle underpins my reforms to the right to live here indefinitely, ensuring settled status is earned by those who have shown a consistent commitment to this country."

And she vowed to come up with a policy that was fair to those who "came here legally" and to British citizens.

A Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain.

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Speaking earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham denied Mahmood had been forced to ditch the plans because Rayner viewed them as "un-British", saying the reforms would need to "strike the right balance".

Asked whether he was "Team Shabana" or "Team Angela," he told LBC: "I'm both of them, I'm Team Angela and Shabana.

"But it just reflects that there's a consultation, there's different not just opinions from politicians, but obviously there's a range of views that have gone into that consultation, so we're in the process now of looking at that."

News.title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
News.content:
Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.

These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones as well as to track criminals.

Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.

We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.

Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.

The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.

The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.
