Sports.title: Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Nothing is over, nothing is done. Or at least not judging by the bravura, balls-out confidence of Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, who remains convinced the past three days of whiplash are simply the drumroll before the big reveal, prelude to some clinching piece of evidence that will swish away the initial finding of guilt on the Premier League’s 100-plus charges.

This appears to be the official City position right now. Rope‑a‑dope litigation. Scooby‑Doo justice. A verdict that is simply exposition, buildup to that moment where we finally get to rip off the zombie mask and reveal the cranky old amusement park owner underneath, with his bulging ring‑binder full of irrefutable evidence of City’s innocence.

This is certainly one way of going about things. Lord Pannick KC, Mystery Machine Chambers. Come for the legal expertise. Stay for the unfathomable brinkmanship.

That great escape may still present itself in more nuanced ways, most obviously in the question of what the actual punishment is here. But even in the current in-between days this feels like the end of an era. The greatest decade in the history of nation-state football projects is over. They’re selling Pep wigs in Woolworths. And we have failed, barring that promised deus ex machina, to paint it sky blue.

So what next? It is understandable there should be a great deal of confusion. This has never happened before. It is without precedent. The common assumption is that events will unfold like this: sanctions first, perhaps as early as midweek. Then an appeal. Then whatever comes next. But someone is suing someone. And it won’t be cheap or quick.

For now, the scale of City’s punishment is the only story in town. A verdict means nothing without the hammer of actual consequences. The triumphalism of those who seem personally invested in seeing City fail could still turn out to be premature.

There are many suggestions of how this may play out. Among the more lenient is a combination of a major fine, a one-season points deduction and a transfer ban. In other words, punishment that looks like punishment but isn’t really. Everyone feels vaguely vindicated. We carry on.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester City chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, issued a statement on Saturday that has only added to the sense of confusion. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

There is the suggestion of political pressure applied by City’s owners, as reported most recently by Bloomberg, with the idea floated that the United Arab Emirates government wishes to see its investment protected as a quid pro quo for its trading partnership with the UK. This is not actually a conspiracy theory. It’s how the world works. Politics is real. Football is not.

At the other end of the scale is a suggestion the Premier League will press for major sanctions as a means of heading off a disastrous round of internecine litigation, club-on-club action that would risk torpedoing the thing we’ve all been watching for the past 15 years. Yes: truth, fair play, stolen glory. But won’t someone think of the brand?

Here is one small suggestion. If the verdict does hold up, the punishment handed down should include a lengthy ban on City having any kind of sponsorship. This would at least speak to the core of the charges, the allegation that state-owned companies were used to funnel in direct investment. It would force City to grow their revenue by more standard means. It may even have a beneficial effect.

Not that anyone is talking about compromise yet. One of the most notable aspects is how utterly entrenched aspects of City’s fanbase seem to be on this. Facts are malleable, principles relative. Everything must be bent to your interests.

There is a very important distinction here. It is entirely legitimate to question the existing rules. Maybe outside investment should be allowed. Spending your own money on your own property, pumping funds into the system, adding not taking: this seems not just reasonable but commendable. How can it be a crime?

This is to wilfully misunderstand the equation. If everyone else is obeying the rules, if the entire culture is based around competitiveness, then this becomes not just deceit and deliberate cheating, but a trashing of the basic idea of sport.

And, in the end, this affects people’s lives in tangible ways. Not just hopes and dreams, but employment, wellbeing, the goals you work for all your life. How many families have been uprooted, incomes affected, moments of happiness scrubbed by outcomes that might have gone the other way?

This is the state of cognitive dissonance described in al-Mubarak’s statement, which is also the only official comment by any party so far. It is not surprising there should be zero acknowledgement of any culpability, or even legitimacy to the charges. Hang on to a rising balloon and you face a difficult decision. Let go before it’s too late or just keep getting higher. Al-Mubarak is in a difficult position here, frontman for a propaganda project that has spectacularly crashed. Faced with this he has trebled and quadrupled down, and in the most tribalist way.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans at the Etihad Stadium in 2012, when they had just won their first Premier League title. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/Getty Images

“This club matters to me,” al-Mubarak begins, a club executive who is, as things stand, guilty of destroying that club’s future prospects. There is dark talk of “media reporting”, with its implication of lies and fake news, as though this is all just another structural obstacle in the way of the true victims here, inherited dictatorial billionaires.

“Here’s what I said to my family,” al-Mubarak goes on, weirdly dragging his own relatives into the picture, before offering once again the most intriguing element, the suggestion there is some key detail here, some game-changing element City are desperate to get out, but which has so far been prevented from entering a properly constituted legal tribunal. “There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident.” This is not a standard line after being found almost unanimously guilty.

So what is he getting at? Part of the problem is the rush to demonise only one side, to see simply bad guys and good guys. In reality, it seems likely the written judgment will heavily criticise the Premier League’s governance.

Rightly so. These charges have been doggedly pursued, but what about, well, everything else? How did an organisation that maintains its serial champions have been cheating for a decade and a half allow this entity into its competition in the first place? How did it fail so completely to regulate it?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

How about, to choose one example, Roman Abramovich, the Kremlin-connected oligarch on whom the British government overnight imposed sanctions as an unfit person, whose own irregularities are well documented? The Premier League has always basically been a TV rights agency masquerading as a regulator. As long as the show rolls on, well, the show rolls on.

This is the only real conclusion to be drawn from any of this. Some kind of governance is being effected here. But this remains a leaking, lurching pirate ship of an organisation. In any sane version of the current timeline there would be pressure for a complete reconsideration of how and why the Premier League exists.

One thing was obvious years before the current state of emergency: countries should not own football clubs. Sovereign wealth funds should not own football clubs. There is an irreconcilable conflict of objectives here. All is fair in foreign policy. Countries will spy, steal and misdirect to gain influence. It is pretty much a patriotic duty to do these things.

But you really don’t need to invite that level of supra-judicial chicanery into your delicate cultural treasure of a sport. What did anyone think was going to happen here? What would the people of the Netherlands think if the UK government bought AZ Alkmaar and began pumping in funds via sponsorship deals with National Rail and the Highways Agency, all the while promising to play fair? This is what the Premier League has permitted. You don’t really get to act surprised when it goes a bit wonky.

View image in fullscreen The sun sets over the Etihad Stadium. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

It is also important to remember that English football hovers like a locust cloud over every other league. The reeling-in of talent and expertise is hugely destabilising. How are you supposed to feel in Germany or Belgium about the fact City and Chelsea have between them spent more than £3bn on transfer fees, all of which is now tainted, apparently put into circulation by something other than a legitimate sporting project?

There is a fair case for Uefa to seek recompense, even to withdraw its patronage until this bandit league gets its own house in order. This won’t happen, because of eyeballs and income flows. But this is down to the balance of power, not any sensible idea of procedure or morality.

What next, then? It is hard to see how a combined 89 charges of failure to provide accurate information or to cooperate with an investigation can be overturned on appeal. But it is also far from impossible. City’s bullishness is presumably based on information from their legal team. The next stage after appeal would be the high court, where different rules on evidence and the law may apply. Perhaps the long game is to get to that stage. It may even work, as it did at the court of arbitration for sport with the Uefa case. Or maybe they’re just planning to spin it out until everyone goes broke, dies or gets into esports.

But in the end, why would you do this? What do you actually want from football? Is proving to the last decimal point that this is all technically admissible really a desirable outcome? The level of sustained, destructive aggression is telling in itself. As are the potential macro-implications.

Most obviously, this case speaks more widely to the way money and power flow in and out of Britain. One version of the endgame is that City’s owners could be forced by the football regulator to sell up. Manchester City are a vast going concern. Imagine the wider shockwaves if this were to happen.

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola with the Manchester City chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

To take one example, a significant amount of the UK property market’s enduring rock‑solid value is built on the idea of inviolable property rights, safety in ownership. Where better to park your funds than a place where the rule of law seems to work for and not against you? London alone is said to have more than £4bn worth of value bound up in dark money. Imagine the ripple effects if a decision on a set of sporting regulations ends with a sovereign state being ordered to forfeit property. Never mind the abrupt lurch into negative equity. It’s enough to make you feel a little pride once more in the power of the wig and the rulebook.

More directly, this remains an existential threat to the league. Not least in the depth of ill-feeling. City’s owners clearly have a deep hostility towards their fellow Premier League members, who are being portrayed as partial and culturally biased. Why would you want to remain part of this organisation? Why would you make any effort to protect it?

Nothing is over, nothing is done. All that seems certain is that this would probably be a good time to hoist the death’s‑head flag and get that old Super League ship rolling again. There might just be a few more takers this time.

Sports.title: ‘Goodison Gazza’ Billy Kenny: ‘The only time I’ve had peace was when I was locked up’
Sports.content:
“I was just a kid and no one was there for me,” Billy Kenny says as he wipes away the tears of hurt and regret on a September afternoon in Liverpool. “I’m angry with Everton for not looking after me.

“Listen, I’m no angel. I’ve played my part, but there are other people who played their part in the demise of Billy Kenny. So I’m still bitter and frustrated today, at the age of 53. It was an absolute waste of talent.”

Kenny used to be one of the most promising young footballers in England, pursued by Alex Ferguson at Manchester United, Kenny Dalglish at Liverpool and Howard Kendall at Everton. He chose his beloved Everton and for a few fleeting months his extraordinary talent shimmered – most memorably during a man‑of‑the-match performance against Liverpool at Goodison Park in December 1992.

His teammate Peter Beardsley called him “the Goodison Gazza” in an eerily prophetic comparison. Kenny played once for England’s under-21s in March 1993, but his ravaging fall echoes the addictions and troubles of Paul Gascoigne.

Kenny discovered cocaine in the early hours of the morning after his greatest game, when he had just turned 19. A cocaine habit spiralled out of control very quickly and he retired from professional football two years later. He had played 23 games for Everton, four for Oldham and two for Barrow. Kenny struggled as an addict for years and ended up in prison.

“I’m clean now,” he says. “I’ve been off the drink and drugs, since my ma died 15 years ago.” Kenny looks up. “It’s my ma’s birthday today. I came off the drugs the day of her funeral and she’s given me the strength to stay sober. I just couldn’t do it while she was alive and that’s what kills me.”

Kenny breaks down twice during our interview, but he tells his story with raw force. He was besotted with Everton, but now the club haunts him. “I ended up being a product of Howard Kendall’s environment,” he says. “For years and years I carried all the blame, but there was no help at all.”

He thinks of Michael Branch, another former Everton player who also wound up in jail. “I spoke to Michael last year and he said at Finch Farm [Everton’s training ground] there are 17 people you can speak to about mental health – whether it’s problems with drink, drugs, your family, your girlfriend. There was no one for me.”

How would life have turned out for Kenny if he had been a gifted player today? “I wouldn’t be talking about misery. I would be talking about glory days and winning for Everton. I feel as though it’s been stolen from me and the fans have been robbed of me as well.”

View image in fullscreen Billy Kenny played 17 league games for Everton despite his talent and retired from professional football at the age of 21. Photograph: Action Images/Reuters

Kenny’s moving new book, written by the Guardian’s Jamie Fahey, who grew up on the same streets in Liverpool, is a penetrating and, yes, sobering depiction of a period in English football when drink addled so many young men. The complex figure of Kendall lies at the broken heart of this story.

“It’s bittersweet when I’m talking about Howard, because I grew up loving the fella,” he says of Kendall, who formed an unforgettable midfield with Colin Harvey and Alan Ball before becoming one of the most successful managers in Everton’s history. “Even today, I’ve got no hatred. He had his own troubles, didn’t he? Where does his alcoholism come from?”

Kenny, at first, hated drinking: “I couldn’t stand it. My dad never touched drugs his whole life, but he would have a couple of pints on a Saturday night. I’d be in bed and my dad would come tell me how good I played for Everton reserves. I had to chase him out because I didn’t like the smell of the ale.

“I then played with my idols in the Everton first team. Kendall always wanted us to go to the Sefton [a pub near the training ground] for a bevvy. As a first-team player I had to go. It was the same for Neville Southall, who never drank. Pat Nevin and Andy Hinchcliffe, too. They’d drop off all the pissed lads at the end. Kendall should have said: ‘Billy, you’re 18, go home.’

“The second time, with the senior pros, I stood with Nevin and the other non-drinkers. But I’ve gone over to the lads with my pint of blackcurrant and lemonade and they’re all laughing at me. A very senior player said: ‘You’d better have a shandy, son, because [Kendall] will sell you if you don’t drink.’

“The next time I dropped my guard, on the ale, and when I got home my head was spinning, spewing up all over my ma’s house. My ma laughed the first time. They really thought I was in a safe place. But I was with a load of alcoholics.

“I don’t care who reads it because I’ve carried this for years. I was just a kid, made up, playing with my idols. If my idols tell me to have a drink I’ll have a drink. I was always drunk from then on.”

In his book, Kenny says “it seemed as though most of the first‑team set-up lived for the booze”.

He describes to me how, for away games, “the first thing on the coach would be the crates of lager and chablis [for Kendall]. On one of my early away games, down to London, I wasn’t really drinking. [On the journey back to Liverpool after the game] I sat in the front with [the assistant manager] Colin Harvey, who I loved. Colin had my best interests at heart and we talked football while they were drinking in the back.

double quotation mark I started to adore the drugs, the birds and the music more than I needed Everton

“We came off the M57 and I’m thinking: ‘Where are we going?’ It’s half 11 [at night] and the coach pulls into the Paradox nightclub. That was Kendall, taking us to the biggest nightclub in Liverpool.”

In January 1993, Kenny did well against Vinnie Jones and the hard men of Wimbledon as Everton won away. He injured his ankle, but he writes: “Kendall told me I’d played a blinder. He said the lads were made up with me and how it would be a real shame if I missed out on the Chinese and a few drinks. I could always put ice on my ankle in the restaurant. Then the killer line: ‘You’ll feel much better after a couple of drinks, lad.’”

Five months later, struggling with injury, Kenny lost himself in cocaine and ecstasy: “I started to adore the drugs, the birds and the music more than I needed Everton.”

His compulsive personality led to “three-day benders”, skipping training and disappearing from football. What would Kenny say to Kendall if his manager were alive today? “I’d say: ‘Howard, you should have looked after me. I shouldn’t have been made to feel I had to drink to play for your team.’”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

When Everton terminated his contract in 1994 Kenny felt abandoned. “I needed help. I needed support. Empathy. Guidance. I received none of it.”

He explains: “Everton sent me to the Priory in Cheshire. But I’m 19 and in group therapy with 60‑year‑old alcoholics who’ve been hiding bottles of scotch in the garden. I couldn’t relate to none of it. They put me in there for two months. Colin Harvey and Paul Power came to see me every day, to get me fit, but Everton were only doing that to sell me.”

Manchester City tried to sign Kenny, but Everton wanted a prohibitive £1m transfer fee. “They’d already done a deal with Oldham behind my back so I got no signing-on fee,” Kenny says. “That’s Everton for you. It’s a badly run club and that still carries on today.”

At Oldham, who were managed by Joe Royle, another former Everton favourite, Kenny felt motivated to try again. But everything fell apart when Royle left – to manage Everton.

View image in fullscreen Billy Kenny says he is getting ‘three or four good days a week’ after 25 years without one. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

At 21, Kenny’s football life was over. The years passed in a drugged-up maze and he was sentenced to nine months in prison – six for drink-driving and three for missing the original trial. “I did five months and got myself in the gym, played five-a-side. No drugs, no drink. In a crazy way the only time I’ve had peace in my life was when I was locked up.”

Kenny was fortunate to escape a 14-month sentence a few years later “because someone was growing cannabis in my house when I was away”. He says: “I had to take the rap for that, but I was lucky. The judge was an Evertonian and I got a suspended sentence. I didn’t want to go to jail then because my ma was dying.”

double quotation mark I’d have been perfect for Fergie. He loved me and I loved it at United

At his mother’s wake, Kenny left his pint on the counter and walked out of the pub. He swore, in her memory, he would never resort to drugs again. He tells me he has kept his promise but “I still get depression”, adding: “I can have a great morning, take the dog out, do an hour on the bags, come home, eat lovely food, and it’s back. But I don’t go round the pub. I don’t phone anyone for drugs. I let it take its toll.”

Kenny’s weathered face brightens. “I’m getting three or four good days a week now where for 25 years I didn’t have one fucking good day. I was either sitting in my house crying or I’d be out, off my head. Now the depression can knock all it wants. I’ve learned to live with it.”

Should he have chosen Manchester United or Liverpool instead of Everton? Both clubs were keen to sign Kenny as a teenager – with Liverpool arranging for him to travel to and from Wembley with the first-team squad for the 1988 FA Cup final when he was 14. “I think about this all the time. As much as I loved the Liverpool staff and the way they treated me, it was out of the question. I’m a born Evertonian. But Man United? I went to United for six weeks in the summer holidays and I saw how Fergie got rid of Kevin Moran, Paul McGrath, Norman Whiteside, Bryan Robson and, later, Lee Sharpe. He wouldn’t stand for any drinking or lack of discipline.

“I’d have been perfect for Fergie. He loved me and I loved it at United. But I’ve given my life to Everton and if I had to do it again I’d probably still go to Everton because I loved the fans. I’m one of them.”

We can see Everton’s new stadium from where we sit and Kenny confirms he has been back to watch the club he once loved so much. “All these ex-players who’re connected to Everton are manufactured Evertonians. I went to the Chelsea game [last season] and it was the same faces, doing the same thing. That’s why our club isn’t moving forwards. Get rid of the dead wood.

“The only legends are the fans. I absolutely love Evertonians and I’m made up when the team does well for them. But that’s it. I just see Everton as the club who never looked after me.”

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel resists change against Czechia despite England defensive errors
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel will resist making drastic changes to his defence despite England going six games without a clean sheet before facing Czechia in the Nations League on Tuesday.

Although Tuchel acknowledged that his side were a “danger to ourselves” when they lost 3-2 against Spain last Saturday, the head coach stood by Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly after their errors against the world champions.

The message was one of continuity as England arrived in Prague for their second game in Nations League Group A3. Tuchel has injury concerns over O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa but is likely to keep the changes to a minimum at the back. James Trafford will continue in goal and Tuchel believes the defeat against Spain was down to individual mistakes rather than structural issues with England’s defending.

“I didn’t see a pattern,” the German said. “It was individual mistakes. I didn’t see a pattern in defending. I think we defended very well in a block when we were organised, but we had just big individual mistakes. But I could not see any defensive pattern that would concern me.

“From a purely defensive approach I felt that we defended much more disciplined, cohesive and organised than in some matches in the World Cup. That was a step in the right direction. We constantly pushed out from our middle block, we tried to go into the opponent’s half and pushed out of the deep block. We didn’t suffer too for long periods of time in defending. We never lost our structure.

“I will not change now because someone made an individual mistake, and they’ve been good for us through all the other matches.”

Two of Spain’s goals came from Guéhi and O’Reilly losing the ball in dangerous positions. “We need to improve these things but when we had the ball we were the biggest danger to ourselves around the box because we just had too many individual mistakes,” Tuchel said. “Purely in defending, I have no concerns.”

Lewis Hall is in line to replace O’Reilly at left-back against Czechia and Trevoh Chalobah will hope to get the nod over Jarrad Branthwaite as Guéhi’s partner in the middle if Konsa is out. England want to reach next year’s finals and losing to Spain means they cannot experiment too much against Czechia, who were beaten by Croatia in their opening game.

The big question is whether Trent Alexander-Arnold replaces Jarell Quansah at right-back and wins his first cap since June 2025. Alexander-Arnold, who did not go to the World Cup, was an unused substitute against Spain.

“He had a very good training week and an excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us,” Tuchel said. “Today was a good training session. Everything is fine. He’s ready to go.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tuchel has explained that starting Trafford in England’s first two Nations League games is to see whether the Leeds goalkeeper can compete at this level. Jordan Pickford, who has been the No 1 since 2018, will return for the trip to Croatia on Saturday and the home game against Czechia next Tuesday.

“We use the Nations League to see where we are with the other goalkeepers,” Tuchel said. “There was no reason from performances to open up this position for competition.

“I think it’s necessary with every other player that we are aware of ‘what if’. If a player that starts a season well, like Traff at Leeds, [he] has the chance to prove it and to play in our style. We just need to see it at some point. We use this competition to actually give him the chance to push on.”

Sports.title: Every saint has a past: how man at heart of City’s first scandal became a United hero | Sean Ingle
Sports.content:
When the Manchester City decision finally dropped, the Guardian’s verdict was damning. “FOOTBALL SENSATION – MANCHESTER CITY’S GRAVE OFFENCES – HEAVY PUNISHMENTS”, the headline read. “It is now proved that the club had for years systematically broken the rules of the Football Association by very unscrupulous means.”

But these words weren’t written last Friday. Instead they were penned more than 120 years ago, at the culmination of English football’s first big illicit payments scandal.

Back then City were a club rapidly on the up, with money and attitude to burn – which might sound familiar. Yet having won the FA Cup in 1904, everything began to unravel.

It started on the final day of the 1905 season, when City were on the verge of winning the title only to lose against Aston Villa in a match that involved punches and literal mud-slinging. Far more seriously, City’s star player, Billy Meredith, was also heard offering a £10 bribe to the Villa captain, Alec Leake, to throw the game.

Some say it was not serious. To this day no one knows the mysterious spectator who reported it. But it created a butterfly effect that led to Meredith being suspended for a season, and ramifications that lasted for decades.

Soon after, when Meredith was seen still hanging around City despite his ban, the FA launched a fresh investigation into the club’s finances. It found that not only was City’s gate money being funnelled into the private accounts of club directors, it was being used to give off-the-books payments to players.

Meredith, for instance, was on £6 a week when the maximum wage was £4. And he was far from the only one being given a little extra on the side. It led to the FA banning 17 players from playing for City again, while two of the club’s directors were banned for life.

View image in fullscreen After the 1906 scandal, Manchester City’s star forward joined Manchester United – what price Erling Haaland following in Billy Meredith’s footsteps? Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme. So is what happened to City all those years ago relevant to modern times? Yes, absolutely.

First off, the 1906 case proves that strong punishments work. While City were hardly the only club to be making similar illicit payments, the FA’s sanctions led to the club slipping down the table, being relegated three years later, and not winning the title until 1937.

That City team also offered an early example of one of football’s immutable laws of gravity. The faster a club rises, the more its foundations may be shaky or unsustainable, and the more it is likely to plummet back to earth.

The other interesting thing in all this? While City had the book thrown at them, Meredith enjoyed a redemption arc that continues to this day.

It helped that some felt he had been unfairly targeted for trying to set up a players’ union and campaigning for the abolition of the maximum wage. The wiry winger could certainly play too, which certainly didn’t hurt either.

Indeed no less a judge than David Lacey, the Guardian’s legendary football correspondent, described Meredith as ranking “with that of Stanley Matthews in the history of the British game”.

And when Manchester United fans voted Eric Cantona as their greatest ever player in 2001, Lacey suggested that a couple of decades earlier they would have gone for George Best, and before that Meredith himself.

The fact that Meredith, who turned out for City from 1894 to 1905 and again from 1921 to 1924, is also in United’s hall of fame marks him out as a unique and substantial force.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Meredith (front row, centre, with moustache and no hat) was a key part of the team that won Manchester United their first league title in 1908. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Intriguingly, those switches across Manchester don’t appear to have attracted much condemnation. Indeed, when Meredith played in the Manchester derby in 1910, the Guardian’s man on the ground was left unimpressed by the lack of fire and venom.

“Both sides tried hard, no doubt; there was no shirking to speak of,” he wrote. “But the game differed in no way that one could see from a hundred other games in which local rivalry has had no place whatsoever. The teams might have represented Penzance and Berwick-on-Tweed respectively for all the evidence the play gave to the contrary.”

In echoes of more modern times, the Guardian’s man also questioned whether modern players cared enough about the shirt on their backs.

“Is it reasonable to expect local or even club fervour in professional football as it exists today?” he wrote after United had won 2-1. “Can local patriotism thrive under a red jersey this year, a blue one the next, and perhaps a white one after that? It does not seem likely.”

Incredibly, Meredith kept playing until he was 49, helped, as the Guardian noted in his obituary, by being a details man whose “mind persistently dwelt on the problems of the game”.

Meredith, who was affectionately known as “old skin” and played with a toothpick in his mouth to help him concentrate, eventually called it a day four months before his 50th birthday when he took over a pub.

Not that it was a quiet retirement. During the Manchester blitz, for instance, a bomb exploded at the back of the pub and a shower of Welsh international caps scattered across the local neighbourhood. It took some time to collect them all given he played 51 times for his country.

Meredith was certainly a smart cookie too. When he was asked about the secret of City’s success, he openly admitted it was because the “club put aside the rule that no player should receive more than £4 a week”.

“Clubs are not punished for breaking the law – they are punished for being found out,” he also admitted. Which applies as much to 2026 as it did all more than a century ago.

Sports.title: Fifa accuses Uefa of ‘misinformation campaign’ against Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
Fifa accused Uefa of waging a “misinformation campaign” and trying to influence the race for its presidency as world football’s governing body urged a US ⁠court to reject a discovery ⁠request linked to a ​controversial investment proposal.

Last month Uefa asked a US federal court for permission to obtain testimony and documents for use in a planned criminal complaint in Switzerland against Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, ⁠over an abandoned plan to transfer World Cup commercial rights into a subsidiary called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

In its response to the filing Fifa said Uefa’s brief contained “numerous false or misleading statements about Fifa and ⁠Infantino”.

“With no basis whatsoever, Uefa suggests that Mr Infantino sought to profit personally from the FFE proposal,” Fifa said in a filing in ​the southern district of Florida, opposing Uefa’s motion for discovery.

“As ‌explained, the FFE plan was subject ‌to approval by both the Fifa member associations and Fifa council, and FFE would have been subject to oversight by both groups within ‌Fifa. Uefa’s suggestions that Mr Infantino violated any law or ethical principle are categorically without merit.”

Uefa declined to comment.

Uefa alleged Infantino developed the proposal in secret with a small group of advisers and investors, bypassing Fifa’s normal governance processes and failing to consult Fifa’s council, regional confederations or member associations.

The filing asked a US court to authorise discovery from Fifa (Americas), Inc and FWC2026 US, Inc, two Florida-based Fifa entities.

Uefa said in the legal filing that investors ‌would have paid $4.2bn (£3.2bn) for a stake in FFE, valuing the business at about $20bn. It added that the valuation significantly undervalued Fifa’s commercial rights and alleged it was not subjected to an open auction ​or tested by an independent valuer.

“Uefa, whether deliberately or through ignorance, conflates equity value with enterprise value,” Fifa said. “It is undisputed that FFE’s ‘initial equity valuation’ – meaning ‘the value that remains for the shareholders after any debts have been paid off’ – was $20bn.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Materials distributed to Fifa’s member associations reveal that FFE’s total ‘enterprise value’ on the other hand – meaning the ’entire value of the business’ – was well over $30bn … Indeed, FFE’s enterprise value was well in ⁠excess of twice the equity value, and therefore far above the value Uefa says would be ​fair.“

The FFE project was abandoned ​in July after opposition from confederations, including Uefa, ​Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and the Asian Football Confederation, over a lack of consultation, with the dispute fuelling demands for ​changes to Fifa’s governance.

Last week ‌Infantino wrote to all 211 ​member associations proposing an independent ​review of the governing body’s decision-making processes. He is up for re-election in March, with Fifa alleging that Uefa’s legal filings were an attempt to influence that election.

“Just before Fifa’s election, Uefa filed this 1782 Application (and three others) spreading misinformation regarding Mr Infantino,” Fifa said. “This court should reject any attempt to influence Fifa’s presidential election based on these grounds.“

Sports.title: Europe’s top-flight clubs to get share of £185m from Club World Cup
Sports.content:
Europe’s top-flight clubs will share half of the $250m (£185m) solidarity pot from the Club World Cup last year, ending a saga that had caused widespread frustration among those who did not participate in the tournament.

Fifa and European Football Clubs (EFC) are close to an agreement that would bring a 50-50 split between sides in Europe and the rest of the world. The fund, set aside to ensure the competition contributes to football’s wider ecosystem, will be distributed once the deal has been ratified.

EFC had sought a share of just over 60% , but compromised after Fifa insisted on a more equal global distribution. A portion of the $125m will be given to all top-division European clubs not involved in the Club World Cup, with amounts varying depending on the number of seasons a side competed at that level between 2021 and 2024.

An amount will also go to clubs with the best performance in Uefa club competitions during that period, again provided they did not play in the tournament in the US in 2025. It raises the likelihood of clubs receiving wildly varying payments. Liverpool, the Champions League runners-up in 2022, would be among those to benefit at the higher end of the scale.

EFC will stage its general assembly in Copenhagen on Tuesday and the agreement is likely to be confirmed after approval by the Fifa council, which is scheduled to meet in Zurich on 15 October.

Clubs from smaller leagues had grown particularly exasperated at the drawn-out timeline for receiving funds that, in many cases, can present a welcome lifeline. The Club World Cup winners, Chelsea, have long since benefited from their £84m payout out of the £740m set aside as prize money.

EFC threatened Fifa it would not cooperate with future Club World Cups if Gianni Infantino did not withdraw his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme. In the same letter, EFC said the lack of a solution on Club World Cup solidarity payments was “of serious disappointment to EFC and our member clubs”.

A joint venture between EFC and Fifa, intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions, remains on the table, but is unlikely to be signed in the near future given the turbulence surrounding world football’s leadership.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Infantino addressed the EFC general assembly in Rome last year, but a repeat performance is not likely this time given the prospect of a direct encounter with adversaries such as the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino spent Monday attempting to boost his standing in Europe by travelling to Riga for the opening of new offices at the Latvian Football Association. The Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, is expected to be among the delegates in Copenhagen.

Sports.title: ‘Football with a smile’: Pocognoli wants happy Gilmour to tee up Scotland success
Sports.content:
Sébastien Pocognoli hopes a “smiling” Billy Gilmour will be central to Scotland’s hopes of improvement following a bruising World Cup.

Gilmour excelled in the second half on Saturday, as Pocognoli’s debut as manager ended in a goalless away draw against Slovenia in the Nations League. The Napoli midfielder missed the World Cup, where the Scots exited at the group stage, through injury. “If you have a player who plays one touch without even looking where he puts the ball it means that he understands the game plan,” Pocognoli said of Gilmour before his Hampden Park bow against Switzerland on Tuesday evening.

“We don’t have a lot of players like this. Even Switzerland don’t. I need to make sure that he finds his smile on the pitch and he was smiling after the game. I saw the Billy from Brighton in Slovenia. At Napoli it is a little bit different, it is more thinking about off the ball. But when he can play he is smiling. He will make mistakes, he played bad passes against Slovenia. But he has to take the risks to play like that to see his qualities.

“I just want Billy to enjoy his football with a smile. If he can do that, the rest will come. I remember him well when he was in Brighton. I thought he was fantastic for them.”

Scotland trained on Monday at Hampden instead of their standard base next door, with Pocognoli keen to familiarise new members of his squad with the venue. “It does not look old but you can feel the history,” he said.

Quick Guide Yakin misses press conference with 'hearing issues' from plane Show The Switzerland head coach, Murat Yakin, missed his team’s Hampden Park press conference with hearing issues as the visitors suffered travel problems on the way to Glasgow. Yakin took training at Scotland’s national stadium and will hope to recover before Tuesday’s Nations League match. A Swiss FA spokesperson said: 'Murat Yakin isn’t at the press conference because he has hearing problems. He struggled with the pressure from the flight so can’t participate in this press conference. He will be at the training session and we hope these complaints will be solved, as has been the case in the past, and he can be in good health for the game.' The Switzerland press conference started late after a two-hour delay to the team's flight. 'There were some problems with the weight as we entered the flight,' the spokesperson added. 'It means we had to land again in Zurich and they had to put more fuel in the engine.' Yakin’s assistant, Davide Calla, took over media duties and said: 'We’ve spent a lot of time looking at Scotland. With the change of coach it will be a different proposition to the Euros [when the teams drew 1-1 in 2024] but we know what to expect. They will be robust, play with a lot of passion and they have a lot of quality players especially in midfield with the ball at their feet. 'In the second half against Slovenia they showed the quality they have,' added Calla. 'It was clear Scotland were better in the second half. It’s an absolute highlight playing at this brilliant stadium. We’ll have lots of motivation to play in this big match.' Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Pocognoli has also warned players not featuring regularly for their clubs that it will become increasingly difficult to win a place in his Scotland squads. Ben Gannon-Doak, Ryan Christie and Aaron Hickey are among key members of Pocognoli’s group who have had restricted domestic minutes this season. While the Belgian is comfortable with that scenario for now, that is likely to change by the time Euro 2028 qualifying begins next year.

“I think Ben will get the games because Bournemouth have the Europa League,” Pocognoli said. “He will play, he will get time. Billy has played in recent weeks since the Champions League has started. So the teams will start to rotate. What concerns me is when March comes. If the players aren’t playing a lot then we will struggle with the physical aspects of the game.

“The demands on the effort are massive. Right now it is OK because it is after pre-season. In November we will see. But we need to have players who have played.”

Sports.title: Nations League: Olise’s late stunner leads France past Belgium, Italy rout Turkey
Sports.content:
Michael Olise’s magnificent late strike gave France a 1-0 Nations League victory over Belgium in Brussels, as Zinedine Zidane made it two wins out of two since being named as the new head coach.

Olise came off the bench late on with the game goalless, and set off from inside his own half to score the winner in the 88th minute. Olise advanced all the way to the edge of the Belgium area before curling a shot beyond the reach of Senne Lammens.

France were missing Kylian Mbappé, who has returned to Real Madrid after injuring his left knee while scoring the winner against Turkey on Friday. The visitors still had the better of the chances with Désiré Doué cracking a shot off the bar in the first half and debutant Lucas Da Cunha striking a post early in the second half.

The contest was heading to an unremarkable goalless conclusion until Olise intervened, having been sent on in the 77th minute in place of Bradley Barcola. France sit top of Group A1 with six points and will host Italy at the Stade de France on Friday, while Belgium entertain Turkey in Liège.

Italy bounced back from an opening 2-0 defeat to Belgium in Rome, as they thrashed Turkey 4-1 on a rainy night in Bursa.

Roberto Mancini’s team dazzled in the downpour, scoring three goals inside the first half-hour as the hosts were punished for defensive errors in their muddy goalmouth. Italy went ahead when Bursa-born fullback Zeki Celik swung wildly at a low near-post corner, deflecting the ball to Alessandro Bastoni who fired into the roof of the net.

View image in fullscreen Michael Kayode celebrates after scoring Italy’s third goal inside the first 30 minutes against Turkey. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters

After 23 minutes, Altay Bayindir flapped at a cross-shot from Michael Kayode and sent the ball into the path of Lazio’s Davide Frattesi, who tucked it home. Four minutes later, Kayode found himself free on the right side of the penalty area, and his near-post shot eluded the Turkish goalkeeper.

Turkey gave the restless home crowd hope in the 47th minute when Gianluigi Donnarumma was drawn to Oguz Aydin beyond the far post. Aydin found Baris Yilmaz who drilled into an empty net, but the comeback lasted five minutes. Pio Esposito headed Italy’s fourth after Sandro Tonali had struck a post.

Yilmaz looked to have cut the gap again with a curling effort but Aydin, bouncing up and down in front of Donnarumma, was offside. Esposito and his older sibling, Sebastiano, also made history in Bursa, becoming the first brothers to start an Italy game together since Aldo and Luigi Cevenini in 1915.

In League B, Northern Ireland were left frustrated after a 0-0 draw at home to Hungary where the hosts passed up chances to take all three points. Patrick Kelly twice went close in the first half, hitting the crossbar with a looping effort, and Isaac Price was denied by Balázs Tóth late on.

View image in fullscreen Northern Ireland’s Patrick Kelly tries to lob the Hungary goalkeeper – but his effort came back off the crossbar. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

Michael O’Neill’s side could not make the breakthrough, though, and there were nervous moments late on as Ruairi McConville blocked Willi Orban’s shot and Pierce Charles saved from Alex Tóth. Northern Ireland sit joint-top of their group alongside Ukraine, who drew 0-0 with Georgia in Tbilisi.

In Group B4, Sweden saw off Poland 3-1 in Solna to earn their second win in two games. Celtic’s Benjamin Nygren pounced at the far post after eight minutes to give the hosts the lead, but Sebastian Szymanski levelled with a shot that hit both posts before going in.

Yasin Ayari restored the home lead when he finished neatly even as he was losing his footing, before Arsenal forward Victor Gyökeres added the coup de grace. Bosnia and Herzegovina are second in the group after winning 4-2 against Romania in Bucharest.

In League C, Aleksa Latkovic’s 89th minute effort clinched a 3-2 win for Montenegro against Armenia to take charge of their group, while Latvia and Cyprus drew 0-0.

Sports.title: Czech Republic vs England LIVE commentary: Tuchel slams ‘madness’ suggestion as Three Lions seek instant recovery
Sports.content:
England take on the Czech Republic tonight and Thomas Tuchel appears to have no plans to rotate his side.

The Three Lions boss has labelled suggestions of giving some of his players a rest to help out their clubs as 'madness'.

4 England lost 3-2 to World Cup winners Spain in their first Nations League game Credit: Getty

England are heading into their second of four games in this new, extended international break after an opening loss.

World Cup winners Spain came from behind to beat Tuchel's men at Wembley on Saturday night, claiming a 3-2 victory.

Harry Kane missed a penalty before La Roja turned the game around, with Mikel Oyarzabal dinking in the late winner.

It leaves England third in Group A3 of the Nations League and in need of three points to keep up with the leaders.

And to make sure they have the best chance of winning, Tuchel seems to be planning to field another strong XI.

He shut down any suggestion that clubs have contacted him asking for some stars to have their minutes limited, following multiple injuries for other nations throughout this break already.

“No, I don’t take calls from Premier League managers," the German said. "I never called any national team coach.

“Why would I start giving the players the impression that it’s okay to take a step back or share a half or to rest one match? Why would I? I would never. It’s madness. We want to win the next match."

Czech Republic vs England on talkSPORT

This Group A3 tie is taking place tonight - Tuesday, September 29.

Kick-off at the Fortuna Arena in Prague is set for 7:45pm UK time.

talkSPORT will have live coverage of the game presented by Adrian Durham.

4 Tuchel has hinted that England are not going to rotate against the Czech Republic Credit: Getty

Commentary comes from Jim Proudfoot and former England captain Stuart Pearce.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.

Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

4 Bellingham is sure to be starting again after an impressive showing against Spain Credit: Getty

Czech Republic vs England team news

Man City full-back Nico O'Reilly has been ruled out of the match while Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa missed training on Monday.

Kane is expected to start up top again while Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon are likely to be in from the off again, along with Elliot Anderson.

Jarell Quansah could be replaced by Trent Alexander-Arnold and Morgan Rogers is another option to come in.

Declan Rice, Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento all pulled out prior to the Spain loss.

Meanwhile, Czech Republic, who lost 2-1 to Croatia in their Nations League opener, have Newcastle's Lukas Hornicek in goal.

Ex-West Ham defender Vladimir Coufal will start at right-back.

4 Kane missed a penalty for the Three Lions at the weekend, but he'll be out to bounce back against the Czech Republic Credit: Getty

Kane takes the positives

Following the Spain defeat, England captain Harry Kane said: "I spoke before that we reached good levels at the World Cup but didn't quite put a full 90 minutes together. Probably similar again here.

"We had a couple of good moments though, that period was as good as we've played in a long, long time and that's the standard we know we can reach.

"We're playing against the world champions, the European champions, and we went toe-to-toe. On another day for sure we'd have won that game.

"We have to take the positives from it. We have to dust ourselves down and go again in a few days."

England forward Anthony Gordon said: "I think it was a bit of a missed chance.

"I thought it was a great game to watch and to play in, some of the attacking play was at the highest level. But I think in a game like that mistakes cost you.

"You always feel like it's you're giving it away rather than them winning it. But of course you could argue both teams because they were as good as us and we were as good as them.

"I'm just gutted about the mistakes."

Sports.title: Harry Kane opens door to Tottenham return with special clause in new Bayern Munich deal
Sports.content:
Harry Kane opens door to Tottenham return with special clause in new Bayern Munich deal

Harry Kane is about to pledge his future to Bayern Munich, but he's still left the door ajar for an emotional return to Tottenham.

Kane's deal with Bayern is set to expire at the end of the season, but both parties are keen to extend his contract.



3 Kane has been at Bayern since August 2023 Credit: AFP

And according to Fabrizio Romano, an agreement between Kane and Bayern is 'very close'.

But there are just a few of the finer details to iron out before the English marksman officially puts pen to paper.

What clauses does Harry Kane want in his contract?

"It's about the length of the contract, how many years, how to sort that clause Harry Kane had in his contract for a Premier League return, for Tottenham matching rights," Romano said.



"So they have something to clarify in terms of clauses, in terms of the length of the contract, but already being almost there financially, I think it's big news for Bayern.

"It's very close."

How good was Harry Kane at Tottenham?

Kane came through Tottenham's academy and went on to become the club's greatest goalscorer, netting 280 times in 435 appearances.



The 33-year-old's brilliance for Spurs was recognised in the form of six inclusions in the PFA's Premier League Team of the Year.

Despite his remarkable goalscoring record with the north London outfit, Kane famously failed to win any silverware with the club.



But that all changed once he moved to Bayern in August 2023.

What has Harry Kane done since moving to Bayern?

Although he endured a trophyless first season with the Bavarians, Kane has gone on to win two Bundesliga titles and the DFB-Pokal.

3 Kane scored a staggering 61 goals in all competitions for Bayern last season Credit: Getty

Kane's haul of silverware has been aided by an otherworldly rush of goals.

Since he joined Bayern, Kane has scored a mind-boggling 152 times in 154 games.



His goalscoring feats have earned him two European Golden Shoe awards, given to the player with the most goals across the top divisions in Europe.

Unsurprisingly, Kane's brilliance in front of goal has him as a serious contender for the Ballon d'Or, although he faces stiff competition from Spain's Lamine Yamal.

Has Harry Kane had the opportunity to leave Bayern?

Rival clubs across Europe had the opportunity to prise Kane away from Bayern in January due to a £57million release clause that was active throughout the month.

The opportunity to nab Kane in a cut-price deal sparked plenty of rumours, with Barcelona and Spurs reported to have an interest in triggering the clause.



3 Kane is already seventh in Bayern's all-time goalscorer list Credit: Getty

However, Kane ultimately stayed put at Bayern.

That looks to be the case for the long-term, too, as both parties work together to continue what has been a successful partnership to date.

When is Harry Kane in action next?

Although Kane's future is bubbling away in the background, his focus is on international matters with England.

The Three Lions are in Nations League action throughout the break and lost their opener against Spain on Saturday.



Kane and his teammates will look to return to winning ways in Prague against Czechia on Tuesday, with kick-off set for 7:45pm.

Sports.title: Ex-Aston Villa star Lee Hendrie reveals playing non-league game saved him after bankruptcy woes
Sports.content:
Former Aston Villa star Lee Hendrie is grateful that he played a National League game on the day his bankruptcy hit the papers.

The ex-England international chillingly reflected on what could have happened when one of his lowest moments made headline news.

5 Hendrie is now a respected co-commentator and pundit Credit: Getty

The one-cap Three Lions ace made 202 Premier League appearances for Aston Villa in a 13-year spell from 1994.

In total, he scored 27 goals and registered 25 assists across 251 top-flight outings and even made his England debut in November 1998.

However, Hendrie finished his career in non-league football after sadly losing his fortune while struggling with mental health issues.

On January 27, 2012, he was declared bankrupt after failing to repay a debt of £235,808.73.

The following day, Hendrie was due to play for Kidderminster away at Stockport County when his finances were splashed across the papers.

And the 49-year-old bravely detailed his account of the ordeal during an appearance on the talkSPORT podcast 'After The Lights Go Out'.

Lee Hendrie on the pain of facing bankruptcy

"I was totally embarrassed," He recalled. "The way my situation had come around was I remember driving into a petrol station, and it was a local paper, and it had a big picture.

"I was actually playing for Kiddy at the time and was playing on the Saturday, and I looked at the paper, and it had me on the front, and it had bankrupt in black capital letters.

5 His only England cap came as a 77th-minute substitute in a 2-0 friendly win over the Czech Republic Credit: Getty

"I thought to myself, 'I can't go into the petrol station. I can't pay for my petrol.'

I sort of went in and sort of ducked down and paid my fuel, and then I thought, I'll go and play football. I think we were playing Stockport.

"I rang the gaffer, Stevie B (Steve Burr) and he said to me, 'Listen, don't worry, the lads are brilliant. They know what they've seen.'

"I was like, do I go or do I not? He said, 'It's up to you. You come if you want. You don't come.' And I actually drove to the game.

"And it was probably a good thing I did, because I think that day, God knows what I could have done, because my head was just gone.

"I was low. And I thought, would it make me feel better about it? And I actually played that day [in a 2-1 defeat for Kidderminster]."

5 Hendrie joined Kidderminster in the National League after leaving Bradford City Credit: Getty

5 Steve Burr (L), ex-manager of Kidderminster Harriers, helped convince Hendrie to play despite news of his bankruptcy Credit: Getty

Lee Hendrie: "I never really had any guidance"

Hendrie, who was reportedly earning more than £30,000 a week at the peak of his career, was then asked how he had got to that point.

He continued: "I find it difficult, but I'm still that person who wants to put a smile on people's faces, still want to be happy and still wear that mask to a certain extent, because I really find it hard to shrug off where I was, what I was, and what I earned.

"Going from those extreme amounts of money and the lifestyle that you live to losing absolutely everything and stripping it back and not being able to do those things, it was a hard lesson.

"I've learned a lot of things. I wish it was the other way around, where I'd learn really early on.

"There was bad advice because, I mean, there's a lot of financial advisors.

"I went into property because all I wanted to do was play football. It was great. I earned the money. I never really had any guidance.

5 Hendrie came through the ranks at Aston Villa Credit: Getty

How did it get to this point?

"I bought my mum a house. I bought dad, my nan and granddad, a house; they looked after us when we'd moved because we weren't a rich family. We were working class.

"I worked on the flowers. My dad had a flower store. So I knew what it was to earn money and what it was like to have money. And I wanted that.

"I wanted to look after my parents. And then to get to a stage where you just take your eye off the ball.

"I got married. I went through a terrible divorce. It went on and on. Similar to when Ray Parlour went through his divorce and it was a massive, it was a massive thing where these solicitors were getting on to the wives and saying, listen, you can take him for half of the money. It's a massive dent then. That's a factor.

"That's going in my pocket, even though it is for my family and kids, which I would not have paid.

"But to take it to the extreme where we could have had a conversation and dealt with it, which we did end up doing in the end, having paid fortunes for solicitors, letters and all the rest of it, which was just a mess.

"In the end, I just said, 'Why are we paying these people when we could sit down?' We've got two girls.

"Let's put it in a trust fund for them. We’re just paying people for the sake of writing a letter."
