World.title: Liberia: ‘Jaw Dropping’ El Niño” Could Test Liberia’s Weak Weather Warning System and Put Thousands of Lives at Risk, Experts Warn
World.content:
The sea continues to wash away at homes in the West Point township, in Monrovia. Credit: Allison Hunter for New Narratives

Summary

Scientists warn that a historically severe El Niño – a climate pattern that disrupts weather around the world – could bring erratic rainfall, and severe flooding, extreme heat, fishing and agricultural disruption to Liberia in coming months.

Experts say the government needs to invest in preparedness strategies now to protect people from to extreme heat and weather in coming months with extreme heat alone predicted to kill 450,000 people globally by February.

Liberia lacks adequate weather stations and relies heavily on global models, limiting its ability to issue accurate, community-specific warnings and meaning millions of Liberians will be left vulnerable.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

The sea off Liberia turns a deceptive shade of calm every year around this time as the rains give way to the dry season – warm, glassy, inviting.



But Nathaniel Blama, Liberia’s former chief environmental regulator, has learned to read that as a warning rather than an invitation.

“When you see the water very warm during that period, it’s time to be afraid because having storm surge, the movement of the current is completely different than normal,” he said. “A lot of people, children, go on the beach. They don’t come back.” Houses and livelihoods are also swept away.

But this year is shaping up to be much worse. New data by climate researchers shows the world is experiencing an exceptionally powerful weather pattern called El Niño—likely the strongest in at least 1,000 years—layered on top of human-caused climate change from burning fossil fuels. This combination means 2027 is expected to be the hottest year ever recorded by scientists.

The climate crisis is already making extreme weather more intense and deadly. Rising heat is now killing one person every minute globally. The El Niño will make this worse, intensifying heatwaves, droughts, and floods across the planet, including Africa. Newly released data from the U.S. based Climate Impact Lab estimates that more than 450,000 people are projected to die globally from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño by February, more than 30,000 in Nigeria alone.

“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” Prof. Friederike Otto of Imperial College London told The Guardian .

In West Africa, where millions rely on rain-fed agriculture, those shifts can be especially damaging. For Liberia, changes in the timing and intensity of rainfall could threaten crops, worsen flooding and increase pressure on already vulnerable communities.

“Farmers could face unreliable rainfall, while hotter, drier conditions threaten crops, water supplies, hydropower and increase the risk of bushfires in places like Wologizi and Foya,” said Isaac Nyaneyon Kannah Teah, a Liberian climate expert.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that occurs when waters in the Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, disrupting weather patterns across the world. It can shift rainfall, intensify heat and bring drought to some regions while causing heavy rains and flooding in others.

Some experts are calling this a “monster” weather event. Temperatures in the Pacific at the heart of El Niño reached a record 3.05C in September. Forecasts project the warming could peak at about 4 C in November and December. A rise above 2C is classified as a very strong, or “super,” El Niño.

Teah said the full impact of the developing El Niño on the country’s current rainy season, ending this month, remains uncertain, but changes in weather conditions in coming months appear certain.

“El Niño may contribute to a hotter and drier January-to-March dry season, placing pressure on water supplies, agriculture, forests and electricity generation,” Teah said. It could also make the beginning of the farming season less predictable, including false rainfall starts followed by prolonged dry spells that damage newly planted crops.

Farmer Oretha Weatoe of James Town, River Cess, looks on as her crops struggle to grow. Photo Eric Opa Doue/New Narratives.

Nearly seven out of 10 Liberians depend on farming for what they eat, so disrupted rainfall could threaten both food and income. Four in every five Liberians is already facing food insecurity. Just 1.6 percent is irrigated, leaving farmers heavily dependent on the rains.

At Liberia’s Meteorological Service, forecasters are already watching the signal build, but they are severely limited by a lack of sophisticated equipment. “We are not even having a marine weather station to give us the actual sea surface temperature,” said Albert Momolu Sherman, director of Liberia’s Meteorological Service, which operates under the Ministry of Transport. “We normally rely on global models.”

Those global models are consistent enough to worry him. He described how an intensifying El Niño fools farmers into planting too early.

“Farmers think that, ‘Okay, the rainy season has started,’ not knowing that this is just a false start,” Sherman said. Then, once the West African monsoon reasserts itself, the rain that finally does come arrives harder and more suddenly than usual, raising the risk of seedlings being waterlogged and communities swamped by flash flooding in a country whose drainage systems were never built for it.

Unlike other countries in the region, the Liberian government does not have a mechanism for warning Liberians about coming heatwaves and heavy rains. The Meteorological Service publishes a ten-day agricultural bulletin meant to guide farmers’ planting decisions. But reaching the people who need it most – in communities without reliable radio, internet or electricity – depends on partnerships with the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, the National Disaster Management Agency and the Red Cross that have yet to fully materialize.

It should not have been like this. International donors made a fund of $10 million available to establish a warning system six years ago. FrontPage Africa/New Narratives documented the suspected corruption and lack of capacity under the Weah administration that led to four-year delays in the project. The Boakai administration reports that it has got the project moving but it has also faced delays.

Teah said it is still too early to determine its effect on Liberia’s entire 2027 season but even if the farmers are spared, they’ll be hit by impacts elsewhere. Because Liberians depend on imports for 80 percent of their food , they could also face higher food prices as El Nino reduces agricultural production in countries from which we import rice and other foods.

Excessive heat will add another dimension. In addition to impacting farming, heat makes it harder for people to work—farmers, fishermen, and construction workers will tire faster in extreme temperatures, earning less money to buy food. Water sources dry up or become contaminated, spreading waterborne diseases that weaken children’s bodies and make malnutrition even more deadly.

A satellite weather-monitoring system used to forecast weather at Roberts International Airport. Photo credit: Liberia Meteorological Service.

For the millions of Liberians who are already food insecure, already eating less nutritious food because they cannot afford better, an intense heat wave could push families from precarious to catastrophic: crops will fail, prices will spike, work will become impossible, and children will face acute hunger. The rural communities hit hardest by heat—with no air conditioning, limited access to clean water, and no cushion of savings—will be the most vulnerable.

The knock-on effects reach further than the farm gate. St. Paul River which supplies the Mount Coffee Hydropower plant near Monrovia can run low as evaporation increases, threatening the electricity supply. It has already reduced electricity generation in recent years as dry-season water levels in the river fell, contributing to widespread power cuts across Liberia. This coming dry season could be worse.

Fishermen monitor the weather as their canoes sit offshore at West Point. Photo by Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon.

Offshore, artisanal fishers face a quieter but no less consequential disruption: warming waters altering fish stocks and pushing dangerous sea conditions closer to shore, threatening both catches and the fishers themselves.

Rising heat brings its own toll for humans: heat stress and other health complications for a population with limited access to cooling or medical care. It will be dangerous for the elderly, infants and those weakened by illness.

Experts said the government has a role to play in helping communities prepare for possible weather-related challenges.

“Closely monitor forecasts from the Liberia Meteorological Service and strengthen preparedness for heat, water shortages, bushfires, agricultural losses and possible flooding,” says Sherman.

The government can also put in measures to save lives including including cooling centers where people can shelter, increased staffing for medical facilities at the hottest times and protections for outdoor workers.

President Joseph Boakai will be immersed in discussion of climate change and the super El Nino during his time at this month’s UN General Assembly. The issue has been a central topic of the meeting with world leaders approving a new declaration to tackle sea level rise with 770 million people live in coastal areas affected by sea level rise. 230,000 Liberians will lose their homes by the end of the century, according to UN models.

Experts said they hope the president comes home from the assembly with a renewed vigor and new ideas to protect Liberians in coming months.

World.title: Liberia: Bon Jallah Seeks Acquittal As DNA Evidence Links Him to Four Exhibits, Defense Points to Crime-Scene Dispute
World.content:
Prosecution Given Until Tuesday to Resist Motion as Criminal Court “E” Suspends Trial; Rwandan Forensic Expert Says DNA Match Cannot Establish When or How Biological Material Was Deposited

MONROVIA — Lawyers representing Peter Bon Jallah have asked Criminal Court “E” to acquit their client, arguing that inconsistencies surrounding the alleged crime scenes and the circumstances of DNA evidence presented at trial raise reasonable doubt.

By Willie N. Tokpah



The motion was filed Monday, September 28, during the 42nd day of jury sitting at the Temple of Justice, following testimony from a Rwandan forensic expert that Bon Jallah’s DNA profile matched biological material found on four exhibits.

Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh, Sr. gave the prosecution until noon Tuesday, September 29, to file a written resistance and suspended the trial pending a ruling on the motion.

The defense does not dispute the DNA match. Instead, it challenges what the scientific evidence establishes about the alleged offenses.

DNA Match Does Not Establish When or How Material Was Deposited

Pascal Bavugirije, Acting Division Manager of the Biology Division at Rwanda’s Forensic Institute, testified that DNA profiles obtained from a white T-shirt, black T-shirt, shorts and boxer matched Bon Jallah’s reference DNA profile.

A forensic report dated January 22 concluded that Bon Jallah could not be excluded as a contributor to the DNA profiles obtained from the four exhibits.

However, Bavugirije told the court that the laboratory could not determine when the biological material was deposited, how it was deposited, or the circumstances under which it came to be present on the clothing.

The laboratory’s role, he explained, was to examine materials submitted by Liberian investigators and compare the resulting DNA profiles with reference samples. It was not tasked with reconstructing the alleged events.

The forensic evidence also included a mixed DNA profile obtained from tissue or toilet paper reportedly collected from a crime scene. According to the report, that profile did not match the reference samples of either Bon Jallah or the alleged victim.

Bavugirije said the unidentified profile could potentially be compared with samples from other individuals if such persons were identified and reference samples obtained.

Defense Challenges Camp Johnson Road Crime Scene

The defense has also challenged the prosecution’s evidence concerning the alleged Camp Johnson Road location.

Two locations had been scheduled for a judicial inspection on September 24: a residence associated with Bon Jallah and the Camp Johnson Road location where the alleged victim testified that one of the incidents occurred.

The Camp Johnson Road site was not visited.

The defense cited testimony from Linsay Gould, identified during the trial as chief investigator of the Women and Children Protection Services, that investigators took the alleged victim to Camp Johnson Road on two occasions but that she was unable to identify the precise location.

Defense lawyers argue that the inability to identify the alleged crime scene undermines that portion of the testimony and contributes to reasonable doubt.

Dispute Over Inspection of Bon Jallah’s Residence

The inspection of Bon Jallah’s residence in the Airfield-Matadi area also became part of the defense’s argument.

According to the court record, representatives of both sides and their lawyers visited the residence on September 24. One room was opened while another remained closed after the family identified one room as the master bedroom and declined to open the other.

Defense counsel Cllr. Wilfred Sayeh argued that testimony before the court had identified the master bedroom as one of the locations where an alleged incident occurred, while the defense maintains that the inspection did not resolve discrepancies concerning the residence.

The defense has further pointed to an alleged difference between the police charge sheet and the alleged victim’s testimony regarding which room was involved.

The prosecution is expected to address those issues in its resistance.

Defense Invokes Criminal Procedure Law

In seeking an acquittal before Bon Jallah presents a defense, lawyers relied principally on Sections 2.1 and 20.10 of Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law.

Section 2.1 provides for the presumption of innocence and requires acquittal where reasonable doubt remains as to whether guilt has been established.

Section 20.10 provides for judgment of acquittal where the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction.

Defense lawyers argued that the prosecution’s evidence has exposed inconsistencies sufficient to justify ending the case at this stage.

Prosecutors requested additional time to respond, saying the defense had raised several issues requiring a detailed answer. Judge Wesseh granted the request but ordered the written resistance filed by noon Tuesday.

Court to Decide Whether Case Continues

The filing of the motion does not constitute a ruling that the prosecution’s evidence is insufficient. The court must now determine whether the evidence presented by the Republic is legally sufficient for the trial to continue.

If the motion is denied, Bon Jallah will retain his right to present evidence in his defense.

If the motion is granted, he would receive a judgment of acquittal. Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law provides the Republic a right to appeal an order granting a motion for judgment of acquittal.

For now, the immediate issue before Judge Wesseh is whether the prosecution’s evidence—including the DNA match on four exhibits and testimony surrounding the alleged crime scenes—is sufficient to allow the case to proceed.

The court’s ruling following Tuesday’s resistance will determine the next stage of the proceedings.

World.title: Liberia: Whein Town Residents Demand Landfill Closure, Cite Rising Health and Water Risks
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE — Residents of Whein Town are demanding the closure of the Whein Town Landfill, accusing authorities of continuing to use a site they say has exceeded its intended lifespan and is exposing surrounding communities to growing health and environmental risks.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Residents interviewed by FrontPage Africa cited increasing mosquito and fly infestations, foul-smelling water they fear may be contaminated, and the presence of rodents and snakes around homes.



They also complained that sections of the wall surrounding the landfill have collapsed, allegedly creating additional entry points for rodents and snakes into nearby residential areas.

‘We Want the Dumpsite Closed’

Samuel Kofi Jones III, Secretary General of the Whein Town Community Leadership, told FrontPage Africa that residents have raised concerns about the landfill for years and have previously protested activities they considered harmful to the community.

Jones recalled an incident around 2012 or 2013 when authorities allegedly brought seized drugs to the area and burned them near the landfill, saying fumes spread into the community.

The incident, he said, prompted residents to protest and demand greater community oversight of activities at the facility.

According to Jones, a community monitoring team was subsequently established, initially comprising eight residents who worked in shifts, including overnight, to monitor activities at the landfill.

He said the team was later reduced to four members because of financial constraints, while stipends have not been paid consistently.

Jones said two batches of community monitors have completed their assignments, while the latest group has worked for about two months awaiting payment.

But for Jones, monitoring is no longer enough.

“If you ask me what I want them to do, I would tell you to close the dumpsite,” he said, stressing that residents do not want the landfill to continue operating in the community.

He said residents remain open to discussions with the government but believe authorities have failed to follow through on commitments made to the community.

The Whein Town Landfill was established in 2011 as a temporary five-year emergency waste disposal site under the Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation (EMUS) Project, managed by the Monrovia City Corporation.

The facility was intended as an interim sanitary landfill to improve solid-waste collection and disposal in Monrovia and Paynesville.

Fifteen years later, however, it remains operational. Residents say the facility has far exceeded its intended lifespan and is now operating in a heavily degraded condition.

Mosquitoes, Flies and Water Concerns

Leon Miaway said mosquitoes have become particularly problematic in the community, especially during the evening.

He said residents often struggle to remain outdoors after 5 or 6 p.m. because of the mosquito population and rely on mosquito nets at night.

Miaway also cited an increase in flies, particularly during the rainy season, saying residents have difficulty eating outdoors without flies coming into contact with their food.

He expressed concern about water sources around the community, particularly following changes to the area where waste is being dumped.

According to Miaway, the new dumping area lacks adequate measures to contain liquid leaking from waste, which he believes has contributed to the pollution of water sources.

He said some residents now have to purchase water for drinking and cooking, adding to household expenses.

“Before you prepare any good food now, it means you have to spend more, even to buy water,” Miaway said.

Miaway also said malaria is common in the community and that children face additional risks when walking barefoot around areas affected by stagnant water.

He said residents have not seen government or humanitarian organizations regularly collecting household data or distributing mosquito nets and other supplies.

“It has been a long while, like, over two, three years now,” he said.

Residents Fear Retaliation

Miaway said residents have held meetings to discuss ways to push for the landfill’s closure but have been reluctant to organize direct confrontations with authorities.

He recalled previous protests in which residents blocked roads and some participants were arrested.

“We don’t want similar things to happen,” he said, adding that residents prefer their community leadership to advocate on their behalf.

Miaway also disputed claims that residents routinely use the landfill for open defecation, saying people living around the facility have access to their own latrines.

He questioned the enforcement of reported safety requirements requiring people entering the landfill to wear protective equipment.

Miaway said residents and some people working at the site can enter without masks or other protective gear.

‘They Are Still Dumping Every Day’

Princess Dennis, another resident, said families living near the landfill are increasingly concerned about illnesses they associate with conditions around the facility.

She cited malaria and other infections among illnesses residents experience and said children are particularly vulnerable.

Dennis said mosquito nets had previously been distributed in the community but did not reach all residents.

She alleged that during some distributions, the exercise stopped around the telecommunications junction, leaving residents in other parts of the community without nets.

But like other residents interviewed, Dennis said the primary demand is not for mosquito nets or other supplies but for the landfill to be closed or relocated.

“I’m upset about the dumpsite here,” she said, appealing to authorities to stop dumping waste at the site.

Dennis said waste continues to be dumped every day despite residents’ concerns.

She also operates a business along the road near the landfill and said the large number of flies affects her customers and forces her to cover her goods.

Water and Cost of Living

Dennis said access to safe water is another major concern.

She said some residents sometimes consume water they consider unsafe because they cannot afford alternatives.

“When we don’t get money, we can drink the water,” she said.

She appealed to the government and other organizations to improve access to safe water.

Amos Moore, called said residents of Whein Town feel betrayed by the Government. Moore said the government has failed to live up to its promise of closing the landfill since its five-year lifespan expired. “We are being used as sacrificial lambs,” he said. It is a shame that the government will unleash such suffering on a large group of its people.”

MCC: ‘Immediate, Aggressive Action’ Underway

In a statement, the Monrovia City Corporation said it is taking “immediate, aggressive action” to address technical challenges at Whein Town, acknowledging that the landfill “has outlived its usefulness” and that the rainy season has compounded the situation.

“The MCC considers the health concerns of the residents as a top priority; as such, we are constantly fumigating the facility and providing routine health care interventions to the residents,” the statement said.

The corporation added that mosquito nets have been distributed and that between March and April 2026, it conducted a free medical outreach for residents.

Addressing claims that garbage is being dumped directly on the ground, the MCC said it remains committed to responsible waste disposal and “would do nothing to endanger the health of the people of Whein Town.”

On the landfill’s future, the MCC said it is at an advanced stage of concluding a public-private partnership framework with a private-sector company for the joint management of the sanitary landfill.

A Community Seeking an End to Dumping

The residents’ accounts depict a community caught between immediate concerns over sanitation, water access and public health and a longer-standing demand for an end to landfill operations in the area.

While the MCC says it is taking measures to mitigate the facility’s challenges and is pursuing a new management arrangement, residents insist that temporary interventions are not enough.

For them, the central demand remains unchanged: close or relocate the landfill and end the dumping that they say has made life increasingly difficult in Whein Town.

Jaheim Tumu contributed to this story.

World.title: Liberia: ULAA Demands Seat at the Table, Warns Boakai Government Against Sidelining Independent Diaspora Voices
World.content:
Diaspora group says Liberians abroad must be valued for more than remittances

Monrovia – The Union of Liberian Associations in the Americas (ULAA) has called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. and his government to back their stated commitment to the diaspora with genuine inclusion, warning that new government-created diaspora initiatives must not bypass or replace independent institutions Liberians abroad have built over decades.

In an open statement issued in New York on September 17, 2026, as President Boakai and his delegation arrived for the 81st United Nations General Assembly, ULAA said the government’s diaspora outreach falls short if it treats Liberians abroad mainly as a source of money and skills while shutting out their critical voices.



“The Government speaks of ‘Mobilizing the Global Liberian Diaspora for National Transformation,'” the statement said. “But the diaspora cannot be valued primarily for its remittances, investments, professional expertise and development contributions while independent diaspora institutions and critical voices are given inadequate space in discussions about the direction of the Republic.”

‘ULAA remains relevant’

Under the banner “ULAA Remains Relevant,” the organization reminded the government that it has served as an organized and independent voice for Liberians in the Americas for more than half a century.

“New government-created diaspora initiatives should complement—not bypass, marginalize or replace—the independent institutions Liberians abroad have built and sustained,” the statement said.

The statement did not name any specific government initiative, but it comes amid the Boakai administration’s push to formalize diaspora engagement.

Beyond economics

ULAA argued that national development cannot be reduced to economics and must address what it called the difficult issues affecting Liberia’s stability and democratic future. It listed border and national security, illicit drugs and trafficking, justice and due process, and “concerns and allegations regarding selective prosecution and political persecution.” It also cited political polarization, governance, accountability, economic opportunity, youth development and national reconciliation.

“These are Liberian issues—and Liberians must have the freedom and space to speak about them,” the group declared.

Call for formal mechanism

The organization called for a “formal and sustained Government–ULAA consultative mechanism,” along with a broader framework that welcomes independent Liberian voices at home and across the global diaspora.

ULAA also drew a contrast between the President’s appearance on the world stage and his administration’s engagement at home. It said that as President Boakai addresses the international community at the UN, his government should show the same commitment to dialogue by listening to the diverse voices of the Liberian people.

“ULAA must have a seat at the table—but the table must be large enough for every Liberian voice,” the statement said. “National development cannot be the conversation of a selected few. It requires inclusion, accountability, open dialogue and the meaningful participation of the Liberian people.”

The statement closed with the slogan “One Liberia. Many Voices. A Shared Future.” It was signed by the ULAA National President, identified in the document as Hon. Mohammad MSG1 Keita.

World.title: After Seven-Year Hiatus, €4.7M Taï-Grebo-Krahn Conservation Project Relaunched
World.content:
MONROVIA — After nearly seven years of suspension, Liberia has relaunched the Taï-Grebo-Krahn Complex Biodiversity Protection Project, a €4.7 million initiative aimed at strengthening the protection of the Grebo-Krahn National Park, improving livelihoods in surrounding communities and enhancing cross-border conservation along the Cavalla River.

By Patience M. Jones,[email protected]

The project, funded by Germany through KfW Development Bank and implemented by the Forestry Development Authority (FDA) in collaboration with the Wild Chimpanzee Foundation (WCF) and local communities, was officially relaunched Thursday at the Royal Grand Hotel in Sinkor, Monrovia.



The project, which was initially valued at €6 million, was launched in 2017 but was suspended in July 2019 following delays in implementation and the failure to meet several financial and administrative conditions required by KfW.

Following discussions between the FDA and KfW after the assumption of office of FDA Managing Director Hon. Rudolph J. Merab, Sr. in February 2024, the project was restructured and its budget reduced to €4,718,065.74.

Under the revised arrangement, the project will focus exclusively on the Grebo-Krahn National Park (GKNP). The original plan to include the Sapo National Park and establish an ecological corridor between the two parks has been removed because of the reduced funding.

The three-year project is scheduled to run from July 2026 to June 2029.

FDA: Conservation Must Benefit Local Communities

Speaking at the launch, FDA Managing Director Rudolph J. Merab said the success of conservation efforts depends heavily on whether surrounding communities see tangible benefits from protected forests.

Merab said Liberia must rethink how its forest resources are managed so that conservation can coexist with sustainable economic opportunities for communities.

His central message was that conservation should not be separated from the needs of people living around protected areas.

“What I am going to bring, whether conservation or commercial, must impact the lives of our people. And if it doesn’t, then we have a problem,” Merab said.

He called for the project to create meaningful benefits for communities while maintaining the protection of Liberia’s forests.

According to Merab, activities around protected forests can create jobs, generate income and contribute to rural economic development, while resources generated through responsible forest utilization can also support conservation.

He urged stakeholders to ensure that the project produces visible and sustainable results for communities.

Project Targets Infrastructure, Rangers and Law Enforcement

Under the redesigned project, the FDA plans to improve infrastructure and equipment for the protection and management of Grebo-Krahn National Park.

The project includes the construction or rehabilitation of ranger posts, headquarters, park warden offices and other facilities, as well as improvements to water and solar power systems.

Infrastructure will be developed in areas including Ziah Town, Tempo, Freetown, Glayway and Youbor.

A dock post will also be constructed to support boat-based monitoring along the Cavalla River.

The project will further provide equipment such as motorbikes, boats and high-beam lights to strengthen surveillance and law enforcement.

By May 2029, the project is expected to support the employment of 33 regularly employed rangers for the protection of the Grebo-Krahn National Park.

It will also support ranger training, community forestry, livelihood programs, small-scale community infrastructure development, road maintenance, community engagement, research and buffer-zone activities.

The project document states that wildlife populations of selected indicator species are expected to increase or remain stable by early 2029.

WCF Pledges Support

Dr. Annika Hillers, Country Director of the Wild Chimpanzee Foundation, welcomed the relaunch, describing Grebo-Krahn National Park as an important part of the Taï-Grebo-Sapo forest complex and one of West Africa’s remaining large connected forest areas.

She said the project comes at a time when communities and the FDA continue to face challenges involving infrastructure, logistics, employment opportunities, sustainable livelihoods, skills training and law enforcement.

Hillers, however, emphasized that conservation cannot be achieved by the FDA and WCF alone.

She called for stronger collaboration among government institutions, particularly in addressing infrastructure and road challenges affecting communities around the park.

“It is teamwork to improve the situation,” Hillers said, pledging WCF’s full commitment to working with the FDA and other stakeholders.

Communities Demand Tangible Benefits

Concerns from local communities also featured prominently during the launch.

A representative speaking on behalf of River Gee County Superintendent Mike T. Swengbe stressed the importance of ensuring that communities living closest to the forest directly benefit from conservation programs.

She recounted concerns from communities that have protected forest areas over the years but have not always seen corresponding development in roads, schools and other basic services.

She urged the FDA and its partners to ensure that benefits promised under the project reach the people living closest to the protected area.

Her message was echoed by Jeremiah G. Sokan, representing District #1 in Grand Gedeh County, who warned that years of delays had contributed to distrust among some communities.

Sokan called on the FDA to approach community engagement with patience and transparency, saying the agency would need to rebuild confidence among residents who have lived with restrictions associated with forest protection for years.

He also urged the government to develop a transition plan to ensure that activities and trained personnel supported by donor funding can be sustained when external funding ends.

Project Suspended in 2019

According to the project overview, the original initiative was conceived to establish an ecological corridor between Grebo-Krahn National Park and Sapo National Park, while strengthening FDA capacity and promoting transboundary conservation.

The project was launched in 2017 but came to a complete stop in July 2019.

KfW subsequently required the FDA to provide financial reports, recruit an external audit firm, transfer remaining project funds back to KfW and work with a KfW-appointed expert to redesign and conceptualize the project.

Following a series of meetings between the FDA and KfW, the project was restructured.

FDA Deputy Managing Director for Community, Conservation and Carbon, Nora G. Bowier, said the FDA has since met the financial and accountability conditions required for the project to resume.

She explained that the project now focuses on Grebo-Krahn National Park, with surrounding communities in Grand Gedeh and River Gee Counties as beneficiaries.

The three beneficiary communities identified in the project document are Konobo, Glio & Twabo, and Glaro.

€4.7 Million Budget

The project’s total budget stands at €4,718,065.74, with major allocations directed toward park management, infrastructure, equipment, personnel and consultancy services.

The budget includes:

€1.3 million for infrastructure;

€300,000 for equipment;

€80,000 for surveillance personnel and rangers;

€130,000 for equipment and field-trip running costs;

€50,000 for strengthening transboundary coordination;

€1.91 million for improvement of Grebo-Krahn National Park management;

€170,000 for studies and analysis;

€410,000 for international consultancy services;

€300,000 for national consultancy services; and

€60,000 for contingencies.

German Government Reaffirms Support

The official launch was conducted by Germany’s Ambassador accredited to Liberia, H.E. Carsten Hölscher, and FDA Board Chairperson Hon. Philip C. Parker IV.

In remarks, Ambassador Hölscher said Germany’s support for environmental protection reflects the country’s longstanding interest in forest conservation.

He described KfW as a state-owned German bank involved in financing projects globally, including those focused on sustainability and environmental protection.

Without the forests, there would not be a good future for all of us,” Ambassador Hölscher said.

FDA Board Chairperson Philip Parker IV also linked the project to the longstanding cooperation between Liberia and Germany in the forestry sector.

He said the renewed partnership through KfW represents a continuation of Germany’s support to Liberia’s efforts to protect its forests and biodiversity.

He urged the implementing partners to ensure that the project addresses the needs and concerns of communities surrounding Grebo-Krahn National Park.

Project Officially Declared Open

Declaring the project open, Ambassador Hölscher said he was pleased to be part of the launch despite arriving in Liberia only recently and not being involved in the project’s earlier preparation.

The relaunch now places the FDA, WCF, the German government, local authorities and beneficiary communities before a three-year implementation period, with expectations that the project will strengthen conservation while producing measurable benefits for people living around Grebo-Krahn National Park.

For communities that have waited through years of suspension, the central test will be whether the project’s promised infrastructure, jobs, livelihood support and conservation benefits reach them as implementation moves forward.

World.title: Liberia: Geneva Reeves-Johnson Foundation Marks 15th World Alzheimer ’s-Dementia Day
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE — The Geneva Reeves-Johnson Foundation, Inc. (GREJOF) has commemorated the 15th anniversary of World Alzheimer’s-Dementia Day, with a call for early diagnosis, increased public awareness, and greater support for people living with dementia and their caregivers.

By Francis G. Boayue

The celebration was held on Friday, September 25, 2026, bringing together high school students and health practitioners under the theme, “The Earlier You Know, The More You Can Do: A Dementia Diagnosis Matters.”



Speaking during the program, GREJOF Director of Programs and Training, John M. Gray, said the foundation is a non-political, non-profit charitable organization established in 2015 in the United States and in Liberia in 2022 in honor of the late Geneva Reeves-Johnson, who died in Georgia, USA, in 2013 from complications associated with Alzheimer’s disease and dementia.

Gray said the foundation continues Reeves-Johnson’s legacy through initiatives focused on mental health awareness, women’s rights, education, skills development, support for impoverished families, and community empowerment.

He said GREJOF’s Youth Empowerment and Mentorship Program (YEMP) seeks to equip young Liberians with skills and knowledge through seminars, vocational training, mentorship, peer discussions, and civic education.

According to Gray, YEMP also encourages young people to become ambassadors for Alzheimer’s and dementia awareness while promoting volunteerism, strategic youth leadership, non-violence, and education.

Serving as guest speaker, Dr. Juliett Whyeayea Diggs, a psychiatry specialist at the E.S. Grant Mental Health Hospital under the Ministry of Health, emphasized the importance of recognizing early signs of dementia and seeking medical assistance.

Dr. Diggs explained that dementia is a group of symptoms resulting from physical damage to the brain and can affect memory, communication, problem-solving, planning, and behavior.

She identified warning signs including memory loss that disrupts daily activities, difficulty planning or solving problems, confusion about time and familiar places, repeated questions, difficulty performing routine tasks, mood changes, withdrawal, and agitation.

“Dementia is not a normal part of ageing,” Dr. Diggs stressed, urging families to seek professional help when they notice significant changes in an elderly relative’s behavior or memory.

She said early diagnosis can help families understand the condition, access appropriate treatment and support, prepare for future care needs, and preserve the affected person’s independence for as long as possible.

Dr. Diggs also called for greater compassion toward people living with dementia, noting that understanding the condition can help reduce stigma and prevent families and communities from misinterpreting dementia-related behavior.

She encouraged communities to have open conversations about dementia and support affected individuals and their caregivers. “Always, the sooner you know, the more you can do,” she said.

World.title: NRPUP Insists Ezra Tembo, Not Kampyongo, Is Leader Of The Opposition
World.content:
The National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) said its president, Dag Hammarskjöld MP Ezra Tembo, is its settled choice for Leader of the Opposition in Parliament. The party rejected claims that Shiwang’andu MP Stephen Kampyongo had been selected for the post. This decision reflects a strong commitment to leadership in zambia.

Party secretary-general Nonde Mubanga said in a statement that a binding decision in Mr Tembo’s favour was taken earlier this month at a properly convened meeting of 34 NRPUP parliamentarians. Luanshya MP Golden Mulenga proposed Mr Tembo, and the motion was seconded by Nyimba North MP Paul Lungu and Chembe MP Kasongo Chomba. This decision is vital for the political landscape in zambia.

The dispute turns on a second, later meeting, which Mr Mubanga said had no power to reverse what the full caucus had agreed. He said that meeting “cannot unilaterally overturn a prior collective decision made by the 34 MPs”. He urged the public, the media and the office of the Speaker to disregard what he called a misleading report now circulating. The future of opposition leadership in zambia is at stake.

The party’s position, he said, stands firm, and the nomination letter recognising Mr Tembo as Leader of the Opposition has already been submitted to the National Assembly of Zambia. Efforts to get a comment from Mr Kampyongo were unsuccessful.

The row has broken out in the first days of the new Parliament. Members of the 14th National Assembly are in induction, and presiding officers are due to be elected on Friday. Opening that induction, Speaker Nelly Mutti urged MPs to enter Parliament with a sense of duty, to disagree without becoming enemies and to hold each other accountable.

The Speaker said the strength of the House would be judged not by the absence of differences, but by its ability to resolve them. She asked veteran parliamentarians not to intimidate new members but to guide them through respectable conduct, and reminded all MPs that the credibility of the House depends on their character, judgment and conduct.

The timetable leaves the opposition little room for a long quarrel. President Hakainde Hichilema will officially open the first session of the 14th National Assembly on October 9. He is expected to outline the Government’s policy direction and priorities for 2026/2027.

Clerk of the National Assembly Loveness Mayaka said the ceremonial opening will take place at Parliament Buildings, and MPs will then consider the pronouncements in the President’s address. NRPUP’s nomination letter naming Mr Tembo is with the National Assembly, and Mr Kampyongo has not responded to requests for comment.

World.title: Hichilema Presses Mopani On Local Content Law And 3 Million Tonne Copper Target
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema called on mining companies to give full effect to the Local Content Law so that more Zambians benefit from the sector. He also challenged Mopani Copper Mines to unlock more copper from its tenements as Zambia pushes towards three million tonnes a year by 2031.

The Head of State made the call in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, when he met Ali Rashed al-Rashdi, chief executive officer of International Resources Holding (IRH). IRH owns Mopani together with ZCCM Investments Holdings (ZCCM-IH). The Local Content Law, which took effect this year, requires mining and related companies to give priority to local businesses for goods, services and contracts.

The President said the Government would make sure the country’s minerals pay off at home. “For our part, we remain committed to ensuring that our natural resources, copper among them, deliver real benefits to our people as we implement the Grow Zambia Agenda,” he said in a statement on his official Facebook page.

He placed Mopani at the heart of the production drive and linked its success directly to the national target. “Raising copper production to three million tonnes a year is central to our Grow Zambia Agenda, and Mopani Copper Mines is key to reaching that target for the benefit of its shareholders and, above all, the Zambian people,” he said.

The President said he was encouraged by progress at the mine but wanted the company to build on those gains and get the most out of the asset. Mopani’s licence area, he said, was extensive and needed more exploration and other techniques to identify and unlock additional mineral resources. He added that the Government had kept its policies, laws and regulations for the sector consistent, giving investors certainty.

Mr al-Rashdi pledged the company’s support. He said IRH remained committed to helping Zambia reach three million metric tonnes and that Mopani would keep exploring tenements that could increase output.

ZCCM-IH board chairperson Phesto Musonda said the mine was already responding, having recorded its highest level of ore mining in the last three months. He said some areas closed for several years were being brought back into operation, raising Mopani’s production capacity, and that ZCCM-IH would keep working with its partners to unlock the asset’s full potential.

The President is in the UAE on a two-day working visit at the invitation of UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. He said partnerships and inward investment were essential to his economic programme. “Our focus in Abu Dhabi is to attract investment and promote private sector-led growth by advancing value addition and industrial development. We look forward to a productive two days,” he said.

Lengwe Bwalya, executive director of the Rhoma Foreign Relations Institute, said the trip had strategic weight as the President’s first foreign trip since his renewed mandate last month. He pointed to the ownership link that makes the UAE central to the copper plan. “Remember, the IRH, under their subsidiary Delta Mining Limited of UAE, holds a 51 percent stake in Mopani Copper Mines on the Copperbelt, which is a key strategic asset in our Grow Zambia Agenda,” he said.

The copper push comes with strong prices. Zambia Statistics Agency statistician-general Sheila Mudenda said refined copper export earnings rose 6.1 per cent to US$1,098.2 million in August. London Metal Exchange prices averaged US$14,353.4 per tonne, up from US$13,525.2 in July.

Refined copper export volumes between January and August reached 608,100 tonnes, 9 per cent higher than the 558,000 tonnes recorded over the same period in 2025. Mining has also carried the Treasury, driving income tax above target this year on the back of favourable copper prices and improved company profits.

Mopani will now continue exploring its tenements under the commitment Mr al-Rashdi gave, while the President completes his two-day programme in Abu Dhabi.

World.title: US Drops Mineral And Data Clauses As Zambia Prepares To Sign $1.5bn Health Pact
World.content:
Zambia is set to sign a revamped US$1.5 billion health assistance agreement with the United States. Washington has agreed to drop clauses that tied healthcare funding to access to Zambian health data and to the country’s copper and critical minerals.

The breakthrough came in bilateral talks on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Mulambo Haimbe met US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Chris Kulukundis, and Washington has since fully decoupled the two agreements.

After the talks, Mr Haimbe confirmed that the disputed terms were gone. “I believe that it has now been agreed that those provisions be replaced completely,” he said. He added that the link between minerals and medicine had also been broken: “The linking, the coupling of the critical minerals agreement with the health assistance… has also been set aside.”

The standoff lasted months and became public earlier this year, when Lusaka rejected an initial five-year, US$2 billion aid package. The Government objected to two conditions in that offer. One demanded unrestricted access to domestic pathogen-tracking data. The other tied the health package to preferential access for American corporations to Zambia’s copper and critical mineral sectors.

Mr Haimbe said the data terms crossed a line the Government would not accept. “The terms regarding data sharing would have violated our citizens’ right to privacy. We maintained that health assistance must be based on humanitarian cooperation, not commercial extraction,” he said.

Zambia is expanding its mining ties with both Western nations and China and has refused to give either side preferential leverage through its public health needs. The minister presented that stance as independence, not hostility towards either partner. “Me being in Beijing does not mean that I’m against Washington, and vice versa,” he said.

With the data-sharing and mineral clauses removed, the revised US$1.5 billion grant has been finalised and cleared for immediate signing. The US will contribute more than US$1 billion directly. The money will go towards stabilising frontline health centres, maternal health networks and infectious disease clinics.

The deal was secured during the same General Assembly session at which Mr Haimbe delivered Zambia’s national statement on behalf of President Hakainde Hichilema, under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation”. In that address, the minister told world leaders that, for Zambia, trust begins with keeping promises and honouring international agreements.

He said the voices of developing countries must matter “in word and in deed”, and that the global system must not protect the interests of the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable. He also invited cooperating partners to back Zambia’s development priorities under the Grow Zambia Agenda, naming health among them.

The revised agreement, without the data and minerals provisions, now awaits signature. Once it is signed, more than US$1 billion from Washington will flow into frontline health services on terms Lusaka has accepted.

World.title: Kavindele Condemns Pardoned Katele Kalumba Over Threats Against Hichilema
World.content:
Former Vice-President Enoch Kavindele described former Finance Minister Dr Katele Kalumba’s remarks and threats against President Hakainde Hichilema as despicable. He said the office of the President commands respect whatever the disagreement.

Dr Kalumba makes the disparaging remarks and issues the threats in a video circulating on various social media platforms. The recording is believed to have been made before the August 13 general election. The former minister has since been arrested for cyber harassment.

In an interview, Mr Kavindele said the conduct was unacceptable and should be condemned by all citizens. He said he had been shaken by what he heard.

“I was deeply shocked by what this man said. Kalumba’s behaviour is despicable and falls far short of what is expected of someone who held the position of Finance Minister in this country,” Mr Kavindele said.

For the former Vice-President, who made the remarks mattered as much as what was said. He said words of that kind, directed at the Head of State, should never have come from a person of Dr Kalumba’s standing, least of all a former Cabinet minister.

He then reminded Dr Kalumba of his own history with the man he attacked. Mr Kavindele said President Hichilema had used his executive powers to pardon Dr Kalumba, which made the hostile remarks a deeply regrettable response.

Dr Kalumba’s legal troubles go back more than a decade. In 2010, he and three others were convicted of corrupt practices and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment with hard labour.

That conviction survived appeal. In December 2022, the Supreme Court upheld the 2010 judgment against Dr Kalumba and his co-accused.

He did not complete the sentence. Dr Kalumba was released from prison on medical grounds in August 2023, having served less than a year of the five-year term.

Mr Kavindele separated the institution from the person holding it. He said political differences could never justify contempt for the presidency.

“Even if you lack regard for the individual holding the presidency, the office itself must be respected,” he said.

He urged citizens to stop insulting leaders and to use their freedom of speech responsibly.

The matter is now with law enforcement. Dr Kalumba faces the cyber harassment allegation, while the video that led to his arrest is still circulating online.

World.title: CDF Empowerment Loans Frozen After Borrowers Repay Only 35 Percent
World.content:
Govt Suspends 2026 CDF Loans As Repayment Rate Sinks To 35 Percent

The Government has suspended the 2026 loan empowerment component of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF). Borrowers have repaid only 35 per cent of the money lent since the expanded programme began in 2021.

Martin Sodala, Director of Planning and Information at the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development, said the freeze would let the ministry recover funds already given to various groups, among them marketeers. The money set aside for this year’s loans has been moved to other areas within the CDF value chain.

The loan window was designed to support enterprises, with priority for youths, women, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable people. A repayment rate of 35 per cent means that for every K100 lent since 2021, only about K35 has come back. Mr Sodala said the suspension was also meant to deal with a poor culture of loan repayment.

“That 2026 loan empowerment component has since been suspended to allow for recoveries to be made from those who got loans,” Mr Sodala said.

He was answering Mupila Kameya, president of the Zambia National Marketeers Credit Association. Mr Kameya raised the empowerment of marketeers at the National Development Coordinating Committee meeting organised by the Ministry of Finance and National Planning.

Mr Sodala told the meeting that the ministry had struggled to get its money back from the outset.

“Those that had initially been given access to loan empowerment funds under CDF, we have struggled as a ministry to recover loans provided,” he said.

The suspension does not stop lending completely. Mr Sodala said disbursements were continuing, but only from money recovered on existing loans. In practice, new borrowers can only be funded when earlier borrowers pay back.

He gave no date for a return to full lending.

“I think we’ll be guided at an appropriate time when the Ministry will make a decision whether we go back to giving out these loans in full,” he said.

For now, he said, the Government’s focus is on recovering the outstanding loans.

The decision falls hardest on marketeers, the group Mr Kameya’s association represents, and they are already under pressure in the capital. Lusaka City Council’s seven-day ultimatum ordering street vendors out of undesignated trading areas in the central business district has reached its deadline.

Lusaka Mayor Chitambala Mwewa said vendors who do not return to their stands will have their trading spaces re-allocated. About 200 of an estimated 8,000 vendors in the central business district have moved voluntarily.

Mr Kameya welcomed the relocation but asked the council for wider consultation. He called for vendors to be profiled and for financial empowerment measures for traders who cannot immediately be accommodated in designated markets.

The rest of the CDF continues to pay for visible projects. In Mwinilunga, North-Western Province Permanent Secretary Colonel Grandson Katambi (Rtd) pointed to Chief Kakoma’s new palace, completed with CDF money.

“The completion of Chief Kakoma’s new palace demonstrates that CDF is delivering visible results,” Col Katambi said.

In Katete, Local Government Service Commission chairperson Laxon Kazabu said the commission had completed a staff audit, a qualification check and a CDF project inspection at the town council.

In Mwandi, local leaders are already encouraging residents to apply for support under the 2027 CDF loans and grants. They want residents to prepare viable project proposals that can create jobs and raise household incomes.

For now the 2026 loan window stays shut. Any money reaching new borrowers will come only from what earlier beneficiaries repay, until the ministry decides to resume full lending.

World.title: HH Challenges Mopani to Ramp Up Copper Production
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has challenged Mopani Copper Mines to unlock more copper from its mining tenements and ramp up production.

The Head of State says this is important as Zambia works towards its target of producing three million tonnes of copper annually by 2031.

President Hichilema says Mopani is a crucial asset in achieving the production target.

He was speaking during talks with International Resources Holding (IRH)-Mopani Copper Mines Chief Executive Officer Ali Al Rashi, as part of his two-day working visit to Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

President Hichilema said he is encouraged by the progress being recorded at Mopani but wants the company to build on the gains and maximise the potential of the asset.

He noted that Mopani’s licence area is extensive and there is a need for increased exploration and the use of other techniques to identify and unlock additional mineral resources.

President Hichilema said Mopani must contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda by increasing production, unlocking mineral resources and creating greater economic opportunities through the mining value chain.

He noted that Government has demonstrated consistency in its policy environment, laws and regulations governing the mining sector, providing certainty for investment.

And Mr. Al Rashi said his company remains committed to ensuring that Zambia meets its target of producing three million metric tonnes of copper annually.

Mr. Al Rashi said Mopani will continue exploring its mining tenements to increase copper production.

Meanwhile, ZCCM-IH Board Chairperson Phesto Musonda said Mopani has recorded its highest level of ore mining in the last three months.

Mr. Musonda said some mining areas that had remained closed for several years are now being brought back into operation, increasing Mopani’s production capacity.

He said ZCCM-IH is encouraged by the progress and will continue working with its partners to unlock the full potential of the asset.

World.title: 2, 720 Vubwi farmers redeem inputs
World.content:
Thirty-four percent of beneficiaries under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) in Vubwi District, have so far redeemed their farming inputs, while 54 percent are expected to redeem after having made the required payment.

Vubwi district has 8, 000 FISP beneficiaries, and a total of 2, 720 have so far managed to redeem their inputs.

District Agriculture Coordinator (DACO), Philimon Lungu has disclosed that government is optimistic that all beneficiaries will have accessed their inputs by November if the prevailing conditions remain unchanged.

Mr Lungu has urged beneficiaries who have received redemption codes to promptly access their inputs to allow them adequate time to prepare for the farming season.

“I must also bring it to your attention that 54 percent of beneficiaries under this programme have already made their deposits out of which 20 percent are yet to access inputs,” he said.

Mr Lungu, who is also Acting District Commissioner (DC), has further encouraged farmers to consider early-maturing and climate-resilient crop varieties as the country and the district anticipate experiencing El Niño conditions.

“We are also advising our farmers to access early-maturing and climate-change-resilient crops as the country and the district anticipate experiencing El Niño conditions. By so doing, they will be guaranteed reduced crop failure,” Mr Lungu said.

He has also confirmed that the district has recorded no irregularities under either FISP or the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) crop marketing programme, particularly involving the distribution of fake or counterfeit seed and fertiliser.

“I should also put it on record that the district has recorded zero irregularities, particularly with regard to fake and counterfeit seeds and fertiliser being supplied to our farmers,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mr Lungu said FRA has so far purchased 240,487 bags of 50-kilogramme white maize, equivalent to approximately 12,024 metric tonnes, under the ongoing 2027 crop marketing season in Vubwi District.

He further said 35,000 bags belonging to farmers are currently at FRA depots awaiting procurement.

He said the district is facing limited storage capacity but assures farmers that government, through the FRA, has safely secured the maize and that no grain will be damaged.

“Despite the limited storage space in the district, government through FRA has safely secured the maize, and I wish to assure the public that no maize will be damaged,” he said.

Mr Lungu said payments to farmers who have sold their maize to the FRA are ongoing and progressing well.

He assured farmers who are yet to receive their payments that they will be paid as the process continues.

On concerns over the shortage of empty grain bags, which are used by the FRA during maize purchases, Mr Lungu said government has provided an additional allocation.

He said the bags will be distributed to all 15 FRA depots in the district this week.

Meanwhile, FISP beneficiary Elizabeth Phiri, who has accessed her inputs, has thanked government for the support and pledged to use the inputs for their intended purpose.

“I know that this support, if properly utilised, will help me and other beneficiaries to eliminate poverty through the enhancement of food security at household level,” Ms. Phiri said.

And farmers, John Sakala and Olipa Banda, who have supplied maize to the FRA but are yet to receive payment, have called on government to expedite the payment process.

The farmers say delays in payment could negatively affect their preparations for the forthcoming farming season, particularly amid the anticipated El Niño conditions.

Responding to the concerns, Mr Lungu assured farmers that government is doing everything possible to ensure that all farmers are paid on time.

He reiterated that the payment process is ongoing and urged farmers to remain patient as the outstanding payments are being processed.

World.title: IOM, Bayer Zambia donate 30 metric tonnes of maize seed
World.content:
The International Organisation for Migration (IOM), in partnership with Bayer AG, has donated 30 metric tonnes of maize seed to vulnerable farmers in five districts of Southern Province to strengthen food security and improve household resilience.

‎

‎The maize seed will benefit farmers in Kazungula, Kalomo, Monze, Namwala and Zimba districts, with each district expected to receive about five metric tonnes of maize seed.

‎

‎Speaking during the handover ceremony in Nyawa Chiefdom in Kazungula, Southern Province Acting Permanent Secretary, Gift Monde in a speech read for him by Deputy Permanent Secretary Yolanta Malunga, said the intervention would help address challenges affecting farmers, including climate variability, prolonged droughts and limited access to quality agricultural inputs.

‎

‎Mr Monde said agriculture remains a major source of food, income and livelihoods for households in the province, but climate-related challenges continue to threaten production, household incomes and nutrition.

‎

‎He commended IOM and Bayer AG for partnering with Government and traditional leaders to respond to the needs of vulnerable farming communities.

‎

‎Mr Monde said the donation has the potential to reach approximately 5,000 farmers through five-kilogram packs or 2,500 farmers through 10-kilogramme packs, depending on the final distribution arrangement.

‎

‎He urged stakeholders to ensure that the inputs reached the intended beneficiaries and were used productively to improve food production and household livelihoods.

‎

‎Mr Monde said the intervention also included Bayer vegetable seeds to enable households to establish backyard gardens and engage in small-scale vegetable production for improved nutrition and additional income.

‎

‎He encouraged women and young people to take advantage of agricultural opportunities, saying farming should not only be viewed as a means of producing food but also as an avenue for enterprise development, income generation and employment.

‎

‎Mr Monde said the initiative is in line with Government’s broader development agenda of promoting production, economic growth, wealth creation and employment.

‎

‎He further urged farmers to adopt climate-smart agricultural practices and make use of the training and knowledge-sharing being provided under the programme to improve productivity and resilience.

‎

‎Meanwhile, Bayer Zambia Country Sales Manager, Rodney Ndou, said the donation was aimed at helping vulnerable farmers prepare for the coming planting season, rebuild their production capacity and strengthen resilience to climate uncertainty.

‎

‎Mr Ndou said access to quality seed, combined with appropriate agronomic knowledge and practical support, could help farmers manage increasingly unpredictable farming seasons.

‎

‎He said the contribution formed part of a wider IOM-Bayer global partnership through which more than 225 metric tonnes of seed would be provided to farming communities in Zambia, Kenya, Nigeria and Ukraine in 2026.

And IOM Chief of Mission, Keisha Livermore, said the donation will help families to recover, grow and build a more secure future.

“Unpredictable rainfall and prolonged dry spells can reduce harvest and put pressure on households. This is why supporting resilience at the community level is very important,” she said.

She said the support is meant to help vulnerable households with high breed maize seed in order to help strengthen food security, improve livelihoods and rebuild resilience to climate shocks.

‎

‎Speaking on behalf of Chief Nyawa, Prime Minister Gideon Siapenya, described the donation as a significant contribution towards improved agricultural production.

He said traditional leadership looked forward to productive fields, improved harvests and stronger household food security.

‎

‎Mr Siapenya thanked Government for its continued partnership with the private sector, saying such collaborations enabled farmers to access important support, including agricultural knowledge and technology.

‎

‎He said traditional leaders would continue encouraging farmers to take agriculture seriously, not only for household consumption but as a pathway to income generation, improved livelihoods and dignity.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 29, 2026
World.content:
press review

Uganda's Tooro Kingdom Faces Succession Dispute Ahead of New King's Coronation

Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo II, a former broadcaster, is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom following the death of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ruled for 31 years after becoming king at the age of three. Kijanangoma, 56, was selected by a 21-member Babiito clan succession committee. However, his appointment has sparked a dispute because members of the late king's family say Oyo left a young son and a will naming the child as his successor. Queen Best Kemigisa has criticised the decision. The kingdom said that the alleged son was never formally presented or recognised and that the selection followed traditional customs. Kijanangoma and Oyo were cousins and both descendants of former King Rukidi III. The new king, who spent more than two decades as a journalist, has pledged to promote unity and development and use his national connections to benefit the people of Tooro. Uganda's traditional kingdoms have no formal political power but retain significant cultural influence.

Conflict Disrupts Ebola Response in DR Congo

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Aid efforts to contain a deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo are being complicated by fighting and the displacement of thousands of people from Kigonze camp in Ituri province. Security incidents, including soldiers searching for weapons and suspected members of armed groups, have prompted families to flee the camp, which houses nearly 19,000 displaced people. The United Nations said that the departures are making it harder for aid workers to assess needs, provide assistance and maintain protection services, while also threatening Ebola surveillance and contact tracing. The outbreak has recorded more than 8,000 confirmed cases and nearly 4,000 deaths. Ituri remains the epicentre despite a recent decline in cases. Meanwhile, infections in neighbouring North Kivu have risen substantially. The World Health Organization says conflict, insecurity, population displacement and limited access to basic services continue to undermine efforts to detect cases, trace contacts and provide timely healthcare.

Zimbabwe Residents Take Govt to Court Over Lake Kariba Ferries

Two Kariba residents have approached Zimbabwe's High Court seeking an order compelling the government to provide adequate, safe and reliable ferries on Lake Kariba following the Mbuya Nehanda disaster that killed 97 people. Fishermen Tonderai Ndevani and Chilumbo Mudenda argued that the government has failed to provide an adequate replacement, leaving communities dependent on the smaller privately operated MV Silverstone or an expensive and lengthy road route. They want the government to provide ferries meeting legal safety standards and submit monthly reports on efforts to restore services. Ndevani said that the ferry was the only affordable and practical way to reach his family in Mola, with the lake journey taking two to three hours and costing US$10 to US$15, compared with up to 10 hours and US$45 by road. The applicants warn that limited ferry capacity could encourage overloading and create another disaster. They are also arguing that the lack of reliable ferry services infringes constitutional rights to freedom of movement and dignity. The case has not yet been set down for hearing.

Kenya Court Blocks Preparations for Proposed Dangote Refinery

Kenya's Environment and Land Court in Malindi has temporarily stopped preparations for the proposed multibillion-shilling Dangote refinery in Lamu County. The interim orders were issued after Salim Tima Swale and 132 other petitioners challenged plans for the project, which was due to hold a groundbreaking ceremony on Wednesday. Justice Jane Onyango ordered that the existing situation on the disputed land in the Hindi/Manda Magogoni area be maintained until October 14, preventing activities including clearing, excavation, fencing, construction and disposal of the land. The petitioners said that they have occupied, cultivated and developed portions of the land for many years and argue that their interests should be considered in any compulsory acquisition process. The court has certified the matter as urgent and will give further directions when the case returns.

Close 

Nigerian Dancer Attempts Seven-Day World Record Marathon

Nigerian dancer Benjamin Daniel, known as Ben Dancer, is attempting to set a new world record by dancing continuously for 168 hours, or seven days. His target is 41 hours longer than the current individual dance marathon record of 127 hours, set by Indian dancer Srushti Sudhir Jagtap in 2023. Guinness World Records has not yet confirmed whether his attempt will qualify as an official record. Crowds of young people have gathered at Freedom Park in Lagos to support him, while videos of the performance have attracted attention on social media. The 33-year-old, who has danced professionally for 18 years, is incorporating Nigerian styles and traditions into the marathon, including Afrobeats, fuji, jazz and zouk, as well as traditional clothing. His team says the performance is intended to showcase Nigeria's cultural diversity as well as his endurance. He is allowed five minutes of rest for every hour of activity, with a medical team monitoring him.

World.title: South Africa: Matlala Back in Court Over Tender Fraud - South African News Briefs - September 29, 2026
World.content:
press review

Matlala Back in Court Over Tender Fraud

Alleged crime boss Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala is set to appear in the Pretoria Regional Court with 13 co-accused in a case involving alleged tender fraud, reports EWN. The 14 accused face charges including corruption, fraud and money laundering over a R228 million South African Police Service wellness contract awarded to Medicare 24 Tshwane District. The State alleged that police officials and company directors manipulated the tender process to favour Matlala. He previously negotiated a plea deal that later collapsed over the proposed prison sentence. The case is expected to eventually move to the High Court.

Taxi Boss Sibanyoni to Testify at Madlanga Commission

Taxi boss Joe Sibanyoni is set to testify before the Madlanga Commission in Pretoria, with his relationship with taxi industry figure Oupa "Bafana" Sindane likely to come under scrutiny, reports SABC News. The commission heard evidence from WhatsApp messages showing Sindane communicating with police officers who allegedly helped facilitate his movements and access to locations linked to Sibanyoni. Sibanyoni's testimony is also expected to address alleged extortion involving him and Sindane in connection with the Moloto Road Project.

Johannesburg Central Business District Faces More Power Cuts

Residents in Johannesburg's central business district face continued power outages after a fire at a central substation left large parts of the area without electricity for five days, reports EWN. The latest outage came just one day after power was restored following a two-week disruption. City Power said that electricity will be restored in phases as teams assess and repair the damaged network, but it cannot confirm when full supply will return.
