This culture of sexual violence endemic in elite institutions like Cornell "has got to stop," said New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at an event in Ithaca, N.Y., on Sunday. She is one of several prominent voices speaking out on the case.

"Those men posted in a group chat. That means it was normal to them. That means it was acceptable to them," she said.

NPR's Brian Mann contributed to this reporting.

World.title: Trump's immigration push has largely spared farms. Idaho dairymen worry it won't last.
World.content:
Trump's immigration push has largely spared farms. Idaho dairymen worry it won't last.

toggle caption Natalie Behring/Getty Images

TWIN FALLS, Idaho — The floor-to-ceiling windows in Rick Naerebout's office afford a sweeping view of the stunning 500-foot-deep, quarter-mile-wide Snake River Canyon. Squint and you can still see what's left of stunt motorcycle rider Evel Knievel's ramp from his failed 1974 attempt to jump the canyon with a steam-powered rocket on his back.

That put Twin Falls on the map in the 1970s. But these days, Twin, as locals call it, and its surrounding fertile river plain are better known as a national agricultural powerhouse, owing largely to the state's multi-billion-dollar dairy industry.

Today it's also an open secret — even in deeply Republican Idaho — that local farms rely heavily on undocumented immigrant labor. Naerebout estimates some 90% of the workers at the state's some 350 dairies may not have legal status.

Sponsor Message

"We're not taking jobs from Americans," Naerebout, the CEO of the Idaho Dairymen's Association says.. "The jobs are physical in nature and you're out in the elements. They just don't appeal to Americans."

toggle caption Kirk Siegler/NPR

American farmers have largely escaped President Trump's ongoing, aggressive immigration crackdown. As the ICE sweeps continue, however, farmers here and across the heartland are growing increasingly uneasy because many couldn't find enough workers even before the recent wave of detentions and deportations.

"If we had a concerted effort to have enforcement activities within agriculture, you could really harm our ability to produce food to feed ourselves," Naerebout says.

In Idaho, immigrants describe a lighter ICE presence

Like a lot of rural and Republican-controlled states, Idaho has not seen the level of immigration enforcement as some of its blue state neighbors, according to interviews with attorneys and immigrant advocates.

Still, twice a week, an ICE deportation plane lands at the tiny Twin Falls airport, in a rural area south of the small city surrounded by farm fields a half-hour drive from Interstate 84. On Tuesdays and Thursdays around noon, Heather Muth and a small group of immigration-rights activists unfurl a banner facing the tarmac that reads "Human Rights, Not Shuffle Flights."

Sponsor Message

"The whole purpose of [these flights] is for them to move around so that their attorneys and their families can't find them," Muth says.

One afternoon, using a telescope, she counted more than two dozen Idaho detainees, in shackles, being loaded from vans onto an ICE-contracted plane, headed to unknown federal detention centers.

"It really makes you wonder, what's going on here and what is this doing to our community," Muth says.

These weekly flights are pretty small. This is no Operation Metro Surge Minneapolis or the MacArthur Park immigration enforcement in Los Angeles. But the sweeps are still casting a chill across this rural farming region that has relied heavily on immigrant labor since the 1950s.

toggle caption Kirk Siegler/NPR

And in nearby Burley, home to milk processing and fertilizer plants, Susan Rios' world has been upended by ICE's crackdown. The 65-year-old farmworker activist and grandmother moved from Arizona to the area as a little girl to pick potatoes. Her daughter and son-in-law, fearing ICE, recently moved to Mexico. The husband is undocumented, so the family decided to self-deport.

"They were seeing how people were being detained and they did not want to take that risk," Rios says. She adds that the couple didn't want their two young daughters to potentially see their father taken away by federal agents.

But since they left, Rios says things have actually been pretty quiet. Nationwide, there have only been a handful of large raids at agricultural facilities in the nearly two years since Trump's sweeps began. Rios says local farms already can't find enough workers, and it's getting worse due to the immigration crackdown.

"I tell everyone, this is your opportunity, for all those that say Latinos are taking your jobs, right now, go to a dairy, go to a farm," Rios says. "I'm sure that you will be hired immediately."

Sponsor Message

Farmers try but can't find any locals to hire

The data backs that up . Last year, Idaho advertised 7,500 jobs through the temporary farm worker visa program known as H2A .

Only four local residents applied.

Rick Naerebout says that's despite the fact that dairy jobs pay more than most service jobs in small-town America.

The labor crisis is even more pronounced in Idaho's dairy industry — the state is now the fourth-largest milk producer in the U.S. — because the work is year-round, not seasonal. So the industry is not eligible for those coveted temporary H2A visas and has to rely on migrant labor.

toggle caption Natalie Behring/Getty Images

"The uneasiness continues to grow," Naerebout says. "The [workers] see all this activity around them, and it's not conducive to having your workforce feel welcomed or comfortable."

Idaho has also gone big for Trump in three presidential elections. Naerebout, a registered Republican, says that for years, multiple administrations — including this one — have mostly looked the other way when it comes to the dairy business's mostly migrant workforce.

"Where we're at now is realizing, OK, the federal government understands the world we live in, but the average Republican voter doesn't," he says.

The dairy industry is flexing its economic muscle, for now

There's only been one known large ICE raid in Idaho since Trump returned to office. It was part of an alleged illegal gambling bust last fall at a horse racing track popular with farmworkers. There haven't been any known large farm or workplace raids here since.

Nampa-based immigration attorney Brandy Perez attributes this to the dairy industry's political clout in deep-red states like Idaho.

"They have the ear of some of our legislators, our governor, and I think it's because of that that we've been able to keep the enforcement at a different level than we've seen in some of the other states," Perez says.

Sponsor Message

More than a year ago, Trump promised action for farmers and their undocumented workers. "We're going to have a system of signing them up so they don't have to go," Trump pledged in July of 2025 .

For now, Naerebout is taking the president at his word.

"But as quickly as we got into this favorable position with the administration, we could fall out of favor," he says. "It's not the most secure place to be."

And they're still waiting for that promised fix from the President and Republican-controlled Congress, which is now in recess until after the midterm elections. A GOP-backed bill with bipartisan support that would remove the seasonal requirement for key agricultural visas has gone nowhere.

And yet cows still have to be milked, every day, all year.

World.title: The Trump administration weakens fuel efficiency standards for new cars
World.content:
The Trump administration weakens fuel efficiency standards for new cars

toggle caption Apu Gomes/Getty Images



The Trump administration announced Monday it's scaling back how fuel efficient American carmakers need to make their fleets.

The Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards set average fuel economy levels for carmakers. The revised rules, which were finalized Monday, will now require carmakers to make their new passenger car and truck fleets up to 1% more fuel efficient each year, aiming for an average of 34.9 miles to the gallon in model year 2031.

This is down from Biden-era rules, which required an annual 2% increase in fuel efficiency with a goal of most vehicles getting, on average, 50.4 miles to the gallon by 2031.

Sponsor Message

The rationale: affordability. Administration officials argue that fuel efficiency technology is expensive, and has helped to drive up the cost of vehicles. They estimate that scaling back the standards will shave about $1,300 off the sticker prices of new cars.

"This administration is delivering relief to families and reviving the beating heart of American manufacturing," said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in an online statement announcing the change.

President Trump weighed in over the weekend on Truth Social: "These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car."

Climate advocates and auto industry observers say the rules change is another step in the Trump administration's efforts to roll back Biden-era climate policies — including cutting the federal tax credit for electric vehicle buyers, delaying federal dollars for a nationwide EV charging program, and striking down federal waivers that let California set its own strict pollution regulations.

In a statement emailed to NPR, Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the Center for Biological Diversity, wrote that rolling back the standards would increase gasoline usage and pollution, "costing consumers at the pump and at the doctor's office."

Sponsor Message

"Trump is tanking sensible mileage standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who're getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump," he continued.

According to AAA, the national average price for gasoline today is close to $4.50 a gallon, and for diesel, a gallon is hovering close to $6.50, just short of last week's record high.

Easing CAFE standards will hinder the industry's realignment toward more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles, said economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University. "It's very bad in the long term, because it slows progress," she said. "Then we make our auto companies less competitive. We give them less practice in making the cars that both Americans will want in the future and that the rest of the world will want." After all, American carmakers hope to continue selling their cars in foreign markets that may have stricter emissions standards. And a future presidential administration could change the rules again.

A legacy of the 1970s oil shock

CAFE standards have been part of the auto industry for decades. In 1975, during that decade's great oil supply shock, Congress enacted rules that encouraged carmakers to make their fleets more fuel efficient in an effort to reduce Americans' dependency on the Middle East for oil.

Since then, the national conversation about fuel efficiency has changed; the U.S. is now the world's largest oil producer, and many regulatory changes have instead been driven by concerns about climate change. Since the early 2010s, the fuel efficiency requirements for passenger cars and light trucks have consistently risen.

In practice, the Biden-era standards meant carmakers needed to make electric vehicles to balance out their gas guzzlers — otherwise they were subject to a fine.

But the Trump administration dropped that penalty last July as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effectively defanging the Biden-era CAFE standards. In December, the White House proposed scaling them back altogether. Soon after, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened a period of public comment.

In its final rule announcing the change, NHTSA also said it's eliminating the ability of carmakers to trade credits amongst themselves for making electric vehicles — a part of the Biden-era CAFE Standards that Republicans often criticized. This rule allowed automakers to buy credits from EV manufacturers to offset making less fuel-efficient vehicles. This helped them meet their CAFE targets.

Sponsor Message

Will easing CAFE standards make cars more affordable?

In announcing the new change, the administration said lowering the CAFE standards will make cars cheaper.

"Instead of allowing manufacturers to design and produce vehicles they believe their customers will want and need, while spreading real-world fuel economy improvements across their fleets, the system has increasingly led manufacturers to try to fit square vehicle pegs in round classification holes to force the adoption of technologies that do not meet the demands of American families," stated NHTSA in the final rule. "All of this adds inefficiency and cost — pushing even more consumers out of an already unaffordable new car market."

"It's true that the price of new cars has gone up quite a lot," says Helper at Case Western. But she contends that much of that is not because of fuel economy standards. Instead, she says, it's because vehicles have gotten larger, they've faced tariffs and supply chain issues in recent years, and they are often loaded with extras like infotainment systems.

A Consumer Reports analysis from 2023 found that between model years 2003 and 2021, vehicles got about 30% more fuel efficient, but attributed the rise in prices to an industrywide shift toward expensive SUVs, rather than from using more fuel-efficient technologies.

And when it comes to the monthly costs of a new car, there are external factors beyond a carmaker's control — like the cost of an auto loan, which is affected both by the Federal Reserve's benchmark lending rate and by an individual buyer's credit score.

"One of the cruxes of vehicle affordability right now is the average monthly payment getting jacked up, because interest rates are so high," says Ellen Hughes-Cromwick, who spent much of her career as Ford's chief global economist and now studies clean energy as a senior visiting fellow at the center-left Third Way think tank.

Sponsor Message

Plus, a cut in the sticker price might eventually be offset by spending on gas. If vehicles are less fuel efficient, that means drivers will need to fill up at the pump more often — which is especially salient in a year of high gas prices due to the war in Iran.

Will carmakers still make fuel-efficient vehicles?

For now, American carmakers are stuck in a kind of jam.

On the one hand, Helper said, a rules change that makes it easier for them to sell trucks and SUVs is "good in the short-term, because they make a lot of profits making these giant vehicles," though they are not as popular outside of the U.S.

This new move "allows the U.S. more of a playground in this protected little Galapagos of an ecosystem where no one else is wanting to compete," Helper continued.

But the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade group representing car and light-truck manufacturers that sell vehicles to the U.S. and that includes automakers such as Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, praised the move. "We're still reviewing the final rule, but NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions," said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the alliance, in an emailed statement to NPR.

"The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand. Today's final rule is an appropriate course correction," he continued.

Ford and Stellantis also both sent statements to NPR. They celebrated the administration's move and said it puts regulations in line with market realities.

"These standards will allow us to offer our customers the freedom to choose from a range of vehicles and powertrains that meet their needs, from brands they love and trust," Stellantis said in their statement, and noted the company is investing more than $13 billion in U.S. manufacturing over the next four years.

Sponsor Message

But in the long term, the CAFE standards change risks hindering American carmakers in a global industry, said Hughes-Cromwick. " The future of the industry is all about the transition to electric vehicles," she said. "The rest of the world is marching on in this transition to EVs. We have a very powerful competitor in terms of the Chinese electric vehicle industry."

"Lowering these standards now, when so many families are already struggling with rising transportation costs, will only make things harder for them. At the same time, lowering the bar for innovation risks a future where the global auto market leaves American industry behind," said Zero Emission Transportation Association executive president Albert Gore, in a statement. The association represents companies that make EVs and chargers.

And automakers may have other reasons not to shift gears too quickly on fuel efficiency: The administration's latest move could face legal challenges, which could take a while to work their way through the courts. Or a future administration could put more aggressive fuel economy standards back in place. For companies that need to make decisions years in advance, to decide which models to build, or which factories to design, the easiest course to keep might be the one they're already on.

World.title: U.S. bans on Canadian booze hit producers on one of the trade war's thorniest fronts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Distiller James Lester has grown used to the on-again, off-again chaos of the trade war, but he's now grappling with a new kind of treatment — being shut out of the U.S. market altogether.

"It's a little sad to be honest," said Lester, founder and operator of B.C.-based distillery Sons of Vancouver.

As of Tuesday at 12:01 am ET, U.S. bans are in effect on some Canadian alcohol products, dairy byproducts, motorcycles and molasses, shutting certain producers out of the U.S. market entirely.

Sons of Vancouver usually ships a few pallets of wheated rye to the U.S. each year — less than 10 per cent of their business overall. But the change is a disappointment for Lester, as he'd been working hard to forge relationships south of the border and expand the business there.

"We still have a little bit available online in the U.S., but that'll be the last of it for who knows how long."

It leaves Lester with few options for his American consumers, since they wouldn't be able to take it back to the States with them even if they came to Canada to buy a bottle.

The import ban heightens the trade war on one of its thorniest fronts — alcohol, which has become a hot-button issue for politicians on both sides of the border throughout the tariff battle.

James Lester founded Sons of Vancouver distillery in 2015. He's grown used to the chaos of the trade war but is disappointed by the U.S. move to ban some Canadian exports entirely from crossing the border, given the hard work he's put into trying to expand into that market. (Andrew Lee/CBC)

Small makers could be hurt most

With import bans stopping the flow of some alcohol products in their tracks, there are lots of individual business owners who stand to be hurt by the ban, according to international trade lawyer with KPMG Law, Robert Glasgow, even if the macro impact isn't massive.

Spirits producers could be hit particularly hard because Canada sends more liquor to the U.S. than it does beer or wine. The U.S. imported $673 million US worth of spirits from Canada in 2025 , compared to $62.1 million US worth of wine and just $19.2 million US worth of beer that same year, according to trade data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

Spirits Canada, the national trade association for the spirits industry, says about 93 per cent of spirits sent outside of Canada are destined for the States — making the loss of the "very important" U.S. market concerning, according to the group's president, Cal Bricker .

But the ban won't apply to barrels of certain kinds of liquor over a certain volume, and tariffs were removed from bulk shipments of certain whiskies and liqueurs when the heightened trade measures were announced earlier this month.

That move will spare big, multinational spirits companies that have bottling and mixing facilities on both sides of the border from some of the impact of the ban, according to Glasgow — leaving smaller players feeling the brunt.

"There's going to be a number of breweries, distilleries, and vineyards — largely the smaller, more independent shops that are more dependent on U.S. Trade and U.S. markets — that this could have some significant impacts for," Glasgow said.

But others in the wine making business have said the 50 per cent tariff rate effectively excluded Canadian products already, and industry groups are calling for more government support to help Canadian vineyards.

WATCH | U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says: U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says | Duration closed caption 3:06 About half of the $2 billion in spirits produced in Canada every year is sold to the U.S., says Cal Bricker, president and CEO of Spirits Canada. 'We sell more Crown Royal in Texas than we do in all of Canada.'

Why booze?

Alcohol has been a focal point in the trade battle since the start, when most Canadian premiers pulled U.S.-made bottles from the shelves of provincially-run liquor stores in March 2025 in response to the U.S. imposing tariffs on Canada.

The move drew criticism from political leaders in certain regions of the U.S. where certain types of spirits are made — like Kentucky, where Governor Andy Beshear appealed to leaders in this country to rethink the move as it threatened bourbon makers in his state.

The White House also cited Canada's "discrimination" against American alcohol , as well as dairy and autos, when announcing new 50 per cent tariffs in July, which hit Canadian booze among other products, including everything from milk to paper products to synthetic wigs.

Despite booze making up a relatively tiny portion of Canada-U.S. trade, Concordia University economics professor Moshe Lander says it's become a thorny issue in the trade war in part because it's so personal.

"We identify ourselves at least in part by the stuff that we drink," Lander said.

Brands like Foster's in Australia or Guinness in Ireland are more than just drinks, they're part of a country's identity, says Lander. He adds the same is true for Kentucky bourbon and California wine, making them politically effective targets.

WATCH | Why booze has become a pawn in the trade war: Why booze is at the centre of Canada-U.S. trade talks | About That | Duration closed caption 10:05 Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. have hit a breaking point over alcohol, with Prime Minister Mark Carney urging premiers to put American liquor back on shelves. Andrew Chang explains how alcohol became a top bargaining chip, how provincial liquor boards complicate trade and what's driving the current tariff standoff. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters and Getty Images)

And despite consumers having a taste for their favourite brand of wine or bourbon, it's relatively easy for consumers to substitute with a local bottle and still have a good night out, KPMG's Glasgow says, making it a smart product for policy makers to target.

"That's a type of retaliation that hits … the country that you're retaliating against harder than it hurts your own markets," Glasgow said.

A year and a half-long hangover

Joan Kautz, head of global sales and marketing for Californian winemaker Ironstone Vineyards, says she understands the strong message sent by taking U.S. alcohol off shelves in Canada.

"I don't like it, but I understand it," Kautz said.

The fight over alcohol has meant wines from the 2,500-hectare vineyard in Lodi, Calif., haven't been available in Canada for a year and a half.

Kautz says they're still selling some products to Alberta, where private-run liquor stores aren't restricting U.S. booze, but it's a fraction of the business Ironstone used to send north of the border.

'Canada is a very important market to us in all aspects,' said Joan Kautz with Ironstone Vineyard. About 35 per cent of U.S. wine exports go to Canada, worth more than one billion dollars US annually. (Ironstone Vineyard)

Historically, she says 20 per cent of the winery's export business went to Canada, making it their most important market outside of the U.S.

"Obviously, it hits financially," Kautz said. "We've been building the market for 30 years and it all went away overnight."

Her family's business exports to dozens of countries, and has been able to focus on other markets as Canadian demand dried up. But for other wineries, the impacts have been greater — some have reportedly filed for bankruptcy or decided to close and sell their vineyards in recent months.

Across booze categories, exports from the U.S. to Canada for 2025 dropped after bottles were pulled from shelves, with spirits sales falling by 70 per cent and wine exports dropping 87 per cent according to the Distilled Spirits Council of the U.S.

As a result of the economic impact, the council has called on U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to resolve the feud over over alcohol, so long-time trading partners can raise a glass together again.

Kautz is still hopeful that will happen eventually. She expects Canadian consumer's memories won't be too short, and they'll still have a taste for California wine when they can eventually get their hands on a bottle.

"There'll be a group that's probably slower to the table," Kautz said. "But you have to be hopeful."

World.title: 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide are caused by infections, study finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For many people, sun exposure, smoking and family history are the first thoughts that come to mind regarding cancer risk factors. While infections are rarely high on the list, new research shows one in eight cancers worldwide are actually caused by them.

These viruses, bacteria and other microbes are the focus of a new paper published Monday in The Lancet Oncology that linked an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 — 12 per cent of all new cases — to these infectious agents.

A team of researchers at The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), an arm of the World Health Organization, conducted the study. They found the largest number of cancer cases attributed to infections globally were caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which can increase the risk of stomach cancer and accounted for 760,000 cases, predominantly in eastern Asia.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) followed close behind. HPV, which causes 100 per cent of cervical cancer cases and also anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and some head and neck cancers, accounted for nearly 750,000 new cases globally, with high rates in sub-Saharan Africa. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) were also linked to a significant number of liver cancer cases.

For the first time, researchers linked even more cancers to infections, expanding their list to include 16 additional ones.

Gary Clifford, a cancer epidemiologist and study co-author based in Lyon, France, said the science has advanced significantly.

"There's been new infectious agents identified in this time as being cancer-causing, and even the infectious agents that we knew about in the past, the evidence has increased about the number of different cancers that they can cause," he said.

Some of those new infectious agents included HIV and its link to cervical cancer, and a very rare virus called Merkel cell polyomavirus that can lead to an aggressive form of skin cancer.

To come up with numbers, researchers first examined which infections cause cancer, then calculated what fraction of these cancers can be linked to specific infections and applied those calculations to global databases of new cancer cases.

Another significant shift is the recognition of the role of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV was linked to about 260,000 cases globally in 2024, and can lead to nasopharyngeal cancer, some gastric cancers and Hodgkin's lymphoma.

"That's quite a big burden of cancer caused by Epstein-Barr virus that was not counted in the past, but is now recognized," Clifford said.

Epstein-Barr virus is also a key risk factor in developing multiple sclerosis , and unlike some of the other infections that have vaccines or antibiotic treatments, there are no available tools to fight against it.

"The fact that we're seeing Epstein-Barr has caused all these chronic diseases — it's increasingly becoming a target that people need to focus on for prevention," he said.

The global report highlights vast regional differences, mostly driven by historical disparities, researchers said. High-income countries that established cancer screening and vaccination programs over the last few decades are doing much better compared to lower- and medium-resourced countries where access to prevention and treatment is limited.

"We really still have a lot of work to do implementing things that we know work and we've known for a long time but haven't really made it into all populations in the world," Clifford said.

In North America, the burden of cancer-causing infections is much lower, but H. pylori and HPV are the most common sources.

Infections causing cancer in Canada

In Canada, according to a 2019 study , the rate of cancers attributable to infections was estimated to be at four per cent. Karena Volesky, an epidemiologist in Montreal, led the Canadian research team while at McGill University.

"It tells us how important each of the 12 infections are," Volesky said of the new global numbers.

While there is a lower prevalence of these forms of infections in Canada, her study estimated these infections lead to more than 7,000 cancer diagnoses each year.

WATCH | HPV vaccination urged: Doctors urge Canadians to get HPV vaccine to prevent cervical cancer | Duration closed caption 2:06 Doctors say Canada is facing a silent health crisis of HPV-related cervical cancer that could be prevented if more people got vaccinated against human papillomavirus, the virus that can cause the disease.

"HPV is certainly an infection that we're keeping an eye on in Canada," said Elizabeth Holmes, the director of health policy at the Canadian Cancer Society.

Holmes said cervical cancer rates had been steadily declining in Canada due to robust childhood vaccination programs, but plateaued last year.

"That's certainly a concern — that we might not meet our goal of elimination of cervical cancer by 2040 unless those rates start to decline again," she said.

Human papillomavirus is transmitted through sexual contact, but the HPV vaccine protects against the most common forms of infection that can cause cancer.

Canada's cervical cancer elimination plan aims to increase vaccination rates to 90 per cent, increase screening rates to 90 per cent and ensure timely followup care after screening.

"Right now, only about five provinces are above 80 per cent, and I think at least one is as low as 66 per cent," Holmes said.

An at-home self-testing HPV kits in Vancouver, British Columbia in January 2024. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The stomach bacteria that can lead to cancer

The infection leading to the most cancer cases is Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium first discovered in the early 1980s that mainly leads to gastric cancers. While the research found the highest burden in eastern Asia in countries like Japan, South Korea and China, it's a problem here, too.

"It's a horrible disease to die from," said Dr. Paul Moayyedi, a leading researcher and gastroenterologist at McMaster University. About 2,000 Canadians die every year from stomach cancer.

Moayyedi wants to see a universal screening program for the bacterium, which can be detected through a blood or breath test, stool sample or endoscopy and treated with a combination of antibiotics over a two-week period.

A microscopic image showing leukemia cells in blue that contain Epstein-Barr virus using a fluorescent stain that causes affected cells to glow green under ultraviolet light. (Paul M. Feorino/CDC)

Helicobacter pylori is associated with crowded living conditions and poor sanitation in childhood. While most people with it can live a long life without any issues, if left untreated, it can cause ulcers and stomach cancer for some.

Moayyedi said stomach cancers may not be seen as high priority compared to other types of cancers, but believes screening programs for those at high risk, such as people with a family history of stomach cancers or First Nations communities, would save lives.

"In consultation with the elders of local communities it would be important to at least offer those groups screening if they would want it," he said.

World.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared.

ShinyHunters c laimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI last Tuesday — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — and gave the law enforcement agency one week to rescind an ⁠unflattering statement about the group.

With the deadline approaching, a ShinyHunters representative sent CBC News a statement Monday saying they were never planning to release the sensitive data, adding that the media and the public have "made many false assumptions and wild speculations."

The group has been linked to dozens of cyberattacks targeting large companies and institutions. ShinyHunters typically demand ransom payments in exchange for not releasing sensitive data, but they have been adamant that was not their intention in this case.

Campaign to 'combat disinformation'

ShinyHunters denied asking the FBI for a ransom, but acknowledged "past operations" could leave them open to misinterpretation.

"The reason why we have stated multiple times that this is not extortion is because since the very beginning we had made our decision that we would never publish this data. We have never intended to nor have we ever planned to," the statement said in part.

The group told CBC News that their actions against the FBI were part of a campaign to "combat disinformation" about their tactics.

"If we made this statement normally then this much attention to our words and intentions would've never been this widespread. We'd have been ignored and disregarded. However, now everyone knows what the issue is and what we are doing."

ShinyHunters took issue with an FBI report from May that said, among other things, the group is known to threaten family members of its targets and threaten to release embarrassing or compromising images of its victims.

ShinyHunters denied ever using those tactics and released a statement following last Tuesday's data breach giving the FBI one week to remove or "correct" the report.

The group shared a 5,000-line spreadsheet of breached FBI data with some journalists, which it said represented only a small piece of its claimed two- to three-terabyte trove.

The sample included names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for what it claimed were thousands of FBI employees.

When CBC News asked ShinyHunters on Monday whether they have taken any steps to ensure the shared data isn't leaked by other sources, the representative said they "cannot guarantee" what will happen to those samples, "because that is out of our control and certain journalists violated our trust."

WATCH | ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for a Canvas hack in May: There's a data breach at Canadian schools. What do we know? | Duration closed caption 7:18 Canvas, a program used by postsecondary schools across Canada, has been hit by hackers. A group called ShinyHunters is claiming responsibility — and asking for a ransom. Emsisoft threat intelligence analyst Luke Connolly lays out what we know.

'Can't trust them,' researcher says

Ian Lin, an ethical hacker and head of research and development at Toronto-based cybersecurity company Packetlabs, says that's concerning.

He says he's seen "a number of researchers" claiming online to have obtained the data, in addition to journalists.

"There's going to be people that are willing to pay a high price for this data," Lin told CBC News.

The hack, which one former FBI operative called a "foreign intelligence service goldmine," has raised concerns about the safety of the agency's employees.

The New York Times reported Monday that the FBI sent out a staff memo acknowledging employees had personal information stolen in a cybersecurity incident, and instructing them to remain vigilant at home and at work and report any unsolicited contacts or threats.

Lin says he does not have high hopes ShinyHunters will keep their word, saying it's common for criminal hacking groups to renege on their promises or to use the same set of data as leverage multiple times.

"Why they did this, I think was for attention. But you still can't trust them to keep safe your data. Because now this is leverage over the law enforcement and FBI. And at any moment they could choose to use this data for their own additional purposes," he said.

"The FBI and law enforcement should all still remain vigilant. There should be massive lessons learned from the FBI side."

World.title: Tessa Virtue says taking on dance without skates is 'terrifying' and 'invigorating'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After years of pursuing precision on the ice, retired Olympic ice dancer Tessa Virtue is embracing the 'messiness' of movement as she returns to her first love, dance, in a new solo performance.

For most of her life, Tessa Virtue has built a career on control.

On the ice, she learned to find the precise balance point on a blade, trust a partner implicitly and make even the most difficult movements look effortless.

With Scott Moir, she transformed ice dance into storytelling built on speed, precision, trust and emotion. Together, they won three Olympic gold medals, three world titles and a permanent place in Canadian sports history.

Now, Virtue is being asked to do something that runs against much of what made her an elite athlete: lose her balance, embrace uncertainty and perform alone.

Her new contemporary dance solo, choreographed by Alyssa Martin, premieres Oct. 15 at the Fall for Dance North Festival in Toronto, where Martin is the artist-in-residence. It is Virtue's first major performance on a stage rather than in a rink — and a return to the art form she first loved.

Virtue says she feels excited and honoured to be asked to participate, but the opportunity has also brought mixed emotions.

"It feels very much like returning to something and also utterly terrifying, but I think that's what's making this feel kind of electrifying and invigorating," she told CBC News.

WATCH | Tessa Virtue wanted to partner up with Scott Moir again: Why Scott Moir won't be Tessa Virtue's dance partner this time | Duration closed caption 1:16 Tessa Virtue reveals she originally asked longtime skating partner Scott Moir to join her on stage. Instead, she's found support through her creative collaborators and the wider dance community.

Dance was Virtue's first love. She began at three, and dance studios became places of comfort whenever skating took her away from home — first at 13, then again when she moved to Michigan at 15.

But returning to dance has not meant simply transferring the skills she developed as an ice dancer onto a stage. Virtue says the two forms demand fundamentally different relationships with the body.

"On the ice, I was technically proficient at finding the balance point on my blade," Virtue said. "In dance, it turns out the momentum and energy that you can create on stage comes from actually tipping off axis and playing with the recovery of that."

For Virtue, that has meant moving away from the controlled perfection demanded by elite skating and toward something looser, riskier and more exposed.

She describes the process as embracing "the messiness and the raw feelings" — a shift she calls cathartic for her nervous system.

The solo also marks the first time in years that Virtue has performed alone. She even asked Moir whether he wanted to join her for a duet.

"He's busy coaching his other athletes and he has a life," she said, laughing.

Instead, Virtue found a new kind of partnership in the rehearsal room and through the wider dance community. Martin says she was drawn to Virtue's performance style long before they began working together.

"There's something that she brings to her performances that is just so authentic and open and generous," Martin told CBC News. "That generosity is not quiet at all. It's quite loud and just so overflowing with this warmth and this power."

The work is set to Céline Dion's It's All Coming Back to Me Now, a song chosen by Martin, who says she immediately knew Virtue could bring power to it.

Robert Binet, Fall for Dance North Festival's artistic director and co-CEO, says the collaboration is exactly the kind of artistic risk the festival hopes to encourage.

"It's a real adventure in bringing two artists who have had very different artistic upbringings and careers together, but who share this absolute love of dance," Binet said.

Tessa Virtue, left, and choreographer Alyssa Martin during rehearsal at a studio space at Meridian Hall in Toronto on Sept. 28. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

He hopes audiences will see Virtue in unfamiliar territory, and recognize that the qualities that made her an extraordinary ice dancer can travel beyond the rink.

"People know her as the most extraordinary ice dancer in the world," he said. "I really want people to see that if you love ice dance, you also love dance, and it's just about people moving to music and sharing parts of themselves with you."

Virtue, meanwhile, hopes audiences remain open to whatever they feel.

"You don't need to know the vocabulary of dance," she said. "You just need to enjoy and remain open to feeling something."

An animated GIF shows Tessa Virtue rehearsing for her solo dance performance in Toronto. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

As for what comes next, Virtue says she's leaving the door open.

"While I might not always feel confident in taking on a challenge, I can always be courageous," she said.

Virtue's solo premieres Oct. 15 at Fall for Dance North in Toronto. The festival runs Oct. 15-25.

World.title: New Princess Diana book 'not about settling scores,' says her brother, Charles Spencer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Charles Spencer says his new book about his sister, the late Princess Diana, is not an attempt to get revenge on his former in-laws, the British Royal family.

"It's not about settling scores," Spencer, a historian, journalist and the 9th Earl Spencer, told CBC Radio's The Current.

"I could have written something much more devastating," he said. "This was the considered version that I thought, 'Yeah, whatever's in here, needs to be in, to give the full story of Diana's life."

The book, Swan Song: Diana, my sister, has prompted a barrage of international headlines over its claims, including that the then-Prince Charles sounded "giddily elated" when Diana died.

But Spencer said he wrote it in part because he's been inundated with interview requests ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death next year.

"I began to think, 'Well, if everyone wants to know the truth, I think it's time for that,' " he said.

Spencer sat down with The Current's Matt Galloway to discuss the book, and his sister's legacy.

Diana and Spencer in 1981, the year she married then-Prince Charles. Spencer was 17 at the time of their wedding. (The Spencer Family/Penguin Random House)

Charles 'upbeat' in call after Diana's death

Diana was arguably the most famous woman in the world after she married Charles in 1981, and gave birth to two sons, William and Harry. But after a tumultuous marriage, the royal couple separated in 1992, finalizing their divorce in 1996.

After leaving the Royal Family, she became a style icon and philanthropist, leading campaigns to clear landmines and challenge stigma around HIV and AIDS .

But she increasingly strained under the glare of the tabloid media and died in a car crash in Paris in 1997, after a high-speed chase while being pursued by paparazzi.

In the book, Spencer claims that Charles sounded "giddily elated" in a phone call after Diana died. Spencer said he'd already received calls from many people wishing to express their shock and offer their condolences.

"He just sounded completely different to everyone else … sort of buoyant … upbeat," he said.

"It was so jarring, particularly among all the sea of other voices."

WATCH | Why Charles Spencer hung up on King Charles: Earl Spencer says Charles 'went nuts' in call after Diana's death | Duration closed caption 0:52 Earl Spencer describes a conversation he had with then Prince Charles in the aftermath of Princess Diana’s death, telling CBC Radio’s The Current host Matt Galloway that Charles ‘went nuts’ when he objected to William and Harry walking behind their mother’s coffin.

Spencer also wrote that he argued with Charles in the days following Diana's death, over palace plans for Princes William and Harry to walk behind their mother's coffin in the funeral cortege. Spencer said he told Charles it would be an ordeal Diana would not have wanted her sons to endure.

"He went nuts and started screaming and shouting," Spencer said. "And then he pulled himself together, I thought — and then, he said, 'We'll forget her soon enough.' "

"I was stunned. And I went, 'I can't believe you just said that,' and hung up on him."

Buckingham Palace responded to the allegations earlier this month.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," the palace said in a statement.

Spencer described the statement as "classic gaslighting."

"They're trying to say maybe it's grief, maybe it was a long time ago, but they're trying to put a question mark over my reliability. It's a tactic, but I don't think it's worked for them."

WATCH | Spencer says Palace is trying to undermine his account: Earl Spencer calls Buckingham Palace’s response to his book ‘classic gaslighting’ | Duration closed caption 0:46 Earl Spencer addresses Buckingham Palace’s response to his book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, telling CBC Radio’s The Current host Matt Galloway that its dismissal of his account is ‘classic gaslighting.

Funeral procession was 'exhausting emotionally'

Princes William and Harry did walk behind their mother's coffin, alongside Spencer and other family members — with thousands of people thronged on either side of their route.

In the book, Spencer describes it as walking through a tunnel of grief, where the reactions of the crowd kept shifting.

"We could walk for 100 metres and it would be silent, you could just hear sobs. And then [further on], people wailing, like it's a biblical thing, a sort of wailing and gnashing of teeth," he told Galloway, adding that some people screamed out their love for Diana and for her two sons.

"For over half an hour, we were just walking with this crashing in from all sides," he said, describing it as emotionally exhausting.

Spencer, centre, with his hands clasped behind his back, walks behind Diana's coffin in 1997. Princes Harry and Prince William are at either side. To their left is the boys' father, Charles, and to the right, their grandfather, Prince Philip. (Dave M. Benett/Getty Images/Penguin Random House)

Some solace came from the late Prince Philip, the late Queen Elizabeth's husband.

"He was very much there for his grandsons, and he took control of it," Spencer said. "He said to the other four of us, the most important thing is to just keep looking ahead."

Spencer hid eulogy from palace

Diana's funeral took place at Westminster Abbey on Sept. 6, 1997. Spencer delivered a eulogy that spoke of her talents, while also delivering sharp criticism of the press and paparazzi.

But at a rehearsal the day before the funeral, he was asked to read his speech for a microphone check in the Abbey. As he climbed the steps to the lectern, "a handful of people, not that many, appeared out of the shadows," he said.

"An alarm went in my brain thinking, 'Hey, this is odd.' And then in that moment I realized they were probably listening … that they were gonna vet it and perhaps veto it," he told CBC.

So Spencer said he'd forgotten the speech at home, and instead started to read from a prayer book.

"I'd hardly read a word when they went, 'That's OK.' And then at that moment I realized that I'd saved the speech."

A handwritten draft of the eulogy Spencer read at Diana's funeral. (The Spencer Family/Penguin Random House)

More than two billion people watched Diana's funeral, with Spencer's eulogy prompting a standing ovation from the crowds watching on screens outside.

But in the days before the funeral, Spencer discovered that the palace had invited the editors of Britain's tabloid newspapers. Believing they had hounded Diana during her lifetime, Spencer called each editor individually .

"I said just please don't come, it's totally inappropriate. Given the circumstances of Diana's death, it's obviously not right that you attend this funeral," he told The Current.

"That really did upset them, but it shouldn't have. They shouldn't have accepted."

WATCH | 'I don't care how famous someone is, you cannot justify vicious, personal attacks': Earl Spencer says ‘vicious’ treatment of Harry and Meghan not OK | Duration closed caption 0:52 Earl Spencer, the brother of the late Princess Diana, addresses the media’s treatment of Harry and Meghan, telling CBC Radio’s The Current host Matt Galloway that ‘vicious, personal’ attacks are never OK.

Harry and Meghan suffering same demonization

Spencer thinks his sister suffered immensely under the glare of the paparazzi, who would provoke her to get the photographs they wanted.

"They would call her the worst words in the world, take a picture and then say, 'Look at her looking upset, she must be deranged or she's mentally unstable,' " he said.

"I mean that is so appalling. As a brother it still makes my blood boil."

He thinks things have improved since the 1990s, but still sees people being demonized in the public eye, including his nephew, Prince Harry, and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex.

"I'm not saying Diana or Harry or Meghan or whatever are perfect people, but they're people. And I do think the public have to remember this," he said.

"Sometimes, I see these appalling comments under newspaper articles from people, and I think those people should be ashamed of piling in on a witch hunt."

Diana with William, left, and Harry on holiday in Austria in 1993. (Tim Graham/Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty Images/Penguin Random House)

Diana the sister, Diana the superstar

On the day she married Charles, Diana "emerged from Saint Paul's Cathedral as a global superstar," Spencer said.

"I certainly didn't see that coming. I mean, she's just my big sister," he said, adding that because he was just 17 at the time, he was "a typical, self-centred, hormonal teenager."

In the years that followed, he learned to focus on his original connection with his sister, by "cutting that away from the Princess Di or Lady Di of the media's imagination and semi-invention."

That wasn't always easy. He remembers one dinner where they met with old friends, who were suddenly sycophantic, having been swayed "into treating her as someone different to the Diana they'd always known."

He said he walked home that night puzzled by the shift and wondering what to do.

"I realized, my job as her brother from that point on was to always just be true, be the same brother," he said.

"And if that meant that sometimes she didn't like what I [said], then it was still good for her, I hope."

World.title: Canada led a 2022 deal to protect the world's nature. Has there been progress since then?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

During a snowy Montreal winter in 2022, Canada welcomed over 180 UN member countries to negotiate an ambitious new agreement to protect nature. The world’s biodiversity was in an unprecedented crisis — with more than one million species facing the threat of extinction, leaders were finally waking up to how close ecosystems were to collapsing.

Steven Guilbeault, then-minister of environment, helped wrangle a consensus and establish a new goal of protecting 30 per cent of global land and oceans by 2030, meant to halt the mass extinction. These spaces would be protected for the long-term goal of conservation, with human activities like fishing and mining banned or heavily restricted.

The agreement also included a promise to help lower-income countries with funding: money to establish and manage these protected spaces.

“That was the compromise in Montreal,” said Guilbeault, while on his way back from Climate Week NYC, held alongside the UN General Assembly to bring together climate advocates and policymakers.

“Those people who wanted more ambition had to agree to commit to more funding, and those who wanted more funding had to agree to more ambition.”

LISTEN | World leaders discuss climate in New York: The Early Edition 7:14 Climate Week taking place to coincide with UN General Assembly in New York It's climate week in New York City - a gathering of top leaders and advocates for a low-carbon future. What on Earth? host Johanna Wagstaffe is there too. She's talking to other meteorologists about how they handle the pressure to speak out - or stay silent - about climate change. She even heard from one weather presenter who quit his job over it.

But that funding is now the main roadblock in reaching the goals of the Montreal agreement. A new assessment report released in New York this week projected that, based on commitments made so far, just 27 per cent of lands and only 12 per cent of oceans will be protected by 2030.

“We have a reasonable shot of reaching our terrestrial targets. We won't be at 30 per cent [but] we'll be close to it,” said Guibeault, who resigned as an MP earlier this year because of the Carney's government's climate rollbacks.

“That's certainly something that should give us comfort. But on oceans protection, there is a lot more work that needs to be done.”

The assessment also comes as Canada, the country where the 2022 deal was made, has shifted its priorities toward fast-tracking resource projects, putting it behind on its own climate targets.

Rich countries need to put up more money: report

Speeding up nature protection and reaching goals will primarily involve increasing funding, according to the assessment, led by international advocacy groups Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean.

The Montreal agreement included a target of $30 billion US per year in international financing for biodiversity conservation in developing nations, of which about $6 billion US of that target is needed specifically to establish protected areas on land and in the oceans.

But international finance has only reached $1.1 billion US per year, it said. This money is supposed to flow from higher-income countries like Canada and Japan to developing ones, meant to create parks and conserved areas, pay for programs like park rangers and support communities and institutions in those regions.

“More money is flowing to countries in the Global South than before, but it's still not enough," Guilbeault said.

The report also said most of the funding is coming from just five major sources: the World Bank; the European Union; Germany; the Global Environment Facility, a multilateral development fund; and the non-profit Rainforest Trust.

The report warned that changes by even one of these funders could jeopardize the total amount.

Still, it also highlighted successes: More than 50 countries already report terrestrial coverage of at least 30 per cent. To date, 20 per cent of lands and 10 per cent of oceans have been protected.

And more help is on the way. This week, Canada ratified the High Seas Treaty, a new global agreement to regulate the oceans and seas currently outside of national jurisdictions. With the majority of world nations now signed on, experts say it will be easier to designate large areas of ocean as protected.

Steve Guilbeault, Canada'a former environment minister, with Huang Runqiu, China's environment minister, at a COP15 press conference in Montreal in 2022. (Paul Chiasson/The Canadian Press)

Oceans protection gets a boost

Until now, 101 countries have ratified the High Seas Treaty. Opened to signatures in 2023, it forms a new kind of international law to govern the oceans, such as new mechanisms to propose conserved areas, to fight climate change and to safeguard marine resources like fisheries that support billions of people.

The treaty has officially come into force last January and its first gathering is set for January 2027.

Canada is leading in ocean protection, as well, by hosting the Our Ocean Conference in Halifax in April. Prime Minister Mark Carney also committed $82 million toward monitoring the ocean — especially in the fast-changing Arctic — and named his wife, Diana Fox Carney, as Canada’s ocean envoy.

Sien Van den broeke, a campaigner with Greenpeace Canada, says the Halifax conference will be a place for countries to showcase commitments they’re making on oceans protection. She expects Canada will make some promises of its own, too.

With the new global treaty, Canada could also support new protection proposals off its vast coastlines. Van den broeke pointed to the Emperor Seamounts , a biodiversity hotspot in the northern Pacific, and the Sargasso Sea , another important ecosystem in the Atlantic, as potential areas the country could champion.

A kelp forest off the coast of California. (Annika Hammerschlag/The Associated Press)

But advocates are also watching nervously as the Carney government has weakened environmental rules back at home, as part of the prime minister's agenda to build major new infrastructure and resource projects amid the ongoing trade conflict with the U.S.

Canada has protected about 14 per cent of its lands and 15.5 per cent of its oceans, according to the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS). Its president, Sandra Schwartz, said that protecting nature is more than just hitting numerical targets.

“Nature really is quite foundational to our way of life and to our long-term success,” she said. “And that's both in terms of economic success as well as our overall well-being.”

As the host country of the 2022 conference that landed the global deal, Canada should lead by example, Schwartz said. But this month, the Carney government introduced a new law that will significantly speed up the federal environmental review process and change how oil and gas pipelines are assessed.

WATCH | New environment fast-tracking laws: Carney faces climate, labour pushback over new nation-building bill | Duration closed caption 2:04 Protesters gathered outside Parliament to speak out against environmental and labour aspects of the government's newly tabled Bill C-39, also known as the Building Canada Strong Act. At least 11 people were arrested.

That comes on top of laws to designate and speed up major projects that have received widespread pushback from environmental groups.

“Canada's going to fall behind,” said Schwartz.

“And it's unfortunate that we appear to be pitting the environment against the economy.”

World.title: B.C. politicians, leaders condemn white nationalist gathering on First Nation reserve
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. politicians and leaders are denouncing a gathering of white nationalists on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve, just east of Kamloops.

Kúkpi7 (Chief) Rosanne Casimir told CBC News on Sunday the nation had received reports that morning of a gathering of about 20 to 30 men, wearing white face masks and black caps, standing together around the reserve while hoisting flags over their shoulders.

In a news release, Casimir said "individuals associated with Second Sons Canada, a group linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology, have been seen and documented within our community.

"White supremacy will not instill fear in generations of survivors and intergenerational survivors who have already carried fear for far too long."

CBC News has verified that video circulating on social media of the gathering is authentic and depicts members of the group Second Sons Canada near the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve.

Casimir said the group was seen on reserve land, and RCMP said they were called to an area on the reserve.

Casimir said the reserve's security told the men they were not permitted to gather and asked them to leave. However, they did not leave until RCMP were called and arrived at the scene.

'Clearly intended to intimidate': RCMP

Kamloops RCMP's officer in charge, Supt. Jeff Pelley, said in a news release Monday that front-line officers from the Tk'emlúps RCMP detachment received a report of the group near Chief Eli Larue Way around 7:25 a.m. PT.

Pelley said officers immediately engaged with the group, which then left the location and "continued throughout various parts of the city."

"The posting of a banner bearing the words 'got bones,' combined with the use of masks to conceal their identities while making such public statements is a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division," Pelley said in the release.

WATCH | CBC investigative unit looks into views of Second Sons: Leaders of growing ‘nationalist’ club praise Nazis, say ‘race war is here’ | Duration closed caption 7:22



He said the RCMP takes the matter seriously and will "continue to engage the group" as part of its investigation.

He asked anyone with information, photos or video, or anyone with knowledge of future gatherings, to contact the RCMP.

Politicians condemn event

Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke out against the gathering in a social media post on Monday afternoon.

"The cowardly act that took place at Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc yesterday, is abhorrent," he wrote on Facebook.

"It has no place in this country. My thoughts are with everyone who are shaken and hurt by this disgusting display of hate."

Carney said the gathering is a reminder of the shared responsibility to confront the devastating legacy of the residential school system.

"Courageous Survivors shared the truth, so that all Canadians could take up the work of reconciliation."

Speaking at the Vancouver International Airport Sunday afternoon, NDP Leader David Eby said there has been a rise "in this kind of white nationalist behaviour" in B.C., adding that more needs to be done "to fight it."

"This is just disgraceful, disgusting behaviour. It's very clear that these people were trying to intimidate, make people feel fearful," he said, adding that the masked men would face severe retribution if their identities were known.

Lorne Doerkson, interim leader of the B.C. Conservative Party, condemned the gathering in a post to social media.

"The white nationalist gathering on Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc land this morning was hateful and meant to intimidate. It has no place in British Columbia," he said.

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, in a post on social media, called the gathering "abhorrent."

"Hate and discrimination of any kind are unwelcome in British Columbia and on behalf of all members of Centre BC, I condemn this behaviour and stand in solidarity with the Tkʼemlúps First Nation," she said.

WATCH | B.C. First Nation on edge after white nationalist gathering: White nationalist gathering puts B.C. First Nation on edge | Duration closed caption 2:32 A gathering of masked white nationalists on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near Kamloops has alarmed the community. Its timing, just days before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, has heightened safety concerns.

'Active club'

Evan Balgord, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network, said the Second Sons have grown to include chapters across the country.

"They are what you call an ‘active club,’ which means they are a white nationalist group, white supremacists, who advocate for guys getting together and training, preparing for what they see as the inevitable use of violence to defend the white nationalist movement, attack their opponents, and ultimately carry out racist mass deportations in Canada," he said.

Balgord said the incident is just the latest in a string of similar demonstrations in various parts of Canada.

He said the white nationalist movement in Canada is currently the largest it has ever been, both in terms of numbers of members and fundraising capacity.

'Not going to deter us': chief

Casimir said the nation's planned events for Truth and Reconciliation Day on Sept. 30 will go ahead.

"We will not be intimidated," she said.

"This is not going to deter us from gathering, reflecting or honouring our survivors and the children who returned home."

Rosanne Casimir, chief of the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc, says the incident won't deter the community from 'gathering, reflecting, or honouring our survivors and the children who returned home.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

But the incident, Casimir said, is an example of a broader problem.

"Everyone should always be concerned because there's so much racism and discrimination out there."

On Monday morning, Casimir told CBC News's Daybreak Kamloops that community safety is the nation's top priority.

She recommended members stay alert and connected, and report any suspicious incidents.

"We're going to continue moving forward and continuing the work of Truth and Reconciliation. And ... if anything, it just reminds us why this work remains so important."

CBC News reached out to Second Sons Canada but did not hear back before publication.

A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.

World.title: What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., currently igniting the internet.

The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7." She alleges they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024.

The lawsuit, filed in New York Supreme Court and viewed by CBC News, alleges the assault happened on campus at the Chi Phi fraternity house, and that one of the frat brothers sent a Snapchat message inviting other members to join them for "free pussy."

It further says that the accused only faced temporary suspensions and "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays" to the university — an allegation Cornell denies.

None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged. But the case has unleashed online fury, drawing comparisons to last year's Hockey Canada sexual assault trial in London, Ont., which saw all five players acquitted.

The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Sept. 28. (Heather Ainsworth/The Associated Press)

On Monday, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.

"Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available — by testimony to the Tompkins County grand jury," district attorney Matthew Van Houten told CBC News in a written statement.

Cornell, in its own statement Monday, said it supported the DA's decision for a criminal grand jury to hear the woman's allegations, but disputed the lawsuit's characterization of how the university punished the accused.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Kyle Kimball, vice-president for university relations, said in a statement posted online.

The statement also said the on-campus Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

Here's what to know about the case and why it's caused so much fury online.

What's in the lawsuit?

According to the lawsuit, the assault began the night of Oct. 19, 2024. Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time, had been drinking with her sorority, and again at a nightclub and then "stumbled" alone at 11 p.m. to the Chi Phi fraternity house on campus to visit a friend — one of the accused.

"Plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past three hours," the lawsuit says. It also says the nightclub served the woman "at least one" alcoholic beverage even though it had marked an X on her hand showing she was underage.

At the frat house, she was given a beer, and her friend allegedly proposed a threesome with another member, to which she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit states.

The accused allegedly took her upstairs and led her to a room with another of the accused. She was pressured to snort ketamine, the lawsuit alleges, adding that she had never used that substance before. They also "plied her" with cannabis and rum, it says, after which the two men "began engaging in sexual acts with plaintiff, all without her consent."

As they engaged in oral and vaginal sex, one of the accused also repeatedly slapped her buttocks, resulting in bruising, the lawsuit says. One of the men left to have a nap, and another entered the room. The two remaining men then began another alleged assault on the woman.

At 1:42 a.m., one of them sent a Snapchat message to the rest of the fraternity, claiming there was "free pussy." The suit includes an image of the alleged message, and some of the purported responses from the accused, including, "like you can walk in and whip it out."

WATCH | Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada trial: Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada sex assault trial | Duration 3:24 Closing arguments in the sexual assault trial of five former world junior hockey players are being presented in court on Monday. All five players have pleaded not guilty. Part of the evidence includes text messages between the accused as a group and also to the complainant. CBC News spoke to several lawyers who aren’t involved in the trial to see how the messages may or may not factor into the judge’s decision.

According to the suit, "multiple" other fraternity members then entered the room. One of them allegedly put ketamine on his erect penis and told the woman to snort it, which she did. The men then began snorting the substance off her naked body, the suit states. Two men took her to another room, where they allegedly assaulted her again.

The alleged incident ended at 5:45 a.m., and Jane Doe passed out. She returned to her sorority house "in a state of shock," the documents state, and soon realized the events were becoming "public knowledge" on campus.

She reported it a few weeks later to the Cornell University Police Department around Nov. 8, 2024. She alleges the seven accused were issued temporary suspensions and allowed "to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays."

The university released a statement and investigated, but ultimately closed it at a later date, according to the lawsuit.

Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the alleged assault and the university's purported handling of it, the lawsuit says. She is suing the seven men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university, Moonies Bar and Nightclub and others, seeking undisclosed damages.

The seven Chi Phi members named in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.

"Ms. Doe has had her dreams destroyed as a result of what has happened to her," her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CBC News in a written statement.

"The fact that her trauma has been made public has been very difficult. However, she has been gratified by the outpouring of support that she has received from the public."

Online backlash to 'the culture of rape'

As the lawsuit made headlines, the backlash was swift. Online, Cornell alumni called on each other to stop donating to the school. Some people publicly turned down their acceptances, and others launched campaigns targeting the university, the local police and the various workplaces of the so-called "Cornell 7."

The seven accused were identified by Cornell's student newspaper editorial board on Sept. 21 in an editorial titled, "Cornell won't, we will."

A screenshot of a Threads post by Dr. Amani Jambhekar posted Sept. 25, 2026. (@ajvictorymd/Threads)

A former South Park writer launched a website to expose the accused. Actors Josh Gad and Florence Pugh posted online condemning the alleged assault and what the lawsuit described as the university's handling of it.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned what she called a "culture of rape" at elite institutions while speaking about the alleged incident, at a town hall in Ithaca over the weekend.

"This is a culture, this is norms, these are practices," said Ocasio-Cortez, according to the Cornell Daily Sun. “What we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore.”

On Monday night, Ithaca Mayor Robert G. Cantelmo called for an immediate moratorium on all student and special event permits, including "Greek life and other student group gatherings," given what he called the "appalling response" by Cornell's administration.

"This is a miscarriage of justice and continues to pose a significant threat to students and residents who may be victimized at unsafe and under-monitored on- or off-campus student events," he wrote in an online statement.

Cornell's response

The university said in a statement Monday that it conducted its own investigation at the time and issued sanctions, including expelling some students and suspending others.

In response to the allegations, Cornell said "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

The school said it conducted an internal disciplinary investigation in 2024. It said a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, and both the woman and the accused testified and presented evidence.

In a statement last week responding to the lawsuit, Cornell said federal privacy law barred it from disclosing specific information on individual students.

People walk through the Cornell University campus on Nov. 3, 2023 in Ithaca, New York. (Matt Burkhartt/Getty Images)

Reopening the case

Van Houten, the district attorney, said Monday that in light of the attention the case has received, he wanted to clarify why the original investigation did not result in criminal charges. He said that Jane Doe went to campus police at the time, but did not, in her initial sworn statement, make any allegations of being gang-raped or drugged.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual," he said.

The prosecutor also said the woman's attorney did not contact him about her statement or about reconsidering the decision not to prosecute.

The Ithaca Police Department said in a statement Monday it was "disturbed" to hear of the accusations, adding that the alleged incident had never been reported to them.

"The Ithaca Police Department learned of these allegations recently through the media,” it wrote.

A woman walks by a Cornell University sign on the Ivy League school's campus in January 2022. (Ted Shaffrey/The Associated Press)

'She was traumatized'

Giuffra, Jane Doe's lawyer, defended his client while blaming the university police investigation.

"In the days following the assault, she was traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode," Giuffra told CBC News.

He questioned why she wasn't contacted by the DA's office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors.

"It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she ... never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint," Giuffra added.

Multiple media now report that the seven accused men have sought legal representation. CBC News has reached out to Jeremy Saland, one of the lawyers identified, and has not yet heard back. But Saland told BBC his client denies the allegations.

His client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat," but "did nothing else," the outlet reported. Saland said his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine."

In a post on Threads Sunday, AI training company Data Annotation Tech wrote it had terminated its contract with one of the accused.

"We are deeply sorry for what happened at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 and extend our concern to everyone affected by the incident," the company posted.

"Any future reinstatement of Matthew Ingalls' contract will be considered only after the civil proceedings are concluded and the court’s findings have been reviewed."
