Final Day: Doors Close at 21:00

The fair opened on Thursday 24 September and closes today, Tuesday 29 September, with shorter hours for the finale: 13:00 to 21:00 instead of the 22:00 close of the past four days. São Paulo Expo sits on Rodovia dos Imigrantes, about 900 metres from Jabaquara metro station on Line 1 Blue.

Closing days at trade fairs are traditionally quieter than the weekend rush. For visitors who have postponed the trip, this afternoon and evening are the last chance to board the boats on display until the next edition.

The Week’s Launches: Bigger Boats, Electric Engines

Brazilian yard Real Powerboats used the show for a double premiere, presenting the new Real 38 Cabriolet and the Real 45 Fly, as documented by Revista Náutica during the weekend. The two models extend one of the country’s best-known sports-cruiser ranges upward in size and comfort.

Schaefer Yachts, Brazil’s flagship yacht builder, brought the project of the Schaefer 26M — at 26 metres the largest yacht the brand has ever designed. Victory Yachts and Wellcraft were among the other exhibitors drawing crowds with new applications of their hulls, from leisure to sport fishing.

On the technology side, engine maker Hidea debuted its first line of electric outboard motors at the show, a signal that electrification is reaching Brazil’s leisure marine market. Lanchas Coral arrived with a new configuration of its Coral 26 featuring joystick control, a handling aid that has spread from premium yachts to entry-level boats.

Beyond the hardware, the first speedboat ever owned by three-time Formula One champion Ayrton Senna anchored the special exhibitions. The display bridged the trade audience and the wider public that rarely walks a boat fair.

Angra dos Reis, on the Costa Verde between São Paulo and Rio, is where much of the boating on show this week is actually lived.

Why This Fair Matters Beyond Six Days

The Boat Show is the largest nautical event in Latin America, and its setting is part of the story: an inland metropolis hosting the trade fair of a coastal industry. São Paulo is where the money, the dealers and the buyers are — the boats themselves mostly end up elsewhere.

That elsewhere is Brazil’s 7,400-kilometre coastline, where leisure boating anchors a wider lifestyle economy of marinas, second homes and charter services. For the expat and second-home communities of Angra dos Reis and Ilhabela, this week effectively sets the industry’s catalogue for the coming season.

The fair also works as a barometer. When high-ticket leisure goods move, it signals confidence among the Brazilian households that drive the top of the consumer economy — and the density of premieres this week, from 26-metre yachts to electric outboards, suggests the trade went into the final quarter with appetite intact.

Practical Notes for the Final Day

Tickets are sold through Sympla, the official ticketing platform. Children under one metre in height enter free, though access to individual stands and boats remains at each exhibitor’s discretion and the responsibility of accompanying adults.

São Paulo Expo offers on-site parking off Rodovia dos Imigrantes, and traffic around the venue builds quickly at opening and closing times. Visitors using the metro can leave at Jabaquara station and cover the last stretch by bus, taxi or on foot.

What We Could Not Confirm

Final attendance and sales figures are not published on closing day; the organisers release them, if at all, after the event. Current ticket prices for the final day were not verifiable on official channels at the time of writing.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the São Paulo Boat Show 2026 close?

The 29th edition closes today, Tuesday 29 September 2026, at São Paulo Expo on Rodovia dos Imigrantes. Final-day hours are 13:00 to 21:00.

What were the standout launches of the 2026 show?

Real Powerboats premiered the Real 38 Cabriolet and Real 45 Fly, Schaefer Yachts presented the 26-metre Schaefer 26M project, and Hidea debuted its first electric outboard line. More than 160 models and around 30 launches were on show across the six days.

Where do I buy tickets?

Tickets are sold through Sympla, the official ticketing platform. Children under one metre tall enter free.

What is the Ayrton Senna exhibit?

The fair displays the first speedboat ever owned by three-time Formula One champion Ayrton Senna, one of the special exhibitions of this edition.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

POLITICS · PARAGUAY

Key Facts — The country Paraguay, landlocked between Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia, is governed by President Santiago Peña of the Colorado Party (ANR) until 2028.

— What happened On Sunday 4 October 2026, 5,043,154 registered voters elect mayors and councils in all 263 districts, according to the electoral court (TSJE), as of September.

— Who is involved 630 mayoral candidates and 2,832 council seats, ABC Color reported from TSJE data on 26 September. The Colorados defend 163 of 261 mayoralties won in 2021 (ABC Color).

— What it means for you Only a physical identity card, valid or expired, is accepted at the polls (TSJE). Alcohol sales stop 12 hours before voting begins, ABC Color reported.

— Still open Turnout, which was 60.55 percent in 2021, and whether the opposition can win Asunción, where one published poll favours the Colorado candidate.

Paraguay municipal elections take place on Sunday 4 October, with 5,043,154 people registered to vote in all 263 districts. The electoral court, the Tribunal Superior de Justicia Electoral (TSJE), confirmed the date and began shipping voting machines on 27 September.

What is on the ballot in the Paraguay municipal elections

According to TSJE figures reported by ABC Color and 1000 Noticias, 630 candidates are running for 263 mayoralties. Councils have 2,832 seats to fill, with an equal number of substitutes.

The court has prepared 14,711 voting tables, each with its own machine, plus 2,094 backup machines. Trucks, river boats and a standby helicopter carry them to remote districts first, then to Central department and the capital.

Mayoralties won in Paraguay's October 2021 municipal elections: Colorados 163 of 261; all other parties and alliances 98. Source: ABC Color, 17 Oct 2021; La Nación, 12 Oct 2021.

Voters mark their choice on a machine that prints a paper ballot with a chip. The paper is counted by hand at each table, and preliminary results arrive through the TREP transmission system on Sunday night.

A test for the Colorados before 2028

In 2021 the Colorado Party won 163 of the 261 mayoralties then in play, ABC Color and La Nación reported. The Liberal Party (PLRA) won 62 on its own and 15 more in alliances, by ABC Color’s count.

In the June 2026 party primaries, Honor Colorado, the faction of former president Horacio Cartes, beat rivals loyal to Mario Abdo, according to CELAG, a regional think tank. The Liberals also changed leadership: Alcides Riveros of Nuevo Liberalismo won the party presidency ahead of senator Ever Villalba, Última Hora reported.

A strong Colorado result would give Peña’s camp a stable base heading into 2028. A weak one, especially in the cities, would hand the divided opposition its first real momentum since 2023.

Asunción, the race to watch

The capital’s previous Colorado mayor, Óscar “Nenecho” Rodríguez, resigned in August 2025 amid corruption allegations, CELAG noted. The party now runs Camilo Pérez of Honor Colorado against Soledad Núñez, backed by the PLRA and allies.

A poll by Ati Snead Consultores, published by El Nacional on 17 September, gave Pérez 52.8 percent and Núñez 34.3 percent. The article did not state the sample size, fieldwork dates or margin of error, so the figures cannot be independently assessed.

Who is voting

Men make up 50.6 percent of the roll and women 49.4 percent, according to TSJE data in ABC Color. ABC Color counts about 1.36 million young voters, roughly 27 percent of the electorate.

Participation is the main unknown. In 2021 turnout was 60.55 percent, meaning almost four in ten registered voters stayed at home.

A home-voting programme will serve 599 people with severe mobility problems in 19 urban districts, ABC Color reported. For background on the country’s politics, see Paraguay Explained: The Country, Its Politics, Its Economy and What to Watch.

What Is Not Yet Known

Turnout and the count in the big cities will not be known until the TREP results arrive on Sunday night. Official district results follow in the days after.

It is also unclear how far a local result will shape the 2028 race. Party primaries for that election are expected in late 2027, and national candidacies are not yet settled.

World.title: Bolivia Food Prices Climb After Diesel Cut; Minimum Wage Now Worth About US$275
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

ECONOMY · BOLIVIA

Key Facts — The country Bolivia, 12 million people, floated its currency in June 2026 and ended fixed-price diesel on 19 September. Most food reaches markets by diesel truck.

— What happened On Monday 28 September, a La Paz mother told Unitel she needs double her old food budget. INE put August inflation at 1.10 percent, 5.02 percent over twelve months.

— The numbers The minimum wage is Bs 3,300 (about US$275) a month. Red Uno found Santa Cruz chicken at Bs 19 a kilo (about US$1.58) on 21 September, from Bs 12 (about US$1.00).

— What it means for you Bolivia food prices hit anyone paid in bolivianos; dollar earners feel little change. Fares and delivered goods also cost more.

— Still open INE publishes September inflation in early October, the first official reading after the diesel change. Wage demands of Bs 4,500 to Bs 5,000 (about US$374 to US$416) are unanswered.

Bolivia food prices are climbing faster than wages, and some families in La Paz say their market budget has roughly doubled. The complaints come ten days after the government ended cheap diesel, the fuel that moves most of the country’s food.

Official data have not yet caught the change. The national statistics institute, known as INE, put inflation at 1.10 percent in August and 5.02 percent over twelve months.

What families told reporters

Mothers shopping in La Paz markets on Monday described the squeeze to the television channel Unitel. One said Bs 200 (about US$17) used to cover her shopping. Now, she said, she sets out with almost a whole wage.

Another, feeding six people, said the household needs at least Bs 700 (about US$58) a week. A third said she now needs “double the budget”, at least Bs 500 (about US$42).

In Santa Cruz, Bolivia’s largest city, the channel Red Uno checked market prices on 21 September. Rice had risen from Bs 7 to Bs 15 a kilo (about US$0.58 to US$1.25).

A tray of eggs went from Bs 24 to Bs 30 (about US$2.00 to US$2.50), Red Uno reported. Neither channel’s check is an official price index.

What the official figures show

INE’s figures tell a calmer story so far. Consumer prices rose 3.01 percent between January and August, helped by a 2.79 percent fall in July.

Monthly change in Bolivia's consumer price index, January–August 2026; 3.01% year to date and 5.02% over twelve months. Source: INE, monthly IPC releases, Feb–Sep 2026.

August’s rise came mainly from chicken, INE said, after 53 days of road blockades delayed restocking at poultry farms. Prices eased again from the second week of the month.

September data will first show the diesel change (Bolivia Diesel Subsidy Ends: Price Rises 83% as Fuel Queues Shrink). Diesel went from Bs 9.80 to Bs 17.95 a litre (about US$0.82 to US$1.49) on 19 September.

A minimum wage worth less in dollars

The national minimum wage has been Bs 3,300 (about US$275) a month since January 2026. President Rodrigo Paz raised it from Bs 2,750 (about US$229).

At the old fixed rate of 6.96 bolivianos to the dollar, that wage was worth about US$474. The peg ended in June. The central bank (BCB) set its official rate at Bs 12.02 per US dollar on 29 September.

Pressure for a raise is building. Víctor Tarqui of the drivers’ confederation told the agency ANF on 21 September the minimum should reach Bs 4,500 (about US$374).

In Tarija, deputy Richard López of the Unidad alliance proposed Bs 5,000 (about US$416), eju.tv reported on 26 September. The government has not responded to either figure.

The case for the reform

The government says the old diesel price cost the state heavily and invited theft. “We cannot buy expensive to sell cheap so that a few can steal it,” Paz said, as quoted by Bloomberg Línea.

Fuel queues that ran for days were shrinking, Unitel reported on 20 September. In December 2025 Paz had also lifted the Renta Dignidad pension from Bs 350 to Bs 500 (about US$29 to US$42) a month, Montero Noticias reported.

Economists still expect a jump in prices. Fernando Romero, a former head of Tarija’s college of economists, told Bloomberg Línea inflation could end 2026 at 17 to 20 percent.

The official projection is 14 percent, the outlet reported, and 2025 closed at 20.4 percent. For the earlier trend, see Bolivia Inflation Slows as Boliviano Loses Value.

What Is Not Yet Known

How far Bolivia food prices rise from the diesel change stays unclear until INE publishes September data in early October. Market checks by television channels are snapshots, not a national measure.

The government has not said whether it will revisit the minimum wage. Fare talks are also open (Bolivia Transport Strike Stops Santa Cruz as Drivers Head to Diesel Talks).

Sources: Unitel (28 Sep 2026); INE (3 Sep 2026); Red Uno (21 Sep 2026); Red Uno, BCB rate (29 Sep 2026); Bloomberg Línea (22 Sep 2026); eju.tv (26 Sep 2026); ANF (21 Sep 2026); El País (Tarija) (27 Sep 2026); Montero Noticias (6 Aug 2026); Unitel (20 Sep 2026). US$ conversions at the BCB official rate of Bs 12.02 per US dollar, 29 Sep 2026. Chart: INE monthly IPC releases, January–August 2026.

World.title: OAS Draft Resolution Demands Nicaragua Revoke Its 2025–2026 Constitutional Changes
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

POLITICS · NICARAGUA

Key Facts — The country Nicaragua, run by co-presidents Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo under a 2025 constitutional reform. It left the Organization of American States (OAS) in November 2023.

— What happened On 28 September 2026 an OAS draft resolution for the foreign ministers’ meeting of 2 October was published. It demands Managua revoke constitutional changes approved in 2025 and 2026.

— Who is involved Peru presented the draft with Colombia and the United States, Divergentes and Confidencial reported on 28 September. The meeting itself was called by a 29–1 council vote on 19 August.

— What it means for you Nothing changes on the ground yet. If adopted, a ministerial group would report within 30 days and could propose coordinated diplomatic, economic and financial steps.

— Still open Whether the wording survives negotiation, whether it passes by consensus, and whether Managua engages with the proposed group at all.

An OAS draft resolution circulated on 28 September asks Nicaragua’s government to revoke the constitutional changes it approved in 2025 and 2026. Foreign ministers of the Organization of American States (OAS) meet in Washington on Friday 2 October to consider it.

The text is a draft, not a decision, and diplomats may still amend it this week to win consensus, Divergentes reported. Its title is “The situation in Nicaragua and its continued collective consideration”.

How the Meeting Was Called

The OAS Permanent Council, the body of ambassadors that runs the organisation between summits, voted on 19 August to convene the ministers. The tally was 29 in favour and one against, Divergentes and Confidencial reported.

Brazil voted against, Mexico abstained and two delegations were absent, according to Confidencial and ACI Prensa. On 23 September the council set the date as 2 October.

OAS Permanent Council vote of 19 August 2026 to convene foreign ministers on Nicaragua: 29 yes, 1 no (Brazil), 1 abstention (Mexico), 2 absent. Source: Divergentes, 19 Aug 2026; Confidencial, 23 Sep 2026; ACI Prensa, 20 Aug 2026.

A Meeting of Consultation of Ministers of Foreign Affairs is the OAS’s top political tool for a crisis. Divergentes notes it had not been used since 2019, for Venezuela.

Which Reforms the Draft Targets

The OAS draft resolution asks Managua to revoke constitutional changes approved in 2025 and 2026 and to restore the separation of powers. The 2025 reform created the co-presidency and lengthened the presidential term from five to six years.

The 2026 reform passed its first reading on 1 September. It bars people the government labels “coup plotters” from politics and would push elections to late 2028.

It still needs a second reading in January 2027; see Nicaragua Faces Blunt UN Criticism as a Reform Delays Elections to Late 2028. Ortega announced on 19 July that he intended to end competitive elections.

What Else the Text Demands

The list includes freeing all political prisoners and disclosing the whereabouts of people who have disappeared. It also seeks the return of citizenship to 452 Nicaraguans stripped of it.

Independent media, civil society groups, universities and business chambers would be allowed to reopen, and confiscated property returned. A monitoring group, cited by Confidencial, counted 68 political prisoners in a report of 25 September.

One clause asks Nicaragua to withdraw security personnel, technology and facilities from outside the hemisphere and end related defence agreements. Confidencial said the draft describes the government’s practices as a threat to hemispheric peace and security.

A Dialogue Track Alongside the Pressure

The centrepiece is a Ministerial Follow-up Group that would seek “rapid and direct dialogue” with Managua, possibly including a visit. It would report within 30 days, and the ministers could reconvene within 45.

The group could then propose gradual collective measures in the diplomatic, economic and financial fields. Former presidential hopeful Juan Sebastián Chamorro called the text “a warning”, though he expects the government to refuse.

Guillermo Belt, a former adviser to the OAS Secretariat, told Confidencial the threat language could open the door to the Rio Treaty. That 1947 pact allows collective defence measures.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is unclear whether the final text will keep the demand to revoke the reforms or the threat language. Nor is it known how Brazil and Mexico, which did not back the August vote, will act on Friday.

No public response from Managua to the draft had been reported by Tuesday morning. Attendance by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has not been confirmed.

Sources: Divergentes, 28 September 2026 (draft resolution presented by Peru); Confidencial, 28 September 2026; Confidencial, 23 September 2026 (meeting date and 19 August vote breakdown); Divergentes, 19 August 2026 (Permanent Council vote); ACI Prensa, 20 August 2026, and Diario Libre, 19 August 2026 (vote breakdown).

World.title: Quito Security Chief Carolina Andrade Resigns After Three Years in Ecuador
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

SECURITY · ECUADOR

Key Facts — The country Ecuador, a dollarised Andean economy of about 18 million people. Quito, its capital, runs its own municipal security office alongside the National Police.

— What happened Carolina Andrade, Quito’s security secretary since May 2023, has resigned. Her exit became public on 28 September 2026; she stays until 30 September (Primicias, Expreso).

— Who is involved Mayor Pabel Muñoz, who received her letter on 24 September, and Interior Minister John Reimberg, who clashed with the city over its camera network in August.

— What it means for you Nothing changes on the street this week. Policing stays with the national force; the city office handles cameras, prevention plans, fire and disaster response.

— Still open Her stated reasons and performance report, due 30 September, and who replaces her. Expreso names a likely successor from unnamed sources; the city has not confirmed.

Quito security chief Carolina Andrade has resigned after more than three years in the post, Ecuadorian media reported on 28 September. She was one of the longest-serving officials in Mayor Pabel Muñoz’s administration.

Her resignation letter cites “personal reasons” and calls the decision irrevocable, according to Expreso, which saw the document. She will stay in office until Wednesday 30 September to hand over the job.

A letter sent on 24 September

The Quito security chief informed the mayor in an official letter dated 24 September, Expreso reported. The news became public four days later, first through Primicias and then across Quito outlets, including Teleamazonas.

She took the job in May 2023, when Muñoz began his term. Her office, formally the General Secretariat for Citizen Security and Risk Management, also oversees disaster planning.

Andrade told reporters she would explain her reasons on 30 September and present a report on her tenure. Until then, only the letter’s wording is on the record.

Next stop: environmental crime in the Amazon

Andrade told Expreso her next role would be at a regional body working on environmental organised crime in the Amazon. Diario La Hora reported that the new job is based in Brazil.

Neither outlet has named the organisation. The move fits her background: before joining the city, she advised the Igarapé Institute, a Brazilian think tank, on climate and security from 2021.

She is a political scientist trained at the Sorbonne in Paris. She also once coordinated intelligence at Senain, Ecuador’s former national intelligence agency, since abolished.

The camera dispute with the national government

Her departure comes after months of friction between the city and President Daniel Noboa’s government over Quito’s surveillance cameras. The resignation letter does not mention that dispute.

On 23 June, Interior Minister John Reimberg told a National Assembly committee that municipal camera systems were being used for purposes other than public safety. He also questioned the presence of former Senain officials in those systems.

On 10 August, Reimberg said the police had taken control of Quito’s camera centre, Expreso reported. He claimed “five or six” mirror rooms were linked to the municipal system and could expose police operations.

Andrade rejected that account and said no parallel room existed. She noted the city’s monitoring centre works inside the same building as ECU-911, the national emergency service.

What she leaves behind

Primicias and Teleamazonas credit her with an agreement with the Interior Ministry to reorganise 108 community police units in the capital. That deal shows the two levels of government could still cooperate.

Her farewell letter lists the city’s security plan for 2023 to 2027 and a disaster-risk plan for 2025 to 2033. Both remain in force regardless of who takes the post.

The change lands while Ecuador remains under a national security crackdown, covered in our report on Noboa’s extended security measures. For wider background, see Ecuador Explained.

What Is Not Yet Known

The city has not named a new Quito security chief. Expreso, citing two unnamed sources, reported that Gustavo Chiriboga, head of the Metropolitan Control Agency since March 2025, is expected to take over.

That appointment is not independently confirmed. The name of Andrade’s new employer, and whether the camera dispute played any part in her exit, are also still unclear.

Sources: Primicias, 28 September 2026; Expreso (resignation letter and new role), Expreso (profile and Reimberg testimony) and Expreso (successor), 28 September 2026; Teleamazonas, 28 September 2026; Diario La Hora, as carried by Cero Latitud, 28 September 2026.

World.content:

COURTS · JAMAICA

Key Facts — The country Jamaica, where a 2022 gun law sets a mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison for certain firearm offences.

— What happened On Monday 28 September defence lawyers withdrew from all criminal courts islandwide. On Tuesday 29 September the action is limited to the Gun Courts (Gleaner, Observer).

— Who is involved The Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association of Jamaica called the action. Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Justice Minister Delroy Chuck defend the law.

— What it means for you Some criminal hearings face delay this week. The associations told members to keep handling urgent remand, emergency bail and constitutional matters.

— Still open Whether the government sets a date for amendments. The Act has a five-year review clause, and the Observer reports a review due next year.

Defence lawyers in Jamaica stayed away from criminal courts across the island on Monday 28 September. They want changes to the Jamaica Firearms Act, the 2022 law that sets 15-year minimum sentences for some gun crimes.

The action continues on Tuesday 29 September, limited to the Gun Courts. The government says it will listen but credits the law with a sharp fall in murders.
