Who called the withdrawal, and why

The Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association of Jamaica issued a joint call. Their members voted overwhelmingly to withdraw services this week, the Observer reported.

Monday’s action covered Parish Courts, Circuit Courts and Gun Courts. It followed a silent protest outside the Supreme Court in downtown Kingston on Wednesday 23 September.

A meeting with Justice Minister Delroy Chuck on Thursday 24 September ended without a timeline for amendments. The lawyers say that is why they escalated.

What the lawyers want changed in the Jamaica Firearms Act

The formal name is the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022. The associations say they do not seek to scrap its 15-year minimum.

“Nothing could be further from the truth,” King’s Counsel Peter Champagnie told a press conference on Monday. He asked that judges gain discretion to go lower in exceptional cases.

Today a judge who finds 15 years unjust must issue a certificate for the Court of Appeal to decide. Champagnie said that review takes “months and months”.

He cited a licensed gun owner in his early 60s serving 15 years for bringing in a spare part. Advocates’ Association president Tamika Harris asked that imitation guns be treated separately from real ones.

The lawyers also say the law removes the incentive to plead guilty. Champagnie said prosecutors and the Chief Justice have raised concerns about the Act too.

Cases before Jamaica's Gun Court as cited by defence lawyer Peter Champagnie KC; 2022 and 2023 not given. Source: press conference, 28 Sep 2026, via The Gleaner and Jamaica Observer.

The government’s case for the law

Holness told his Jamaica Labour Party executive on Sunday 27 September that he is open to improvements. He said the matter was discussed at length in the National Security Council.

He cited murders down 23 percent so far this year, after a 43 percent fall last year. He argued the law, policing and international partners together produced that result.

Chuck has called the Act “clearly working”, the Gleaner reported. The Observer said he has no intention to disturb the 15-year minimum.

Disputed numbers from the Gun Court

Champagnie challenged the claim that the law cut gun cases. He said the Gun Court had 508 cases in 2019 and 403 in 2021, before the Act.

By his count there were 363 in 2024 and 389 in 2025. These are his figures; court data were not published alongside them.

Both sides stress common ground. The lawyers say they back tough penalties for violent gun crime, and Holness said the review should not be adversarial.

For background, see Jamaica Explained: The Country, Its Economy, Its Politics and What to Watch. On court delays, see Trial in Killing of Jamaican MP Paulwell’s Baby Daughter Moved to 2027.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not known how many hearings were postponed on Monday. Neither the courts nor the associations had published a count as of 29 September.

It is also unclear whether lawyers will extend the action beyond Tuesday. The government has not said when a draft amendment could reach Parliament.

Sources: The Gleaner, “Bar fight”, 29 September 2026; Jamaica Observer, withdrawal of services, 28 September 2026, lawyers’ press conference and Holness on the Firearms Act review, 29 September 2026.

World.title: Who Is Costa Rica Really Competing With for Tourists?
World.content:
Costa Rica’s tourism board says the real rivals are not its neighbors. The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) places the competition in faraway destinations such as Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and New Zealand, which it considers comparable in nature and outdoor activities, rather than anywhere in Central or Latin America.

Business chambers in tourism see a much wider field. They count Panama, Colombia, Mexico and the Dominican Republic among Costa Rica’s rivals depending on the market segment, and they warn that a stronger colón has made Costa Rica noticeably more expensive for visitors.

The ICT’s position is not new as in May 2025, then-Tourism Minister William Rodríguez rejected comparisons with neighboring countries by likening Costa Rica to a luxury car that does not compete with a $15,000 or $20,000 vehicle, and he named the Maldives, Thailand, the Seychelles and Sri Lanka as the true competitors.

The institute has kept that stance under the new administration. Tourism Minister Marcos Borges has described Costa Rica as offering a unique product, while acknowledging that tourism is a highly competitive industry in which it has to stay ahead. Some data support the institute’s view. Figures from the U.S. National Travel and Tourism Office show Costa Rica has held roughly one-third of U.S. travelers to Central America, with shares of 32.1% in 2022, 33.6% in 2023, 32.7% in 2024 and 33.4% in 2025.

However, a closer look suggests growth has been less convincing. Air arrivals rose only about 1% in 2025, and the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur) contrasted that result with gains of 4% in Colombia, 5% in the Dominican Republic, 6% in Mexico and 10% in Guatemala. Costa Rica opened 2026 with double-digit growth in the first months of the year, but momentum has faded since.

Cumulative air arrivals through August were up 5.8%, and just 2.7% from the United States, as tourist numbers lag behind a fast-growing supply of rentals. Hans Pfister, president of the National Chamber of Ecotourism and Sustainable Tourism (Canaeco), said the competition depends on the segment. In wildlife ecotourism, he said, Costa Rica can go up against African safari destinations, while for regional biodiversity it competes with Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Chile.

Within Central America, Pfister said, the main rival is Panama, and on a global scale he pointed to Australia and New Zealand. Canatur, for its part, has repeatedly cited Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Colombia and Panama as benchmarks in its public statements. The disagreement reflects two different definitions of competition. The ICT measures it by similarity of product, while the chambers also weigh competition within specific segments and on the balance between price and quality.

Pfister described Costa Rica’s differentiation around nature, biodiversity and sustainability as solid, but said the advantage has narrowed as other destinations develop comparable offerings, some with the added appeal of novelty. He said value for money has become critical.

According to Pfister, stability, physical and legal security, and hospitality still justify a premium price. The limit comes, he said, when those qualities stop matching the cost of a stay and price begins to look like a competitive disadvantage rather than a premium for quality or sustainability.

That calculation has shifted quickly. The U.S. dollar averaged 648.76 colones in 2022 and 450.93 colones through August 2026, a difference of about 30%, and the dollar-colón exchange rate has hovered near record lows in recent weeks. The stronger colón hits the industry from two directions. Tourism businesses earn much of their revenue in foreign currency but pay wages, services and supplies in colones, while the same trip becomes more expensive for visitors spending dollars.

Canatur says the appreciation is affecting the operations, competitiveness and financial stability of its member companies. Canaeco has warned of significant effects on small and medium-sized businesses and of a threat to the small eco-lodge model that helped set Costa Rica apart, a strain already visible in tourism job losses tied to the strong currency.

The ICT acknowledges that exchange rates can influence how travelers perceive value and calls the rate a relevant factor in the competitive environment. It says, however, that it lacks sufficient comparative evidence to conclude that Costa Rica has lost ground to other destinations across the board.

The effect may be showing up in how long visitors stay rather than whether they come at all. According to ICT data, air travelers spent an average of $1,848 in 2025, the second-highest figure since 2006, but stayed just 10.3 nights on average, down from 12.2 in 2024 and 12.9 in 2023 and the shortest stay in 20 years.

Canatur has said higher costs may not keep tourists away but can lead them to book fewer nights, compress their itineraries or visit fewer places within the country. The figures alone do not establish cause and effect. Pfister also pointed to infrastructure, mobility and security as challenges that could weigh on competitiveness in the coming years.

The ICT itself said its main challenge for the next three to five years is ensuring that tourism growth is matched by greater service capacity, citing tourism infrastructure, connectivity and destination management. As a measure of visitor experience, the ICT pointed to results from the travel analytics firm Mabrian.

Between January and August 2026, the tool scored Costa Rica 91 out of 100 for overall perception, 88.3 for product and 93.2 for perceived safety. Costa Rica has long chosen to compete on quality rather than price, and few dispute that the country offers something distinct. Whether that distinction continues to justify a steadily rising bill will depend as much on roads, safety and public services as on beaches and rainforests.

World.title: Costa Rica Could Be Home to More Than 40,000 Fungal Species, Study Finds
World.content:
Costa Rica is known around the world for monkeys, sloths, toucans, sea turtles and an enormous variety of plants, but one of the richest forms of biodiversity we have here is much easier to overlook, growing in the soil, on fallen trees, among wet leaves and sometimes almost completely out of sight.

A major study led by researchers at the University of Costa Rica suggests the country could be home to more than 40,000 species of fungi, even though scientists have formally documented fewer than 7,000 so far, highlighting just how much remains to be discovered in a country already considered one of the world’s biodiversity hotspots.

Researchers Melissa Mardones, Julieta Carranza-Velázquez and Carlos Rojas examined 78,333 records of fungi collected in Costa Rica over roughly 170 years, using specimens stored at the University of Costa Rica, the National Herbarium and collections in other countries. Their study, published earlier this year in the scientific journal Plants, People, Planet, pulled together one of the most complete pictures yet of the country’s fungal life.

By combining those collection records with species already reported in scientific publications, the researchers raised the number of fungal species known from Costa Rica from 5,676 to 6,789, an increase of nearly 20%. The bigger finding, however, is how much may still be missing.

Scientists used several methods to estimate how many fungal species could actually exist in Costa Rica, including comparisons with the number of plants and arthropods already known and information from modern DNA-based studies. Those calculations produced estimates ranging from about 6,900 species to as many as 40,373.

That upper figure should not be confused with 40,000 species that scientists have already found and are waiting to name. Instead, it is an estimate of how large Costa Rica’s fungal population could eventually prove to be if scientists were able to search the country much more thoroughly, particularly in places where little collecting has taken place.

The existing collections make clear how incomplete that work remains. Nearly 80% of the 78,333 records had been identified only as far as their genus, meaning researchers knew the broader group the fungus belonged to but had not determined its exact species. Among the specimens identified to species level, the database contained 2,862 different species, and almost 90% of those appeared in the collections five times or fewer.

In practical terms, many Costa Rican fungi are known from only a handful of specimens collected over more than a century, making it difficult to determine whether they are genuinely rare or whether scientists simply have not spent enough time looking for them.

Where researchers have looked also makes a major difference. The southern Talamanca mountain range, the Osa Peninsula and parts of central Guanacaste are among the better-studied areas, while the Nicoya Peninsula, the Central Pacific and several forest zones along the Pacific side of the Guanacaste mountains remain poorly represented in the collections.

Those gaps mean that areas already popular with residents and tourists could contain large numbers of fungal species that have never been formally recorded, while less accessible forests may hold an even greater amount of unexplored diversity.

Costa Rica’s rainy season also appears to play an important role in when fungi become visible. Researchers found a median of 98 specimens collected per calendar day during the dry season, compared with 181 during the rainy season, when moisture creates better conditions for many fungi to produce mushrooms and other visible reproductive structures.

The researchers caution that historical collecting habits can influence those numbers, since scientists may simply have spent more time looking for fungi during wetter months, but the overall pattern remained strong enough to show a close connection between rainfall and fungal activity.

The project also tells part of the story of biological research in Costa Rica. Collections expanded slowly through much of the early 20th century, then grew dramatically between 1990 and 2015 during the years when the former National Biodiversity Institute, known as INBio, carried out extensive field work around the country. Collecting declined sharply after that period, reinforcing concerns among researchers that completing the country’s fungal inventory will require sustained funding and many more years of work.

That matters for more than simply adding new names to a list. Fungi break down dead vegetation, recycle nutrients, help trees and other plants absorb water and minerals, support healthy soils and form relationships with much of the plant life found in Costa Rica. Some species can also cause diseases in crops, while others have potential uses in medicine, agriculture and biological pest control.

Researchers say Costa Rica’s existing collections provide something else that may become increasingly valuable: a record of where fungi were found and when they appeared. By returning to the same places in future decades, scientists may be able to see whether changing temperatures, rainfall patterns, land use or other environmental pressures are altering fungal populations.

The study recommends more field work in poorly sampled regions, better identification of specimens already sitting in collections, more consistent recording of where fungi are found and the creation of a national fungal culture collection that could preserve living samples for future research.

Fungi also remain largely absent from international conservation efforts compared with mammals, birds and plants, despite their importance to forests and other ecosystems, and researchers noted that tropical fungi are particularly poorly represented in assessments such as the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List.

For a country like ours that has spent decades building its international reputation around biodiversity and conservation, the findings are a reminder that much of Costa Rica’s natural wealth may still be unknown, including thousands of species that could be growing unnoticed just beneath the forest floor.

World.title: Police investigating death threat targeting Customs chief at western border
World.content:
Police investigating death threat targeting Customs chief at western border

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are reviewing surveillance footage after a threatening message targeting a senior Customs officer was discovered at the western border on Monday morning.

Police confirmed during their press briefing that officers responded to the cargo area at the Customs Department after a piece of cloth bearing a written threat was discovered.

Investigators processed the scene and are now reviewing surveillance cameras in the area in an attempt to determine who placed the message.

The writing reportedly contained a threat and the surname of a specific individual.

Public reports identified the person targeted as Luis Betancourt, the Officer in Charge of Customs at the western border.

Police said security guards are already stationed in the area but additional security measures will now be put in place.

Investigators have not publicly identified a suspect or established a motive for the threat.

World.title: Police charge Dan Lopez with attempted murder in Alfred Mahler shooting; .223 rifle recovered
World.content:
Police charge Dan Lopez with attempted murder in Alfred Mahler shooting; .223 rifle recovered

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say Dan Lopez has been arrested and charged in connection with the shooting of Alfred Mahler in the Maya Ranch area of the Cayo District.

During Monday’s police press briefing, investigators confirmed that Lopez was charged with attempted murder, dangerous harm and use of deadly means of harm.

Police also reported recovering a .223 rifle which investigators believe was used in the shooting.

Lopez was taken before the court on Monday.

Mahler was shot last week while travelling in the Maya Ranch area. Previous reports indicated that he was struck by gunfire after a vehicle reportedly followed the vehicle in which he was travelling.

Police had earlier confirmed detaining a person and recovering a .223 rifle as part of the investigation.

The Maya Ranch area has been the subject of an ongoing land dispute involving farmers and private landowners.

The investigation into the shooting continues.

World.title: Gunmen block driver on highway, beat him with firearm and steal vehicle near Sandhill
World.content:
Gunmen block driver on highway, beat him with firearm and steal vehicle near Sandhill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are searching for two armed men accused of carjacking a motorist near Sandhill on Saturday after reportedly following him along the highway and firing shots.

According to police, a man reported that he was driving on the highway when another vehicle began following him.

He reportedly heard gunshots before the other vehicle overtook him and blocked his path, forcing him to stop.

Two armed men then exited the vehicle, struck Kumar in the head with a firearm, dragged him from his vehicle and drove away with his vehicle toward Belize City.

Police launched a search and later located both Kumar’s vehicle and the suspects’ vehicle in the Maxboro area.

Police say both vehicles were processed for evidence, but the suspects had already fled.

Investigators also confirmed that the vehicle allegedly used by the gunmen was registered to a rental company in the Cayo District.

Police are working to identify and locate the two suspects.

World.title: Four gunmen rob businessman in Independence; getaway vehicle later found at banana farm
World.content:
Four gunmen rob businessman in Independence; getaway vehicle later found at banana farm

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery in Independence in which four gunmen reportedly held up a businessman and escaped with cash, documents and a firearm.

Police say the complainant reported that he was at his business establishment on Sunday when a Kia vehicle arrived.

Four men reportedly exited the vehicle, all armed with firearms, and held him up.

The robbers allegedly stole a 9mm pistol before demanding the keys to a safe. Police say the men subsequently removed documents and an undisclosed amount of cash before fleeing the area.

No one was injured during the robbery.

The suspected getaway vehicle was later found abandoned at a banana farm in the Bella Vista area.

Police say investigators are searching for four suspects and the investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Senior police officer exchanges gunfire with suspected burglars in Ladyville; one man hospitalized
World.content:
Senior police officer exchanges gunfire with suspected burglars in Ladyville; one man hospitalized

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an attempted burglary in Ladyville that escalated into an exchange of gunfire between a senior police officer and two suspected burglars early Sunday morning.

The incident occurred at around 4:00 a.m. on Compassion Lane, where a senior officer reportedly responded after being alerted to a burglary in progress.

Police say the officer encountered two men armed with crowbars who appeared to be attempting to pry open burglar bars, a door and a window at a residence.

The officer reportedly ordered the men to stop, but police say one of them fired shots in his direction. The officer took cover and returned fire.

A short time later, Deon Grant of Belize City arrived at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital suffering from gunshot injuries. Police say Grant is suspected of being involved in the incident and remained hospitalized in stable condition at the time of the briefing.

Scenes of Crime personnel recovered crowbars and several expended shells from the area, while damage was observed on the home’s window and door.

Police say no surveillance cameras have yet been located in the immediate area and the investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Police reviewing surveillance footage in murder of Dangriga basketball player Antonio Flowers
World.content:
Police reviewing surveillance footage in murder of Dangriga basketball player Antonio Flowers

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say investigators are reviewing surveillance footage as they seek to identify the gunman who shot and killed 25-year-old Antonio Flowers in Belize City on Sunday night.

Flowers, also known as “Tonio,” was walking in the Antelope Street area at around 9:30 p.m. on September 27 when police say he was followed by a man who pulled out a firearm and fired several shots in his direction.

Flowers was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

Police confirmed during Monday’s press briefing that Flowers was known to police and had previously been dealt with in connection with criminal matters. Investigators have not disclosed a motive for the killing.

Flowers was originally from Dangriga and had family in the Antelope Street area.

Flowers was also involved in basketball. Previous reporting identified him as a player with the Dangriga Dream Ballers.

Police say surveillance cameras in the area are now being reviewed in an effort to identify a suspect.

World.title: Vega’s delivery truck overturns on Santander road
World.content:
Vega’s delivery truck overturns on Santander road

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Vega’s delivery truck overturned on the Santander road this afternoon.

Photos from the scene show the white truck lying on its side off the roadway, with its cargo spilled across the roadside and into the bushes. Boxes, packs of toilet paper and other goods can be seen scattered around the vehicle.

People were seen at the scene gathering and sorting through the spilled items.

There is no word yet on what caused the truck to overturn or whether anyone was injured.

BBN will update as more information becomes available.

World.title: New STEAM pavilion coming soon for Bishop Martin High School
World.content:
New STEAM pavilion coming soon for Bishop Martin High School

By Zoila Palma: Ground was officially broken today for a new STEAM Pavilion at Bishop Martin High School in Orange Walk Town, aimed at expanding opportunities for students in science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics.

The new facility will feature a fully equipped science laboratory, an engineering makerspace and a modern recording studio, providing students with spaces to develop practical and creative skills.

The project is supported through a national partnership between the Government of Belize, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Global Partnership for Education through the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology’s Skills for the Future Program.

World.title: ‘We are not breaking ranks’
World.content:
TWO defence lawyers representing murder accused Andre Ruddock appeared in court on Monday as his trial continued, despite colleagues maintaining a pledge to withdraw legal services from all criminal matters islandwide in pursuit of amendments to the Firearms Prohibition Restriction and Regulation Act 2022.

But according to attorney Anthony Williams, he and fellow counsel Venice Brown did not break ranks with their colleagues. Instead they had a duty to their client which had to be fulfilled.

“We want to make it very clear that we are not breaking ranks with our colleagues. Myself and Miss Brown are 150 per cent in support of our colleagues. However, there is a difference — the Jamaica Bar Association knows about it and they also sanctioned it. The difference is that when you are in a part-heard matter you can’t just go and strike like that. You have to seek the permission of your client in writing,” Williams told the Jamaica Observer.

“If you don’t seek the permission of your client in writing, then you can be deemed to have neglected your client and you can be sanctioned as well. Also, the court can proceed with the matter and the judge can possibly cite you for contempt of court,” Williams explained.

He added that in the absence of defence attorneys a judge may decide to proceed in a part-heard matter because lawyers are expected to be present. He said that if they don’t turn up, they do so at their own peril.

“The situation is different when you are in a part-heard matter, and the lawyer, whoever he or she is, cannot just abandon their client just like that; they have to seek the client’s permission. And in this particular case our client said, ‘Run with it.’ There are many other lawyers who are in the same position, but we have not abandoned our colleagues,” Williams stressed.

In addition to Williams and Brown, a number of attorneys showed up for their clients on Monday at the Home Circuit Court for various reasons, including that some were not in agreement with the protest action.

Essentially, the defence lawyers are arguing that the Act removes discretionary powers from judges, as it mandates a 15-year minimum sentence for an illegal gun possession conviction.

Williams’ client, Ruddock, is being tried in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner in what has been described as a human sacrifice ritual at Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion St James. Ruddock allegedly cut Gardner’s throat on the instruction of his now deceased pastor, Kevin Smith.

Smith died in a car crash in St Catherine a few days later while being transported to Kingston to be charged with the incident.

On Monday the fourth witness in the case, a police sergeant based in St James, returned to complete his testimony which he started last week.

He described the scene at the church as “evil, fluid and chaotic”.

“People were moving from one direction to the next. One body was seen close to the pool area,” the witness recalled.

He explained that members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) made their way through barbed wires to gain access to the compound of the church where three people, including Gardner and two male members of the church, lay dead.

One of the men was allegedly killed by Smith, while the police were said to have shot dead the other man who had rushed toward them with a knife. Based on the sustained gunfire and the sacrificial-type activities that were taking place at the church, the security forces had to call for adequate back-up, which included support from the military.

“The soldiers got to the barbed wire. I saw them climbing over and onto the church premises. On reaching the premises I shouted out to them. Police, accompanied by army personnel, proceeded towards a person who was kneeling behind the column at the entrance gate. I observed them accosting this person. They arrested him and carried out a search of him. The police and soldiers then forced open the big entrance gate,” the witness said.

“When they got there, the man was still in the kneeling position with white cloth over his head. He stood up and the officers searched him. When he stood up, from where I was standing [on the roof] I couldn’t see his face. I could only see the height of the person who was about 5 feet two or three inches tall. At that time there were a lot of police personnel and soldiers around this man. They took him on[to] the roadway and I couldn’t see what took place from there,” the witness said, without being able to say who the man was.

World.title: Debutants Tru-Juice remaining calm despite table-topping JPL start
World.content:
Tru-Juice FC striker Daniel Roberts celebrates after scoring the winning goal in the club’s 1-0 victory over Molynes United in the Jamaica Premier League at Stadium East on Sunday. (Photo: JPL)

DESPITE Tru-Juice FC’s strong start to their debut Jamaica Premier League (JPL) season, Assistant Coach Craig Richards says it’s too early to be thinking about the play-offs.

The newly promoted club lead the JPL stadings on seven points after a 1-0 win over Molynes United at Stadium East on Sunday. Striker Daniel Roberts’s 62nd-minute strike was enough as Tru-Juice stay unbeaten after their first three games. They also join Montego Bay United and Waterhouse as the only two clubs who have yet to concede.

Richards says he was pleased with the team’s execution, after nearly a week of preparation.

“We knew that it was going to be a tough-fought game. We know how the Molynes team plays and we’ve been training all week to nullify them — and we also worked on ways to hurt them and it paid dividends,” he said.

“When we play against certain teams, we really assess them and train accordingly, so I’m very pleased. There are parts of the game that I’m disappointed with but there are aspects that I’m very pleased [about], and that’s football. I’m pleased we got three points on the board, and we look forward to the next game.”

Tru-Juice have attracted several top players to join their inaugural season, including Reggae Boyz Alex Marshall, Gadail Irving, and Tafari Chambers.

The Linstead based-club caught the eyes of many during their opening game when they thrashed reigning Caribbean Cup champions Mount Pleasant FA 4-0 and held last season’s semi-finalists, Montego Bay United, to a goalless draw.

Although starting on a positive note, Richards says they’re not placing too much pressure on themselves.

“Our objective is to play quality football and maximise on the points and [see] wherever that leads us,” he said. “Our aim is to compete. And competing can lead us to good places but as it relates to [the] objective [of] top six or whatever, if that should come then we are very welcoming for that but for now we’re taking it three games at a time.

“This is our first season. There are quite a number of teams that have been competing in this competition for some time so they have some experience. While we have experienced players, the club itself is in its first season so we continue to set different objectives at different points of the season, and we’ll see where that leads us.”

Mount Pleasant Head Coach Theodore Whitmore was pleased his team got off the mark after their 2-0 win over Dunbeholden at the Dunbeholden Sports Complex.

After losing their first two games of the season, goals from Trayvone Reid and Nicholas Nelson ensured the St Ann-based club picked up all three points.

“It doesn’t feel like three, it feels like six points,” Whitmore said. “I think we would have met our objective when we got two goals this afternoon; we didn’t concede, we kept a clean sheet, so I think it’s something that we can build on.

“When you look at the table and see Mount Peasant at the foot, nobody expects that. It wasn’t pleasing even for the fans that travel with us every Sunday, so it’s very pleasing [to beat Dunbeholden]. We look forward to the next one; and it gives us now a momentum going into the next game and into the semi-final of the Caribbean Cup.”

Sunday’s results

Molynes 0, Tru-Juice 1

Dunbeholden 0, Mount Pleasant 2

Portmore United 4, Humble Lion 1

Cavalier 3, Arnett Gardens 2

Racing United 0, Mobay United 1

Waterhouse 2, Treasure Beach 0

Tivoli 1, Phoenix Chapelton 1

World.title: ALL THE KING’S MEN
World.content:
Hunain Shah (second right) of Jamaica Kingsmen celebrates with teammates (from left) Keemo Paul, Andre Russell, and Vitel Lawes after getting the wicket of Roston Chase during their Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League T20 match with St Lucia Kings in Gros Islet, St Lucia, on Friday, August 21. (PHOTO: CPLT20)

JAMAICA Kingsmen Head of Operations Atishai Mansingh says a strong collective effort will be needed to continue cricket’s revival on the island.

The Kingsmen finished runners-up of the recently concluded Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL), after losing to the Antigua and Barbuda Falcons in the final in Barbados.

It was a remarkable run for the Jamaican franchise in their first season as the Kingsmen, having been inactive for the 2024 and 2025 seasons after former owner Kris Persaud sold the franchise and moved on to the now-champions Falcons.

This season also saw the return of CPL to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019, with four games hosted in Kingston.

While pleased with the franchise’s start, Mansingh says he’s focused on helping to grow the sport locally.

“CPL coming back is not going to solve all of the issues that we have in Jamaica cricket,” he said. “It’s a spark, and what we do with that spark is what will determine whether this moment becomes a temporary celebration or the beginning of a genuine revival — and the revival is going to start from the top down.

“We want to encourage all of public and corporate Jamaica to see the highest-paying sport for what it is. The fact is, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park this year, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park next year, but we have to work towards filling Sabina Park in the years coming, because if this park is seen as a football park, as an entertainment park, for the history that it holds, every single one of us are failing. Filling Sabina Park is not about the Kingsmen putting on social media s and giving away tickets. It’s about the teamwork [and] the support which is needed to to build these cricket structures in Jamaica.”

Mansingh says cricket’s development locally cannot be driven solely by finances but must also be fuelled by passion for the sport.

“Players cannot rebuild it alone. The Government and sponsors, though we always request them, also cannot build it alone. Clubs, schools, families, businesses and supporters must all play a part,” he said.

“If we don’t put the love into the sport, who’s going to? [People] say, ‘Who’s going to fix cricket?’ ‘CPL come, they have money, they’re going to fix it’, ‘This person have money so they’re going to fix it’. Money is not going to fix this; it’s the love that we all possess for the sport that’s going to bring the happiness back to the sport.”

Mansingh says more emphasis needs to be placed on women’s cricket as well, with the debut of the Jamaica Empress team in the Women’s CPL providing a good starting point.

“Cricket is not just about a man with a ball and a man with a bat,” he said. “The women are equally important for this sport’s growth. The Kingsmen launched the first-ever Jamaica women’s CPL franchise, the Jamaica Empress. It has given an opportunity to women to see the sport as a way of employment. A sport that was always seen as a gentleman’s sport has now been seen as just simply a sport.

“That is very crucial, because when the likes of Hayley Matthews, Stafanie Taylor, Chinelle Henry are able to go to tournaments across the world and earn US$250,000 [$38 million] for a six-week tournament, that is eye-opening to state that this sport is not just going to fill the pockets of men any more but it’s going to create structures and systems for young girls to say, ‘I want to be like them when I’m older.’ ”

World.title: Wolmer’s Boys student dies after collapsing during class
World.content:
Wolmer's Boys School Gate file photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — A fourth-form Wolmer’s Boys High School student has died following a medical emergency at the school on Monday, the school has confirmed.

In a statement, the Wolmer’s Joint Board of Management indicated that the student collapsed during class and was rushed to hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

The board expressed profound sorrow at the passing of the young man, describing it as a deeply painful loss for his family and for the entire Wolmer’s community.

“The Joint Board extends its heartfelt condolences to his parents, relatives, friends, classmates, teachers and all whose lives he touched,” the statement read.

The school said it is providing support to affected students and members of staff and urged the public to refrain from circulating unverified information concerning the circumstances of his passing.

World.title: Lt Stitchie, dancehall icon who found new calling in gospel, dies at 60
World.content:
Lieutenant Stitchie (Photo via Instagram)

Veteran deejay Lieutenant Stitchie has died.

Observer Online understands that the entertainer, whose given name was Cleveland “Cleve” Laing, died at hospital on Monday, just one day before he would have celebrated his 61st birthday.

The tragic news comes less than 24 hours after the entertainer’s wife, Sophia Laing confirmed that he had been hospitalised with a low blood count and was receiving treatment at the Kingston Public Hospital.

READ: Lt Stitchie hospitalised with ‘low blood count’

The pioneering dancehall entertainer whose career spanned the formative years of the genre before he made a transition to gospel music, had been ailing for some time. His health issued stemmed largely from a debilitating stroke in the first week of September 2024.

Stitchie emerged from the competitive sound-system culture of Spanish Town in the early 1980s, working alongside figures including Papa San, Wickerman and Major Worries. His breakthrough came in 1986 with the humorous Wear Yuh Size, followed by Natty Dread, before his career expanded internationally with a recording deal with Atlantic Records in 1988.

But perhaps the most defining chapter of Stitchie’s life came when he left secular dancehall behind and devoted himself to ministry after becoming a born-again Christian in 1997. He subsequently built a thriving career in gospel reggae as his transition did little to diminish the respect he commanded within the wider entertainment fraternity.

His death is expected to reverberate across both communities, with artistes who shared stages, sound systems and recording studios with him likely to reflect on the contribution of a man who managed to reinvent himself without losing his place in Jamaican music history.

World.title: Jamaica has second-longest work week in the Americas, longest in Caribbean — report
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica has been listed as the country with the second-longest average work week in the Americas and the longest in the Caribbean for 2026, according to a report shared by the World Population Review.

Eclipsed only by 28th-placed Honduras, whose population works an average of 44.20 hours per week, Jamaica placed 35th on the list, with locals working an average of 43.45 hours per week.

Men put in slightly more time than women, with their average listed as 44.55 and women at 42.14 hours per week.

Guyana was directly below Jamaica in 36th spot, with its population spending an average of 43.29 hours at work per week; far down the list at 61, with an average of 41.46 hours per week, was Haiti.

The three countries outpaced the global average of 38.67 hours per week.

The report, which relies on data collected by the International Labour Organization (ILO), noted that higher-income countries with a cultural emphasis on work/life balance generally have shorter official work weeks compared to countries with longer work weeks and rank higher on the world’s happiest countries list.

In contrast, countries with a longer work week, while often ranking as hard-working countries, usually have fewer worker protections, reduced amenities and a populace that is less happy and possibly overworked.

The Caribbean country with the shortest average work week was Barbados, with 34.47 hours per week on average.

With a 31.86-hour weekly average, Canadian citizens were listed as having the shortest work week in the region of the Americas, while the shortest globally was Yemen at an average of 22.95 hours per week.

World.title: Jamaica welcomes first cohort of Ghanaian healthcare workers
World.content:
Forty-three Ghanaian specialist nurses arrived in Jamaica.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica on Monday welcomed the first cohort of Ghanaian healthcare workers as part of ongoing efforts to strengthen the country’s healthcare workforce and support the delivery of quality healthcare services.

The majority of the 43 nurses will be assigned to the Western Regional Health Authority (WRHA), which manages health facilities in St James, Westmoreland, Trelawny and Hanover and the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), which oversees Kingston & St Andrew, St Thomas and St Catherine.

The nurses, who are specialists in various areas, including critical care, paediatrics, operating theatre, nurse/midwife, emergency, oncology and mental health/psychiatric, will also serve in the other two health regions and at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI).

Their arrival follows the signing of a Bilateral Health Cooperation agreement between the two countries earlier this year, which aims to place 400 healthcare workers in Jamaica.

“We warmly welcome the Ghanaian nurses and look forward to the valuable contribution they will make to our health system and the people we serve. This is not only in keeping with our Vision for Health 2030 plan but is fully aligned with the Ministry of Health & Wellness Jamaica’s Human Resource for Health (HRH) Stabilisation Strategy,” said Minister of Health & Wellness, Dr Christopher Tufton in a statement on Monday.

The ministry said the four-year agreement between Jamaica and Ghana has established a structured framework for the voluntary recruitment and temporary deployment of Ghanaian health professionals, particularly nurses and doctors, to support Jamaica’s healthcare system while promoting bilateral cooperation and ethical international recruitment practices.

It added that Jamaica and Ghana will further strengthen their partnership in health through additional technical cooperation in areas such as primary care reform, national health insurance and management of non-communicable diseases, among others.

World.title: Defence attorneys to withdraw services from courts islandwide Monday
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Following unsuccessful discussions with the Ministry of Justice, defence attorneys have been directed to withdraw legal services from all criminal courts islandwide on Monday as clashes over minimum mandatory sentences in the Firearms Prohibition Restriction and Regulation Act 2022 continue.

The action is expected to affect Parish Courts, Circuit Courts and Gun Courts.

Another day of industrial action, specifically targeting the Gun Courts, is scheduled on Tuesday.

A joint statement from the Jamaican Bar Association (Jambar) and Advocates Association of Jamaica (AAJ) indicated that members had voted overwhelmingly in favour of withdrawing legal services this week.

The vote followed a silent protest on Thursday in front of the Supreme Court in downtown Kingston by association members, where they lobbied for a review of the mandatory minimum sentences applied to certain gun crimes in the 2022 law.

READ: Lawyers protest mandatory minimum sentences under Firearms Act

Maintaining that the legal fraternity does not oppose stringent measures against violent gun crime, it emphasised that the legislation as currently constructed contains structural gaps and rigid mechanics that undermine the broader legal framework.

They described “significant shortcomings, gaps and statutory weaknesses” impacting the justice system, including what the attorneys describe as the erosion of judicial discretion, the dismantling of guilty plea incentives and the practical friction with statutory sentencing discount frameworks.

A meeting was held with Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Delroy Chuck on Thursday to address the issues, but the lawyers say those discussions concluded without any definitive legislative timeline to address their concerns.

READ: Chuck to meet with protesting lawyers over Firearms Act discontent

The associations, however, urged attorneys to manage urgent remand list matters, emergency bail applications involving juveniles or vulnerable persons, and time-sensitive constitutional applications in a manner that ensures no client’s fundamental rights are prejudiced during this period.

The associations say they are again calling for urgent and meaningful legislative amendments to ensure the justice system functions efficiently for all Jamaicans.

World.title: EU’s net payers insist on ‘several hundred billion euros’ in budget cuts
World.content:
However, many net contributors — those who pay in more than they get out — want their bills cut. Others, including those who stand to gain most from the funding, want to see spending increased.

"Our six countries alone finance almost 40% of all Member States’ contributions. While net contributors as a whole are in the minority, they shoulder around three-quarters of the total financing burden," the letter reads. A 60% nominal increase in the size of the budget compared to the current one, they argue, is "simply not realistic."

In a bid to lessen the financial pressure on national capitals, the Commission wants to create new powers to raise revenue directly through bloc-wide taxes (known as own resources), with e-cigarettes, vapes and cryptocurrency transactions all being considered. That, however, has not satisfied more frugal nations.

"The EU budget is ultimately paid for by European citizens. That remains true whatever financing mechanism or own resources we invent," the letter cautions.

The Irish presidency is due to present a new negobox — a detailed breakdown of the proposed budget with fresh figures — in the coming days. Leaders will then hold talks over its content at a two-day summit in Brussels from Oct. 15.

Negotiators are eager to get a deal by the end of the year to ensure the budget is in place when the current one expires, and to prevent discussions being roiled by national elections in France, Poland and other countries.

World.title: EU weighs axing exam board
World.content:
The European Personnel Selection Office, created in 2002, is the gateway for EU civil servants and designed to pick the best and brightest from thousands of applicants. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images

The European Personnel Selection Office is under growing scrutiny amid high-profile failures and accusations of no longer being fit for purpose.

BRUSSELS — The European Commission is considering major changes to its civil service exam board amid a budget squeeze and growing criticism — including possibly scrapping it, two EU officials told POLITICO Brussels Playbook.

The European Personnel Selection Office, created in 2002, is the gateway for EU civil servants and designed to pick the best and brightest from thousands of applicants. But it’s under increasing scrutiny amid high-profile failures and the fact that the EU has fewer jobs to offer due to pressure on its long-term budget.

One scenario is simply to “get rid of EPSO,” said an EU official involved in the thinking about reforms, granted anonymity to speak about the plans. The last open hiring round — which drew a record 174,922 applicants — proved “completely unmanageable,” the official said, adding that “the cost of administering this sort of mass exam is out of proportion to what we get out of it.”

World.title: What does Andy Burnham have to prove today?
World.content:
It’s the new prime minister’s big day in Liverpool – but will he explain what Labour conference slogan “hope again” actually means?

After a series of major speeches with little substance so far from his cabinet colleagues, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy wonder whether Andy Burnham is saving all the juicy details for himself.

Could there be some policy surprises – with the pensions triple lock seemingly on the table?

And with Reform inching back ahead in the latest polling, the duo ask who Labour views as their main opponent heading into the next election: Reform or the Conservatives?

Plus, Sam has a scoop on the PM’s latest plans to bring back drinking at the footie.

Remember, Politics At Sam And Anne’s will be back later with a special de-brief edition on the Burnham speech.

World.title: Gastein health conference gets underway
World.content:
Welcome to Tuesday’s Morning Health Care! It’s the first day of Gastein and Claudia and I will be here all week, so we’re going to need gossip to survive. There are rumors about a place where people dance in a cage to let their hair down; if you know anything, do tell. What happens in Gastein …

Get in touch: [email protected], [email protected]. 

DRIVING THE DAY

A LITTLE LESS CONVERSATION, A LITTLE MORE ACTION: The slow implementation and inefficiency of health policy across Europe is hampering the bloc’s ability to respond to major challenges like climate change, health security, AI and workforce issues, says Clemens Martin Auer, the president of the European Health Forum Gastein. Europe doesn’t have a lack of ideas or technical skills to tackle major problems facing the sector, but rather an implementation problem, he told Morning Health Care in an interview ahead of his last conference as head of the forum, with his final day on Oct. 31. “The older I get, the more impatient I am with the slowness of our policy implementations,” he said.

More action needed: As health experts, industry representatives, and everyone in between descend on Gastein, Austria, for a four-day health conference, Auer is calling for more action. “We are living in really challenging times, and my observation is that we don't do enough to change the situation.”

Pharma: Capricious U.S. health policies, including a push by the Trump administration to reduce domestic drug prices (more on this below), were creating global uncertainty and impacting where drugmakers were investing, Auer said, pointing to increasing investment in China. Health systems in Europe could only be counterbalanced if countries were willing to pay more for products like generics to shore up supply chains, he said. “If you want to safeguard that supply, then you have to be willing to pay more for them.” His comments come as the pharma industry is set to play a major role at the conference across multiple panels, with U.S. policies and European drug prices running as an undercurrent in most major discussions on health security, accessibility, and competitiveness.

Competitiveness: Auer pointed to the Draghi report, which proposed a plan to increase competitiveness more than two years ago. “ Do we see any implementation, substantial implementation? The economic numbers and data are getting worse.”

World.title: Trump, diesel and Europe’s new energy squeeze
World.content:
Another surge in energy prices risks making life even more expensive for Europeans — especially once winter rolls around.

So when EU energy ministers meet in Dublin today, affordability will be at the top of their agenda. On the show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss just how bad the price spike is and how the cost of gas could play out at ballot boxes across Europe.

Next, what does it take to ensure people who want to live in the countryside can stay in the countryside? We discuss the Commission’s “Right to Stay” initiative, which aims to help people stay in rural areas rather than leaving to the big cities for better jobs, schools and services.

And finally, the Commission is considering big changes to EPSO: that’s the body that runs competitions for permanent EU jobs. The system is slow, costly and was described by one insider as “completely unmanageable.”

Have you applied for an EU job via EPSO? What was your experience like? Let us know on our WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: Brits want to get closer to the EU — and even Farage’s voters agree
World.content:
“The public now often looks to Europe for overseas alliances, particularly as the U.S. is increasingly perceived as at best unreliable and at worst adversarial,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at public research company Public First, which conducted the poll for POLITICO. “But it’s not straightforward for the government. ‘Getting closer with Europe’ is not the same as ‘reversing Brexit,’ and Burnham will have a challenging needle to thread to appease his pro-European wings without reopening wounds the public would prefer stayed closed.”

The Brexit referendum a decade ago divided the country, cost two prime ministers their jobs and triggered often bad-tempered divorce negotiations between London and Brussels that took years to complete.

Public First asked respondents for their views on moving the country closer to the EU and accepting EU rules. Some 31% said Britain should build a “closer” relationship with Brussels, but only if it did not mean complying with the EU’s rulebook. But 39% wanted “much closer” cooperation even if that did require the U.K. to follow some EU rules again.

The poll also confirms how the Brexit debate has carved the country into two blocs — pro and anti. Supporters of parties on the left were far more likely to back a closer EU relationship than those on the right. Green Party voters were the keenest of all: 64% said they’d support much closer EU ties even if that meant applying more EU rules. Older voters were less keen on closer ties to Brussels.

Among Reform UK voters, 51% said they want a closer relationship — twice the 25% who want more distance from the EU. That poses a potential challenge for party leader Farage, a career Euroskeptic. The finding could also provide ammunition for Labour politicians who want Burnham to be more ambitious about his plans to upgrade the U.K.-EU relationship, potentially including a return to the bloc’s customs union, single market or even full EU membership again.

As Burnham prepared to deliver his Tuesday speech to party members and activists in Liverpool, a succession of ministers and others gave their views about what kind of closer relationship with the EU he should pursue.

World.title: Mélenchon’s plan to beat the far right: Grab the first-time voters
World.content:
But polls show the plan is working at the moment.

A survey conducted by Cluster17 exclusively for POLITICO last week had Mélenchon tied for second place with center-right candidate Edouard Philippe at 19%. And a Harris Interactive poll released Monday showed the pugnacious former teacher at 18% — against 16% for Philippe. Le Pen remained well ahead of the pack in both surveys, receiving more than 30% of the vote.

The Cluster17 poll showed 47% of respondents younger than 35 backed Mélenchon. That’s more than twice the 22% that Le Pen, who placed second among that demographic, was seen receiving.

Strategists from Mélenchon’s party, France Unbowed, told POLITICO that they believe young voters, working-class citizens and those with immigrant roots will be motivated to head to the polls for the first time to back their champion given his platform.

Mélenchon is the only leading candidate accusing the French state of pushing systemic racism and Islamophobia and denouncing police brutality. He is Israel’s most vocal critic on the French political stage. And he has promised ambitious policies to tackle climate change, including shifting towards 100% renewable energy.

Road to the second round

France Unbowed points to the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis — a former home of French royalty, now one of the capital region’s poorest suburbs and home to a large working-class population, many of them of immigrant descent — as potential proof of concept.

World.title: Send rejected asylum-seekers out of EU ASAP, urges Greek minister
World.content:
Plevris emphasized that the plan does not entail establishing return facilities but rather designates return countries. “We’re not talking about centers, in the sense that someone whose asylum is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country,” he said. “If your asylum has been rejected, you will either return to your country of origin or to a third country outside the EU.”

According to two EU diplomats familiar with the issue who were granted anonymity to discuss the matter freely, the first deal will be with Rwanda. Uganda and Uzbekistan are also reportedly under discussion as possible return countries.

Plevris said the countries under consideration already have large migrant populations and camps to accommodate them, adding that the Core Group nations “are open to whatever framework the countries there want — whether they want to talk about camps, or broader integration programs.”

Rwanda has been at the center of various offshore migration plans. In 2022, the U.K. announced a controversial multimillion-pound deal with Kigali to deport asylum-seekers to the country to have their claims processed. The scheme was abandoned after years of legal challenges.

The timetable proposed by Plevris might be ambitious, given that several crucial elements of the agreement remain up in the air. The minister said members of the Core Group are currently in discussions with international organizations to establish monitoring processes that would ensure human rights are respected in third countries to which migrants will be deported.

“Obviously, we’re not going to transfer this authority elsewhere,” he added. “We want to have the expertise and the presence of international organizations, but the responsibility lies with the five countries, jointly.”

World.title: Sabotage halts Syria gas pipeline in latest attack on energy sector
World.content:
An apparent explosion on an eastern gas pipeline in Syria halted gas flow to power stations in the latest act of sabotage against the Mediterranean country's energy facilities, authorities said Tuesday.

 

"A fire broke out Monday evening in a gas pipeline between the Al-Shoula area and Deir ez-Zor due to the explosion of a sectional valve caused by sabotage," the official SANA news agency reported.

Quoting an official at the Syrian Petroleum Company, SANA added that "the fire halted gas flow from the Al-Jabsah plant to power stations".

It remains unclear who was behind the sabotage at this time.

Eastern Syria's Deir ez-Zor province, home to the country's main oil and gas fields, has seen persistent attacks since the so-called Islamic State terrorist group's defeat in 2019.

IS group remnants regularly target energy infrastructure in the region in asymmetrical attacks meant to subvert Damascus' push to fully secure its energy logistics.

A gas pipeline at the same facility was struck in what Syrian authorities also described as deliberate sabotage on 18 August.

Syrians across the country have been complaining about rising fuel prices, as authorities cite the Iran war as the reason for the hike.

Earlier this month, Syrians across the country took to the streets to protest the price increase.

Before the 2011-2024 war, which ravaged the country's infrastructure, Syria produced 30 million cubic metres of gas per day for electricity generation, according to Energy Minister Mohammad al-Bashir.

Today, production has dropped to 8.5 million cubic metres, while demand ranges between 22 and 25 million cubic metres, according to al-Bashir.

In June, Damascus signed a contract with US oil giant ConocoPhillips to develop the country's gas sector as the new authorities, who toppled longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad in 2024, seek to attract investment to support post-war reconstruction.

The Al-Jabsah facility is one of Syria's main gas processing plants, located in an area that was returned to the central government's full control earlier this year.

World.title: UK's biggest AI supercomputer may have to wait until 2030s for enough power
World.content:
The launch of the United Kingdom’s largest planned AI supercomputer, due to open next year, could be delayed until the 2030s because of problems securing enough electricity.

 

The project was announced as part of the first tech deal between the United Kingdom and the United States, as Britain pushes to expand its artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

The site is being developed in Loughton, east of London, by UK-based start-up Nscale, which counts US chipmaker Nvidia among its investors.

In 2025, Nscale announced plans to install around 23,000 Nvidia AI chips in the data centre and link them together to form what it says will be the UK’s largest AI supercomputer. That computing power is intended to support Microsoft’s Azure cloud services.

However, UK Power Networks (UKPN), the company that will connect the site to the local power grid, has told Nscale that the grid will not be able to supply enough electricity to the site until the early to mid-2030s, according to UK AI industry newsletter The Morning Intelligence.

In an interview with the newsletter, UKPN pointed to work needed on the wider national transmission network.

National Grid, which maintains that network in England and Wales, said it was working with the national system operator NESO and local network operators to speed up connections.

Nscale is looking at generating power on-site and is speaking to UK Power Networks about ways to accelerate the connection, the Morning Intelligence added.

Soaring data centre electricity consumption in Europe

The UK start-up says the data centre could eventually expand from 50 to 90 megawatts of power — enough, if used continuously, to consume as much electricity in a year as about 315,000 typical UK homes, based on 2026 figures from UK energy regulator Ofgem.

The Loughton site is part of Nscale’s wider plan to install nearly 59,000 Nvidia AI chips across data centres in the UK.

Across Europe, demand for data centres is growing while authorities are tightening rules for new data centres amid growing pressure on electricity grids.

Data centre electricity consumption across Europe is projected to rise from 96 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 236 terawatt-hours by 2035, according to UK-based energy think tank Ember.

Earlier this month, Scotland halted new hyperscale AI data centre approvals amid concerns over whether the country’s energy grid can cope with rapidly rising demand.

Amsterdam has restricted new data centres and expansions over concerns about space and power, while a bill proposed by Denmark’s government in August would give large electricity users, including data centres, a lower priority for grid connections.
