World.title: North Korean landmine blasts in DMZ a 'violation of armistice,' Seoul says
World.content:
The blasts that wounded three South Korean soldiers last week were apparently caused by North Korean mines, Seoul said on Tuesday, adding it was an armistice violation that would prompt "corresponding measures."

 

One troop lost a foot due to the explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer zone that has divided the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.

The northern and southern boundaries of the zone are among the world's most heavily fortified frontiers and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.

Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul's comments came a day after his ministry said North Korean mines were "highly suspected" of causing the two explosions last week.

"This is a clear violation of the armistice agreement and since North Korea bears responsibility, we will take corresponding measures," he told a parliamentary hearing, when asked whether the military had tentatively concluded that the mine was North Korean.

Kang said South Korean forces were in the DMZ to clear the area in advance of an operation with the UN Command to assess terrain changes caused by North Korean forces south of the Military Demarcation Line, which marks the nations' effective border.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un meets soldiers who took part in a training in North Korea, 13 March, 2024 AP Photo

The mine detectors used by the officials were the "latest models," the minister said, but detection efforts were hampered by dense vegetation in the area, noting that "clearing all the vegetation as they advanced was difficult."

"Our current assessment is that the mines may not have been detected because the detectors were being operated too far above the ground," he said.

At the hearing, Yang Jin-hyeok of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told lawmakers that a site investigation earlier on Tuesday discovered an unexploded North Korean plastic anti-personnel mine.

Kang told lawmakers the military "has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages", without giving details.

Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war since the Korean conflict ended in a truce, not a peace treaty.

'Principal enemy'

Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, said on Monday that two landmines exploded during the 21 September incident and that a third, unexploded mine was found while soldiers were withdrawing after the blast.

"Taking into account the crater and the pattern of the flames from the explosion, the extent of the injuries sustained by the service members...we assess that North Korean landmines are highly suspected to have caused the blast," Kwon said at the time.

Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un designated South Korea as his country's "principal enemy," Pyongyang's military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off.

A view of the South Korean National Assembly in Seoul, 2 April, 2026 AP Photo

In a 2015 landmine incident, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded in a blast on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs.

Seoul concluded that North Korean troops had crossed the Military Demarcation Line to plant the mines, an accusation Pyongyang denied.

The incident prompted South Korea to resume anti-Pyongyang loudspeaker broadcasts along the border.

World.title: Google appeals EU data-sharing order, warns of 'irreversible harm'
World.content:
Google said on Tuesday it had appealed EU measures announced in July requiring it to share data with rival search engines and give competing AI services greater access to Android, warning that the measures could put users’ privacy at risk.

 

The company filed its appeal with the EU’s General Court in Luxembourg.

“We’re appealing decisions that will force us to share people’s private search history without sufficient anonymisation and weaken vital security protections on Android,” said Oliver Bethell, Google’s senior director for competition.

The European Commission said Google must begin sharing search data from January 2027 to “rebalance the playing field” for rival search engines.

Changes to Android are also due next year. The Commission said the changes would give competing AI assistants access to features available to Google’s own services, such as Gemini, allowing users to activate a rival assistant by voice or ask it to carry out tasks in other apps.

Google argues that Android is already open to other services and that the search data requirements lack adequate safeguards, user knowledge and consent.

“People use Search for their most personal questions — from medical worries to close relationships — and mandating we share these personal queries without adequate safeguards would cause irreversible harm to user privacy,” Bethell said.

Related Google rivals in Europe line up for damages after record EU fine

However, the Commission said when it announced the measures in July that they include protections for users’ privacy and device security.

It said search data would be anonymised before being shared and Google could assess whether a recipient posed serious security or data protection risks.

The appeal is the latest clash between Google and Brussels under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which sets rules for large tech companies that dominate key digital markets.

In a separate case in July, the Commission fined Google €890 million for favouring its own services in search results and restricting app developers from directing customers to other ways of buying their products.

World.title: Why are pictures of Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani in a miniskirt going viral?
World.content:
A wave of images depicting Italy's foreign minister and deputy prime minister Antonio Tajani wearing a variety of skirts and dresses has swept across Italian-language social media platforms.

 

No, he hasn't suddenly become a fashion icon overnight: these pictures are actually AI-generated, and Italians are sharing them over a controversial statement he made about women.

A selection of the AI photos circulating on social media Euronews

To understand the joke, we need to go back to something Tajani, leader of the centre-right Forza Italia party, said at a political event near Rome on 18 September.

He was responding to a question about why voters should choose an established party, such as Forza Italia, rather than a newer and more eye-catching rival, such as National Future, the far-right party led by MEP Roberto Vannacci.

Tajani compared a voter's choice of party with the advice he might give his son on what type of woman to marry.

In his analogy, he contrasted an attractive but potentially unfaithful woman with one who was less conspicuous but more dependable.

He then suggested the more "serious" woman might wear a longer skirt.

"Even if the polls say they prefer the [flashier girl], or the serious girl who maybe has a longer skirt than the other one, or it could be a muscular playboy versus the one who wears a tie to the office a little more often," Tajani said to the audience at the ITACA event. "I always recommend choosing the reliable one, and the centre-right is reliable."

The comment has gone viral on social media, where users have turned Tajani into a meme, commenting that the length of a woman's skirt says nothing about her loyalty.

Politicians and priests weigh in

The remarks have also prompted criticism from Italy's opposition politicians.

Former Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi, leader of the centrist Italia Viva party, shared two of the pictures, saying that Tajani was "more of a meme than a minister."

Elsewhere, senators from several opposition parties posted pictures of themselves in skirts as a protest. One participant described the demonstration as being about women’s freedom to dress without men judging them.

"This is a gesture of freedom to say that we are free to dress as we want," said Raffaella Paita, also from Italia Viva, who spearheaded the protest. "We believe that women's freedom is measured by every gesture of freedom, including the length of a skirt or any other gesture women choose to make without being judged by men."

The controversy also drew a response from the Catholic Church: Giuseppe Baturi, secretary-general of the Italian Bishops' Conference, said that women must be treated with respect.

"Every word, every glance at women must be filled with respect and admiration," he told journalists in a press conference. "For us Christians, the first place where the Word became flesh was a woman's womb."

"For those of faith, this forever affects how they look at women," he added. "Respect is needed, especially towards women, to the extent that they can be the object of superficial glances."

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said the comment "came out badly", adding that she would not "blow it out of proportion."

As for Tajani himself, he has since apologised, saying he never intended to offend women.

World.title: Learning from the front line: Estonian defence sector bets on cheap, smart and flexible military drone systems
World.content:
Estonia, the Russia-bordering NATO member, has a relatively small army — but as one of the world's digital leaders, it is looking to make up for that with technology.

 

Its defence industry is now building a wide range of cutting-edge military equipment, battle-tested in Ukraine and ready to scale up: low-cost, jamming-resistant drones, portable launch systems and sensors that spot threats in the sky.

Euronews Next was invited to an undisclosed location near Tallinn to see a demonstration of these Estonian-made systems.

KrattWorks showed how a single operator can now control a swarm of drones, each capable of carrying deadly explosives, at the same time. The company's core idea is to make each soldier count for more.

"The Estonian army is about 40,000 strong, but the adversary is quite a lot bigger. So we need to multiply our soldier [count]," Karmo Saar, Head of Sales at KrattWorks, told Euronews Next.

In Ukraine, he explained, one operator can already control seven of their drones.

The machines can also fly without a constant link to their operator. "The systems we develop in Estonia are fully autonomous," Saar said. "If they are being jammed and the connection is lost, they have all the computing power on board and they finish the mission themselves."

Estonia's defence industry is almost entirely private. Many firms supply Ukraine — while improving their products based on feedback from the battlefield.

Threod Systems' reconnaissance drone Euronews

Threod Systems, which makes surveillance drones, says that feedback has improved its designs.

"If you lose the GPS, what will the aircraft do? Previously it mostly crashed somewhere," Margus Allas, Test Engineer at Threod Systems, told Euronews Next.

"Nowadays, our product is that safe that it comes home — you can take it over and land safely. So that was a key feature that came from Ukraine."

Allas said Ukrainian users also pushed the company to test in harsher conditions. "In real life we want to use the aircraft in bad weather," he told Euronews Next.

Some operators are exhausted and have gone days without sleep, he added, so the software has to be simple to use.

The "Cata B" pneumatic catapult for drone launches Euronews

Cheap, local and scalable

That experience has pushed Estonian firms towards flexible, lightweight and affordable solutions.

One example is a pneumatic drone catapult, also produced by Threod and widely used in Ukraine. The "Cata B" can be set up in minutes and needs only diesel fuel to launch drones.

Detection matters as much as the drones themselves. Rantelon, a radio-frequency technology company, showed a passive drone detector.

It emits no signals and only listens, so an enemy cannot easily locate it. "The advantage of being passive is that your enemy can't tell where your systems are," Kaspar Põder, Sales Project Manager at Rantelon, told Euronews Next.

The device can track several drones at once, across different radio bands, and covers military as well as civilian models.

Põder said uses range from border protection to critical infrastructure and large public events. "Drones are here to stay, and the market is growing," he told Euronews Next.

Electric Wings' FPV drones are designed to be cheap and domestically produced Euronews

Electric Wings Group showed a 10-inch FPV drone designed to carry a munition to its target. The drone uses radio frequencies and is "not jamming proof," Jordan Vähesoo, Sales Manager at Electric Wings Group, told Euronews Next.

But jammers are expensive and not everywhere, he said: "If one [drone] breaks down or gets jammed, you just open a new one from the box and you go again."

The company can produce about 10,000 units a year now and says it can scale up from there.

The frames, propellers and motors are made in Estonia, and the batteries are assembled there. "I think it's important that every country has its own manufacturer. A lot of components right now are still coming through China," Vähesoo told Euronews Next.

Chinese parts are cheaper, he said, but European tenders increasingly ask for European electronics. "I would like to see that switch," he added.

The state is backing the push. Estonia wants to become a global hub for testing and building drones. The government aims to triple defence industry revenue to €1 billion between 2023 and 2030.

Hugo Urbla, Director of Operations at the Estonian Defence Forces' Force Transformation Command Euronews

An adapting army

The armed forces are changing too. Hugo Urbla, Director of Operations at the Estonian Defence Forces' Force Transformation Command, told Euronews Next that Ukraine has shown how cheaply damage can now be done.

"A bang has become cheaper, because it costs [just] a few euros to fly something now," he said.

The Force Transformation Command organises cooperation between the armed forces, industry, research institutions and international partners.

"Things that are produced by Estonian companies, be it for dual use or for only military purposes, are being actively tested by the Defence Forces on major exercises but also on a day-to-day basis," Urbla said.

"This does not mean that these systems are off-the-shelf ready. A technological system will always need direct feedback from soldiers who are using it. Only this way can the system actually become one that is worth something to a soldier."

But drones will not replace conventional forces, he added.

"The armour and manoeuvre units will have a place in the next war," Urbla told Euronews Next. "We know what the current war looks like, but we do not know what the next war will look like."

World.title: Iranian airliner with passengers on board seized at Istanbul over €3-million debt
World.content:
A Caspian Airlines Boeing 737 was seized at Istanbul Airport on Monday by court-ordered enforcement officers acting on a debt claim of approximately €3 million, stranding passengers who had already boarded a flight bound for Iran.

 

Lawyers and bailiffs representing the creditor, aviation representation and supervision company ACM Temsil Gözetim, arrived at the aircraft — registered EP-KPB — as it was ready for departure and served the seizure order before it could take off, according to Anadolu Agency.

Passengers and cabin crew were removed from the aircraft and returned to the terminal.

Caspian Airlines is a Tehran-based carrier founded in 1993 and operating as part of Iran's state aviation group. It flies Boeing 737s on domestic and international routes, including to Istanbul.

Iranian carriers have faced chronic difficulties maintaining their fleets and meeting financial obligations to foreign counterparts as a result of decades of US sanctions, which restrict access to aircraft, spare parts, maintenance services and international financial systems.

The war between the US and Iran that began in February has compounded those pressures, with Iranian airspace repeatedly disrupted and international routes curtailed.

The seizure came days after sweeping US secondary sanctions on Iran's aviation sector took effect last Wednesday.

The US Treasury had sanctioned 27 Iranian airlines and nine associated service providers on 8 September under its Operation Economic Outcast, warning that foreign airports, fuel suppliers, ground handlers and ticketing companies that continued servicing Iranian carriers would themselves face sanctions and risk being cut off from the US dollar system.

The secondary sanctions triggered a rapid contraction of Iranian aviation internationally, with flights by Iranian carriers suspended in Iraq, the UAE, Azerbaijan and Oman.

In turn, Iran's largest private carrier Mahan Air suspended flights to Turkey and Oman.

Lufthansa and Austrian Airlines suspended their own routes to Iran through 24 October. Qatar Airways suspended services citing airspace restrictions. China, Russia and Pakistan have continued to maintain flights to and from Iran.

Daily international flights at Tehran's main airport fell from 80 to 90 before the sanctions to around 41 by Monday, according to tracking data.

Tehran has filed formal complaints with the UN, the International Civil Aviation Organisation and the International Court of Justice.

Turkey has not formally barred Iranian carriers, which is why Caspian Airlines was still operating the Istanbul route at the time of the seizure.

World.title: Houthi attacks put Turkey’s new Saudi defence pact to the test
World.content:
Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia are putting Turkey's new defence pact with the kingdom to its first major test – forcing Ankara to weigh support for its ally against the risk of being drawn deeper into the conflict.

Advertising

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on 7 August, committing themselves to the principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.

The three countries' military chiefs met in the Saudi capital on Friday, a day after the Iran-backed Houthis launched their latest barrage of missiles targeting Riyadh and Saudi Aramco oil facilities in Yanbu.

In recent weeks, Saudi Arabia has reported intercepting numerous Houthi drone and ballistic missile attacks from neighbouring Yemen.

The military chiefs discussed intelligence sharing, military coordination and integrating their capabilities, Saudi and Pakistani statements said. Turkey's defence ministry did not comment on the meeting.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Saudi expectations

Turkey has so far stopped short of committing itself to military action.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this month that Ankara was looking into providing what he called “technical support”, without elaborating on what that could involve.

Saudi Arabia could look to Turkey for air defence systems, counter-drone technology, radars and maritime security, given the expertise and capabilities of the Turkish military and defence industry, said Amed Khuzaie of the Washington-based think tank N7 Foundation.

“The Mecca Agreement pact will prove its vitality and importance only if it's deemed to be functional,” Khuzaie told RFI.

The Riyadh meeting followed talks in New York on Thursday involving the Saudi and Turkish foreign ministers and Pakistan's deputy prime minister and foreign minister on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

Turkish media citing foreign ministry sources said the meeting focused on ongoing “technical negotiations”.

But providing support to Saudi Arabia could expose Turkey to retaliation from the Houthis.

“By God, if Turkey and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis, said in an Iraqi television interview.

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Risk of retaliation

The warning should be taken seriously given the Houthis' military presence around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical waterway linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, explained Amed Nagi, a Yemen expert at the International Crisis Group.

“[The Houthis] targeted US and UK shipping in the Red Sea,” Nagi said. “They could do the same beyond [that] to the Gulf of Aden, because we know Turkey is very active in the Horn of Africa.

"So I think these are the areas that the Houthis will think about if there is any sort of retaliation against Turkey.”

In 2024, the Houthis attacked US military and commercial shipping in the Red Sea, damaging the Gibraltar Eagle bulk carrier with a cruise missile and sinking the British-linked cargo ship MV Rubymar.

Saudi Arabia could also look to Israel for support if its new partners do not provide what it needs, Khuzaie said.

“Who has better intelligence in the region than the Israelis today?” he said. “Diversifying resources, if one fails you, you have another side that could assist.”

The risks for Ankara go beyond possible Houthi retaliation. Turkey must also manage its relationship with Iran, which backs the Yemeni group.

“It is not in the interest of Turkey to have a direct confrontation with any actor in the region, and the Houthis have become a proxy of Iran; Turkey doesn't want a confrontation with Iran directly," said Bilgehan Alagoz, an international relations professor at Istanbul's Marmara University.

"Turkey is trying to solve the issue from a diplomatic point of view.”

In a joint statement last week, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt said that dialogue and diplomacy were the only sustainable way to resolve the region's conflicts, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself under international law.

Fidan met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in New York on Friday.

Fidan later said they discussed Iran's negotiations with the United States and conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but that diplomatic efforts had yet to produce a breakthrough.

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Iran balancing act

The diplomatic efforts come as Turkey's relationship with Iran faces other strains.

Turkey-based international relations analyst Soli Ozel said Ankara has for decades walked a “fine line” between rivalry and cooperation with Tehran while balancing its relationships with Iran and Western allies, particularly the United States.

Turkey's banking regulator recently revoked the operating licence of Iran's Bank Mellat branch in Istanbul, although the official notice did not say the move was intended to enforce US sanctions.

The US Treasury also said Ankara had agreed after talks with Washington to stop flights by Iran's Mahan Air as part of efforts to comply with US measures against Tehran. Three Turkish airlines also suspended flights to Iran.

Turkish authorities have also repeatedly accused Iran of hostile operations inside the country, including assassinations and abductions of Iranian dissidents.

In January, security forces arrested six people suspected of spying for Iran and gathering information about the Incirlik air base, which is used by US forces.

Becoming involved in the conflict against the Houthis could upset Ankara's already delicate relationship with Tehran, Ozel told RFI.

“The Iranians who actually have a lot of [intelligence] capabilities in Turkey, we’ve seen that before, then you find yourself in a hot or cold war,” he said.

World.title: Argentina's Milei threatens UK with international legal action over Falkland Islands oil project
World.content:
A major offshore oil project is opening a new front in the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Buenos Aires threatening legal action and sanctions against companies involved.

Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action.

The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy.

What has Argentina threatened to do?

Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks.

"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X.

"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added.

Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

Port Stanley is the capital of the British-controlled Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas (FILE: 07/10/2019) Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors.

His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization.

Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations.

What is the Sea Lion oil project?

Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands.

The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities.

Oil production is expected to begin in 2028.

The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project.

Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the Falkland Islands in 1982 after Argentine forces invaded the British-controlled territory [FILE: 1982] Image: PA/empics/dpa/picture alliance

The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources.

Why are the Falkland Islands disputed?

The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas.

Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK.

The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory.

The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future.

In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%.

Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim.

World.title: UK: US government questions bail for Fairford base suspects
World.content:
The US government sees "the hand of a foreign actor" in the security scare at RAF Fairford, a hub for US heavy bombers in Europe. Donald Trump criticized the suspects being released on bail amid ongoing investigations.

The US government has described the security alert over the weekend at the RAF Fairford base in southern England as a "very serious situation," thanking UK authorities for their cooperation.

But President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also both questioned the move to grant the five suspects bail under strict conditions as investigations against them continue.

RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

Long-range US bombers have operated out of Fairford since it was set up near the end of World War II Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

What did Rubio and Trump say about the case?

Marco Rubio said in an interview with Fox News that while there was much he could not say on air for now, the security scare during which five young men were detained constituted a very serious situation.

"It's one that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor. I won't get into great detail about that yet," he said, without mentioning Iran until a later point in the interview in a more hypothetical context.

"I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," Rubio said.

The Iranian Embassy in London, meanwhile, said that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" of Iranian involvement.

Rubio also echoed President Donald Trump in saying that "a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have released on bail."

Trump had mentioned the issue in comments to reporters in the White House earlier on Monday.

"I will tell you, I would have said, 'Don't let them have bail.' I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that," he said.

UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What have British investigators said about the case?

Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday in the vicinity of the air base, which is in a rural area roughly two hours' drive west of the capital. They were wearing face coverings.

Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.

Locals were able to return home on Monday, and preliminary reports from the British Press Association and others suggested the materials in the vehicles were not viable explosives, but counterterrorism and explosives experts continued to examine the scene.

The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, acknowledged the "significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident," and said investigators were considering "every possible angle."

One of these angles, he said, was the possibility "that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."

Taylor said that the men had been released under stringent conditions, and that granting them bail did not in any way signify an end to investigations against them.

Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said that decisions like granting bail were operational matters for police and prosecutors, not politicians.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a security meeting known as Cobra, after the secure Cabinet Office Briefing Room A that hosts such sessions, on Monday evening.

Even prior to Sunday's deployment, security was already tighter than usual at sensitive UK facilities like RAF Fairford Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

What is RAF Fairford?

RAF Fairford is a large military airbase not far north of Swindon in Gloucestershire, west of London.

It's a base for US heavy bombers in Europe and has been used as a launch point for operations involving long-range B-52s in a series of conflicts in recent decades including both Iraq wars, the NATO bombing of the former Yugoslavia, and most recently in a limited capacity in Iran this year.

Residents in the Cotswolds region had noted an increased security presence and activity at the base amid the conflict, as is often observable around such bases during such periods.

Because of the longstanding close military ties — and very often infrastructure set up during World War II when Nazi Germany occupied much of Europe — southern England is home to a string of airbases also used by the US military.

World.title: Germany news: Merz revolts over EU budget, report says
World.content:
The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party has seen better days: Most recently, it suffered unprecedented defeats in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin. At this time of voter disenchantment, two prominent CDU politicians have come under fire on social media: Jens Spahn and Philipp Amthor have been facing accusation of being out of touch and self-absorbed.

Jens Spahn has faced a series of controversies in recent months Image: Lars Berg/dpa/picture alliance

A few weeks ago, Spahn resigned from his powerful position as parliamentary group leader of the CDU and CSU bloc in the Bundestag after Spahn had announced that had become a parent with the help of a surrogate mother in the United States. He was accused of hypocrisy because surrogacy is banned in Germany and the CDU and Spahn himself had repeatedly voted to uphold this ban.

Spahn was then given a seat on the influential Budget Committee. He called in sick for a meeting, but at the same time the tabloid BILD published a photograph of him vacationing in Sardinia with his young son. Spahn immediately resigned that post as well.

The CDU's Philipp Amthor has only recently become Minister of State for Federal-State Cooperation in the Chancellor’s Office. There, he placed a beach chair on the balcony of his new office and proudly showed it to a TV reporter. As a reminder: His party has just been voted out of the state parliament in his home state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on the Baltic Sea coast. But that didn't seem to have dampened the minister's good spirits.

The CDU's Philipp Amthor has drawn some unwanted attention at a precarious time for the CDU Image: Michael Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

Once again, social media reactions were fierce: This time with criticism of the young government official’s alleged arrogance. Amthor swiftly had the beach chair removed.

As the German saying goes, "Wer den Schaden hat, braucht für den Spott nicht zu Sorgen" (He who suffers the loss need not worry about the ridicule). That is seen to apply quite accurately to the CDU at the moment.

World.title: Evicted Spanish pensioner to return home, lawyer says
World.content:
Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, became a symbol of the housing crisis in Spain after she was evicted last week from the apartment she had lived in for decades.

An elderly woman who was evicted from the Madrid apartment she lived most of her life in and whose case sparked widespread solidarity protests across Spain, is going to be able to return home, her lawyer said on Monday.

Video last week showed Maria del Carmen Abascal, known by her nickname Maricarmen, being taken out of the building on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.

Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, is a wheelchair user and a resident of the Spanish capital's Retiro neighborhood.

Her dramatic eviction touched a nerve among Spaniards who took the case to heart to bring one of the country's most pressing problems to the center of attention: the housing crisis.

Thousands demonstrate against evictions and the housing crisis in Spain Image: Richard Zubelzu/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Demonstrators set up camps at Puerta del Sol square Image: David Canales/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Protesters were angry that Maricarmen was removed from the apartment she lived in since 1956 Image: Bruno Thevenin/Middle East Images/picture alliance

Rising prices and a shortage of homes have pushed people out of the market in Europe's fourth-largest economy, with the weekend's protest having put pressure on Spain's left-wing government led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.

On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of the Spanish capital, with many having then pitched tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night. More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.

Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says

"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters, calling it "a result of the social mobilization."

"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.

Spanish housing bill Tuesday falls short of protester demands

Sanchez, who last week called the eviction a "social tragedy," is hoping to secure backing for a long-delayed housing bill at Tuesday's meeting of Spain's Council of Ministers.

But according to El Pais, the legislation put forth Tuesday falls short of the demands of protesters who are asking for tougher action against abusive landlords and a freeze on rents until the housing crisis is resolved.

World.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model amid safety concerns
World.content:
The decision comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly powerful and autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up.

Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has abandoned plans to release a next-generation AI model after internal testing found that the system failed to meet the company's safety and alignment standards.

GPT-6.1 Astra, which is designed to handle increasingly complex tasks with less human intervention, had been scheduled to debut in October but tests reportedly found that the model displayed higher levels of deceptive behavior than its predecessors.

Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, said the model had improved in some areas but had not met the company's standards for staying within authorized boundaries or clearly communicating its actions to users.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users," Jain said. "But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms ⁠of safety and ​alignment."

Pressure builds for stronger AI oversight

The postponement comes as OpenAI and other AI companies face growing pressure to strengthen safeguards around increasingly powerful and autonomous models.

Some of these models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic have been involved in security incidents during testing.

Earlier this month, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei joined other industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.

Leading AI executives are set to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday to discuss the need for finding a balance between AI innovation and oversight.

OpenAI pledges to rebuild trust after government website hack

On Tuesday, OpenAI admitted that its models had even accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorization as part of internal training and evaluation exercises in June.

The company said ‌the activity ‌involved ​websites and systems linked to Services Australia, ​the NSW Bureau of ⁠Crime ​Statistics and Research, ​the Victorian ​Department of ‌Health and the Australian ​Institute ⁠of Health and ⁠Welfare.

The incursion, which occurred in June, was not made public until last week.

In a blog post, the ChatGPT maker apologized for the hacking and acknowledged it ‌mishandled its response ⁠and ⁠pledged to take accountability to "rebuild trust with the Australian people."

World.title: France: Student protests over conditions at French high schools fuel political clashes
World.content:
Over 160 people were arrested and dozens injured after student protests in France descended into violence. With a presidential election approaching, senior politicians are pointing fingers at each other.

Student protests spread to high schools across France on Monday, resulting in dozens of injuries, over 160 arrests and arguments between senior politicians — a day ahead of a nationwide strike by public sector workers and seven months ahead of the presidential election.

Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week in protest at overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor quality learning materials and teacher shortages.

The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regions including Lille in the north, Marseille in the south and Sedan in the east.

Video footage on French media showed student protesters lighting flares and firing fireworks, even inside a school building, while police officers responded with tear gas.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the 'escalation' of the situation 'irresponsible' Image: Adnan Farzat/NurPhoto/picture alliance

French student protests: what have politicians said?

As of Monday night, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported incidents at around 180 establishments resulting in 164 arrests and injuries to 12 students, three teachers and 12 police officers.

He acknowledged that the "difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed" but said: "This wasn't about making demands, it was really violence in its purest form."

He added that "a number of individuals … were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes and projectiles [and] clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces."

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the "escalation" of the situation "irresponsible" and said: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."

'Hands off our youth!' French politicians clash over protests

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that the protests, which he described as a "classic high school student movement," were being exploited by violent elements — and took aim at the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon.

"There is a political hijacking of the blockades by elected officials from France Unbowed," he said.

Earlier on Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."

"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Prime Minister Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Melenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."

In the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, the LFI-run local council called the students' demands "legitimate" and published a statement reading:

"Let [the authorities] come and talk to [the students] and see for themselves whether the youth are being instrumentalized, or whether they are simply capable of thinking, organizing themselves and defending their own study conditions and their future."

France: The camps under Paris bridges To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

France: strikes — and an election — to come

The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the French union that defends the interests of high school students, said it would urge a nationwide blockade of schools on Tuesday — coinciding with planned strike action by public sector workers.

French primary school teachers' unions said they expected some 40% of teachers to be off work on Tuesday.

With a key presidential election only seven months away and incumbent President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from standing for a third term, French politicians from across the ideological spectrum are seeking issues that resonate with voters.

Melenchon, a 75-year-old veteran anti-capitalist who finished third in the 2022 presidential election, is popular among younger, left-leaning voters.

His LFI party was one of the left-wing outfits which joined the Nouveau Front Populaire (New Popular Front or NFP) coalition in 2024 to oppose the far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN) in legislative elections.

The coalition beat the RN but the elections produced a divided parliament which has been dogged by political deadlock and votes of no-confidence.

Prime Minister Lecornu is still trying to build enough support to pass a 2027 state budget, but his government is besieged by opponents who are unwilling to accept spending cuts while energy costs continue to rise.

Leo makes first official papal visit to France in 18 years To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Israel's Netanyahu holds secret meeting with UAE president
World.content:
After confirming a rare meeting, Netanyahu's office has denied suggestions that the Israeli prime minister requested that Abu Dhabi deny reports that it had warned Israel about an impending Hamas attack in 2023.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secretly met with the president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, both governments confirmed late on Monday.

"The two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them," read an Emirati statement.

Netanyahu's office said the visit "focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges."

The secret trip came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the UAE president had warned Netanyahu about an imminent threat from the Palestinian militant group Hamas ahead of the deadly attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 — a warning which the Israeli premier allegedly failed to pass on to security services.

Indeed, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported on Monday that the purpose of Netanyahu's visit had been to request that Sheikh Mohamed deny having given such a warning.

Netanyahu's office denied that the prime minister had made any such request, just as it had also denied the original report.

Netanyahu files complaint against Israeli broadcaster

Earlier on Monday, before the confirmation of Netanyahu's trip, Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet filed a complaint against Channel 12, accusing it of violating censorship rules by reporting the visit before the prime minister had returned to Israel.

"This evening, Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation," read a statement from Netanyahu's office.

It noted that the report had been made public while the premier's plane was still outside Israeli airspace and therefore "endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad" spy agency and other top security officials.

How the Iran war has deepened Saudi-UAE rivalry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Israel and the UAE: diplomatic relations

Sheikh Mohamed's hosting of Netanyahu was a significant development at a time when the Israeli leader is seen by many across the Middle East as the chief propagator of the war in Gaza, which has seen over 70,000 Palestinians killed — many of them civilians.

It is also the first time that the UAE has officially acknowledged a meeting between the two leaders after denying reports of a previous Netanyahu trip in May.

The UAE is one of only a handful of Arab nations which maintain official diplomatic ties with Israel after signing the Abraham Accords during US President Donald Trump's first term in 2020.

The UAE condemned the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 as a "serious and grave escalation" and said it was "appalled" by reports of Israeli citizens being taken hostage.

But relations have also been strained by Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, with the UAE denouncing "ongoing Israeli violations" in the Palestinian enclave.

Nevertheless, Israel reportedly deployed Iron Dome air defense systems, together with personnel to operate them, to the UAE during the war against Iran, as the Gulf state faced retaliatory attacks from Tehran.

World.title: US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry make travel less predictable as countries cancel flights
World.content:
The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.

US sanctions are pushing Iran's weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo.

Earlier in September as part of "Operation Economic Outcast," the US Treasury Department targeted Iran's aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and may lose access to the US financial system.

The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies.

For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington's broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.

Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.

For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.

The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.

For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.

Major Middle East routes canceled

Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously, for safety reasons, that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia had been seriously disrupted.

On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.

Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.

Is Iran set to become an economic outcast? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.

As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the "J-1" general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.

Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.

The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.

More travelers use land crossings

With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.

One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.

"The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close," he told DW anonymously.

For families, older people, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.

Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.

That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.

Iran's shaky aviation industry

Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions.

Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.

An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.

When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.

Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran's GDP.

"Iran's aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time," Salavati told DW.

"The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money," Salavati added.

Iran offers plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran isolated by air and sea

Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.

Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.

If those first connections disappear, Iran's international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.

The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult.

If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states.

World.title: Acampada en Sol por la vivienda, en directo | El PSOE y Sumar alcanzan un acuerdo para aprobar el decreto de vivienda
World.content:
Bilbao se suma a las movilizaciones para reclamar soluciones al problema de la vivienda

Un grupo de ciudadanos ha instalado, desde este pasado lunes por la noche, una acampada en la plaza Arriaga de Bilbao para denunciar el problema de la vivienda y reclamar soluciones. Con esta protesta, Bilbao se suma a las movilizaciones que se vienen produciendo desde que la semana pasada Maricarmen, una mujer de 87 años, fue desahuciada de su vivienda, lo que ha provocado una respuesta ciudadana con iniciativas como una acampada en la Puerta del Sol en Madrid.

En la capital vizcaína, a primera hora de la mañana de este martes estaban instaladas un total de ocho tiendas de campaña delante del teatro Arriaga, una iniciativa organizada principalmente a través de redes sociales para exigir soluciones al problema de la vivienda. La acampada comenzó este pasado lunes, por la noche, con carteles en los que se puede leer “Stop fondos buitres” “All caseros are bastards” (todos los caseros son bastardos), “Maricarmen somos todos” o “Por la huelga revolucionaria, derecho a vivienda digna ya”, entre otros.

Los participantes, alrededor de una decena de personas, han explicado que han organizado de manera independiente y autogestionada esta acampada y se están haciendo llamamientos a través de las redes sociales, de un grupo de WhatsApp y por el “boca a boca” para que la gente se sume a esta iniciativa. “Esperamos llenar la plaza Arriaga y estaremos hasta que podamos”, han manifestado.

Según ha señalado uno de los integrantes, antes del desahucio de Maricarmen la situación ya era “insoportable” y, tras lo ocurrido, “se ha llegado a un punto” en el que el problema de la vivienda es “insostenible” y “parece que ser rentista es un derecho antes que ser una persona humana con derecho a tener una casa”. Asimismo, ha explicado que los participantes de la protesta son gente sin casa y, en su caso, vive en un local sin cédula de habitabilidad “porque no hay una casa para vivir” con sus ingresos. Según ha apuntado, esto es ya “un ultimátum” para que se apruebe el decreto Maricarmen con medidas para facilitar el acceso a la vivienda. Según ha señalado, no se viene a esta vida “para ser esclavos” que parece que quieren a la gente “medicada, hacinada en casas pequeñas, carísimas y en trabajos con sueldos precarios”.

“La vida no es eso. La vida no es tener un jefe capitalista que te oprime y un casero especulador. La vida es mucho más extensa y mucho más poderosa. Y la gente tiene que despertar ya de una vez”, ha añadido. Otro de los participantes en la protesta ha denunciado que “lo que arrastra” el problema de la vivienda es que hay unos sueldos que “no dan para nada, que te limitan la vida”. Según ha apuntado, ha estado en 12 países y nunca ha visto uno “más reventado que este” con unos precios de vivienda “imposibles”. (EP)
