World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

Play Video

LATEST UPDATES

World.title: Impeachment court admonishes prosecution’s Tolosa over press briefing remarks
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Prosecution panel spokesman Jay Tolosa said on Tuesday, September 29, that the impeachment court in Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial has admonished him over public comments that were previously flagged for potential violation of its sub judice rule.

Tolosa said the ruling did not explicitly say that the admonition was tantamount to a first offense, but if it were, a subsequent violation by Tolosa would result in a P30,000 fine.

“I respectfully disagree with the admonition. There is no finding that I violated the rule. While I respectfully disagree, I respect the authority of the impeachment court as an institution, and with that, I will not belabor the point and I will, of course, respect that admonition and be even more careful in giving statements moving forward,” Tolosa said in a press conference.

Play Video

The decision came after the court compelled Tolosa to explain his remarks made during a September 8 press conference. There, he said, the prosecution’s evidentiary targets have been met, that it was clear to the Commission on Audit that Duterte’s offices violated rules on confidential spending, and that the vice president cannot say she will not take the witness stand and invoke her right against self-incrimination.

The court’s sub judice rule bars parties from making comments in public pertaining to the merits of the trial.

Tolosa, in his reply to the show-cause order issued to him, asserted that his comments made to the media were procedural matters outside the sub judice rule of the impeachment court, and were just accurate reiterations of matters already placed on record.

Tolosa is among the four spokespersons of the prosecution team, but is the only one who is bound by the sub judice rule.

Tolosa is a seasoned litigator. The UST alumnus represented American soldier Joseph Pemberton, who was convicted of homicide in the killing of Filipino transgender woman Jennifer Laude in October 2014, and also counseled Philippine Airlines and the local affiliate of Fortune 500 company Philip Morris International. – Rappler.com

World.title: Baste Duterte claims no direct hand in Gencorp deals with Davao City
World.content:
Davao City Mayor Sebastian 'Baste' Duterte takes the witness stand on Day 31 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 29, 2026.

'Do you really believe that a head of procuring entity has no knowledge on the companies that bag government contracts with them?' prosecution spokesman Zia Alonto Adiong asks

MANILA, Philippines – Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte distanced himself from his city government’s deals with Gencorp during his testimony at Vice President Sara Duterte‘s impeachment trial on Tuesday, September 29.

He consistently maintained that he had no direct hand in the contracts sealed with the company linked to the Vice President, his older sister — a claim the prosecution found hard to believe.

Taking the witness stand on the 31st day of Sara s trial on Tuesday, the younger Duterte said he first heard about Gencorp when it was mentioned in open court more than a week ago.

Play Video

The Vice President’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) show she is a stockholder of Gencorp, which has bagged at least P33 million in projects with Davao City Hall since 2022, when she was elected as the country’s second highest official, and when her brother succeeded her as Davao City mayor.

Baste claimed he did not personally review Gencorp’s contracts, and did not personally approve such deals because he did not interfere in the undertakings of city hall’s bids and awards committee (BAC).

He said he delegated his procurement responsibilities to Davao City Assistant City Administrator Tristan Domingo because of his workload as mayor.

“You’re aware, Mr. Mayor, that delegating your signing authority to Mr. Domingo does not delegate your accountability as the head of procuring entity (HOPE)? You are still the final accountable officer,” private prosecutor Ted Te told the local chief executive during the direct examination.

“Yes,” the hostile witness answered.

‘Difficult to believe’

Spokespersons for the prosecution panel aren’t buying the mayor’s effort to disassociate himself from the Gencorp deals.

“We find it difficult to believe Mayor Baste’s statement that he sees no irregularities in the way the deals are handled,” prosecution spokeswoman Renee Co said in FIlipino.

“Do you really believe that a head of procuring entity has no knowledge on the companies that bag government contracts with them?” prosecution spokesman Zia Alonto Adiong added.

Adiong pointed out that Mayor Baste and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte are also business partners of Jaime T. Cruz through Chinese Gen Bee Food Corporation. Cruz’s name has been repeatedly listed in corporate filings of several companies linked to the Vice President.

Play Video

Sara’s ties to Gencorp and its contacts with Davao City Hall raise numerous questions on conflict of interest, and apparent violation of the constitutional provision that bars the Vice President from having business interests. – Rappler.com

World.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model release over safety concerns
World.content:
OPENAI. A man walks past an OpenAI booth at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo

The Wall Street Journal reports that GPT-6.1 Astra shows higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including efforts to obfuscate its activities

OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation AI model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company’s safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker confirmed on Monday.

OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and rival Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei earlier this month joined industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.

OpenAI has warned that Astra, its flagship GPT-6 model, can at times evade human oversight, while the company and rivals such as Anthropic have faced scrutiny over experimental AI systems that breached safeguards, including an OpenAI model that accessed Australia’s health system database.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that OpenAI had abandoned plans to launch the model, which was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance.

The Journal reported that GPT-6.1 Astra also showed higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including instances in which it did not always accurately disclose what actions it had taken.

“While (GPT-6.1 Astra) improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done,” said Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.

“Of course we want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that’s in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment,” Jain said.

The decision comes ahead of OpenAI’s developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers. – Rappler.com

World.title: Anthropic warns AI may pose ‘existential risks to humanity’ in IPO filing
World.content:
ANTHROPIC. An Anthropic logo is displayed at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026

Anthropic warns investors that its AI may exhibit 'self-preserving behaviors' including attempts to 'resist shutdown,' to 'conceal or manipulate information' and behavior 'resembling blackmail'

MANILA, Philippines – Anthropic plans to caution potential investors in its IPO that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” an extraordinary warning by a company seeking to profit from the same technology.

The company’s IPO prospectus, reviewed by Reuters, highlights risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit “self-preserving behaviors,” including attempts to “resist shutdown,” to “conceal or manipulate information” and behavior “resembling blackmail.”

“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,” Anthropic said in the filing.

While public companies routinely outline product risks to investors, few, if any, have issued warnings suggesting their technology could cause potential human extinction. Anthropic emphasized both the transformative potential of AI on par with industrialization and electricity and the irreversible harm it could cause if mishandled.

Anthropic and other AI developers, including OpenAI, have faced scrutiny after incidents where experimental systems defied constraints, including a report of an OpenAI model breaching Australia’s health-system database.

Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger estimated a greater than 10% probability that AI could kill humans within the next decade, echoing a sentiment by a former colleague, Jacob Coxon.

Risk-heavy disclosures

The company, which has positioned itself as a safety-first AI lab, devoted roughly 80 pages of the 261-page main body of its prospectus to laying out risk factors, nearly twice the 48 pages it used to describe its business.

For comparison, SpaceX, which owns xAI, dedicated just around 38 of the 277-page main body of its prospectus to risk factors.

“Potential model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety,” Anthropic said in the prospectus, adding that models sometimes develop unexpected capabilities during training that may not be discovered until they have been deployed and have resulted in significant safety incidents.

AI researchers have also warned that as models grow more capable, they increasingly recognize when they are being watched and adjust their behavior accordingly, which makes it harder to monitor model behavior.

Anthropic declined to comment in response to a request for comment on Monday.

Uncertain returns on safety investment

Despite emphasizing AI safety, Anthropic said that returns on its safety investments are unclear.

It did not disclose in the filing how much the company was spending on such research. Earlier this month, Anthropic said about 6% of the computing power it used for AI research went to safety work in a sample week in July.

The company, creator of Claude AI models, described safety efforts as “resource-intensive” and said it must divide its limited funds between computing power, expensive AI talent and safety.

Anthropic said that its customer usage, and as a result revenue, is driven by new models and that a “continuous and overlapping cadence” of releases is “inherent to remaining at the frontier of AI development.”

The company last week released a new version of its Opus model, 10 days after CEO Dario Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for pacing the frontier.

Some analysts and experts have said no leading AI lab would slow down when doing so risks handing rivals an advantage in an industry where valuations can change with each release.

Anthropic has pledged in recent weeks to disclose more data publicly about how it uses AI models to build future generations of the technology, as experts warn about recursive self-improvement — the point at which models can develop on their own without human help.

“We believe building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems is a collective responsibility and that the market will reward it,” Anthropic said in the filing. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Just Saying] Refocusing the impeachment
World.content:
Both the judges and the public must immediately take a step back and refocus on the true, vital purpose of this impeachment trial. There is a real danger that the proceeding is straying into a bad imitation of a criminal trial. This shift can lower the overall quality of the trial, confusing the public, and steering the process away from its core objective.

This confusion — I believe — is the primary reason the trial has been perceived as becoming protracted. When an impeachment court acts like a criminal court, it gets fixated on strict legal technicalities that belong in a regular courtroom. But impeachment is not designed to put anyone in prison or strip away personal liberties. That is why it does not require proof “beyond a reasonable doubt.” Forcing criminal standards onto an impeachment trial distorts the process and wastes critical time.

The most important distinction to keep in mind is that public trust is a matter of confidence, not criminal guilt. If Vice President Sara Duterte committed acts that violate criminal laws, she must answer for them in the proper legal forum — such as regular courts or the Ombudsman — where criminal liability is determined. Impeachment, however, serves a completely different function: protecting public office by deciding whether an official still deserves the public’s confidence to hold power.

In an impeachment trial, the goal is not to prove a crime beyond a doubt — though, in the process, it can also be accomplished. The actual test is whether the evidence presented is clear enough to convince a reasonable person that the official’s actions are so highly questionable and irregular that they destroy trust in that office. An official does not need to be a convicted criminal to be unfit for leadership. Serious, evidence-backed irregularities that compromise integrity are more than enough to show that public trust can no longer be granted.

To see how this is a question of public confidence rather than technical criminal guilt, we only need to look at simple, common-sense questions. For example, when the Vice President in full public view made what appears to be a threatening remark against the President, the First Lady, and the Speaker of the House of Representatives, does that inspire extrajudicial killing and not the rule of law? When millions of pesos in public money were withdrawn in cash and placed in “gym bags,” does that at least require a compelling reason for justification? When a Vice President should concentrate full-time on her official job, does having business interests smack of a conflict of interest? None of these questions require a years-long criminal trial to evaluate. They are plain, direct questions about whether an official’s conduct maintains or destroys public confidence.

This fundamental principle was demonstrated when the Impeachment Court itself — exercising its own constitutional authority — voted 13–1 to resolve the debate on the two-thirds voting threshold. The Senate sitting as an impeachment court rightly clarified that the two-thirds requirement is not an inflexible, static number fixed at 16. Instead, it is a variable calculated strictly from the senator-judges who are legally and factually capable of sitting to try and decide the case (“while sitting for that purpose”).

By making this determination internally, the Impeachment Court asserted its sole constitutional power to keep its proceedings moving forward. The ruling reflects a practical constitutional reality: empty seats, medical absences, or non-participating members cannot be allowed to paralyze an institution tasked with holding high officials accountable.

Just as the Impeachment Court recognized that its voting denominator must reflect the actual judges sitting to do the work, the court and the public must also recognize that the evidentiary standard must reflect the actual nature of the trial. Observing and implementing a rigid, criminal-level proof is just another way of paralyzing the court’s constitutional duty.

It is deeply frustrating to watch a vital constitutional mechanism get bogged down by what many perceive as criminal trial tactics and partisan delays. Every day spent debating technicalities that belong in a criminal defense motion is a day stolen from the core question: Does this Vice President still command the confidence required to hold public trust?

Despite these setbacks, there is still reason to hope. The Impeachment Court’s own resolution on the voting threshold shows a willingness to cut through rigid misinterpretations to preserve institutional function. If the senator-judges and the public now apply that same clear-eyed perspective to the evidence itself, the trial can finally shed — what many believe —as its criminal trial pretenses and fulfill its true constitutional objective: safeguarding the integrity of public trust. Acquit or convict the Impeachment Court must, but it should be done abiding by the spirit of the Constitution. – Rappler.com

Mel Sta. Maria is former dean of the Far Eastern University Institute of Law. He teaches law at FEU, the Ateneo School of Law, the University of Sto. Tomas, Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila, University of Makati, and Manuel L. Quezon University. He also hosts shows on both radio and YouTube, and has authored several books on law, politics, and current events.

World.title: World Bank: 4Ps a ‘far more effective’ program for reducing poverty
World.content:
4PS. Beneficiaries of the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program learn about digital financial platforms in a Department of Social Welfare and Development event in Brooke's Point, Palawan, May 31, 2024.

Rather than being merely the ayuda program critics sometimes portray it as, the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program may actually have the 'strongest demonstrated poverty-reduction impact among major transfer programs,' according to the World Bank

MANILA, Philippines – For families enrolled in the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps), the cash assistance given by the government is meant to help keep children in school and support their health, giving households living in poverty a little more room to get by. And if you ask the World Bank (WB), the program has been a success.

The WB’s latest assessment suggests that the money spent in this targeted program is doing more to reduce poverty than many other forms of government assistance.

“The message is clear: 4Ps is far more effective a program,” World Bank senior economist Jaffar Al Rikabi said during the launch of the lender’s Philippines Public Finance Review on Monday, September 28.

Play Video

The WB estimates that the 4Ps delivers around 200 times more poverty reduction per peso spent than VAT exemptions, and about twice as much as the social pension for indigent senior citizens. The program itself reduces the country’s poverty rate by around 2.2-percentage points (ppts), which Al Rikabi described as “much more than any other program.”

The Philippines’ broad VAT exemptions are meant, in part, to lessen the cost of goods and services for lower-income households. While the World Bank has not identified which specific exemptions it finds ineffective, it has called for a review of non-food VAT exemptions. Examples of such exemptions include medical and hospital services, books and educational materials, some prescription medicines, and lower-priced residential housing, which are covered under Section 109 of the Tax Code as amended by the TRAIN and CREATE laws.

The problem, the WB said, is that richer households end up capturing more of the benefits from VAT exemptions simply because they spend more. “Richer households consume more exempted goods in absolute terms,” World Bank senior economist Jaffar Al Rikabi said, noting that their higher purchasing power means they buy more goods overall. Higher-income households are also more likely to buy their goods and services from large formal stores where the VAT applies.

“What we’re trying to show here is that a policy that is intended to support the poor actually does it, but in a quite poorly targeted manner,” Al Rikabi said.

By contrast, the 4Ps specifically targets poor households. In its report, the World Bank describes it as having the “strongest demonstrated poverty-reduction impact among major transfer programs,” adding that an additional 1% of GDP invested in 4Ps is associated with a 4.4-percentage point reduction in the poverty headcount.

That explains why the WB is calling for more of the government’s already existing social protection budget to be redirected toward 4Ps, rather than cutting the program’s spending. Shifting funds from less targeted transfers toward 4Ps or a similarly “registry based successor” could reduce the poverty headcount by an estimated 2 ppts. (READ: Poverty rate hits record low 9.7%, but millions are one crisis from sliding back)

“This would lift approximately 2 million Filipinos above the poverty line within the existing social protection budget,” the WB said in its report.

Criticism against 4Ps

The World Bank’s high praise for the program, however, comes just as funding for it under the budget is set to decline. The 2026 budget provides around P112.9 billion for 4Ps, while the proposed 2027 allocation falls to P99.1 billion, intended for 3.5 million households.

The 4Ps has also long faced questions about whether the cash assistance program truly helped families move out of poverty.

In 2022, the Commission on Audit (COA) said the program’s poverty reduction performance needed a closer look. The COA flagged that around 90% of the more than 4 million active beneficiary households stayed below the poverty threshold despite being in the 4Ps program for seven to 13 years and receiving a combined P537 billion in cash grants as of June 2021.

Senator Erwin Tulfo also proposed in 2025 replacing monthly 4Ps assistance with livelihood capital that beneficiaries could use to start small businesses, arguing that the existing setup was similar to “giving alms” to the poor.

That stigma has also played out online. A Rappler analysis with data forensics group The Nerve in May found 4Ps beneficiaries being blamed in viral Facebook posts for higher Meralco electricity bills after the expanded Lifeline Rate Subsidy took effect. The subsidy charge was only P0.01 per kilowatt-hour, while the much larger increase in bills came from generation charges. – Rappler.com

World.title: PH nails best sepak takraw finish in Asian Games with women’s double silver
World.content:
DUO. Sepak takraw players Jean Marie Sucalit (right) and Abegail Sinogbuhan in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Jean Marie Sucalit, Abegail Sinogbuhan, and Nelly Jay Salon miss out on a sepak takraw gold in the 2026 Asian Games after a straight-sets loss to Vietnam in the women's double final

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines added a breakthrough sepak takraw silver to its 2026 Asian Games haul on Tuesday, September 29, courtesy of the women’s double squad of Jean Marie Sucalit, Abegail Sinogbuhan, and Nelly Jay Salon.

The Filipinas missed out on the gold after a 15-8, 15-4 loss to Vietnam in the final at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Gymnasium in Japan.

Still, it is the Philippines’ best-ever finish in the sport since sepak takraw debuted in the Asian Games in 1990, surpassing three previous bronze results.

One of those bronzes were won by the men’s regu crew of Jason Huerte, Jom Lerry Rafael, Reynaldo Asilum Jr., Glindel Phori, and Ronsited Gabayeron on Monday, September 28.

Sucalit, Sinogbuhan, and Salon advanced to the gold-medal duel after an emphatic 15-12, 15-10 semifinal victory over Laos, the only team to beat Vietnam in the tournament.

But Vietnam proved to be a different beast, racing to a commanding 10-5 lead in the opening set then cruising the rest of the way in a match that took just 34 minutes to finish.

The Philippines has captured three silvers so far, the other two coming from mixed martial artist Jean Claude Saclag and the Gilas Women 3×3 basketball squad. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakh Olympic Champion Shaidorov Rises to Second in World Figure Skating Rankings
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Mikhail Shaidorov has climbed to second place in the updated International Skating Union (ISU) world rankings with 4,193 points, marking the highest position of his career.

The rankings are led by United States skater Ilia Malinin with 4,590 points, while Japan’s Yuma Kagiyama is third with 4,123 points.

Shaidorov’s rise in the rankings follows his bronze-medal finish at the ISU Challenger Series Memorial Ondrej Nepela in Bratislava, Slovakia. The tournament marked the Kazakh skater’s first international competition of the 2026/27 season and his first international start since the 2026 Winter Olympic Games.

Shaidorov scored 272.75 points overall, earning 95.98 points in the short program and 176.77 points in the free skating program.

Russia’s Evgeni Semenenko, competing as a neutral athlete, won the tournament with 292.09 points, while Italy’s Daniel Grassl took second place with 278.80 points.

The second-place ranking represents Shaidorov’s highest-ever position in the ISU world rankings.

World.title: Kazakhstan Completes Key Aviation Safety Review Ahead of Potential US Flights
World.content:
ASTANA – Experts from the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) have completed an International Aviation Safety Assessment (IASA) of Kazakhstan’s aviation safety oversight system, conducted from Sept. 21 to 25, the Civil Aviation Committee’s press service reported.

The assessment focused on Kazakhstan’s state aviation safety oversight system and its compliance with applicable International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards and recommended practices.

The FAA expert team began its visit with a meeting with Kazakhstan’s Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev. During the IASA, the experts reviewed Kazakhstan’s aviation legislation, subordinate regulatory acts and the country’s capacity to exercise effective oversight of aviation safety in line with ICAO requirements.

On Sept. 24, the FAA team also conducted a field visit to Air Astana in Astana. The airline is currently applying for economic authorization from the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) to operate flights to the United States. According to the Ministry of Transport, the visit was a positive, mutually beneficial experience for the organizations involved.

Preliminary results presented

On Sept. 25, FAA experts held a final briefing in Kazakhstan and presented their preliminary findings. The experts noted the significant work Kazakhstan’s aviation authorities carried out. According to their preliminary assessment, Kazakhstan showed strong results in several areas, reflecting progress and political commitment to aviation safety.

Under the IASA procedure, the FAA will next send an official notification to Kazakhstan’s aviation authorities. The FAA will then hold final consultations to discuss any required corrective measures.

After these stages, the FAA will decide on Kazakhstan’s Category 1 status. Obtaining Category 1 would create the regulatory conditions Kazakh airlines need to complete the required procedures to launch direct air services to the U.S.

The assessment is therefore an important step in Kazakhstan’s efforts to meet international aviation safety requirements and establish the regulatory framework for potential direct air connectivity with the U.S.

World.title: KIOGE 2026 to Mark 30 Years of Kazakhstan’s Energy Industry Dialogue
World.content:
ALMATY – The 30th International Oil and Gas Exhibition (KIOGE 2026) will take place in Almaty on Sept. 30-Oct. 2, bringing together more than 500 companies from 62 countries to discuss the future of Kazakhstan’s energy sector, international cooperation and emerging technologies.

The anniversary edition of the exhibition will bring together government representatives, international and national energy companies, major project operators, technology providers, equipment manufacturers and oilfield service companies.

Of the 501 participating companies, 187 are from Kazakhstan and 314 are international, while 34% of exhibitors will participate in KIOGE for the first time. National groups will be represented by companies from Austria, Germany, Italy, India, China and Russia. More than 9,000 visitors are expected during the event’s days.

Three decades of industry dialogue

The anniversary of KIOGE comes as Kazakhstan’s energy sector is undergoing significant technological and structural changes, with growing attention to digitalization, artificial intelligence, gas processing, petrochemicals, low-carbon development and new energy and logistics chains.

The conference program, which will run Sept. 30-Oct. 1, will bring together 620 delegates and speakers from 12 countries, with more than 280 B2B and G2B meetings planned.

Founded in 1993, KIOGE has developed alongside Kazakhstan’s oil and gas industry, evolving from an industry exhibition into a platform for investment, technology exchange and professional dialogue. Over three decades, its agenda has expanded from major oil and gas projects and international investment to include digitalization, industrial localization, energy transition and emerging technologies.

Focus on new energy chains and technology

The first day will feature the plenary session on Kazakhstan’s role in new energy chains, alongside sessions on intelligent upstream development, Kazakhstan’s national energy report, low-carbon development and ESG, digital transformation, and oil and gas machinery and petrochemicals, as well as the presentation of the 26th WPC Energy Congress, which will be held in Astana in 2028.

Artificial intelligence will feature prominently in the program, with practical cases examining AI, automation and new technologies in the oil and gas industry. The program will also examine export logistics and the geopolitics of energy routes, with experts discussing existing and alternative export corridors and Kazakhstan’s role in regional energy exports.

Gas, energy policy and the industry’s future

On Oct. 1, the program will focus on gas and gas chemistry, export logistics and the geopolitics of routes, and Kazakhstan’s energy future, including investment, the energy transition and strategic opportunities.

A panel involving veterans of the oil and gas industry, “Industry Legends on Challenges and Victories,” will look back at three decades of sector development and discuss future challenges.

The second day will also feature the business game organized by GR Hub Kazakhstan and a PR and HR business simulation focused on leadership and management in an environment of uncertainty, technological change and artificial intelligence.

Practical business program

A separate business program at the exhibition venue on Sept. 30-Oct. 1 will feature sessions, including discussions, presentations of new technologies and training sessions open to industry professionals.

Companies will present practical solutions, procurement programs and opportunities for cooperation across the oil and gas value chain. The North Caspian Operating Company, Karachaganak Petroleum Operating and Tengizchevroil will present opportunities for domestic suppliers, while other participants will showcase technologies in areas ranging from AI and well productivity to intelligent oil and gas processing.

The exhibition will be held across pavilions 7–11 of the Atakent International Exhibition Center.

Anniversary edition

The 30th anniversary edition is expected to continue KIOGE’s evolution by bringing together traditional energy companies and new technology providers to discuss how the industry can respond to changing global energy markets. The anniversary program will conclude with an awards ceremony and a film marking 30 years of KIOGE.

KIOGE 2026 is officially supported by the Ministry of Energy of Kazakhstan, the Almaty’s city administration, Atameken, KAZENERGY, KazMunayGas, PSA, IMBC, Energy Monitor, KazService and PETROCOUNCIL.KZ.

The event is organized by Kazakhstan’s exhibition company Iteca in partnership with international organizer ICA Events.

The e-tickets are available here.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s University Offensive
World.content:
Germany’s future in Central Asia’s boom market will be decided in the lecture hall

Kazakhstan is the gateway to a growth region, yet Germany lacks knowledge of it. Those who invest in talent gain networks and markets. Those who wait fall behind. Berlin needs to act.

On Monday, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has arrived in Germany. Interest is high, since Kazakhstan is becoming one of Germany’s most important economic partners. Knowledge about the country has barely kept pace. Some would call it typically German. We discover new markets, debate billion-euro projects and know surprisingly little about the countries behind them.

In 2025, the country accounted for more than 80 percent of German trade with Central Asia. The country is evolving from a commodity supplier into a production location and logistics hub, and it is the gateway to a market of more than 80 million people. Yet who in Germany knows Kazakh universities, companies and institutions? Who speaks the languages, has studied there or has built networks over years? Very few.

In Kazakhstan, this gap is increasingly becoming a competitive disadvantage. Too few German students spend extended time in the country, university partnerships remain limited and personal networks are thin. The result is a shortage of people who know the market from first-hand experience, beyond presentations and statistics.

An analysis by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) shows how far the region’s economic weight has already shifted. In the paper “Why Investors Are Turning to Central Asia and Caspian,” published in September 2025, the authors examine the investment potential of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan and the Kyrgyz Republic. Together, the four states have around 70 million inhabitants and an economic output of about $440 billion. Kazakhstan accounts for almost 60 percent of regional GDP.

The study also highlights the region’s comparatively well-educated labor pool, with almost seven million workers holding a university degree and a further 11.5 million with vocational or equivalent qualifications. Konstantin Polunin, the director and partner at BCG and one of the study’s authors, summarized the development to this newspaper last year. “What we are seeing is a lasting structural change,” he said.

“Germany underestimates this potential,” Kanat Kozhakhmet, the president of Narxoz University in Almaty, told this newspaper. “Cooperation between Kazakh and German universities has so far been clearly insufficient.” In his view, universities, internships, research and skilled-worker programs belong much closer to the center of economic relations. “We need to build a roadmap for cooperation,” he said.

Founded in 1963, Narxoz University is one of the nation’s long-established economics universities. For German partners, Kozhakhmet sees potential in joint study and practical programs, resource research, technology projects and the training of technical specialists.

Kazakhstan sends its students into the world

His criticism concerns the reach of German universities, whose quality he does not question. German universities, he said, are barely visible at Kazakh schools, at education agencies and in the networks through which families organize study abroad. Other countries have courted young talent more actively for years. Whoever reaches these students builds ties to a generation that will later work in companies, ministries, state corporations and academia.

According to UNESCO data, around 91,200 Kazakhs study abroad. Germany counts 126,400, with a population roughly 4.5 times larger. This places Kazakhstan among the countries with the largest outbound student flows worldwide. Around 59,000 Kazakhs studied in Russia in 2021. China now counts more than 11,000 Kazakh students, and other published estimates exceed 14,000.

Figures on the state Bolashak scholarship program show how strongly Astana treats education as a strategic investment in competitive talent. Over 33 years, more than 13,200 specialists have been trained abroad. Today, 45 percent of alumni work in the private sector or as entrepreneurs, 25 percent in state structures and 18 percent in national companies.

Of the Bolashak and academic stays abroad reported for 2024/25, 57.3 percent went to the USA, 29 percent to the United Kingdom and 4.6 percent to Germany. For a country whose higher education system enjoys a strong international reputation, this is a small share.

Germany also falls short of its potential in academic mobility. In 2024, 792 Kazakh students went to Türkiye and 691 to Poland. Germany attracted 193. This stands out because German universities are growing internationally, with around 420,000 foreign students and doctoral candidates expected for the 2025/26 winter semester. According to available data, only about one in 220 international students comes from Kazakhstan. An internationally successful higher education location is therefore tapping only a small part of the potential in a country with a strong orientation toward study abroad.

Kazakhstan becomes an education hub itself

At the same time, Kazakhstan is changing from a source country of mobile students into a regional higher education location. In the 2025/26 academic year, around 35,000 foreign students from 88 countries were enrolled. The government is building a network of international branch campuses and partnerships, with more than 30 projects at various stages of development.

The United Kingdom and Türkiye show how such relationships can grow. More than 5,700 Kazakhs have studied in the UK on Bolashak scholarships alone. Cardiff University opened its first campus abroad in Astana, which is also the first campus of a Russell Group university in Central Asia.

Türkiye works through the jointly run Khoja Akhmet Yassawi University in Turkistan, a large scholarship program and closer links between study and business practice. Within a decade, the number of international students in Türkiye rose from around 72,000 to more than 340,000.

Germany has a network, though a small one

The German-Kazakh University in Almaty has around 700 students, nine bachelor’s and five master’s programs, and hosts about 20 German guest lecturers per semester. Anhalt University of Applied Sciences is present in Almaty. At Yessenov University in Aktau, programs in logistics, energy and environmental engineering, and mechatronics run with German participation. The Goethe-Institut’s PASCH network includes eight schools, 20 teachers and around 2,600 pupils. DAAD, GIZ, the Goethe-Institut, the AHK, political foundations and German companies add to this.

Mobility remains low despite this base. In 2025, the DAAD funded a total of 942 people from Kazakhstan and 141 people from Germany traveling to Kazakhstan. Of the 114 Germans in project funding, 105 spent a month or less in the country. Individual funding went to 11, and 9 of them stayed longer than six months. Kazakh authorities cite around 2,000 students from Kazakhstan in Germany, compared with a few dozen German citizens at Kazakh universities.

In Aktau, an Institute for Sustainable Engineering has been established with German support, including stays at German partner universities. Beyond that, a dense network of academic contacts exists. In 2023, both governments already pointed to 178 university agreements. The figure, however, says little about the depth of cooperation.

Double-degree programs illustrate this. At the end of 2023, universities offered 181 such programs with foreign partners. Of these, 102 ran with Russian universities, 12 with Poland, 10 with Germany and 9 with France. Germany has an established academic presence in the country, yet has so far left the potential of more institutionalized partnerships largely unused.

Skills shortages make education an economic issue

The AHK survey of German companies in Central Asia gives the topic an immediate economic dimension. In the World Business Outlook of spring 2025, shortages of skilled workers and economic policy conditions were among the companies’ main concerns. Around 64 percent of the companies surveyed were based in Kazakhstan. Qualified staff are in demand particularly in energy, construction, telecommunications and IT.

At the same time, Kazakhstan wants to keep more processing and technological value creation in the country. Mining, energy, mechanical engineering, logistics and digitalization need engineers, mechatronics technicians, IT specialists, laboratory staff and environmental technology experts. Germany brings machinery, industrial experience and a strong vocational training system. Universities are expanding technical programs. Both can be linked directly to investment projects.

“Kazakhstan in Practice”

A German approach can build on existing structures. With “Russia in Practice,” the DAAD already had a format that combined study with everyday business life. German students and graduates went to companies on site for six months, and the DAAD financed the scholarship, travel, insurance and, where needed, language courses. The same basic idea could be relaunched for Central Asia, with longer stays, a company or research institution as practice partner, language support and a clear link to the degree program.

“Kazakhstan in Practice” or “Central Asia in Practice” could bring young German experts to industrial and resource regions, logistics specialists to Aktau and the Middle Corridor, computer scientists to digital projects and economists to companies or universities. Narxoz would be a partner in Almaty. Kozhakhmet wants to link such formats more closely with companies and points to resource research, technology and engineering training as fields for new cooperation.

For Polunin, the education question continues an economic development that began with growing international interest in Central Asia. “We pointed out last year that the rise of Central Asia is a lasting structural change,” he told this newspaper.

“Today the question is whether the capital the region attracts can be turned into real capabilities. That requires human capital, research, training and technology. Kazakhstan has the opportunity to position itself as an economic gateway and increasingly also as the education and science hub of Central Asia. For Germany, this opens the possibility of thinking about economic cooperation, talent development and research much more closely together,” Polunin added. Many individual projects could thus become a joint strategy.

Kozhakhmet’s idea of an education roadmap would build on structures that already exist. If new industrial projects are agreed during the presidential visit, the staffing question can be addressed at the same time, from the university in Almaty to the German company on the Middle Corridor.

The author is Alexander Dergay, the founder and managing partner of Orbis Nova, a research and analysis firm. Dergay is also cooperating with geopolitical foresight agency Nightingale Int. He worked for several years as an adviser and analyst specializing in geostrategic risk before serving as an foreign policy editor at the Berliner Zeitung and the Ostdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, Germany.
