World.title: Clock starts for ‘hard man’ judge as nine-week ICAC probe finally wraps
World.content:
Former judge Fabian Gleeson, SC, known as “the hard man of the NSW Court of Appeal”, will have 180 days after final submissions to hand down his findings from the blockbuster corruption inquiry into illegal Liberal Party donations, after more than nine weeks of evidence wrapped up on Tuesday. The Independent Commission Against Corruption’s high-profile inquiry code named Operation Rosny has finished its public hearings after 38 days of evidence from 20 witnesses, which included former Liberal powerbrokers, fugitive developer Jean Nassif, and a private investigator. ICAC presiding commissioner and one-time feared rugby back-rower, Fabian Gleeson, SC. KATE GERAGHTY The commission has set a “standard time frame” of 180 days after final submissions for a report to be tabled to NSW parliament; however, witnesses in previous high-profile ICAC inquiries have waited longer for findings. Former premier Gladys Berejiklian waited almost 20 months for a finding that she engaged in serious corrupt conduct for breaching the public trust by not disclosing her secret romance with disgraced MP Daryl Maguire.



Gleeson, who was described “affectionately” as the hard man of the Supreme Court in his swearing-out ceremony in May 2025, said he would impose “page lengths” on submissions, in a sign he does not want lengthy delays to his final report. The final Operation Rosny witness was former Strathfield Labor councillor Sharangan Maheswaran, who was alleged to have engaged in blackmail and/or offences under the Surveillance Devices Act while waging a pressure campaign to force Strathfield’s then-mayor Matthew Blackmore to resign from the role. Sharangan Maheswaran arrives at the ICAC on Tuesday. Sam Mooy The ICAC heard on Tuesday that private investigator Shane De Kauwe invoiced Nassif’s development company $134,000 for surveillance of Blackmore, which then-Labor councillor Maheswaran convinced Toplace to pay. Maheswaran, who was also the lawyer for Toplace, said the surveillance work had a “tangential” connection to Nassif because Blackmore had “linked up” with another individual who Maheswaran believed was targeting him because of his connection to the disgraced developer.



The commission heard on Tuesday that Nassif’s daughter Ashlyn raised the payment to De Kauwe as a personal expense for Maheswaran to cover, but he convinced her Toplace should pay the invoices because he was already owed money. Related Article Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Former Strathfield councillor Sharangan Maheswaran wraps final day of public hearings “I believe that Toplace paid it on the basis that I was insisting that I need to get this paid, and I will offset it against other liabilities you owe me because I regard the targeting of me by this individual to be linked to Toplace Pty Ltd,” Maheswaran said. Maheswaran told the commission he only became aware De Kauwe was making covert audio recordings after he was provided with highly detailed notes. He said when he asked De Kauwe to explain something in his surveillance notes, the private investigator said he would “go back and check”.



“That’s when it became apparent that he’d taken a recording. Now, Mr De Kauwe also said to me that he might record if there was obvious criminality involved and he said he was entitled to do so,” Maheswaran said. Maheswaran told the commission he then sought legal advice for himself about the legality of making these recordings, which he passed on to De Kauwe. He has been ordered to provide that advice to the commission. However, last week De Kauwe told the commission he only began to make audio recordings of Blackmore after receiving legal advice from Maheswaran, and his understanding was if he suspected criminality, he could record the conversation. Maheswaran also offered to “stir up” Blackmore to try to capture damaging comments on a covert audio recording, the ICAC has heard. De Kauwe texted Maheswaran to let him know Blackmore was at a cafe. “Have you got a good audio on him? If so I’ll stir him up,” Maheswaran said.



Maheswaran told the commission he thought he could prompt Blackmore into talking about council-related matters, and “things I thought he was orchestrating on the council at that point”. Maheswaran later texted Labor councillor Karen Pensabene that he thought Blackmore realised he was “being watched”. “Did we get caught?” Pensabene asked. “Nah, but he was highly suss,” Maheswaran replied. Maheswaran told the ICAC that Pensabene was aware of the surveillance but may not have been aware of the covert recordings.

World.title: Socceroos v Brazil LIVE updates: Australia get another shot against Brazil in Brisbane
World.content:
The starting line-ups are in ... and the Socceroos are unchanged, which is a bit of a surprise. I was sure that Tony Popovic would look at rotating a few players, but I guess he thought that Friday night’s team worked well and wants to give them another run together to see if they can repeat the dosage against Brazil.

Remember, after tonight, they have only two more games (in November) until the Asian Cup starts in January, so there really isn’t much time for experimentation. This is close to Australia’s strongest possible XI; the sidelined Jordan Bos, Cristian Volpato and Mohamed Toure all probably would have been in the mix to start, but they’re injured.

And as for Brazil? A whopping seven changes. It’s easier to tell you who’s kept their spots: Raphinha, who wears the captain’s armband, Vinicius jnr, Bruno Guimaraes and Danilo. So no Endrick or Estevao.

Their goalscorer in Townsville, Rayan – the forward from AFC Bournemouth whose last-gasp header saved the Selecao from an almighty embarrassment – has been elevated into the starting line-up. Good for him. Meanwhile, goalkeeper Otavio and midfielder Gabriel Bontempo have been named for their international debuts. Where else would you want to do that than Suncorp Stadium?

World.title: This once fringe sex act is now ‘normal’ – and women are ending up with permanent brain damage
World.content:
NationalWomen's health This once fringe sex act is now ‘normal’ – and women are ending up with permanent brain damage Wendy Tuohy September 29, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Women in their early 20s risk becoming a generation with higher stroke risk at a younger age because of the “epidemic” of sexual strangulation, also known as the consensual practice of “choking”, forensic and research experts warn. Dr Amelia McLean, of the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, said the increase in the number of patients who had been sexually strangled is so striking that clinicians are worried normalisation of it will leave a generation with increased risk of brain injury. Dr Amelia McLean, at the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, is seeing an increase in sexual strangulation. Chris Hopkins After a 16-year-old Sydney girl died in August following what police believe was strangulation during consensual sex, the federal government floated banning choking pornography – the main source of the popularisation of reducing oxygen to the brain to heighten sexual sensation. But McLean has also been alarmed by TikTok and YouTube tutorials outside of pornography that offer advice on how to slow blood supply in the neck’s main vessels “safely”.



“There are some TikTok clips, also on YouTube, including one that has gone viral which basically is a young woman explaining how to strangle yourself or someone else ‘safely’. She points to the carotid arteries and how to compress them to cut off blood supply to the brain … to be someone’s ‘hand necklace’,” said McLean, who works in VIFM’s clinical forensic medical unit. Related Article Analysis

Consent crisis Porn industry ‘has blood on its hands’ as sexual choking rates soar That the comments under the YouTube version were mostly positive reflects a lack of knowledge that even minor pressure could cause damage, including small tears to the lining of blood vessels, known as arterial dissection, that may trigger catastrophic events, immediately or later, McLean said. Sexual strangulation is now so common a feature of sexual assault – some cases of which begin as consensual encounters – that some young patients she examines believe the choking element is unremarkable, she said. “We examine patients after sexual assault, and we have noticed it seems to be quite generational. If I see someone in their mid-30s, it’s uncommon to hear there’s been strangulation, but when it’s someone in their early to mid-20s or younger, it’s very, very common,” McLean said.



“To the extent where we will not be aware strangulation has taken place, and when we do ask them they say, ‘Oh, yeah, of course that happened’ – as opposed to it being unusual, they don’t seem particularly alarmed about that part of it.” Related Article Exclusive

Crime More than 1000 people charged in first year of domestic violence choking laws McLean and non-fatal strangulation research experts such as University of Melbourne Professor Heather Douglas say it is essential that young people are informed about the serious and cumulative harms to brain function risked by even mild blood-flow restriction, but in a way that does not alienate them. Harm can include hypoxic and anoxic brain injury – causing brain cells to die – cognitive defects such as amnesia, short-term memory gaps, disorientation, and heavily impaired decision-making or executive function, incontinence, cardiac arrest and miscarriage. Choking can also cause convulsions, seizures and death. The teenager who died in Sydney’s northern beaches is reported to have experienced seizures before losing consciousness.



Frequent exposure to sexual strangulation also correlates with higher rates of mood disorders including depression, anxiety, loneliness and emotional distress. Related Article NSW State Parliament Social media algorithms in spotlight after spate of alleged Sydney schoolboy assaults Douglas last year studied the understanding of risk among young people – the primary demographic using sexual strangulation outside longstanding niche-sex communities – and concluded one reason strangulation has become so accepted is because understanding of the danger is low. She previously studied the use of sexual strangulation among 4702 people aged 18-35 and found 57 per cent had been strangled at least once and 51 per cent had strangled someone at least once. Young women (61 per cent) were more likely than young men (43 per cent) to report ever having been strangled by a partner, and young men (59 per cent) were more likely to have done it to a partner than young women (40 per cent). Douglas said clinicians such as McLean are right to be alarmed: “Yes, you might have a generation at risk of stroke, or a generation who might have mild-to-severe brain injury as a result of this behaviour.



“But the prohibition narrative can be something young people don’t respond to, when older adults are saying, ‘never do this’.” Sexual choking merchandise is available on mainstream shopping websites such as Etsy. Etsy Consent for sexual activities was often assumed to be carried over from one event to the next, with no ongoing negotiation, placing those being strangled regularly at higher risk of longer-term cognitive issues, she said. “There is really clear evidence coming out of the US comparing young women who have never been strangled with those strangled three or four times in the previous month – and there are clear changes to how the brain looks, the time it takes to problem-solve, and clear changes to the memories [of those strangled],” said Douglas, a longtime violence-against-women academic. These studies demonstrated that as well as increasing stroke risk, the practice may cause “a generation of young women who might have mild-to-severe brain injury as a result of this”.



Related Article Consent crisis ‘Do you know that is wrong?’ The question the attorney-general had to ask her son In New South Wales, women’s health services have recently reported a huge surge in the number of people concerned they have an acquired brain injury after being strangled, including during sex. The practice is considered so mainstream that a wide range of heavy pet-style slip chains for women’s necks remain on sale on popular mainstream shopping platforms such as Etsy, and articles promoting erotic asphyxiation as an advanced kink appear in publications, including Women’s Health. Dr Neil Goldie, service director for emergency medicine at Monash Health, compared the cumulative effects of non-fatal strangulation with the incremental harm caused by multiple concussions. “A bit like with concussions in football players, people may not notice it at the time, but 10 to 15 years down the track, there might be significant sequelae [chronic conditions or complications resulting from a prior trauma],” he said.



“It can have catastrophic effects of death, or repeated minor hypoxic brain injury causing cognitive decline or memory losses that wouldn’t necessarily be picked up at the time and may become evident later. It’s going to be really hard to measure.” McLean says an influencer-driven campaign to promote accurate knowledge about potential brain damage from disruption of oxygen during consensual sex, even when it does not leave visible marks, is needed urgently, and the VIFM is considering launching its own. Dr Amelia McLean is examining increasing numbers of sexual-assault survivors whose assailants have used sexual strangulation on them. Chris Hopkins Non-fatal strangulation is also common in family violence attacks, and research has shown it is a strong indicator of potential escalation of violence and homicide. Police laid 1000 charges in the first year after laws criminalising it as a standalone family violence offence came into force in Victoria in late 2024. The prevalence of choking in domestic violence situations is probably underreported, as the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare states only about 8 per cent of sexual assault incidents are reported.



Dr Amy Webster, manager of policy, advocacy and research at Sexual Assault Services Victoria, described sexual strangulation as “a manufactured sexual act that has become a lot more common as it’s been promoted and normalised by porn, social media and the manosphere”. Related Article Crime What to know about the Tates, the misogynist influencers facing rape, sex trafficking and child porn charges “It’s presented as common and pleasurable, and many people think they should be consenting to it, or consent isn’t needed, or that sexual strangulation can be done safely: but we know that’s not true,” she said. The practice had changed the way sexual-assault crisis care is provided, making it more complicated, Webster said. The sector had noticed a significant increase in sexual strangulation in stranger assaults, casual encounters and family violence incidents in the last five years. Jennifer Fielding, unit manager Women’s Emergency at the Royal Women’s Hospital, agreed with McLean that women who have experienced sexual strangulation as part of assault or family violence often do not think to mention it because it is considered so routine.



“Because they see it as normal, they don’t like to place blame when it happens, there’s that minimisation, their outlook on it is different,” she said. “The scary thing is that because of this normalisation, they may not recognise they are at risk until it’s too late.” And her colleague Amanda Morris, senior program manager of family violence, agreed that as multidisciplinary professionals strive at the hospital to raise awareness and reduce harm from sexual strangulation, messaging about serious danger must be balanced so that women feel comfortable disclosing it. “We need high-quality, trauma-informed messaging regardless of where [women] are – on social media, in medical [systems], seeing it on the news – so they can choose to seek help,” she said. If you or someone you know needs help, contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service on 1800 211 028. World.title: The ‘unheralded’ organ: Why kidney disease is so difficult to detect
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessIllness The ‘unheralded’ organ: Why kidney disease is so difficult to detect Abby Seaman September 29, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Greens leader Larissa Waters announced on Monday night she will step down due to a decline in her health. Waters has been managing pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD). “For some time now I’ve been quietly managing chronic kidney disease alongside doing the work I love. But recently it’s taken a downturn, and I need to be honest with myself about not being invincible,” she said in a statement. Senator Larissa Waters will take some time away from parliament after a decline in her health. Alex Ellinghausen Only 7.4 per cent of Australian adults self-reported having the condition. But about 14 per cent show biomedical signs of CKD. However, the disease can be asymptomatic, and many people don’t realise they have it until it’s too late for treatment.



What is chronic kidney disease? The kidneys’ primary function is to filter the blood and remove waste products. Jonathan Craig, vice president and executive dean of the College of Medicine & Public Health at Flinders University, explains that individuals don’t need their kidneys to function at 100 per cent but CKD occurs when kidney function deteriorates to a level that cannot keep up with the body. “All of us pass urine, and urine contains a number of chemicals which, if left in the body, would cause damage … But as kidney function declines through a number of diseases, it reaches a level that the body is adversely impacted by the build-up of toxic waste,” Craig says. Because the kidneys play such a vital role, CKD impacts the entire body.



Related Article Cancer The bowel cancer symptom women can often miss “The kidneys are one of these unheralded, fabulous organs that we have that just go about their business, but if the kidneys do fail, that affects all parts of us,” Craig says. There are many causes of kidney disease, with diabetes being the leading cause in Australia, accounting for about 36 per cent of new cases. Other causes include high blood pressure, immune diseases, congenital conditions or genetic disorders. For a small portion of people with CKD who suffer from kidney failure, the only treatment is dialysis or organ replacement. Craig says studies into the quality of life of people with kidney failure show it is worse than living with some cancers, and in some cases cannot be treated.



“The treatment is really just life preservation, with dialysis – that requires being attached to a machine three times a week for up to five hours a day, which is, as you can imagine, pretty brutal,” Craig says. Only 7.4 per cent of Australian adults self-reported having the condition. But about 14 per cent show biomedical signs of CKD. Getty Images What are the symptoms? Most CKD is unrecognised, and kidney function can decline without signs or symptoms. “We’re aware we have symptoms and signs that say that the body has got a problem … The problem with chronic kidney disease is that it’s slowly progressive in many cases,” Craig says.



Often it is found through a blood and urine test at a point where kidney function cannot be returned to what it was. Symptoms that can indicate poor kidney function are general, such as tiredness, malaise and itching. “Let’s say we start at 100 per cent of kidney function. Those symptoms might only become apparent when you are down to 20, 30, 40 per cent of kidney function. So you have to lose a lot before those symptoms become evident,” Craig says. Chief executive of Kidney Health Australia Chris Forbes says CKD is a “silent killer”, as 50 per cent of people living with kidney disease die prematurely of a heart attack or stroke. “A staggering 2.5 million Australians with signs of CKD have no idea they have it, putting them at serious risk of life-threatening complications,” Forbes says.



And Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experience disproportionate levels of kidney disease. “Regardless of whether they live in urban, regional or rural areas, compared with the general population, they are twice as likely to develop kidney disease and four times as likely to die from kidney disease,” Forbes says. The rate of incidence of kidney failure in remote and very remote areas of Australia is up to 20 times higher compared to non-Indigenous people. Is it possible to prevent chronic kidney disease? The general advice is to minimise the risks by living as well as possible.



Related Article Wellness Once Emily realised what chemicals were in her beauty products, she couldn’t turn back “These are old and somewhat boring things like smoking and diet and physical activity and stopping diabetes, managing diabetes appropriately, controlling blood pressure appropriately. “Some of these things we clearly can’t avoid, right? We can’t avoid ageing. We can’t avoid being born with a genetic disorder that gets passed down to us,” Craig says. Newer diabetes drugs, like SGLT2s and GLP1s, Craig explains, have been helpful in some people with diabetes in preventing complications to the kidneys. “There are some medications, as well as specific medications for specific kidney conditions, but those behavioural biomedical risk factors are the major issues from a population perspective.”



Prevention is key, says Forbes. “A simple kidney health check could save your life,” Forbes says. “We need every Australian to take this seriously. Early detection is the key to preventing kidney failure and the need for dialysis or kidney transplant.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: She’s an Australian law professor. Her husband says they ‘don’t do consent’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAbortion Opinion She’s an Australian law professor. Her husband says they ‘don’t do consent’ Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor September 29, 2026 — 7:00pm

September 29, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a recent episode of The Dr Jo Show, Australian furniture designer James Howe said that within his marriage to Dr Joanna Howe, the podcast’s host, “consent isn’t even a frickin’ thing”. “Like for me, like, I just … I don’t do consent. We don’t do consent,” the father of five said. James’ comments came during a broader discussion about sexual consent education and the government’s digital duty-of-care bill, which the Howes believe amounts to “school-based indoctrination” and “brainwashing”. James and Joanna Howe on The Dr Jo Show podcast. YouTube Joanna appeared to agree with her husband of 17 years’ comments, and as a successful influencer among Australia’s far-right, she immediately understood the impact of James’ words.



“They’re going to clip that up online, and you’re going to sound really bad,” she said laughing. Related Article Violence Government, parents, teachers: ‘It is everyone’s responsibility to be part of combating this culture’ James replied: “I don’t give a f---. Like, I do marriage, man. Like, I don’t, I don’t do consent,” James replied. But as it turns out, both James and Joanna Howe definitely do give a f---. Not only about an education model that aims to reduce Australia’s appalling national rates of sexual violence, but also about our abortion laws. Over the past 18 months, Dr Joanna Howe, a law professor at Adelaide University and a Rhodes scholar, has become one of Australia’s most recognisable, prolific, and aggressive anti-abortion activists.



Until recently, it felt as if conservative Christianity’s renaissance was something only happening in Donald Trump’s America. Mormon women are among the most popular reality TV stars, tradwives are some of the highest-paid influencers in the world, the White House is stacked with self-identifying men of God driven by implementing their ideological agendas – usually at the expense of women and minorities – and the president prefers sitting down with far-right podcasters than journalists. This has created a conservative cultural zeitgeist that’s spread beyond the Atlantic and found an audience around the world, including here in Australia. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson with Dr Joanna Howe. YouTube/The Dr Jo Show On her YouTube channel, Dr Howe boasts almost 50,000 subscribers, and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has appeared on her show multiple times. On Instagram, she has over 150,000 followers, while James Howe has close to 200,000 – even after a sizeable drop following his comments about consent. Joanna Howe has used her platform to attack politicians who identify as Christian but are pro-choice, and said a podcaster who spoke about her experience having a termination was “celebrating her abortion”. She described Chanel Contos – the woman behind the Teach us Consent and Fix our Feeds campaigns – as “moronic”.



She has also consistently promoted her own anti-abortion protests. Related Article Political leadership Pauline Hanson has views about who should pay for kids. It’s a logic that doesn’t add up In the days before releasing the podcast episode which caused the furore earlier this month Joanna Howe organised a protest in Sydney where NSW One Nation leader Mike Newman told the crowd his party wanted abortion “stopped”. The next day, Newman told News24 he had misspoken, clarifying that One Nation seeks to ban “sex-selective abortion and late-term abortion” only, not abortion entirely. One Nation’s federal deputy leader Barnaby Joyce also attended and spoke at another of Howe’s anti-abortion rallies in June.



In the lead-up to that event, Howe circulated an image on social media of what she said were two babies named Ruth and Emma, who had been birthed on a bathroom floor after their mother had received a medical abortion and was left alone by doctors. The image Dr Howe was circulating was almost certainly a photograph of sugar glider joeys – not human fetuses – something even she later conceded, according to reports in The Guardian. Despite this knowledge, she continued to use the images to promote the rally and described the misinformation as “insignificant details”. NSW One Nation leader Mike Newman, with Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce. James Brickwood “Even if … the picture of Ruth and Emma is sugar gliders, like, does it really even f---ing matter?” she posted on social media.





Related Article Opinion

Fertility Why aren’t women having children? Ask men Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor When discussing the backlash to her podcast episode – which has since been removed – and growing calls for Adelaide University to fire the academic, Dr Howe told my colleague Bronte Gossling this week, “I think that what this [outrage] is really about is that I am leading a movement to end abortion in this country and that goes against the establishment view.” That may be true. But it’s equally plausible that a lot of people are simply outraged with what James Howe said. If Joanna Howe and her supporters want to end abortion while simultaneously supporting ineffectual education models like abstinence, consent is more important than ever. Katy Hall is a senior editor and regular columnist. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Clearly knocked out’: Top neurologist questions Watson’s fitness for grand final
World.content:
A leading neurologist says he will be stunned if there is an independent concussion consultant willing to clear Connor Watson to play in the NRL grand final after he was “clearly knocked out” in the preliminary final. The Roosters named Watson in the No.14 jersey for Sunday’s showdown against Newcastle but will have to gain clearance from an independent doctor if the representative utility is to take the field. Connor Watson gets knocked out on Friday night. Nine Watson’s head collided with the knee of Dolphins forward Kulikefu Finefeuiaki in his first minute on the field on Friday night. After an on-field head impact assessment, Watson was deemed to be displaying category-two concussion symptoms, which were upgraded to category one a few minutes later. Under the NRL’s concussion rules, players suffering a category one concussion must be stood down from training and playing for a minimum 11 days.



In Watson’s case, the decider will be played just nine days after his collision. Provided Watson was symptom-free on Saturday, the day after the game, and has not suffered a concussion the past three months nor had more than five concussions in his career, the Roosters are entitled to ask the NRL to review the category-one classification. Connor Watson suffered a head knock in the preliminary final against the Dolphins. Getty Images That would require the NRL to seek an independent concussion specialist to meet with Watson and review his case. As of Tuesday night, the Roosters had yet to make that application to head office. Regardless, at least one respected neurologist said Watson should not be risked.



Professor Mark Parsons a neurologist for nearly 30 years, has worked with numerous NRL players and said it was almost impossible to imagine Watson would be able to take the field based on what he had seen. “Personally, I don’t think you can justify an early return for Connor Watson, medically or legally – you can’t take a risk with this condition because it’s too dangerous,” Parsons said. Loading “I’d be very surprised if an independent neurologist would clear him. I’ve seen plenty of NRL players over the years. They’ll tell you they are fine, but now we can do neurophysiological tests to give objective evidence of how the brain is functioning. “A lot of expert authorities suggest 11 days isn’t long enough when there has been a category one head injury where there has been a loss of consciousness – and looking back at the replays of the incident on Friday night, he definitely got knocked out and lost consciousness.



“It’s worth mentioning the reason an early return is so dangerous is that if the player suffers even a minor head knock, before his brain has fully recovered, it can lead to massive brain swelling with permanent brain injury, and even sudden death.” Related Article NRL 2026 ‘Shouldn’t be mentioned in the same sentence’: Knights No.7 feeling weight of Joey’s jersey Parsons made it known he lived in the Hunter, but had no affiliation with the Knights. Tolu Koula failed a HIA during Origin I when he was knocked out by Newcastle captain and Queensland fullback Kalyn Ponga, and returned to play a club game in eight days. However, Koula was deemed to have suffered category two symptoms that night. Roosters officials insisted they would follow the protocols, and had previously demonstrated that they took a conservative approach when bringing their players back from concussions.



Meanwhile, Adam Gee will officiate his second NRL grand final, with Chris Butler to work as the bunker official. Gee has previously officiated the 2023 grand final between Penrith and Brisbane. Ashley Klein, who oversaw all three Origin games, but was demoted to bunker duties last weekend after failing to award an escort penalty to the Warriors in the final minute of their semi-final loss to Newcastle a week earlier, misses out.

World.title: Teacher charged with rape of Newington student still on education department payroll
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Teacher charged with rape of Newington student still on education department payroll Daniel Lo Surdo September 29, 2026 — 6:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The former Newington College teacher accused of raping a student at the prestigious private school was working at a secondary college in Sydney’s southern suburbs until her arrest, and is still being paid by the Department of Education while she confronts a string of child abuse offences. Deandra Kontou, 32, was last week charged with nine offences, including aggravated sexual assault, four counts of sexual assault, and using an electronic device to groom her victim, who was aged under 16 at the time. Teacher Deandra Kontou in a staff school photo taken this year. She taught geography for two years at Newington, where she also led a year 7 mentorship group, before she was abruptly moved on in November 2019 once the allegation was conveyed to college staff. Kontou, who went by her maiden name Haralambidis while at Newington, was teaching at Georges River College Senior Campus, Oatley, until she was arrested at her Sutherland home last week. She had been permanently employed by the Department of Education at the co-educational senior school since 2024, where she taught society and culture, history and geography.



Kontou was removed from the school as detectives prepared charges against her, and the NSW Education Standards Authority has revoked her accreditation. She remains on the public payroll, having been put on “alternative duties” while banned from teaching children under the conditions of her bail. The charges Kontou faces don’t relate to her time at the Oatley school, and she is not accused of any criminal wrongdoing while employed by the Department of Education over the past two years. Kontou worked as a teacher at Newington College for two years. Kate Geraghty Mark Morrison, acting deputy head of Newington’s Stanmore campus where the secondary college is based, wrote to staff and parents on Monday and apologised for interrupting the school break with such “distressing news”. “Please know that our thoughts first and foremost are with the [alleged] victim, survivor and their family,” Morrison said, in an excerpt of the letter seen by this masthead.



“I acknowledge that this news may land differently for you depending on your personal circumstances and tenure at the College. We did feel it was important that you heard from the College and if you have any concerns, please contact me.” Kontou’s employment at Georges River College while under investigation by the NSW Police over the Newington allegations has raised concerns among parents and students, who have been rocked by the charges facing the teacher. Detectives restarted their investigation into Kontou in 2025 after initially probing the incidents at the time. Related Article Crime Former Newington teacher charged with rape, grooming student One Georges River parent, whose daughter was taught by Kontou and who requested anonymity to protect the identity of her child, wrote to the principal on Tuesday saying she was “deeply concerned” by the allegations the teacher now confronts. “I would like reassurance regarding the processes followed in relation to staff screening, risk assessment and student safety,” the parent wrote.



“I am not seeking confidential information about any individual, but I believe parents are entitled to understand how student welfare and safety have been protected in this situation.” Kontou was granted conditional bail in Sutherland Local Court last Wednesday to return to her home in Sydney’s southern suburbs. She is banned from entering schools or undertaking teaching jobs that require contact with children, contacting the alleged victim and any prosecuting witnesses, or being in the company of a child without another adult present. There are about 2000 students across Newington College’s Stanmore and Lindfield campuses. The school, founded in 1863, started accepting girls into its classrooms this year following a highly contentious decision that led to courtroom showdowns and a broader culture war over the merits of all-boy schools and toxic masculinity. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Jason Winstanley named as RNZ’s next chief executive
World.content:
Jason Winstanley has been named as RNZ's new chief executive and will take up the role in 2027.

He will replace current RNZ head Paul Thompson, who is leaving the organisation at the end of the year after 13 years in the top job.

Winstanley's start date and transitional arrangements are still to be confirmed.

After a radio career spanning more than 25 years, Winstanley is currently the chief audio officer at NZME. He has also worked as head of talk at Newstalk ZB, assistant content director at ZM, and content director of The Hits.

RNZ board chair Brent Impey said there was a very strong field for the chief executive role.

"Jason combines a deep understanding of radio audiences with proven experience leading teams and delivering results in a fast-changing media environment," Impey said.

World.title: Electricity bills set to increase for Wellingtonians
World.content:
Audio player for " Wellingtonians may pay more for electricity network " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/regions/1653642%2Felectricity-bills-set-to-increase-for-wellingtonians

Wellingtonians may pay more for electricity network Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Wellington Electricity is looking to increase lines charges by nearly 30 percent across the region in the coming years.

The company said ageing infrastructure, a move away from gas, and increased storms are putting pressure on its network.

Consumer NZ says that will be tough on households already rationing electricity to get by.

'We can't wait' - Electricity boss

Wellington Electricity chief executive Greg Skelton said from 2028, charges could increase by between an extra $144 and $168 for a year, on top of the $600 annual bill Wellingtonians already pay - an extra $12 to $14 per month.

Chief executive Greg Skelton said the company needed to spend $1 billion over the next 15 years.

"There's no choice - we can't sit back and go let's wait another decade, if we do then the network...won't provide the service that people are used to."

Lines charges are set every five years and are regulated by the Commerce Commission. The company is planning to ask the commission to allow it to increase its prices, and has started consulting with Wellington residents.

Skelton said the city had 65,000 households still using gas, but expected that would soon change, with more drivers turning to electric vehicles, and households looking at installing solar.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Wellington Electricity had some of the lowest lines charges in the country, Skelton said, because it had a lot of assets underground and up to now, relatively high gas usage.

"The modelling we've done shows that once solar gets to around 25 percent of the consumers with solar, then there isn't much more room for anyone else."

He said the company was also looking to increase its 90 staff to 150, and improve its IT systems to be able to process more data.

At the moment the company could only access information from some of its substations in some of the city's suburbs - it could not see detailed information about how much electricity was being used and at what time on specific streets.

He said some infrastructure was now ageing, and investment would need to target larger substations in the city first - which cost between $2 million and $4m to replace.

Skelton said a lot of "excavation and trenching work" of roads would be needed to fix the underground cable system to link this back to the national grid.

Staff would be holding drop-in centres in areas from November to talk to residents about the plans, and what it wanted to see from more investment.

'People already rationing electricity - Consumer NZ

Lines charges made up about 35 percent of people's power bills in the rest of the country - in the capital Wellington Electricity said it was about 25 percent.

Lines charges are incorporated into people's power bills, and include distribution - the cost of poles, substations and lines, and also transmission - the cost charged by Transpower to operate the National Grid.

Inside the Wellington Electricity control room. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Consumer NZ's Powerswitch manager Paul Fuge said while investment was necessary to keep the network reliable, Wellington Electricity's increases came at a time when people were struggling.

"People are rationing their use of electricity to the point where it's affecting their health and well-being.

"One in five households told us in our latest survey they have gone to bed cold, gone to bed early to stay warm to cut back on heating. And that's really unfortunate in a first world country like New Zealand."

Fuge said he expected lines charges elsewhere in New Zealand to also increase, as the pressures of weather events, electrification, and ageing infrastructure converged.

Throughout New Zealand total power bills had increased by 20 percent over the past two years, Fuge said, with a large share being due to network or lines charges.

The costs of infrastructure providing every day essentials like water, power and roads was becoming debilitating, Fuge said.

"The increases are more than inflation, and more than an increase in household incomes - and that's what's worrying, because these aren't 'nice to haves'."

Fuge said people needed more help to get into lower-cost alternatives like solar and more efficient appliances.

World.title: New human waste dumping plan to be considered by Otago council
World.content:
Central Otago District Council could backtrack on plans to truck treated human effluent onto farmland after discovering the proposed site near Lauder might not be able to handle all of its sludge.

The council will decide on Wednesday on how to deal with a growing volume of treated wastewater sludge, with staff warning that Cromwell's ponds urgently need de-sludging and geobags containing thousands of cubic metres of dried sludge - dating back a decade - need moving.

The original recommendation was to dump the waste on land near Lauder, using a non-notified consent that already allows Wānaka's sludge to be disposed of at the property.

Audio player for " Locals rally against plans to dump waste in small town " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/country/1650345%2Fnew-human-waste-dumping-plan-to-be-considered-by-otago-council

Locals rally against plans to dump waste in small town Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The move was expected to save at least $600,000, compared with the estimated $1.6 million cost of carting the sludge to Southland's Winton landfill.

The proposal had angered Federated Farmers, but in a late addition to the agenda on Tuesday, staff recommended sending the stored sludge to Winton landfill instead, because the Lauder site might only be able to take half of Cromwell's sludge.

The total cost of transport to Winton and de-sludging the ponds was now estimated to be more than $3 million including contingencies.

The report said sludge from the Alexandra wastewater treatment plant might still go to the Lauder site, because it could be accommodated within the consent conditions.

The updated report said the council had received three tenders to remove the geobags and de-sludge the Cromwell ponds.

"Given the recently raised concerns by the consent-holder at Lauder, there is an increased risk that there could be interruptions to the program of work for removal of the geobag material. Delays in transporting this material will result in a variation to the contract being required and contract cost increases," the report said.

"Following assessment of the tender prices, staff believe the cost impacts of potential delays outweigh the cost efficiency of transporting the material a shorter distance to Lauder."

If personal hygiene products were found in the geobags, it would affect the ability to spread sludge at Lauder, the report said.

The Otago Regional Council, which granted the original non-notified consent to the Queenstown Lakes District Council in January, said it was taking community concerns seriously and there was a regular compliance and monitoring programme in place.

Speaking before the agenda item was updated, Federated Farmers Otago president Anna Gillespie said the plan had annoyed local farmers who had copped flak about water quality in the area and had worked hard to make improvements.

"They're angry that it could have gone through non-notified and there wasn't any consultation and they're angry that it's happening," she said.

"The feeling is that if it had been a notified consent then we could have stopped it rather than it going ahead."

Federated Farmers wanted the original consent reconsidered, Gillespie said.

"It's absolutely staggering that the council is even discussing this after the recent outcry over Wānaka trucking its treated excrement to a Lauder farm," she said.

Gillespie said the practice of spreading treated effluent on land was not new but the Lauder site was highly unsuitable.

"Experienced local farmers know what a farm like this - with porous gravely soils and low rainfall - can realistically produce by way of crops to soak up effluent nutrients," she said.

"We all understand the desire to save ratepayers' money but this shouldn't be at the expense of water quality in a sensitive catchment upstream of public water intakes."

The decision to dump treated human effluent from Wānaka on the Lauder property has prompted outage from locals worried about the potential impact on their water and health.

In the initial staff report to councillors, Three Waters group manager Julie Muir said testing of the sludge from the Alexandra site and geobags stored at Cromwell met the consent requirements for disposal in Lauder.

The report initially recommended councillors approve plans to transport the sludge to Lauder because it was the most cost-effective and legally compliant option for Central Otago ratepayers despite community unhappiness about the consent.

Earlier this year, Beca reviewed the capacity and ability of the Cromwell treatment plant to cope with increased demand because of growth, finding that it needed immediate and ongoing treatment upgrades to ensure the nitrogen limits were not triggered.

The Cromwell wastewater ponds were de-sludged a decade ago into geobags that allow the sludge to dry over time and reduce transport costs.

About 20,000 cubic metres of sludge was identified in the ponds, which would cost an estimated $2.8-$3.2 million to remove.

"Dried sludge contained in geobags on this site needs to be moved and the ponds de-sludged again as a matter of urgency," Muir said.

"This work is required to ensure that a consent condition which will require a reduction in nitrogen loading is not triggered.

"Once this trigger is reached then the nitrogen and ammonia limits on the consent reduce significantly which will require alternative more costly treatment methods."

Otago Regional Council chief executive Richard Saunders said the consent was non-notified based on an assessment of information supplied as part of the application process.

Council staff had since spoken with local residents and interested parties about their concerns, he said.

"The issues raised have primarily related to water quality, odour, human health and the consent process. The consent was processed in accordance with the Resource Management Act and is now subject to regular compliance audits," Saunders said.

Saunders said the concerns included any impact on the sensitive Manuherekia catchment area.

"We are aware through our engagement with the Manuherekia community that there are a number of concerns about the potential for adverse effects," he said.

"We are taking these concerns seriously and will continue to engage with the community on them."

The council had a regular compliance and monitoring programme underway for the site but Saunders did not rule out a potential review of the resource consent and said information from the community was helping to inform the council's response.

"It is too early to say what if any changes may be sought through this process," he said.

The Central Otago District Council has an annual sludge management budget of $1.15 million, which historically included $530,000 to remove sludge from Alexandra to Winton landfill each year.

Lauder School Bed and Breakfast co-owner Karolina Kasparova said the community was not happy to have treated sludge at its doorstep.

"We have our own water scheme and obviously we run business and we need our water to be safe, and the farmers and many people around are concerned about it," she said.

She wanted Central Otago District Council to rule out sending waste to Lauder.

"I think it would be quite outrageous," she said.

"I'm sure that none of us would be happy for other council to bring their waste here."

Audio player for " Locals rally against plans to dump waste in small town " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/country/1650345%2Fnew-human-waste-dumping-plan-to-be-considered-by-otago-council

Locals rally against plans to dump waste in small town Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

'Hamstrung with a lack of decent scientific information'

Central Otago Environmental Society co-chair Matthew Sole was concerned about any treated effluent being discharged to land near Lauder.

"We feel we're really hamstrung with a lack of decent scientific information behind whether this can actually be done ecologically and effectively," Sole said.

He wanted to know how issues like biohazards, chemicals, heavy metals and microplastics would be effectively managed.

He was also worried about the possible fast-track housing projects in the region.

"The government's proposing putting a cap on our rates. I really think we should be putting a cap on our growth until we can ... fund the necessary infrastructure to deal with all of this," he said.

There was a bit of a hypocrisy given our expectations for agriculture, he said.

"We discuss all the farming effluent issues in public, why when it comes to our human waste are kept out of the loop?

District mayor Tamah Alley was surprised when she first heard about the non-notified consent from a member of the public.

She has since spoken to locals and said the community had raised valid concerns.

"It is something that they understand there is a time and a place for discharge to land," she said.

"There are some concerns locally as to whether or not that particular piece of land is fit for purpose."

The council had an appetite to deal with the district's own waste so it was not shipping its problems elsewhere.

"Councils do need to be responsible for ensuring that when growth plays its part and creates waste like this, that we have plans for how that waste will be dealt with that are sustainable, that are financially responsible and that are environmentally responsible," Alley said.

Queenstown Lakes District Mayor John Glover said the council currently used the AB Lime landfill at Winton to dispose of the majority of sludge from its wastewater treatment plans.

"The separate consent between SJ Allen and Otago Regional Council that allows SJ Allen to dispose a proportion of its total sludge volumes at the Lauder site was not driven or issued by Queenstown Lakes District Council, and could only have been achieved with the willing consent of the rural landowner," he said.

"The pressure that growth is putting on our local infrastructure, and in turn on our own communities, is well known."

World.title: Dannevirke rest home criticised over poor care and delayed cancer diagnosis
World.content:
An elderly rest home resident was found with maggots in a wound on her leg after ongoing problems with flies from a nearby paddock that neighbours tried to control with fly spray.

The woman was one of several residents at Eileen Mary Residential Care and Retirement Village in Dannevirke who did not get a proper standard of care.

A non-verbal woman was living with an aggressive form of undiagnosed breast cancer, while a 94-year-old woman's family weren't told she was "actively dying" until hours before her death and it was too late for them to see her.

The families complained to the Health and Disability Commissioner about the treatment their family members received at the aged residential care facility between 2022 and 2024.

The commission received four complaints and a coronial referral relating to the standard of care provided to residents with high and complex needs.

At the time, the facility was owned by Eileen Mary Age Care Limited but it was sold to new owners in November 2024.

The new operator reported that investment in care systems and staffing has improved the standard of care, occupancy and resident satisfaction.

Four complaints, one investigation

The four complaints were combined into a single investigation with deputy health and disability commissioner Rose Wall finding the facility breached the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers' Rights on multiple occasions.

The first complaint was laid by the son of a 94-year-old woman living at the rest home.

She was admitted to the care facility on 21 January, 2022 for hospital-level care after hospitalisation for exacerbation of congestive heart failure. She also had a history of dementia, leaking leg oedema and wounds on her legs caused by the leaking.

She needed extensive help with daily living, including personal care and mobility.

It was noted that she had dry, fragile and itchy skin.

On 23 January, she had a small wound on her leg and the centre's wound care plan instructed staff to cover it with absorbent pads and change the dressing every two days.

Clinical records show that the wounds were reviewed regularly, and on 9 February, 2022 it was documented that the absorbent dressings needed to be covered with two layers during replacement.

On 20 February, 2022, a nurse found maggots in the woman's wound during a routine dressing change. The moisture and exudate levels of the dressing before its change were not recorded.

An ambulance was called and paramedics assessed the wound and advised staff to follow up with her GP the next day. The GP advised staff to continue Betadine washes and review the wound if it deteriorated further.

An event report noted that fluid in the woman's wound may have attracted flies from a nearby sheep paddock during the warm weather and fly season.

Clinical records note that the woman's neighbours had brought in fly spray and a portable fan to remove the flies from her room. No other pest control measures were implemented by Eileen Mary staff.

The woman died after the complaint was made.

Wall was "critical of the care provided" to the woman and said it was "inadequate overall".

"Specifically, I am critical of the lack of pest-control measures implemented by Eileen Mary Age Care Limited, the standard of adverse event reporting, and the lack of compliance with the Wound and Skin Care Policy.

"I am also concerned to learn that Eileen Mary Age Care Limited placed reliance on [the woman's] neighbour to contain the pest, rather than actively taking the lead."

Complaint two

The second complaint related to a woman who died of complications from advanced breast cancer while living at the rest home.

The HDC received a referral from the coroner about the care provided to the woman. The coroner raised concerns around the timely recognition of the woman's breast changes and escalation of care by Eileen Mary Age Care Limited in 2023 and 2024.

The woman had an intellectual disability that meant she was non-verbal.

Eileen Mary Age Care Limited said that the woman did not have a breast cancer diagnosis or a family history of breast cancer when she was admitted to its care home, but Te Whatu Ora documentation showed that her family had a history of maternal breast cancer and non-maternal history of other forms of cancer.

Because the woman could not verbalise her pain levels she was to be given paracetamol if she called out or appeared unsettled.

However, progress notes make regular references to her "calling out", "screaming", and being "unsettled" and "restless" and she experienced these behavioural symptoms almost daily over March and April 2024.

Primary care notes on 2 May, 2024 record that she had been "noted by staff to be agitated over recent weeks". This was not escalated to her nurse or GP for review.

Regular skin checks found the woman had redness on her left leg, right arm and armpit and on 25 April, 2024, a caregiver noted a lump on her right breast.

The lump was escalated to a nurse who did not assess its size or signs of redness, swelling, or pain on palpation. There was no further documentation about the breast lump until 30 April, 2024.

A small lesion also developed on her breast.

A nurse reviewed the woman on 2 May and referred her to hospital, which found the woman had advanced breast cancer and returned her to the rest home for palliative care but no end-of-life care plan was commenced by the facility.

She died that month.

Wall found the home breached the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers' Rights.

"There was a lack of timely recognition of the changes in [the woman's] breast. In my opinion, Eileen Mary Age Care Limited staff did not utilise critical thinking to establish the underlying reasons for the acute changes in [her] health.

"I am also critical of the lack of an end-of-life care plan to support the last days of [the woman's] life."

Wound care and communication

The other complaints involving women at the rest home all related to failed wound care.

A pressure wound on one of the women was infected and resulted in the woman contracting sepsis.

When her condition deteriorated, an ambulance was called but the ambulance service's entry into the care facility was delayed for 30 minutes because no access was provided.

Eileen Mary Age Care Limited said that its expectation was that someone would monitor the care facility entry to allow external services to access the resident promptly. It acknowledged that this did not occur and that this delayed the woman's care.

Documentation from the ambulance service indicates that on arrival, there were concerns about the care provided, specifically that oxygen was not given to the woman and the wound dressing was "old", "tattered at the edges and in parts not even stuck to skin", "weepy", and "pungent", and that the wound appeared necrotic.

Her daughter also complained about delays in staff informing her mother had been "actively dying".

She was only informed about the deterioration in her condition in the early hours, meaning family were unable to spend time with her before she died later that day.

Wall found Eileen Mary Age Care Limited breached the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers' Rights in all cases.

Rest home apologises

Eileen Mary Age Care Limited accepted the HDC's findings and apologised to the residents and families affected.

It acknowledged the need for wound care plans for chronic skin conditions, documentation of dedicated management plans, and consistent oversight of residents by RNs.

Eileen Mary Age Care Limited said recruiting experienced staff remained a persistent challenge and that this made providing a high standard of care more difficult at the time.

Eileen Mary had made changes since November 2024 including further educating staff on wound care management, refined handover processes and improved communication between its staff and families.

The commissioner made several recommendations to the new operator of the care facility.

They included audits on dead patients to make sure end-of-life care plans were established and audits on patients with chronic pain to make sure their conditions were being managed appropriately.

It also wanted the facility to consider implementing weekly reviews of at-risk residents to make sure correct care is maintained.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Associates dumped drugs and guns as fatally injured man carried from Wairarapa shooting
World.content:
The owner of a red ute - which carried the fatally injured Doreion Hard from the scene of a daylight shooting in a Wairarapa supermarket car park - says she tried to staunch the man's bleeding as the vehicle's occupants dumped drugs and guns.

Hard died after he was shot in the back following what prosecutor Tim Bain described as a "drug deal gone sideways" in a car park in Featherston in March 2025.

Tuesday is the second day of the murder trial of Pelikai Taukei'aho and Tauave Sue at the High Court in Wellington.

On Monday lawyers for the Crown told the jury that four men - including Hard - had conspired to rob the defendants after arraigning a meeting to purchase several ounces of cocaine on 22 March, 2025.

On Tuesday the woman slumped in her chair as she told the court she had remained with her truck rather than give the vehicle up to the men - acquaintances of hers - who demanded she take them to Featherston.

After meeting up with another vehicle carrying Hard in the supermarket car park, three of the men readied firearms - putting them in their waistbands.

Hard and one other walked towards the defendants who were waiting in a grey Holden Cruze.

Prosecutor Tim Bain described the incident where Hard was shot in a Featherston supermarket car park as a "drug deal gone sideways". Supplied

The two men opened the car doors and lent into the vehicle. The woman said she heard them yelling aggressively and suspected one man had hit the occupant on the driver's side.

The woman would later tell police the two men had guns pointed at the defendants.

As the altercation was taking place a third man stepped behind the Holden scattering Z-nails behind the vehicle's tyres while the remaining man stayed in the driver's seat - with her in the back.

The witness said the rear left hand side window of the vehicle shattered suddenly, seconds after the three men returned to the vehicle.

"I think Doreion shot the gun," she said.

"We were just moving and then the window, bang, and then a quick glance and I see [the defendants] jump out of the car. That's when I heard another bang and Doreion grabbed my arm and said he'd been shot.

"I pulled him forward to try and find where he'd been shot to stop the bleeding.

"They were too busy worried about hiding everything. I was just trying to keep him awake," she said.

Tauave Sue has pleaded not guilty to the murder of Doreion Hard. Mark Mitchell

The woman said the ute headed south stopping on the way to dump the firearms and a bag taken from the grey Holden.

Nearer to Greytown the ute made other stops as two of the male passengers made their own way to avoid arrest.

"I'm still trying to keep Doreion awake. **** gets out. He says he can't get caught by police et cetera. Then we get to Carterton and that's where we stop," the woman said.

Police and ambulance arrived soon after but Hard would die from his injuries.

Panic as shots ring out

A witness to the fatal shooting spoke of panic in the Featherston car park as shots rang out on the sunny afternoon.

He said at least one of two men appeared to brandish a firearm as they robbed the occupants of the grey Holden.

Another removed packages from the back of the car as the occupants held their hands in the air.

The witness said he stopped in his tracks when he saw a man walk away from the car as he appeared to tuck a firearm into his waistband.

Pelikai Taukei'aho has pleaded not guilty to the murder of Doreion Hard in Carterton on 22 March 2025. Mark Mitchell

Moments later Taukei'aho sprang from the Holden and opened fire on the red ute carrying the men as it left the scene - fatally wounding Hard.

The witness said the shots "sounded like firecrackers" as Taukei'aho and Sue climbed out of their car and walked - away from him - towards the ute as it made its escape from the car park.

Another witness said he saw a man holding "a small dark, probably black, object," as up to four shots rang out.

"It was quite clearly a gunshot, I'd been in the military for 22 years. I know what a gun sounds like.

"Three or four [shots] from memory. It was all over very quickly," the witness said.

Defence lawyer Louise Szrayni pressed the witness about the order and timing of the events he saw.

"You can imagine what it's like. There's people panicking left right and centre. It was all over in the space of 30 secs," the witness said.

He said he was focussed on the man who appeared to have a gun, "it was almost like tunnel vision" he told the court.

But he countered defence lawyer Karun Lakshman's assertion that his military experience meant he was "unfazed" by firearms.

"I think anyone who isn't phased by guns and gunshots is a scary person," the witness said.

World.title: Whakaata Māori-Curia poll reveals major shift in Te Tai Tonga race
World.content:
Incumbent MP Tākuta Ferris could lose his electorate seat of Te Tai Tonga, with a new Whakaata Māori-Curia poll showing him trailing behind every other candidate in the country's largest electorate at 15 percent support, behind Labour's Mananui Ramsden with 30 percent, Te Pāti Māori candidate Lisa Marie Murch with 17 percent, and Green Party candidate Lisa Te Morenga with 16 percent.

All four candidates will go head-to-head in a live debate on Tuesday night at 7pm on the Te Ao Māori News Facebook page, Te Ao Māori News YouTube page, Whakaata Māori, and MĀORI+, moderated by Julian Wilcox and Maiki Sherman.

The exclusive poll results were commissioned by Whakaata Māori as part of its Whakatau 2026 election coverage series.

The survey was conducted from September 14 to September 24 by Curia Market Research, which also polls for the National Party and the New Zealand Taxpayers' Union.

The poll surveyed 500 Māori voters aged 18 and older in Te Tai Tonga, including 420 by phone and 80 through an online panel. The margin of error is plus or minus 4.5 percent with a 95% percent confidence level.

Returned support for Labour as Ferris struggles

The poll indicates that Te Tai Tonga could swing back to Labour if voters deliver a 7 November election result close to their preferences recorded during the survey period.

In modern times, the Māori electorate, covering Te Waipounamu, Rakiura, Wharekauri, and parts of Te Ika-a-Māui, including Te Whanganui-a-Tara, has most often been held by Labour MPs from the Tirikatene dynasty for 72 years, with only brief periods of representation by New Zealand First and Te Pāti Māori MPs.

However, Tākuta Ferris, who defeated long-serving MP Rino Tirikatene in the 2023 election, is running as an independent following a dispute within Te Pāti Māori that led to his departure from the party.

Candidate support and approval

The poll produced mixed views on Ferris:

Approval Ratings: Despite low voting preference, Ferris received positive net approval: 29 percent said he had done a good job and 11 percent said he had done a poor job, giving a net rating of +18 percentage points.

Demographics: Voters aged 18-39 were significantly more likely to rate Ferris as good (37 percent) compared with those aged 60 and older (15 percent). Conversely, voters over 60 were more likely to rate him as poor (24 percent) compared with younger demographics (8 percent).

Gender & Age Splits: Wāhine were more likely than tāne to support Green candidate Lisa Te Morenga (21 percent vs 10 percent). Her support was highest among those aged 18-39 (24 percent) compared with older age brackets.

When asked how important it is for an electorate MP to stand up to their party, 3 percent rated it very important, 43 percent somewhat important, 14 percent not that important, and 3 percent not at all important.

Party vote preferences

The poll showed Labour leading party vote preferences at 28 percent, followed by the Greens (14 percent), Te Pāti Māori (11 percent), New Zealand First (6 percent), National (6 percent), Opportunity (4 percent), and Free Palestine (4 percent), with 10 percent of voters remaining undecided.

The data also highlights a generational divide, showing that Labour support was lower among 18-39-year-olds (16 percent) than among 40-59-year-olds (42 percent) and those aged 60 and older (37percent).

Te Tai Tonga voters were asked to rate their highest priorities for improving Māori outcomes.

Honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi ranked highest at 30 percent, followed by reducing poverty and homelessness (24 percent), improving health and education outcomes (20 percent), mental health and addiction support (13 percent), and addressing Māori unemployment (10 percent).

World.title: Tauranga City Council chief executive Marty Grenfell steps down
World.content:
Marty Grenfell has resigned as Tauranga City Council chief executive.

In a statement, Mayor Mahé Drysdale said Grenfell's last day in the office will be on Friday.

Councillors and staff have been under fire following a review of the January landslide at Mount Maunganui that claimed six lives.

The review found the landslide was preventable, with "one competent consultant after another" identifying the hazard over two decades.

Grenfell earlier maintained he had not offered his resignation because he was confident he was the best person to lead the organisation through what he described as a "difficult period".

Drysdale had also backed his chief executive, saying he was in a "good position" to urgently put in place mitigation and risk management.

The mayor today said he respected Grenfell's decision and thanked him "for his unwavering commitment to public service in our city over the past eight years".

"During this time, Mr Grenfell has helped lead Tauranga City Council through periods of significant growth, change, and challenge. I thank him for his contribution and wish him all the very best for the future," Drysdale said.

World.title: Five-week delays in cancer diagnoses as specialists overwhelmed with work
World.content:
Specialists who diagnose cancers are warning that backlogs are resulting in an unacceptable five-week delay.

The recommended time for an urgent sample diagnosis is 48 hours and non-urgent is five days.

The Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia supports the government's increase in screening initiatives, but said more specialists are needed to work through the increased samples.

Its vice-president for New Zealand Associate Professor Diane Kenwright told Checkpoint there is a five week wait for cases to be diagnosed.

"It means that patients have to wait to know whether they've got cancer or not for five weeks. It breaks my heart actually knowing that I can't give the best service to patients."

Associate Professor Diane Kenwright. Diane Kenwright

Kenwright said such delays could result in adverse outcomes for patients.

"My fear is that a cancer will be in the routine pile rather than the urgent pile," she said.

"In the routine pile, it will wait up for five weeks to be diagnosed and that's five weeks before surgery and five weeks before chemotherapy can begin."

Audio player for " Cancer specialists overwhelmed with work " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1653504%2Ffive-week-delays-in-cancer-diagnoses-as-specialists-overwhelmed-with-work

Cancer specialists overwhelmed with work Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

The government has expanded screening for some cancers including bowel cancer, resulting in more samples.

Kenwright said the Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia wrote to the health minister before this year's Budget, asking for $3.7 million to train 23 pathologists and close the staffing gap.

"It's a bit like a traffic jam. We need more pathologists in order to be able to cope with more samples and we need to be able to train more pathologists so we can do it in the future too," she said.

But she said there was no funding given towards that goal in the Budget.

"Pathology services are right on the knife edge. We are working so hard every day, but still can't get through the work that's sent to us," Kenwright said.

"We really support the government's screening initiatives, but they forgot one thing, and that's the people who make the actual diagnosis and read the biopsy."

Health Minister Simeon Brown said he recognised changes to screening programmes will create more demand, and Health New Zealand was working to understand that, and confirm funding.

A plan for how pathology services are resourced was being developed, he says, and the College of Pathologists will be invited to contribute.

He expected Health New Zealand to keep working closely with the sector so patients received their results as quickly as possible.

World.title: Silver lining for Freo captain after grand final injury nightmare
World.content:
Fremantle have had some badly needed good news in the wake of its AFL grand final disaster, confirming captain Alex Pearce will not need surgery.

The Dockers are confident the key defender will return to training in the pre-season.

As the post-mortem continues following Saturday's devastating loss to Brisbane, Fremantle said Pearce suffered a partially ruptured Achilles tendon, as well as a calf strain.

Pearce was giving chase early in the third quarter of the grand final when he suddenly fell to the ground.

Two trainers helped him from the field, with one of the most shattering images of the loss being Pearce hobbling past the premiership cup on crutches at the post-game presentations.

Brisbane coach Chris Fagan and several of his players offered their best wishes to Pearce soon after the final siren.

Alex Pearce went down with his injury during the third quarter of the grand final. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Coach Justin Longmuir said losing the Dockers' defensive general cost them, especially during Brisbane's last-gasp comeback.

"Thankfully Alex has not had a complete rupture of his Achilles tendon and he will not require surgery," Fremantle football boss Joe Brierty said on Tuesday in a club statement.

"Scans have revealed a partial tear of his Achilles tendon and also a significant calf strain.

"As it stands, we expect Alex to return to training in pre-season."

Also on Tuesday, chief executive Simon Garlick was the latest key Docker to defend Wharfie Time and dismiss its activation as a factor in their heartbreaking loss.

Lions coach Chris Fagan and several of his players have said since that they had a plan if Wharfie Time was sounded, vowing they would try to use it to their own advantage.

But Garlick followed Longmuir and Brierty in denying Wharfie Time had torpedoed the Dockers.

"We know teams, including ours, have scenario plans for being a few goals down or up with a few minutes to go," Garlick told SEN.

"Brisbane executed that plan exceptionally well on Saturday, clearly. It's clearly a plan they would've had regardless of Wharfie Time."

It remains unclear whether Wharfie Time is now sunk.

"Our fans love Wharfie Time. We've just lost a grand final in the most heartbreaking way," Garlick said.

"We're not about to throw out things that make us who we are.

"We'll work through that."
